sections.name: 兰江岸边
sections.content_zh:
兰江岸边

我们所研究的诸葛村在浙江省兰溪县的西部，是"古今第一良相"诸葛亮一支后裔聚居的血缘村落。建村之初，曾经称为高隆村，显然从诸葛亮高卧隆中的事迹隐括而来，到明代后半叶，渐渐转向以姓氏为村名，这是当地普遍的习惯。

兰溪县属金华府，即婺州，位于钱塘江的中上游。钱塘江的中游叫富春江，溯江而上，富春江在严州府（今名梅城镇）分为新安江和兰江（又名瀫水）。唐代诗人杜牧有句："越嶂远分丁字水，腊梅迟见二月花。"清代诗人赵锡礼也有句："江流燕尾分还合，山扫蛾眉断复连。"这"丁字水"和"燕尾"，说的就是严州府的水形。新安江自西流来，上游便是经济和文化都很发达的皖南。兰江自南流来，上游有婺江和衢江，分别来自东南方的婺州和西南方的衢州，都是富庶的浙江省的腹地，它们相会在兰溪城的西侧。

兰溪县治在严州府南不足百里，舟楫半日可到。《光绪兰溪县志·形胜》里写的兰溪的山形水势可谓十分雄壮：

兰溪由金华玉壶山翔舞起伏，直走大河之滨，融结为县治。后枕层峦，前挹九峰，西北则寿昌、建德诸山，排衙列戟，周围环拱。兰阴一山，屹立横亘，近如屏障。衢、婺两港皆数百里奔流至此，汇成巨渊。

但是，位于丘陵区的兰溪，县境内并不利于农业。《光绪兰溪县志·田赋》说：

邑当山乡，罕平原旷野，涧溪之水易涨易涸，往往苦旱。厥田惟黄壤，厥赋中下。

兰溪县的农业处于中下水平，然而从宋室南渡以来，人口压力却逐渐增大。《宋会要》说："渡江之民，溢于道路。"《建炎以来系年要录》则说："四方之民，云集二浙，百倍常时。"据光绪《兰溪县志》，北宋大中祥符年间，兰溪县人口主客户共一万九千三百三十三户，南宋绍兴中为二万二千九百六十一户，净增三千六百二十八户。

正像晋商和徽商一样，故土的不利于农业，迫使他们在商业上求出路，终于成了全国最大的封建性商帮，兰溪也有大量的人弃农从商。兰溪人经商占有地利，它和皖南的徽州、赣北的景德镇、江南的苏州和本省的杭州，都相去不远。这些城镇，从宋、明以来，都是商业和手工业最发达的，兰溪与它们都有水路交通。它北邻的严州城在南宋就有水驿站，叫瀫水驿。诗人杨万里从江西奉诏赴杭州行在，乘船在瀫水驿夜宿，写下了几首诗，其中一首：

系缆兰溪（兰江）岸，开襟柳驿窗。
人争趋夜市，月自浴秋江。
灯火疏还密，帆樯只更双。
平生经此县，今夕驻孤艭。

灯火帆樯，且有夜市可趋，严州这时候已经相当繁华了。

兰溪也有重要的陆路交通。明清时期，从北京到福州的驿路经过兰溪城，有驿站，名为兰皋驿。它的马站有正马与备马各二十五匹，马夫二十五名，防夫六名。

有这样的地理位置和交通，所以，元代邑人王奎作《重建州治记》说：

然其地当水陆要冲，南出闽、广，北拒吴会，乘传之骑、漕输之楫，往往蹄相劘而舢相衔也。

因此，农业容纳不下也养活不了的人口，纷纷转向商业和手工业。

兰溪的手工业和商业发展相当早。唐开元元年（713）陈藏器著《本草拾遗》就说"火腿产金华者佳"，金华火腿大量产于兰溪。北宋《太平寰宇记》说："酒出兰溪美。"南宋周密《武林旧事》里提到"兰溪酒曰瀫溪春"，《谈荟》也说"兰有瀫溪春酒"。这些都是农产品加工。真正的手工业则有北宋熙宁年间在县东开铜矿，在兰江边建造船场，为浙中造船中心。据张秀民著《南宋刻书地域考》，兰溪是婺州四个刻书点之一（另外三个为东阳、义乌、金华）。又据《浙江通志稿》，纸币的使用，也始于婺州，初见于宋绍兴元年（1131），时称"钱关子"。因为婺州屯兵，到杭州贩运的商人向婺州地方政府交现金，换取"关子"，到杭州兑现。关子初时是一种汇票，后来成为货币。

到了明代后半叶，随着东南一带资本主义经济兴起，兰溪的手工业和商业更加繁荣。兰溪一县的赋税将近金华府八县总数的三分之一。万历《兰溪县志》说：

业手工者为攻金之工、攻石之工、陶工、冶工、缝衣絮业之工、捆履织席之工。

近而工商者籍籍也，远而业商者，或广、或闽、或川、或沛、或苏杭、或南京，以舟载比比也。

本志载，当时兰溪有机户四百七十一户、匠户一百六十三户、纸户五十七户、窑灶十七户。光绪《兰溪县志》则说，明代兰溪有"住坐"匠人九十三户、"轮班"匠人五百九十四户、"存留本府"织染局机匠共一百六十三户。这在当时是比较多的。

明清易代之际，浙江遭到严重破坏，婺州更有"金华三日"的大屠杀，酷烈不下于"扬州十日"。明末清初大戏剧家李渔（1611—1680）诗《婺城乱后感怀》说："有土无民谁播种？子遗翻为国踌躇。"但不久经济便有所恢复。康熙四十四年（1705），兰溪发生了染踹工匠罢工，平息之后，立了一块"禁碑"，碑文里说：

兰邑商贾环聚，人烟稠密，而布铺一项，需有染坊七家、踹坊十家、工匠三百余人。

这规模很不小了。到乾隆十四年（1749），兰溪人开设祝裕隆布店于邑城，后来在金华、龙游和本县游埠镇都有分号，这是早期的"连锁店"。

由于兰溪的特殊地位，四方商贾纷然而来。康熙四十八年（1709），在兰溪设闽南公所。乾隆十六年（1751），设江西会馆；二十一年（1756），设新安会馆。此后，陆续有越郡公所、江南公所、四明公所和东阳、义乌、永康、台州等会馆。其中，徽州人（新安人）与兰溪的关系尤其密切。早在明代，万历《兰溪县志》说："徽贾纷集，市兴矣！"徽州人对兰溪商业、银钱业和典当业等的发展起了不小的作用。正德年间邑进士章懋进贡明武宗的蜜枣就是徽商泰荣漆号精制的。清道光三年（1823），徽州人程圣文在兰溪开墨店，产名墨。

兰溪商人也分赴外地建造会馆，如扬州。李渔撰扬州兰溪会馆联：

一般作客，谁无故土之思，常来此地会会同乡，也当买舟归瀫水；
千里经商，总为谋生之计，他日还家人人满载，不虚骑鹤上扬州。

渲染故土之思，渲染满载还家，反映出当时的商人虽然不辞千里谋财，依然是封建性的，观念中还设有摆脱土地的束缚。

太平天国战争，浙江省破坏惨重，兰溪也遭大难。光绪《兰溪县志·序》说："咸同之间，历洪杨大劫，民人存者仅十之三，田地多温、台客民垦种。"（前知县秦簧撰）幸而灾后恢复很快，同治年间兰溪已经有银楼二家、钱庄十五家，光绪时，典当业兴起，兰溪有码头三十二处，甚至有了专业的码头，如药业码头、煤炭码头等等。

兰溪城的繁荣带动了县境内一些村镇的繁荣。早在明代，章懋在平渡镇渡口的《待渡亭碑记》里写道："凡四方舆马之经行，负担之往来，日以数千。居民数百家，咸以货殖为业。"另有香溪镇，万历六年（1578）建制为镇，设巡检司和税司，得税为县城税收的五分之一多。离诸葛村只有十五华里的永昌镇、离诸葛村四十余里的游埠镇，也都是工商业很繁荣的大镇。

兰溪的各行各业中，有一项很特殊而又很发达的行业，就是中药业，当地人俗谚说："徽州人识宝，兰溪人识草。"草就是中药。康熙《兰溪县志》记载，明代上交两京礼部药材有半夏、前胡、穿山甲等十种。光绪《兰溪县志》则记万历六年杂赋中有药材十二种；记载兰溪物产，有药属三十七种，其中说到岘山出产红党参。诸葛村就在岘山脚下。但兰溪人主要是经营药材，开药店批发、贩运，并不重视种植药材。据《兰溪实验县商业概况》（1935）说：

浙东各县多产药材，因兰溪交通便利，多集于此……甚至闽、赣、皖南，需要药材亦皆仰给焉。且本县习药业者亦较各业为夥……凡浙东各县药店，兰溪人开设者实居多数。

到各县或外省开设药店的兰溪人形成父传子、亲带亲的"药帮"，有专门的行话，叫"药切"。在县城，有一个瀫西药业公所，于清乾隆九年（1744）建立了一座一千多平方米的药皇庙。道光十九年（1839），公所在兰江建船埠，设义渡，称药皇渡。

世代经营药业，精通中药的鉴别和加工炮制，带动了医术。早在宋代，兰溪县城就有药局，"储药饵，以施济百姓之疾苦者，名曰惠民药局"（见光绪《兰溪县志》）。康熙《兰溪县志》则记载了一所医学，"医学旧在三皇庙侧，元初设学，即宋之官酒务基而建三皇庙，因设医学以附其侧，由其主祭"。历代名医辈出，宋代就有郭时芳，"回生起毙，百不失一"；元代有何凤为婺州医学教授；王开在大都的公卿间行医二十余年；明代以后就更多了，而且有不少著作传世。

兰溪县的药业从业人员中，诸葛村人又占了绝大多数。"瀫西"指的就是兰江以西，诸葛村是瀫西最重要的药材专业村。

1992年
sections.content_en:
By the Lanjiang River

The Zhuge Village we studied is in the western part of Lanxi County, Zhejiang Province. It is a blood-relation village inhabited by descendants of a branch of Zhuge Liang, the "best prime minister of all time." At its founding, the village was called Gaolong Village, obviously derived from Zhuge Liang's story of living in seclusion in Longzhong. By the latter half of the Ming dynasty, it gradually changed to a surname-based village name, a common local custom.

Lanxi County belonged to Jinhua Prefecture, also known as Wuzhou, located in the middle and upper reaches of the Qiantang River. The middle reach of the Qiantang River is called the Fuchun River. Going upstream, the Fuchun River divides at Yanzhou Prefecture (now Meicheng Town) into the Xin'an River and the Lanjiang River (also known as Fushui). Tang poet Du Mu wrote: "Yue peaks far divide the T-shaped water, winter plums late see February flowers." Qing poet Zhao Xili also wrote: "The river current like swallow tails divides and joins, mountains like eyebrows break and reconnect." These "T-shaped water" and "swallow tails" describe the water formation of Yanzhou Prefecture. The Xin'an River flows from the west, its upper reaches being southern Anhui with highly developed economy and culture. The Lanjiang River flows from the south, with the Wu River and Qu River in its upper reaches, coming from Wuzhou in the southeast and Quzhou in the southwest respectively — both wealthy hinterlands of Zhejiang Province — meeting at the western side of Lanxi City.

The county seat of Lanxi is less than a hundred li south of Yanzhou Prefecture, reachable by boat in half a day. The "Guangxu Lanxi County Annals · Topography" describes Lanxi's mountains and waters as quite magnificent:

Lanxi, from Yuhu Mountain in Jinhua, dances and undulates, going straight to the great river, forming the county seat. Behind it are layered peaks, before it are the Nine Peaks, to the northwest are mountains of Shouchang and Jiande, arranged like guards in formation, surrounding and arching around. Lanyin Mountain stands erect and stretches horizontally, close like a screen. The Qu and Wu ports both flow hundreds of li to this point, converging into a great deep pool.

However, Lanxi, located in a hilly area, is not favorable for agriculture within its county. The "Guangxu Lanxi County Annals · Land Tax" says:

The county is in mountainous terrain, rare are plains and open fields; stream waters easily rise and dry up, often suffering drought. Its fields are yellow soil, its tax rating is middle-lower.

Lanxi County's agriculture was at a middle-lower level, yet since the Song court moved south, population pressure gradually increased. "Song Huiyao" says: "People crossing the river overflowed the roads." "Jianyan Yilai Xinian Yaolu" says: "People from all directions gathered in the two Zhe regions, a hundred times more than usual." According to Guangxu "Lanxi County Annals," during the Northern Song Dazhong Xiangfu period, Lanxi County had a total of 19,333 households (both registered and guest); during the Southern Song Shaoxing period it was 22,961 households, a net increase of 3,628 households.

Just like the Shanxi merchants and Huizhou merchants, their homeland's unfavorable agriculture forced them to seek出路 in commerce, eventually becoming the largest feudal merchant guilds in the country. Lanxi also had large numbers of people abandoning agriculture for commerce. Lanxi people had geographical advantages for business — it was not far from Huizhou in southern Anhui, Jingdezhen in northern Jiangxi, Suzhou in Jiangnan, and Hangzhou in their own province. These towns, since the Song and Ming dynasties, were the most developed in commerce and handicrafts, and Lanxi had water transportation connections with all of them. Its northern neighbor, Yanzhou City, had a water post station in the Southern Song called Fushui Station. Poet Yang Wanli, traveling from Jiangxi to Hangzhou by imperial order, spent the night at Fushui Station by boat and wrote several poems, one of which:

Tying the cable at Lanxi (Lanjiang) bank, opening the willow station window.
People rush to the night market, the moon bathes in the autumn river.
Lamps sparse then dense, masts single then double.
Having passed this county all my life, tonight I moor a lonely boat.

With lamps and masts, and a night market to visit, Yanzhou was already quite prosperous at that time.

Lanxi also had important land transportation. During the Ming and Qing periods, the post road from Beijing to Fuzhou passed through Lanxi City, with a post station called Langao Station. Its horse station had 25 regular horses and 25 spare horses, 25 grooms, and 6 guards.

With such geographical location and transportation, therefore, Yuan dynasty local Wang Kui wrote in "Record of Rebuilding the Prefecture Office":

Yet its place is at the hub of land and water, south to Fujian and Guangdong, north to Wu and Kuaiji, post horses and transport boats often have hooves rubbing and prows touching.

Therefore, the population that agriculture could not accommodate or support turned to commerce and handicrafts in large numbers.

Lanxi's handicrafts and commerce developed quite early. In the first year of Tang Kaiyuan (713), Chen Zangqi's "Materia Medica Supplement" said "ham produced in Jinhua is excellent," and Jinhua ham was produced in large quantities in Lanxi. Northern Song "Taiping Huanyu Ji" says: "Wine from Lanxi is excellent." Southern Song Zhou Mi's "Wulin Jiushi" mentions "Lanxi wine called Fuxi Spring," and "Tanhui" also says "Lan has Fuxi Spring wine." These were all agricultural product processing. True handicrafts included copper mining east of the county in Northern Song Xining period, and shipyards built by the Lanjiang River, making it the shipbuilding center of central Zhejiang. According to Zhang Xiumin's "Research on Southern Song Book Printing Regions," Lanxi was one of four book printing sites in Wuzhou (the other three being Dongyang, Yiwu, Jinhua). Also according to "Zhejiang Tongzhi Draft," the use of paper money also began in Wuzhou, first seen in the first year of Song Shaoxing (1131), then called "money coupons." Because Wuzhou stationed troops, merchants trading to Hangzhou paid cash to the Wuzhou local government in exchange for "coupons," redeemable in Hangzhou. Coupons were initially a type of bill of exchange, later becoming currency.

By the latter half of the Ming dynasty, with the rise of capitalist economy in the southeast, Lanxi's handicrafts and commerce became even more prosperous. Lanxi County's taxes were nearly one-third of the total of eight counties in Jinhua Prefecture. Wanli "Lanxi County Annals" says:

Handicraft workers include metalworkers, stoneworkers, potters, smelters, tailors and quilt-makers, sandal-makers and weavers.

Nearby, merchants and craftsmen are numerous; far away, those in commerce go to Guangdong, Fujian, Sichuan, Pei, Suzhou-Hangzhou, or Nanjing, with boats carrying goods everywhere.

The annals record that at that time Lanxi had 471 weaving households, 163 artisan households, 57 paper households, and 17 kiln households. Guangxu "Lanxi County Annals" says that in Ming dynasty Lanxi had 93 "resident" artisan households, 594 "rotating" artisan households, and 163 weaving and dyeing bureau artisans "retained in the prefecture." This was relatively many at that time.

During the Ming-Qing transition, Zhejiang suffered severe destruction, and Wuzhou had the "Three Days of Jinhua" massacre, as cruel as the "Ten Days of Yangzhou." Late Ming-early Qing great dramatist Li Yu (1611-1680) wrote in poem "Feelings After the Chaos in Wucheng": "With land but no people, who will sow? Survivors hesitate for the country." But the economy soon recovered. In the 44th year of Kangxi (1705), a strike by dyeing and fulling craftsmen occurred in Lanxi; after it was平息, a "prohibition stele" was erected, with the inscription saying:

Lanxi City has merchants gathering, dense population, and for cloth shops alone, there are seven dyeing workshops, ten fulling workshops, and over 300 craftsmen.

This scale was not small. By the 14th year of Qianlong (1749), Lanxi people opened the Zhuyulong cloth shop in the county city, later having branches in Jinhua, Longyou, and Youbu Town in the county — an early "chain store."

Due to Lanxi's special position, merchants from all directions flocked here. In the 48th year of Kangxi (1709), the Minnan Guild Hall was established in Lanxi. In the 16th year of Qianlong (1751), the Jiangxi Guild Hall was established; in the 21st year (1756), the Xin'an Guild Hall. Thereafter, there were successively the Yuejun Guild Hall, Jiangnan Guild Hall, Siming Guild Hall, and guild halls for Dongyang, Yiwu, Yongkang, Taizhou, etc. Among them, Huizhou people (Xin'an people) had especially close relations with Lanxi. As early as the Ming dynasty, Wanli "Lanxi County Annals" said: "Huizhou merchants gathered in crowds, the market prospered!" Huizhou people played a significant role in the development of Lanxi's commerce, banking, and pawnbroking. The honey dates presented to Emperor Wuzong of Ming by Jinshi Zhang Mao in the Zhengde period were exquisitely made by the Huizhou merchant Tai Rong Lacquer Shop. In the third year of Qing Daoguang (1823), Huizhou person Cheng Shengwen opened an ink shop in Lanxi, producing famous ink.

Lanxi merchants also went to other places to build guild halls, such as in Yangzhou. Li Yu wrote a couplet for the Lanxi Guild Hall in Yangzhou:

All being guests, who lacks thoughts of homeland? Often coming here to meet fellow townsmen is like buying a boat to return to Fushui;
Traveling a thousand li for business, always for livelihood, someday returning home fully loaded, not in vain riding a crane to Yangzhou.

Rendering thoughts of homeland, rendering returning home fully loaded, reflects that merchants of that time, although willing to travel a thousand li for wealth, were still feudal in nature, their mindset not yet freed from the bonds of land.

The Taiping Rebellion caused severe destruction in Zhejiang, and Lanxi also suffered greatly. Guangxu "Lanxi County Annals · Preface" says: "During the Xianfeng-Tongzhi period, after the great Hong-Yang catastrophe, only three-tenths of the people survived, and fields were mostly reclaimed by Wenzhou and Taizhou migrants." (Written by former county magistrate Qin Huang) Fortunately, recovery after the disaster was rapid. During the Tongzhi period, Lanxi already had two silver shops and fifteen money shops; in Guangxu period, pawnbroking rose, and Lanxi had 32 wharves, even specialized wharves such as medicine wharves, coal wharves, etc.

The prosperity of Lanxi City drove the prosperity of some towns within the county. As early as the Ming dynasty, Zhang Mao wrote in "Record of the Waiting Ferry Pavilion" at the Pingdu Town ferry: "All four directions' carriages and horses pass through, burdens come and go, daily in thousands. Several hundred resident households all make a living from trade." There was also Xiangxi Town, established as a town in the sixth year of Wanli (1578), with an inspection office and tax office, collecting more than one-fifth of the county seat's tax revenue. Yongchang Town, only fifteen li from Zhuge Village, and Youbu Town, more than forty li from Zhuge Village, were also large towns with prosperous industry and commerce.

Among Lanxi's various trades, one special and highly developed industry was traditional Chinese medicine. Local proverb says: "Huizhou people know treasures, Lanxi people know herbs." Herbs are traditional Chinese medicine. Kangxi "Lanxi County Annals" records that in the Ming dynasty, medicinal materials submitted to the two capitals' Ministry of Rites included pinellia, peucedanum, pangolin scales, etc., ten types. Guangxu "Lanxi County Annals" records twelve types of medicinal materials in the miscellaneous taxes of the sixth year of Wanli; recording Lanxi's products, there are 37 types of medicinal herbs, mentioning that Xian Mountain produces red codonopsis. Zhuge Village is at the foot of Xian Mountain. But Lanxi people mainly dealt in medicinal materials, opening pharmacies for wholesale and transport, not emphasizing cultivation. According to "Commercial Overview of Lanxi Experimental County" (1935):

Counties in eastern Zhejiang mostly produce medicinal materials; due to Lanxi's convenient transportation, they gather here... even Fujian, Jiangxi, and southern Anhui needing medicinal materials all rely on it. And those in this county practicing the medicine trade are more than in other trades... of pharmacies in various eastern Zhejiang counties, those opened by Lanxi people are actually the majority.

Lanxi people who opened pharmacies in other counties or provinces formed a "medicine guild" with father teaching son and relatives bringing relatives, with specialized jargon called "medicine talk." In the county city, there was a Fuxi Medicine Guild Hall, which in the ninth year of Qing Qianlong (1744) built a Medicine Emperor Temple of over 1,000 square meters. In the 19th year of Daoguang (1839), the guild hall built a boat dock on the Lanjiang River and established a free ferry, called Medicine Emperor Ferry.

Generations of operating the medicine trade, mastering the identification and processing of traditional Chinese medicine, drove the development of medical art. As early as the Song dynasty, Lanxi City had a medicine bureau, "storing medicines to relieve the people's sufferings, called Huimin Medicine Bureau" (see Guangxu "Lanxi County Annals"). Kangxi "Lanxi County Annals" records a medical school, "the medical school was formerly beside the Three Emperors Temple; in early Yuan it was established, building the Three Emperors Temple on the site of the Song official wine office, thus establishing the medical school attached to its side, with its chief officiating." Famous doctors emerged through dynasties: in Song there was Guo Shifang, "reviving the dead, not one failure in a hundred"; in Yuan there was He Feng as Wuzhou medical professor; Wang Kai practiced medicine among nobles in Dadu for over twenty years; after Ming there were even more, with many works passed down.

Among Lanxi County's medicine industry practitioners, Zhuge Village people accounted for the vast majority. "Fuxi" refers to west of the Lanjiang River, and Zhuge Village is the most important medicinal material specialty village in Fuxi.

1992

sections.name: 来到了关麓村
sections.content_zh:
来到了关麓村

自从研究乡土建筑以来，每次选题，我们都向偏僻的地方去找，找那些被冷落了的村子，因为它们最容易在无声无息中消失而不留下一点点资料。1994年春末，结束了江西省婺源县的第二轮工作，该寻找下一个课题了，我们还是没有打算到相邻的歙县和黟县去。那里的民居，早已驰名国内外，用不到我们去关心了。

仅仅是为了过路，我们到了屯溪。屯溪市城乡建设委员会的陈继腾先生陪我们到歙县和黟县的几个著名村落看了一看。那些村落的完整、房屋的精美和文化含量之高，确实非常难得，但没有使我们动心。村落密不透风，封闭的小巷遮没了所有的住宅，只有在水塘岸边，那些住宅才得以喘一口气，展现它们的个性。这样的村落太教人感到沉重。虽然学术工作的选题不能以个人好恶为准，但既然可选的题材还很多，我们何必不找一个能使我们激动的。

陈继腾先生曾经亲手测量过黟县全境，熟悉那里大大小小的村落。终于有一天，他带我们到了钱塘江水源西武岭下的关麓村。这是一个默默无闻的小山村。

刚刚进村，我们就被吸引住了。三十几幢住宅，疏疏朗朗，大多舒舒服服亮出自己秀丽多变的身姿。有生气勃勃的马头墙，有柔和而富张力的拉弓墙，还有的墙像破浪前进的船头，弧形的，缓缓地弯过去。在这些墙头跌宕起伏的轮廓之下，我们见到了一个精雕细刻的水磨青砖门楼，又一个，还有一个，一个挨着一个，一个比一个漂亮。一条小溪，哗哗地从它们前面流过。溪上的青石板桥，对着一座八字墙门，门边白粉墙上漏窗里探出一枝鲜红的天竺子。沿着小溪走，溪边石条凳上袒开古铜色胸膛的人们，微笑着招呼我们。村里，院墙后东一株枇杷树，西一株柿子树，掩映着楼上细巧的格扇窗。棕榈树的叶子，在粉墙上投下图案般的影子。在竹林沙沙的轻声中，我们推门进了几户人家，大多是三合院，素净清雅，尺度宜人，十分安逸。意想不到的是，堂屋里、卧室里居然都有满顶满壁的图画，幅面都很大，有"百子闹元宵"，有"九世同居"，还有我们说不出名堂的壮观的战争场面。最教人感到家庭生活的温馨的是婴戏图和母婴图。天真的娃儿，一只手捂住耳朵，一只手去点燃爆竹；或者依偎在妈妈的怀里，享受妈妈粉腮的抚爱，年轻的妈妈，脸上洋溢着慈祥而幸福的光彩和母性的庄严。天棚上或是嬉水的鲤鱼泼刺，或是穿花的蛱蝶翩跹，也有山水和花鸟。我们以前只知道徽州建筑的"三雕"，就是木雕、砖雕和石雕，从来没有听说过彩画，这次一见，大感惊喜。家具不但都是古色古香的，而且完整成套。堂屋里的条案、八仙桌、太师椅；卧室里的满顶床、净桶柜、梳妆台、衣橱，都还闪亮着硬木和黄铜配件的光芒。连陈设和许多日常用品都是老年代的，条案上的掸瓶、插屏、座钟，书房里的砚台、笔架、水盂，一一都在，而且还照传统的方式放置着。

我们虽然喜爱乡土建筑和乡土文化，研究它们，给它们做记录，但是，我们一向并不希望看到生活停滞不前。这种心情一直是非常矛盾的，有时候很困扰我们。不过，见到关麓村这样一个难得的古老乡村的标本，我们还是觉得很幸运。

在溪头，我们遇见了一位粗手粗脚的老人家，向他请教，那么精彩的壁画是由什么样的人来画的呢？他回答：请漆匠呀！然后微微一笑，说，齐白石不就是画这种彩画出身的吗？我们听了，心中不觉一惊，立即决定把关麓村选作下一个研究对象。按照我们一贯采用的工作方法，我们选题，希望村落保存得比较完整，比较典型，有丰富的历史文化内涵，更希望它还保存着宗谱。但是，关麓村的宗祠、庙宇、文馆之类都已荡然无存，宗谱也在"文化大革命"中完全毁掉，我们选定它的时候却没有考虑这些。我们准备不惜为它修正一下我们的研究方法。

到了秋天，田头的桕子树像火焰般一簇一簇燃烧起来的时候，我们开始了关麓的第一轮工作。我们住在村子中央一个农家里，天气已经很凉，两人合盖一条短被，盖不住脚丫子。好在工作顺利，豆浆很浓，白薯又很甜，日子过得快活。将近一个月的时间里，我们测绘、摄影、访问，认识了许多朋友，得到了他们热情的帮助，尤其是汪亚芸先生、汪景恒先生和汪祖武先生。汪亚芸先生七十岁出头，年轻时在屯溪的绸布店里学徒，后来当了兵，50年代回村安居，孑然一身，喜好读书，尤其注意文史，所以不但对村里情况知道得多，而且对徽州一般的风尚也比较了解。他把珍藏的乡人的书信、短笺、账单、婚书等等借给我们看，最有价值的是乾隆三十三年（1768）一份分家阄书。汪景恒先生是中年人，四十岁不到，在村里当电工，因为他父亲觉民先生（1989年去世）长期在村里当私塾和小学教师，对村里情况最熟悉，所以他也听说一些。他借给我们觉民先生写的一份关于村子建筑情况的短文，还把秘藏的一幅祖先画像和敕封诰命给我们摄影。汪祖武先生刚刚六十岁，从县电影放映队退休回家，住在关麓村东一华里的宏田村。他父亲也曾经在关麓村当过私塾和小学教师。他读书多，知识丰富，兴趣广泛，因为自小不曾离乡，又颇留心，所以知道很多村里的事。他的住宅是一所大四合院，有前后两个大花园，种着珍木异卉，还有一口不小的鱼塘。我们去拜访的时候，推开门，满院的菊花正开得热闹，照得人眼花。我们在他家里抄录了一个房派的谱图，宗祠的楹联，祖坟的碑文。他送了我们一份几年前他写的关麓村住宅调查报告。

这轮工作，收获不少。原来关麓是一座十分典型的徽商血缘村落，在清代，作为主姓的汪姓人家全都从商，经济很宽裕，少量农田由外来的小姓耕种，他们是佃户或者佃仆，佃仆对主家有人身依附关系。徽商一向以儒商自许，知书达理。他们的乡里生活，有相当高的文化品位，以至小小的村里竟有十几幢"学堂屋"。这个村落，从选址定居、结构布局、房屋的类型和形制，直到住宅里的家具、陈设和各种日常用品，都鲜明地反映着徽商的家庭生活方式和文化修养，也反映着农村中的社会阶级分化。过去，村子的公共生活很发达，这是农业社会里封建宗法制的传统文化和徽商的市井文化的特殊结合。这样的公共生活也同样鲜明地反映在村落的规划和建设上。虽然关麓村的宗祠和庙宇等等已经在近几十年里全被破坏，但它的住宅区却还保持着旧貌，没有多大变动。

看来，巧得很，关麓村的种种特点大体上符合我们研究工作的选题要求，我们没有必要修正我们的工作方法。这使我们非常高兴。

过了些日子，我们更加见识到关麓村住宅建筑的精致。除了彩画和门窗格扇之外，牛腿、灯笼钩、花架、垫斗、压画条也都有很高的恰如其分的装饰性。青砖雕花门头更是丰富多彩。在其他地区很少见的固定式家具，尤其独运匠心。作为富裕的徽商的家，这些住宅里不但有壁橱、百宝格、神龛、吊柜和床铺，此外，窗台有暗设的小屉子，床铺后有秘室，樘板里有夹层和暗门，等等，都设计得非常机智巧妙。

我们到家家户户楼上杂物堆里去翻看，有一二百年历史的瓷灯台、整套的瓷餐具、烛台、气死风灯、灯笼、鱼缸、糕饼模子，还有玲珑精巧的各式鸟笼。有些鸟笼像座宫殿，里外两三层。这些东西艺术质量之高，使我们大为兴奋。连粗制的日用竹木器，如筷子筒、蒸屉、提篮、水勺、斗笠、烘笼、小板凳、儿童便器等等也无不使我们钦佩制造者的智慧，并且感到极大的审美满足。

我们在婺源工作的时候，听说过佃仆制，在关麓，我们亲眼看见了旧时给人吹唢呐的乐户、照料新婚夫妇的红婆和被买来的不知自己姓名和年龄的丫环。我们竟有机会为一位八十七岁的佃仆送终、送葬。

但是，我们仍然十分遗憾，因为关麓汪氏的宗谱确实已经没有了。这使我们难以了解村子的历史。

第二年5月初我们再去的时候，又见到了一幅奇丽的景色，整个黟县都浸没在金黄色油菜花无边无际的海洋里了。大地那样恣肆放纵地展现它的灿烂和辉煌。我们高高兴兴住进了农家，开始第二轮的工作。老朋友们更加亲热，新朋友多了起来。终于有一天，一位新朋友，汪祯祥，从柜子里翻出两本秘藏的线装本子给我们。毛边纸，对折八行，红丝栏，用毛笔书写，里面除本房崇德堂派的谱图之外，全是他祖父的杂记，内容涉及祭祀、请封、商业经营、房地产、善行义举、乡贤行状、买卖奴仆、婚娶丧葬、社会治安等，它们比宗谱更详尽、更具体、更贴近生活，非常生动地刻画了从清道光年间到民国年间徽商乡里的生活情景。读着这两册杂记，我们兴奋不已。花几天时间抄录完毕，我们就到处去询问有没有类似的本子，先后竟又借到了几本，可惜都没有汪祯祥这两本无所不录的杂记，而只有几个房派的谱图，叫作"祖宗本子"。不过，它们毕竟使我们多知道了一部分关麓汪氏的谱系，从而推断了一些事情的大致年代。我们的研究条件终于还是勉强具备了。

对关麓和附近的村子的了解越多，我们越为黟县农村过去堂皇的建筑景观感到吃惊，简直不可思议。关麓村的宗祠、庙宇、文昌阁、学堂、牌坊，等等，曾经组成绵延二里多的壮丽的建筑群。它们是徽商故里社会历史的见证、文化建设的丰碑。而离关麓村不过五里七里，还有更大更繁荣的村子。只是经过近几十年的社会大变动，它们中有许多竟连废墟都见不到了。虽然遗址上油菜花那么繁密可爱，我们心中依然惆怅万分。寻寻觅觅，只在路边捡到一块残石，模模糊糊可以辨认出雕着一头狮子。汪祖武先生说，那是当年辅成文会泮池边的栏杆柱。辅成文会是一幢大门为五凤楼的三进的大建筑物，包含文昌阁、乡贤祠、明伦堂、义塾和花园。50年代中期，村里的当权人为卖瓦片把它们拆掉时，竟动用了劳改犯。

汪景恒先生给我们看几份资料，其中之一是发表在《黄山》杂志1988年11月号上的一篇文章，题目叫"风沙向小桃源袭来"，作者余治淮。文章写的是关麓村汪氏总祠和村前去西武岭的古驿道的破坏经过。他先是描写汪氏总祠的"巍然庄重"和它前面月塘的"绿荷满池、芙蓉多姿"，然后说：

不料，时光转到了风光明媚的1983年，古祠和月塘却飞来了一场灾难。生产队长姜某，借口年久失修（按：所谓年久失修，就是两年前姜某揭卖了祀厅后坡的瓦，以致梁架遭雨淋朽），召集一伙人，擅自将宗祠拆毁，将砖、木、石料兜卖一空，发了横财。村里人愤然联名上告，开始姜某还提心吊胆地过了一段日子。可县里对关麓村民的来信……如同泥牛入海，这件事不了了之。农民们是最讲实在的，队长可以带头拆祠堂、卖公产，他们又为什么不可以损公肥私呢？于是，月塘周围的二十四根石柱，一百零八块栏板也就今日三、明日四地进了寻常百姓家，派上垫脚石、砌墙脚的用场了。

古人以修桥补路视为人生最大的善举和功德……旧时各村都立有乡规民约……1979年冬天，岭下村二十余户农民要建造新屋，他们打上了西武岭古驿道的主意。开始人们还是悄悄地撬走几块断裂的石板，后来，大伙一哄而起，一夜之间，一段长达五十余米路面的石被撬挖掳掠一空。冬去春来，这段被毁的古驿道，坑坑洼洼，雨水冲刷出一道道曲曲弯弯的沟壑，像是雄关（按：指村后西武岭上的西武关）用泪水描绘出的一个个留等人们解答的问号。

问号问的是什么呢？作者没有说。

这篇文章发表之后，又过去了一二十年，现在的情况就更加凄凉了。而且村村如此，不独关麓。关麓村中，连那条全村人赖以生活的小溪，也变成了秽臭的垃圾沟，水牛泡在溪里便溺，修理房子的碎砖烂瓦也往里扔；两岸的石条有些已经挖走，有些已经倒坍。住在那些足可称为文化珍品的房子里，人们对它们的精美毫无感受，不但不去爱惜它们，反而天天用很粗暴的方式在摧残它们。明万历进士谢肇淛经桃源洞进黟县盆地的道中，写了一首诗："春风篱落酒旗闲，流水桃花映碧山。寄语渔郎莫深去，洞中未必胜人间。"照这些年的情况继续下去，曾经被称为小桃源的黟县，真是未必有什么胜景，不堪再深去了。要问的：一个问题是何以至此，一个问题是如何重整。

提这样的问题或许是不适当的。但这情况更反衬出我们工作的重要和急迫。我们还是加紧干罢！

1995年秋
sections.content_en:
Arriving at Guanlu Village

Since we began researching vernacular architecture, every time we choose a topic, we look for remote places, seeking villages that have been neglected, because they are most likely to disappear silently without leaving any records. In late spring 1994, after completing the second round of work in Wuyuan County, Jiangxi Province, it was time to find the next project. We still had no intention of going to the neighboring She County and Yi County. The folk houses there were already famous at home and abroad, and didn't need our attention.

Merely to pass through, we went to Tunxi. Mr. Chen Jiteng of the Tunxi Urban and Rural Construction Committee accompanied us to visit several famous villages in She County and Yi County. The completeness of those villages, the exquisiteness of their houses, and their high cultural content were indeed rare, but they did not move us. The villages were airtight, with closed alleys obscuring all residences; only by the ponds could the houses catch their breath and show their individuality. Such villages felt too heavy. Although academic topic selection should not be based on personal preference, since there were still many topics to choose from, why not find one that could excite us?

Mr. Chen Jiteng had personally surveyed all of Yi County and was familiar with its villages, large and small. Finally one day, he took us to Guanlu Village at the foot of Xiwu Ridge, the source of the Qiantang River. It was an unknown small mountain village.

As soon as we entered the village, we were captivated. More than thirty residences, spaced generously, most comfortably showing their graceful and varied forms. There were vibrant horse-head walls, soft yet tension-filled bow walls, and some walls like prows of ships breaking waves, arc-shaped, curving gently. Beneath the undulating silhouettes of these wall tops, we saw an exquisitely carved water-ground blue brick gatehouse, then another, and another, one next to another, each more beautiful than the last. A small stream gurgled past in front of them. A bluestone bridge over the stream faced a splayed-wall gate; by the door, a branch of bright red nandina berries peeked through a lattice window on the whitewashed wall. Walking along the stream, people with bronze chests bared on stone benches smiled and greeted us. In the village, behind courtyard walls, a loquat tree here and a persimmon tree there framed delicate lattice windows upstairs. Palm leaves cast pattern-like shadows on the white walls. In the soft rustling of bamboo, we pushed open doors into several households, mostly three-sided courtyards, plain and elegant, with pleasant proportions, very comfortable. Unexpectedly, the main rooms and bedrooms actually had paintings covering entire ceilings and walls, with large formats — "Hundred Children Celebrating Lantern Festival," "Nine Generations Living Together," and spectacular battle scenes we couldn't name. Most heartwarming for family life were the infant play scenes and mother-infant scenes. Innocent toddlers, one hand covering an ear, the other lighting a firecracker; or nestled in mother's arms, enjoying the caress of her powdered cheek, the young mother's face radiant with kind happiness and maternal dignity. On the ceilings were splashing carp playing in water, or butterflies flitting through flowers, as well as landscapes and birds-and-flowers. We had previously only known the "Three Carvings" of Huizhou architecture — wood carving, brick carving, and stone carving — never having heard of painted decoration. Seeing it this time, we were greatly surprised and delighted. The furniture was not only antique but complete sets. The long altar table, square table, and armchairs in the main room; the canopy bed, commode cabinet, dressing table, and wardrobe in the bedroom — all still gleamed with hardwood and brass fittings. Even the furnishings and many daily items were old-fashioned: the duster vase, table screen, and mantel clock on the altar table; the inkstone, brush rest, and water bowl in the study — all present, and still placed in the traditional manner.

Although we love vernacular architecture and culture, researching them and recording them, we have never wished to see life stagnate. This feeling has always been very contradictory, sometimes troubling us. However, seeing Guanlu Village as such a rare specimen of an old village, we still felt very fortunate.

At the stream head, we met a rough-handed old man and asked him: what kind of people painted such wonderful murals? He answered: hire lacquerers! Then with a slight smile, he said, wasn't Qi Baishi originally a painter of such decorative paintings? Hearing this, our hearts jumped, and we immediately decided to choose Guanlu Village as the next research subject. According to our usual working method, when selecting a topic, we hoped the village would be relatively well-preserved, typical, with rich historical and cultural connotations, and especially hoped it still preserved genealogies. But Guanlu Village's ancestral halls, temples, and academies had all vanished, and the genealogy was completely destroyed during the "Cultural Revolution." We hadn't considered these when choosing it. We were prepared to revise our research methods for its sake.

By autumn, when the tallow trees by the fields burned like flames cluster after cluster, we began the first round of work in Guanlu. We stayed at a farmer's house in the center of the village; the weather was already cool, and two of us shared one short quilt that couldn't cover our feet. Fortunately the work went smoothly, the soybean milk was rich, the sweet potatoes sweet, and life was happy. In nearly a month, we surveyed, photographed, and interviewed, making many friends and receiving their enthusiastic help, especially Mr. Wang Yayun, Mr. Wang Jingheng, and Mr. Wang Zuwu. Mr. Wang Yayun was in his early seventies; as a young man he had apprenticed in a silk and cloth shop in Tunxi, later became a soldier, and returned to settle in the village in the 1950s. Alone and unmarried, he loved reading, especially literature and history, so he not only knew much about the village but also understood general Huizhou customs. He lent us his collected villagers' letters, notes, bills, and marriage contracts; the most valuable was a family division document from the 33rd year of Qianlong (1768). Mr. Wang Jingheng was a middle-aged man, under forty, working as an electrician in the village. Because his father, Mr. Wang Juemin (died 1989), had long been a private tutor and primary school teacher in the village and knew the village best, he had also heard things. He lent us a short essay about the village's architecture written by his father, and allowed us to photograph a secretly preserved ancestor portrait and an imperial edict. Mr. Wang Zuwu had just turned sixty, having retired from the county film projection team and returned home, living in Hongtian Village, one li east of Guanlu. His father had also been a private tutor and primary school teacher in Guanlu. He was well-read, knowledgeable, with broad interests; having never left the village since childhood and being observant, he knew many village affairs. His residence was a large four-sided courtyard with two big gardens front and back, planted with rare trees and flowers, and a sizable fish pond. When we visited, pushing open the door, the courtyard was full of chrysanthemums in full bloom, dazzling. At his home we copied a branch genealogy, ancestral hall couplets, and tomb inscriptions. He gave us a residential survey report of Guanlu Village he had written a few years earlier.

This round of work yielded much. It turned out Guanlu was a very typical Huizhou merchant blood-relation village. In the Qing dynasty, the Wang family as the main surname all went into commerce, with comfortable economies; a small amount of farmland was cultivated by outsider minor surnames, who were tenants or bond servants, with bond servants having personal dependency relations with their masters. Huizhou merchants always prided themselves as "Confucian merchants," educated and cultured. Their village life had quite high cultural taste, so much so that the small village had more than ten "school houses." This village, from site selection and settlement, structural layout, house types and forms, down to furniture, furnishings, and various daily items in residences, all clearly reflected the Huizhou merchants' family lifestyle and cultural cultivation, as well as social class differentiation in the countryside. In the past, the village's public life was highly developed — a special combination of traditional feudal patriarchal culture in agricultural society and the urban culture of Huizhou merchants. Such public life was also clearly reflected in village planning and construction. Although Guanlu Village's ancestral halls and temples had all been destroyed in recent decades, its residential area still retained its old appearance without major changes.

It seemed, coincidentally, that Guanlu Village's various characteristics generally met our research topic requirements, and we had no need to revise our working methods. This made us very happy.

After some time, we further appreciated the refinement of Guanlu Village's residential architecture. Besides painted decoration and door/window lattices, the corbels, lantern hooks, flower shelves, bracket blocks, and painting rails all had highly appropriate ornamentation. Blue brick carved gateheads were especially rich and varied. Fixed furniture, rarely seen in other regions, was particularly ingenious. As wealthy Huizhou merchants' homes, these residences had not only wall cabinets, display shelves, shrines, hanging cabinets, and beds, but also hidden small drawers under windowsills, secret rooms behind beds, interlayers and hidden doors in partition panels, etc., all designed very cleverly.

We rummaged through junk piles upstairs in every household, finding porcelain lamp stands one or two hundred years old, complete porcelain tableware, candlesticks, windproof lanterns, paper lanterns, fish tanks, cake molds, and exquisitely crafted birdcages of various styles. Some birdcages were like palaces, with two or three layers inside and out. The high artistic quality of these items greatly excited us. Even coarse daily bamboo and wooden objects — chopstick holders, steamers, carrying baskets, water ladles, bamboo hats, warming baskets, small stools, children's chamber pots, etc. — all made us admire the makers' wisdom and feel great aesthetic satisfaction.

When working in Wuyuan, we had heard of the bond servant system; in Guanlu, we personally saw musicians who formerly played suona for people, "red women" who attended to newlyweds, and maidservants bought without knowing their own names or ages. We even had the opportunity to attend to the dying and funeral of an 87-year-old bond servant.

However, we still felt very regretful, because the Wang family genealogy of Guanlu was truly gone. This made it difficult for us to understand the village's history.

When we went again in early May the following year, we saw another marvelous sight — all of Yi County was submerged in an endless ocean of golden rapeseed flowers. The earth so wantonly displayed its brilliance and splendor. We happily moved into the farmhouse and began the second round of work. Old friends became closer, and new friends multiplied. Finally one day, a new friend, Wang Zhenxiang, took out two secretly preserved thread-bound books from a cabinet. Mao-bian paper, folded in eight columns, red silk borders, written in brush — besides the genealogy chart of the Chongde Hall branch, they were all his grandfather's miscellaneous notes, covering sacrifices, imperial honors, business operations, real estate, charitable deeds, local worthies' biographies, buying and selling servants, marriages and funerals, social security, etc. They were more detailed, specific, and close to life than genealogies, vividly depicting the life scenes of Huizhou merchants in the village from the Daoguang period of Qing to the Republican era. Reading these two notebooks, we were thrilled. After spending several days copying them, we went around asking if there were similar books, and eventually borrowed several more, though unfortunately none had the comprehensive notes of Wang Zhenxiang's two books, only branch genealogy charts called "ancestor notebooks." Still, they let us learn more of the Guanlu Wang family's genealogy, thereby inferring approximate dates of some events. Our research conditions were finally barely adequate.

The more we learned about Guanlu and nearby villages, the more astonished we were by the grand architectural landscape of Yi County's countryside in the past — simply incredible. Guanlu Village's ancestral halls, temples, Wenchang Pavilions, schools, memorial archways, etc., once formed a magnificent building complex stretching over two li. They were witnesses to the social history of Huizhou merchants' hometowns and monuments to cultural construction. And only five or seven li from Guanlu Village were even larger and more prosperous villages. It was only after the great social upheavals of recent decades that many of them couldn't even be found as ruins. Although the rapeseed flowers on the ruins were so dense and lovely, our hearts were still filled with melancholy. Searching and searching, we only found a broken stone by the roadside, on which a carved lion could be vaguely recognized. Mr. Wang Zuwu said it was a railing post by the pond of the former Fucheng Literary Society. The Fucheng Literary Society was a large three-courtyard building with a phoenix-tower gate, containing a Wenchang Pavilion, local worthies' shrine, lecture hall, charity school, and garden. In the mid-1950s, when village authorities demolished them to sell tiles, they even used labor-reform prisoners.

Mr. Wang Jingheng showed us several materials, one of which was an article published in the November 1988 issue of "Huangshan" magazine, titled "Wind and Sand Strike the Small Peach Blossom Spring," by Yu Zhi Huai. The article described the destruction of the Wang family's main ancestral hall in Guanlu Village and the ancient post road to Xiwu Ridge. He first described the main ancestral hall's "majestic solemnity" and the moon pond in front with "lotus leaves filling the pond, hibiscus in varied beauty," then said:

Unexpectedly, time turned to the sunny 1983, and disaster struck the ancient hall and moon pond. The production team leader Jiang, on the pretext of disrepair (note: so-called disrepair meant that two years earlier Jiang had sold the tiles from the back slope of the worship hall, causing the beams to rot in the rain), gathered a group of people and unauthorizedly demolished the ancestral hall, selling all bricks, wood, and stone, making a fortune. Villagers angrily signed a joint petition; at first Jiang lived in fear for a while. But the county's response to the villagers' letter... like a clay ox entering the sea, the matter ended without resolution. Peasants are most practical; if the team leader can lead in demolishing the ancestral hall and selling public property, why shouldn't they line their own pockets at public expense? So the twenty-four stone pillars and 108 railing panels around the moon pond gradually found their way into ordinary homes, used as stepping stones and wall foundations.

The ancients regarded building bridges and repairing roads as the greatest good deeds and merits... In old times every village had village regulations... In the winter of 1979, more than twenty peasant households in Lingxia Village wanted to build new houses, and they set their sights on the ancient post road of Xiwu Ridge. At first people quietly pried away a few broken stone slabs; later, everyone joined in, and overnight, a section of road over fifty meters long was stripped bare. Winter passed and spring came; this destroyed ancient post road, pitted and uneven, with rain washing out winding gullies, looked like the heroic pass (note: referring to Xiwu Pass on Xiwu Ridge behind the village) drawing question marks with tears, waiting for answers.

What did the question marks ask? The author didn't say.

After this article was published, another ten or twenty years passed, and the current situation is even more desolate. And it's like this in every village, not just Guanlu. In Guanlu Village, even the small stream that the whole village depends on has become a foul-smelling garbage ditch; water buffalo soak and defecate in it, broken bricks and tiles from house repairs are thrown in; some stone strips on both banks have been dug away, some have collapsed. Living in houses that could well be called cultural treasures, people feel nothing for their exquisiteness; not only do they not cherish them, but they daily destroy them in crude ways. Ming Wanli jinshi Xie Zhaozhe, passing through Taoyuan Cave into the Yi County basin, wrote a poem: "Spring wind, village fences, wine flags idle, flowing water, peach blossoms reflecting green mountains. Tell the fisherman not to go deeper, the cave may not surpass the human world." If things continue as they have these years, Yi County, once called the Small Peach Blossom Spring, truly may have no scenic spots left, not worth going deeper into. The questions to ask: one is how it came to this, another is how to restore.

Raising such questions may be inappropriate. But this situation only underscores the importance and urgency of our work. We'd better hurry up and get to it!

Autumn 1995

sections.name: 徽商村里的生活
sections.content_zh:
徽商村里的生活

徽商，无论是资本还是人手，都在不同程度上依赖宗族关系，作为商帮，他们的封建色彩很浓，一般仍扎根于宗族居留的那方土地。他们长期在外面奔走，但把妻儿老少留在故乡。故乡是封建而保守的。康熙《徽州府志》主撰人赵吉士在《寄园寄所寄·泛叶寄》里写道："新安各姓，聚族而居，绝无一杂姓搀入者，其风最为近古。……父老尝谓，新安有数种风俗胜于他邑：千年之冢，不动一抔；千丁之族，未尝散处；千载之谱系，丝毫不紊；主仆之严，数十世不改，而宵小不敢肆焉。"康熙以后三百年间，变化甚微。

封建传统销蚀着商业资本的积累。徽商在外服贾有了积蓄，常常要带钱回家买些土地，建造房屋。土地不多，眷属大多不耕种，佃给小姓，收取租谷。徽州的村子一般都是血缘聚落，但村子里总有些外姓人，他们大多是来自外地的穷困农民，势单力薄，是为小姓。关麓村的小姓，多从安庆、怀宁、铜陵、潜山一带来，被称为"江北佬"。来时孤身，一扁担家私，在承租的地块上或者村边搭草棚暂栖，也有住在东家家里的。住稳了之后，把家小接来落户，在村边造一些小房子。东家的租谷不一定都能收上来，如汪丕鉴在他手记录本中的《遗嘱》里说："田租四百余租，实收一百宽余租；豆租一百余租，实收三十余租。"有些凭中买的田地，远在祁门，从来不曾亲见，租谷更无从收起。商人眷属并不完全靠租谷生活，主要靠商人定期由职业"信客"送来的汇款，关麓人称为"吃信壳"。商人只把土地当作不怕偷盗的财富来储存罢了。

承租的佃户中，有一部分叫作"臧获"，他们对东家有一定的人身依附关系，也称"伴当"、"庄户"或"佃仆"。他们与东家的关系，世代传承，所以赵吉士说"主仆之严，数十世不改"。这些人除了租田纳谷之外，还要给东家无偿服劳役，主要是各种贱役，如男子要抬轿、扛丧（即抬棺，要结过婚的才可）、挖坟穴、守坟、挑担、吹打，妇女均为大脚，要接生、当红婆（婚礼时照料新娘）、给"孺人"和小姐抬轿，姑娘则当丫环，等等。这些人身份很低，因此赵吉士说："徽俗重门族，凡仆隶之裔，虽显贵，故家多不与缔姻。"嘉庆《黟县志·风俗》则说："重别臧获之等，即其人盛赀厚富，行作吏者，终不得列于辈流。"

在关麓村，臧获不依附一家一户，而依附所租土地的主人所属的房派、支派，如"三家"、"六家"、（老）"七家"、承德堂、崇德堂和"志顺公后裔"等。主家所属派中某家有事，臧获便去服役，如果人手不够，他们会自行邀请依附于其他房派的臧获来帮助，主家不必出面。这些劳役虽然依"制度"说是无偿的，但因多属"红白喜事""添丁增口"之类，所以赏钱不少。例如，新春元日，他们到东家门前扫几笤帚地，说几句吉祥话，便有厚赏；新妇花轿抬到祠堂，他们堵住大门唱喜庆话，要女家给封赏后才让开大门，放花轿进去。年时节下主家做年糕、清明馃，会送给他们一点。因为"有利可图"，所以各房派的臧获互相间不得侵越，而且子孙都把这种关系当作权利继承。

这种佃仆制度由来已久。关麓村的臧获，来源大多是：一、在外地经商时买的家僮或婢女，带回村来在家中服役，长大后准予毁券自立，成为佃仆；二、以婢女招亲，入赘为佃仆；三、因"种主田、住主屋"，将来还要"葬主山"，沦为佃仆；四、佃仆的后代，世世为佃仆。前述乾隆三十三年（1768）华桧的析产阄书里有一条："绕绛岭头系承桃之产，照之滋公阄书分法管业，今与仆人王六、婢女春秀住歇。"春秀有卖身契，王六有招赘文书。崇德堂定规，清明节给之滋府君、之滨府君和恺府君（华桧）扫墓时，要给仆人叶禄、叶六各烧"冥包一个"，他们的坟就在主山。这两例主仆名分是很典型的。

大户买婢女的习惯一直沿袭到民国年间，所以关麓村目前还有些当过婢女的老妇人，如篾匠汪朝立的母亲原为"双桂书屋"汪永梁（汪庭辉之子）家的婢女。她们不知道自己的姓氏和原籍，但都在土地改革后婚配，已经没有佃仆身份。我们在1995年春季调查时，见到八十七岁的项福春，土改后他原是本地小姓，因娶了"六家"汪昌泰家的婢女，成为佃仆，是个吹唢呐的乐户。土改后他妻子仍然一直在村里帮忙红白诸事。50年代，他妻子去世了，没有儿女，又续弦了一位"二婚"妇女，带来一个女儿。60年代初，大饥荒，村里饿死了不少人，妻子熬不下去，跟着一个过路的祁门铁匠走了。不久，有人看见铁匠又到村子里来了一趟，说项福春的妻子在外面饿死了。铁匠走后，女儿就失踪了，可能是铁匠把她召走了。80年代村人又给他找了一个男孩过继为孙子，但并不跟他过日子。男孩淘气，不好好读书，只等着继承他土地改革时分来的一间房子。两年前，项福春一度病危，村里给他募捐了两千元丧葬费，后来病愈，钱由村妇女主任保管着。我们离村之前，1994年4月14日下午5时，这位全村最后的昔日佃仆因疝气引发败血症去世。他去世前两小时仰卧在床上，我们给他拍了一张照片。村里人给他办丧，按照古例，埋在主家的查里岗坟地里。那个孙子来尽孝，捧头、摔盆、举着哭丧棒送葬，穿一身毛边丧服（缞服），是用化肥袋子改做的，帽子上"尿素"两个字清晰可见。

东家们把给佃仆住的庄户房造在村子边角或者坟地旁，小小的，不同他们的高堂华屋混杂。

高堂华屋里住着徽商眷属，据清闲斋《夜谭随录》云："新安风俗勤俭，虽富家眷不废操作。"虽然并不种田，却还纺绩、种菜。乾隆年间古筑人孙学治《和施明府源黟山竹枝词》之一道："北庄岭下女绩麻，西武岭边女纺花。花布御冬麻度夏，有无相易各成家。"这是妇女生活的真实写照。妇女们受着封建礼教沉重的压迫，被丈夫抛在村里，侍候公婆，养育儿女。而丈夫却往往在外面再婚，另有家业。正如《二刻拍案惊奇》卷十五里说的徽商汪朝奉娶二夫人："这个朝奉，只在扬州开当中盐，大孺人自在徽州家里，今讨去做二孺人，住在扬州当中，是两头大的……"关麓习俗，经商人从外地归来时妻子从菜园回家要先进后门，洗了脚，梳洗打扮，才能与丈夫相见。

丈夫很少回来。他们十二三岁便出外学徒，十六七岁回家完婚，过三个月就再出去。从此多则一年回来一次，少则三四年一次，甚至有十几年才回来一次的。但徽商都有叶落归根的意识，五十岁上下，就给儿子们分家经营，自己退而养老，回家赋闲。在外地有二夫人的，也要每年在家住几个月。

到清代晚期，有一些人成了食利者，斥资入股，自己不参与经营，而长期在乡闲住。如崇德堂的丕鉴和他的父亲德麒，就有多年这样的生活。

这些家居的人形成乡绅的主体。其中有一部分热心乡土建设、文化教育和祠下管理，对村子的影响很大。

关麓村在乡商人的生活，虽然远不如淮扬一带的徽商那样奢侈豪华，却也相当优裕。他们熟悉长江中下游富庶的城市，多少会把那里的一些风习带回老家，从而突破老家千百年的"俭啬"旧俗。他们起造的中型住宅，雅洁精致，家具陈设都很整齐细巧，考究品位。他们未必经常鲜衣美饰，但大多备有靓装丽服。有一张民国十八年（1929）十月十七日"皖省王祥茂皮局"（在安庆）开给汪悔初（丕洽）先生的发票，写的是"滩羊皮马褂筒一件，价洋贰拾捌元，当收洋贰拾叁元，两讫"。另有一张胡美辉裁缝店给汪悔初的工洋清单，开列十四件衣服。其中有哔叽驼绒袍一件，花大呢夹袍一件，哔叽夹袍一件，哔叽裙一条，法布夹袄裤一套，纺绸裤一条，麻纱女褂一件，等等。工洋一共拾贰元壹角伍分。可见他们的衣着质量很高。

他们出门稍远便乘轿子。有些类似原始旅行社的行业为他们服务。如有一封"黟城安庆信局"致汪悔初的信保存下来，内容便是洽谈安排赴安庆的轿子和旅伴的。关麓村东大约两三华里，赴古筑镇大道的一个陡坡下，有过一家轿子行，那地名就叫石屋行。轿行除了接送客人外，还有喜庆用轿出租。

民国年间，这个五百多人小村子有二十家出头的商店。其中有一家怡昌号南货店，是"八家"四、六两房兄弟开的，经营南北杂货、两洋海味，还卖猪肉、豆腐和油盐等日用品，自设糕点作坊。它在全县都可称大店。有一家滋生堂中药店，自制丸、散、膏、丹，有坐堂医生。有一家新荣馆子店，卖炒菜、红烧肉和各味面条。甚至还有汪观榜和李东楷两家银匠店，主要营业是把银锭剪成散碎银两，便于使用，或者把散碎银两铸成银锭，以便携带，也代客加工金银首饰。虽然它们有些生意是为过路人和附近小村的，仍然可见关麓村生活的富裕。

关麓村的婚丧、祭祀也很铺排。在外地去世的，都要把棺木运回来，一般要三十六名杠夫轮流。如丕鉴手记录本里有两条资料：一、"昭志公在外寿终，殁在垅坪位育典，去世道光十九年，搬柩往黟，请县主点主。合族办族规，做七日奠祭，热闹异常，用银二千余两"。二、"令训公殁于安庆恒吉绸缎庄，次年（按：道光二十三年）搬柩往黟，请县主点主，开五日祭奠，办合族饼胙。受礼，各亲戚一名，世谊外各同寅官不辞谢。在众祠开吊，幛挂满堂"。令训是昭志的儿子。到1936年，"六家"汪懋坤（锦章，九十三世）在安庆去世，还要用十二个杠夫把棺木抬回来。

关于婚筵，丕鉴手记中也有一则资料。丕鉴的继子懋长（慰祖，1911年生）结婚的时候（1937年4月）："初四日上头饭，男客四盘二碗八桌，女客廿余桌，走动下人、庄上（按：即佃仆）二三桌。次日正期系四月初五日，拜天地，中饭男客四盘二碗亦八桌；夜，男客鱼翅花烛酒亦八桌；夜限鱼翅席四点心、八大碗、八小碗、四中碗、十二碟。正期初五日女客亦与上头饭一律，计廿余桌；走动、庄上、鼓乐二桌。夜限女客十桌，翅席二桌，茶与男客一样。共吃亥（按：即猪肉）约一百八十余斤，海菜洋廿余元，酒洋十元，红帖蜡烛约洋廿元，开门、斟酒洋十八元，加轿税洋八元，鼓乐吹席洋八元，共计用三百余元，加批书、送日子计二百四十余元。"这时候丕鉴因连遭水火灾、"北兵"掠夺和土匪抢劫，已经很潦倒，生意早已收歇，坐吃祖业，尚有这等排场，则昭志、令训时代婚筵盛况可以想见。

徽商向来不废诵读，称为"儒商"。他们虽然十二三岁便外出学徒，但童年经过学塾的旧学教育，有相当不错的文化素养。日常也有些风雅的文化生活。家家堂屋里有中堂和条幅的字画，有木板刻的楹联，有些人家且有收藏字画、书籍和文玩的爱好。道光《黟县续志》记他："字晓山……少孤，善事母，友爱诸弟。弱冠，师皖江何龙，写山水人物，有生动之致。后益肆力倪、黄、沈、董诸家，寒暑不辍。称其画者谓风神秀润，青出于蓝。"本志又记关麓汪烈（汪光烈）："邑增生，性醇谨，孝友克敦，好古博雅，尤工翰墨，临池学钟、王以下及宋、元、明诸家，而薜枕米南宫者最久。惜年四十而殁，未竟所学，今流传片纸，人争重之。"同治《黟县三志·文苑》里有一位汪占晋，"廪生，少受父廷深训，邃于经学，词章亦工，著有《桐轩文钞》"。

关麓村这样杰出的人物并不多，但直到民国初年，一般男子还颇善翰墨，书法亦佳，日常燕处，朋友间也有论诗品画的雅好。汪亚芸先生现存顾耀南、汪仲琴和一位署名为"旭"的长辈致他父亲汪丕洽柬帖数封，都很有情致。如顾书之一："委题画媚，本思兴到书之。不意稍写数字，竟心手不应，将尊画写污，殊与愿违，并负尊命。可见无根柢之事，不能运用如耳。罪甚。"又有顾未题款识的书稿两页："吾乡步直老人在道咸间为一时名士，善诙谐，文字特超而画尤自成一家，惟不轻应人之求耳。今搜求老人之画，益如凤毛麟角，殊罕觏。迩丙寅重九节，过舅家，见壁悬画松一轴，笔老气苍，绝非时手能臻此境。读其款识，果为步直老人之作，爱玩之余，因向表嫂要求割爱。表嫂乃慨然以此见赠。心喜拜嘉，爰志数语，永表谢意。时丁卯冬识于皖垣。"这些乡绅们生活中的文化氛围，由此可见一斑。

商人们虽然自诩"儒商"，生活富足，毕竟还不能完全抹去传统的"士农工商"社会品级观念在他们心里投下的阴影。他们总要借各种封建性关系提高自己的社会地位。前述昭志和令训的丧事，都请县主"点主"，即在神主牌位上给"主"字点一个红色点子，便是这种心态。更进一步的，是花钱捐一个空官衔。他们从少年时代就要学做生意，不可能通过科举获得功名，但他们有钱，可以用救灾助赈或其他各种名义出钱捐官，代替十年寒窗苦功。有些人还为父亲、祖父和儿子买封。例如，昭志于道光十四五年（1834-1835）用垅坪典盈余银三千两囤积贩运棉花，得利五百两整，到道光十七年（1837），"拨此银，请上代四品诰封卷，从生父上一代国僖公则也赠朝议大夫（按：另一处记为中宪大夫，例授州同知），生父光晖公诰赠朝议大夫（按：另一处记为中宪大夫），本身昭志公亦请例赠朝议大夫"。"候至同治初年，用以人（按：即丕鉴）生父德麟公（按：疑应为"德麒公"）名请三代五品衔诰封。上代先王父（按：即令训）诰赠、先父（按：即德麒）例赠（奉政）大夫"（按：所言三代仅举二代。更上一代昭志已曾请封）。这次是由令训极善理财的孀居夫人叶氏出的钱。得到诰封之后，"于同治年间在族祠（按：即世德堂）挂诰匾，已祠崇德堂亦挂诰封匾。办族规饼，办合族规，中海参席，晚鱼翅席，都十桌。有往无往概请来吃"。丕鉴本人还于"光绪廿年在湖北鄂湘赈捐，例加捐蓝翎奉政大夫，同知衔，遵照省例，历捐县丞，指分江西试用县丞"。德麒还是"候选布理问监生"，他的胞弟德培是"候选盐课大使正堂，江西候补巡检"。

"八家"也有几个"大夫"。其中一个是九十世经商的六房令钟。至今还有纪念他受诰封为奉政大夫时的彩色画像，像上恭书光绪十八年（1892）三月诰封的全文。他的儿子德澄也是奉政大夫并授同知衔，"八家"的始祖、八十九世昭溆为奉政大夫，都是由德澄讨封的。

有钱有闲的寄生生活有很大的腐蚀性。清代末年和民国年间，关麓村的乡土生活发生了一些变化。有些浮浪之人放荡而不自检点，赌博、抽鸦片、嫖娼。赌场很多。村子西北角，"六家"的汪丽声（来久）家曾是大烟馆。迁住鲍村的"八家"汪丕玉是个青帮头子，本世纪40年代霸占了关麓村村口几间商店屋开了一家客店，聚赌并容暗娼，且曾图财谋害一位客商。一里路外的宏田村，靠近接武桥，有两个大宅院，土名"下围墙"，一个是大烟馆，另一个住清音班。清音班是一种地方小戏班，平日应召到喜庆人家演唱堂会，也卖淫，亦娼亦优。民国八年（1919）腊月十三日晚上，丕鉴在他的手记录本上写下了这样一段话："……伊二房（按：九十一世德培，德麒之弟）丝毫分文乌有，概都败清败了，足见土话油干火无，弃世矣！搬来之物，废当票满当了有一百余张，计算洋有四五百元。换过了金叶金共有一二斤。有废票谱换金的。留得刻下价大，可谓巨富之家人也。实深可惜。此可罕见、罕有也。此记。魁銮家物、衣、首饰、赤金叶可谓黟县头一家，也遭败人。可惜，可惜！真正不少也。"这些人家的败落都不是因经营挫折或遇意外，而是由于坐享其成的子弟的腐化。

1995年

附记

1994年秋至1995年春我们在关麓村调查时，尚有硬木雕花鸦片烟床两张。村民相告，村中挖房基和翻菜地时，常可见鸦片烟具。我们采集了一件。汪祖武先生说，他外祖父就是一夜间赌光了家产的，而他母亲仍嗜赌如命。"三家"汪亚芸先生说："三家""六家"等房派的败落，主要由于子孙腐化。"八家"子孙都比较谨严，连吸烟的都没有，所以发达。
sections.content_en:
Life in a Huizhou Merchant Village

Huizhou merchants, whether in capital or manpower, relied to varying degrees on clan relations. As a merchant guild, they had strong feudal characteristics and generally remained rooted in the land where their clans resided. They traveled extensively for business but left their wives, children, and elders in their hometowns. The hometown was feudal and conservative. Zhao Jishi, chief compiler of Kangxi "Huizhou Prefecture Annals," wrote in "Jiyuan Jisuo Ji · Fanye Ji": "All surnames in Xin'an live in clan settlements, with absolutely no mixed surnames entering; their customs are most archaic... Elders used to say that Xin'an has several customs superior to other counties: thousand-year-old tombs, not a handful of soil moved; clans of a thousand men, never scattered; thousand-year genealogies, not the slightest disorder; strict master-servant relations, unchanged for dozens of generations, and villains dare not act recklessly." In the three hundred years after Kangxi, changes were minimal.

Feudal traditions eroded the accumulation of commercial capital. When Huizhou merchants accumulated savings from business, they often brought money home to buy land and build houses. The land was not much, and family members mostly did not cultivate it, instead tenanting it to minor surnames and collecting rent grain. Huizhou villages were generally blood-relation settlements, but there were always people of other surnames in the villages, mostly poor farmers from elsewhere, weak and powerless, called minor surnames. In Guanlu Village, minor surnames mostly came from Anqing, Huaining, Tongling, and Qianshan, called "Jiangbei laolao" (northerners). They came alone with a shoulder pole of belongings, temporarily sheltering in thatched huts on rented plots or by the village edge, and some lived in the master's home. After settling, they brought their families to settle and built small houses by the village. The master's rent grain was not always fully collectible. For example, Wang Pijian wrote in his hand-recorded "Will": "Field rent of over 400 zu, actually collected just over 100 zu; bean rent of over 100 zu, actually collected just over 30 zu." Some land purchased through intermediaries, far in Qimen, had never been personally seen, and rent was even harder to collect. Merchant families did not live entirely on rent; they mainly relied on remittances sent periodically by merchants through professional "letter carriers," called "eating letter shells" by Guanlu people. Merchants treated land merely as wealth that couldn't be stolen.

Among tenant farmers, a portion were called "zanghuo" (bond servants), who had certain personal dependency relations with their masters, also called "bandang," "zhuanghu," or "dianpu." Their relations with masters were hereditary, so Zhao Jishi said "strict master-servant relations, unchanged for dozens of generations." Besides renting land and paying grain, these people also had to perform unpaid labor for masters, mainly various menial tasks: men carried sedan chairs, bore coffins (only married men could), dug graves, guarded tombs, carried burdens, played music; women were all big-footed, delivering babies, serving as "red women" (attending brides at weddings), carrying sedan chairs for "ladies" and misses, and girls served as maids, etc. These people had very low status, so Zhao Jishi said: "Huizhou customs value clan lineage; descendants of servants, even if wealthy and prominent, old families mostly do not intermarry with them." Jiaqing "Yi County Annals · Customs" says: "Strictly distinguishing bond servant ranks, even if they become wealthy and serve as officials, they ultimately cannot be ranked among peers."

In Guanlu Village, bond servants did not attach to individual households but to the branch or sub-branch of the landowner, such as "Three Families," "Six Families," (Old) "Seven Families," Chengde Hall, Chongde Hall, and "descendants of Zhishun Gong," etc. When a family in the master's branch had an event, bond servants came to serve; if short-handed, they would invite bond servants attached to other branches to help, without the master needing to intervene. Although this labor was "unpaid" according to "system," since it mostly involved "weddings and funerals," "births," the tips were substantial. For example, on New Year's Day, they swept a few broomfuls in front of the master's door and said auspicious words, receiving generous tips; when the bride's sedan chair arrived at the ancestral hall, they blocked the gate singing celebratory songs, only letting it pass after the bride's family gave rewards. During festivals, when masters made New Year cakes and Qingming cakes, they would give some. Because "there was profit to be made," bond servants of different branches did not encroach on each other, and descendants inherited these relations as rights.

This bond servant system had long origins. The zanghuo in Guanlu Village mostly came from: 1. House boys or maids bought while doing business elsewhere, brought back to serve at home, and when grown, allowed to tear up their contracts and become independent, becoming bond servants; 2. Maids who招赘 husbands, who became bond servants; 3. Those who "planted master's land, lived in master's house," and would eventually "be buried on master's mountain," becoming bond servants; 4. Descendants of bond servants, who were bond servants for generations. The aforementioned family division document of Hua Gui from the 33rd year of Qianlong (1768) had a clause: "Raojiangling head is inherited property, managed according to Zhizi Gong's division document, now lived in by servant Wang Liu and maid Chunxiu." Chunxiu had a deed of sale, Wang Liu had a marriage document. Chongde Hall stipulated that when sweeping the tombs of Zhifu Fujun, Zhibin Fujun, and Kai Fujun (Hua Gui) during Qingming, servants Ye Lu and Ye Liu would each be given a "hell money packet," and their graves were on the master's mountain. These two examples of master-servant status are very typical.

The custom of wealthy families buying maids continued into the Republican era, so Guanlu Village still has some elderly women who were maids, such as the mother of bamboo craftsman Wang Chaoli, originally a maid in the "Double Cassia Study" of Wang Yongliang (son of Wang Tinghui). They didn't know their surnames or origins, but all married after land reform and no longer had bond servant status. During our investigation in spring 1995, we met 87-year-old Xiang Fuchun. After land reform he was originally a local minor surname; because he married a maid of the "Six Families" Wang Changtai's family, he became a bond servant, a musician who played the suona. After land reform his wife still helped with weddings and funerals in the village. In the 1950s his wife died, childless, and he remarried a "second marriage" woman who brought a daughter. In the early 1960s, during the great famine, many starved in the village; his wife couldn't endure and left with a passing blacksmith from Qimen. Soon after, someone saw the blacksmith return to the village, saying Xiang Fuchun's wife had starved to death outside. After the blacksmith left, the daughter disappeared, possibly taken by the blacksmith. In the 1980s villagers found him a boy to adopt as grandson, but the boy didn't live with him. The boy was naughty, didn't study well, only waiting to inherit the one house Xiang Fuchun received in land reform. Two years earlier, Xiang Fuchun was critically ill; villagers raised 2,000 yuan for his funeral, but he recovered, and the money was kept by the village women's director. Before we left the village, at 5 PM on April 14, 1994, this last former bond servant in the village died of sepsis caused by a hernia. Two hours before death he lay supine in bed, and we took a photo of him. Villagers held his funeral, according to ancient custom burying him in the master's Chali Gang cemetery. The adopted grandson performed filial duties, held the head, broke the pot, carried the mourning staff, wearing a rough-hewn mourning garment (cui garment) made from fertilizer bags, with the words "urea" clearly visible on the hat.

Masters built houses for bond servants at village corners or by cemeteries, small, not mixed with their own grand houses.

In grand houses lived Huizhou merchant families. According to Qingxianzhai's "Yetan Suilu": "Xin'an customs are diligent and frugal, even wealthy families do not stop working." Although they didn't farm, they still spun and wove, grew vegetables. During Qianlong, Guzhu native Sun Xuezhi wrote in one of "He Shi Mingfu Yuan Yishan Zhuzhi Ci": "Women at Beizhuang岭 twist hemp, women at Xiwu岭 spin flowers. Cloth for winter, hemp for summer, exchanging what they have to make homes." This is a true portrayal of women's lives. Women suffered heavy oppression from feudal ethics, left in the village by husbands, serving in-laws and raising children. Husbands often remarried elsewhere with separate families. As recorded in Volume 15 of "Erke Pai'an Jingqi": Huizhou merchant Wang Chaofeng took a second wife: "This merchant only runs a pawnshop and salt business in Yangzhou; the first lady stays at home in Huizhou, now taken as second lady, living in Yangzhou pawnshop, it's 'two big heads'..." In Guanlu custom, when a merchant returned from elsewhere, his wife coming home from the vegetable garden had to enter through the back door first, wash her feet, groom and dress, before meeting her husband.

Husbands rarely returned. They left for apprenticeships at twelve or thirteen, returned home to marry at sixteen or seventeen, and left again after three months. Thereafter they returned at most once a year, at least once every three or four years, some only once every dozen years. But Huizhou merchants had the consciousness of "fallen leaves returning to roots"; around fifty, they divided the business among sons, retired to old age, and returned home to idle. Those with second wives elsewhere also had to live at home for several months each year.

By the late Qing dynasty, some became rentiers, investing capital without participating in management, living idly in the village long-term. For example, Pijian of Chongde Hall and his father Deqi lived such lives for many years.

These home-dwelling people formed the main body of the local gentry. Some were enthusiastic about local construction, cultural education, and ancestral hall management, having great influence on the village.

The life of home-based merchants in Guanlu Village, although far less luxurious than Huizhou merchants in the Huaiyang region, was quite comfortable. They were familiar with the wealthy cities of the middle and lower Yangtze, and brought back some customs, breaking through the village's thousand-year-old "frugal" traditions. The medium-sized residences they built were elegant and refined, with furniture and furnishings neat and delicate,讲究 taste. They didn't always wear fine clothes, but most had beautiful outfits. An invoice dated October 17, 1929 (18th year of Republic), from "Wan Sheng Wang Xiangmao Leather Shop" (in Anqing) to Mr. Wang Huichu (Piqia), reads: "Lambskin jacket piece, price 28 yuan, received 23 yuan, settled." Another labor list from tailor Hu Meihui for Wang Huichu listed fourteen garments, including serge camel-hair robe, large wool lined robe, serge lined robe, serge skirt, cotton-padded jacket and trousers, silk trousers, linen woman's jacket, etc. Total labor cost 12.15 yuan. This shows their clothing quality was high.

They took sedan chairs for any distance. Some proto-travel agency businesses served them. A letter from "Yicheng Anqing Letter Bureau" to Wang Huichu survives, discussing arrangements for sedan chairs and travel companions to Anqing. About two or three li east of Guanlu Village, at the foot of a steep slope on the road to Guzhu Town, there was a sedan chair shop; the place was called Shiwu Hang. The shop not only transported passengers but also rented festive sedan chairs.

During the Republican era, this village of over 500 people had more than twenty shops. One was Yichanghao South Goods Store, opened by brothers of the "Eight Families" fourth and sixth branches, selling north-south groceries, foreign goods and seafood, also selling pork, tofu, oil and salt daily necessities, with its own pastry workshop. It could be called a large store in the whole county. There was Zisheng Tang Chinese medicine shop, making pills, powders, ointments, and pellets, with an in-house doctor. There was Xinrong Restaurant, selling stir-fries, braised pork, and various noodles. There were even two silversmith shops, Wang Guanbang and Li Dongkai, whose main business was cutting silver ingots into碎 silver for use, or casting碎 silver into ingots for portability, also processing gold and silver jewelry for customers. Although some business served passersby and nearby small villages, it still shows the prosperity of Guanlu Village life.

Weddings, funerals, and sacrifices in Guanlu Village were also lavish. Those who died elsewhere had their coffins brought back, generally requiring 36 pallbearers taking turns. For example, Pijian's notebook had two records: 1. "Zhizhi Gong died away from home, at Longping Weiyu pawnshop, died in the 19th year of Daoguang, coffin moved to Yi, county magistrate requested to 'dot the master.' Whole clan held clan regulations, seven-day memorial, very lively, costing over 2,000 taels of silver." 2. "Lingxun Gong died at Hengji silk shop in Anqing, next year (23rd year of Daoguang) coffin moved to Yi, county magistrate requested to 'dot the master,' five-day memorial, clan cakes and meat distributed. Gifts received, one from each relative, beyond friendship all colleagues did not decline. Mourning opened in public ancestral hall, scrolls filled the hall." Lingxun was Zhizhi's son. By 1936, when Wang Maokun (Jinzhang, 93rd generation) of the "Six Families" died in Anqing, twelve pallbearers were still needed to carry the coffin back.

Regarding wedding banquets, Pijian's notebook also has a record. When Pijian's adopted son Maochang (Weizu, born 1911) married (April 1937): "Fourth day head meal, male guests four plates two bowls eight tables, female guests over twenty tables, servants and bond servants two or three tables. Next day proper day fifth of fourth month, worship heaven and earth, lunch male guests four plates two bowls also eight tables; evening, male guests shark-fin wedding banquet also eight tables; evening limited shark-fin banquet four dim sums, eight big bowls, eight small bowls, four medium bowls, twelve dishes. Fifth day proper female guests same as head meal, over twenty tables; servants, bond servants, musicians two tables. Evening female guests ten tables, shark-fin two tables, tea same as male guests. Total pork about 180 jin, seafood over 20 yuan, wine 10 yuan, red cards and candles about 20 yuan, door-opening and pouring wine 18 yuan, sedan chair tax 8 yuan, musicians 8 yuan, total over 300 yuan, plus engagement documents and date-giving over 240 yuan." At this time Pijian had suffered floods, fires, "northern soldiers" plundering, and bandit robbery, was already destitute, business long closed, living off ancestral property, yet still had such extravagance — one can imagine the grandeur of wedding banquets in Zhizhi and Lingxun's time.

Huizhou merchants never abandoned reading, called "Confucian merchants." Although they left for apprenticeships at twelve or thirteen, their childhood old-style education in private schools gave them fairly good cultural accomplishment. Daily life also had elegant cultural activities. Every family's main room had central scrolls and hanging calligraphy/paintings, wooden-carved couplets; some families had hobbies collecting paintings, books, and scholarly objects. Daoguang "Yi County Continued Annals" records him: "Style Xiaoshan... orphaned young, served mother well, friendly to brothers. At twenty, studied under He Long of Wanjiang, painting landscapes and figures with vivid effect. Later diligently studied Ni, Huang, Shen, Dong masters, never stopping in heat or cold. Those who praised his paintings said elegant and moist, surpassing the master." The same annals also record Guanlu Wang Lie (Wang Guanglie): "County government student, pure and prudent, filial and friendly, fond of antiquity and elegance, especially skilled in calligraphy, studying Zhong, Wang and Song, Yuan, Ming masters, most admiring Mi Nangong. Unfortunately died at forty,未竟所学, today even a scrap of his writing is treasured." Tongzhi "Yi County Three Annals · Literary Garden" has Wang Zhanjin: "Government student, young trained by father Tingshen, deep in classics, also skilled in prose, author of 'Tongxuan Wenchao'."

Guanlu Village had few such outstanding figures, but until the early Republic, ordinary men were quite skilled in calligraphy, and in daily leisure, friends enjoyed discussing poetry and appreciating paintings. Mr. Wang Yayun still preserves several letters to his father Wang Piqia from Gu Yaonan, Wang Zhongqin, and an elder signing "Xu," all quite refined. For example, one from Gu: "Commissioned to inscribe painting, intended to write when inspired. Unexpectedly after writing a few characters, mind and hand didn't respond, soiled your honored painting, contrary to wish and your command. Shows things without foundation cannot be applied freely. Very guilty." Another unsigned manuscript: "Our native Buzhi old man was a famous scholar in Daoguang-Xianfeng, good at humor, writing especially transcendent and painting uniquely his own, but rarely complied with requests. Today seeking his paintings is increasingly rare. Recently on Double Ninth Festival, visiting uncle's home, saw a pine painting on the wall, brushwork old and vigorous, far beyond contemporary ability. Reading the inscription, indeed Buzhi old man's work; after enjoying, asked cousin's wife to part with it. She generously gave it. Joyfully accepting, wrote these words to express gratitude. Winter of Dingmao year in Wanhuan." The cultural atmosphere in these local gentry's lives is evident from this.

Although merchants prided themselves as "Confucian merchants" and lived comfortably, they could not completely erase the shadow of traditional "scholar-farmer-artisan-merchant" social hierarchy in their hearts. They always sought to improve their social status through various feudal relations. The aforementioned funerals of Zhizhi and Lingxun both requested the county magistrate to "dot the master" — putting a red dot on the "master" character on the ancestral tablet — reflecting this mentality. Further, they bought empty official titles. Having learned business from youth, they could not obtain scholarly honors through examinations, but they had money and could buy official titles through disaster relief or other means, replacing ten years of hard study. Some even bought titles for fathers, grandfathers, and sons. For example, Zhizhi, in the 14th-15th years of Daoguang (1834-1835), used 3,000 taels surplus from Longping pawnshop to hoard and trade cotton, profiting 500 taels; in the 17th year of Daoguang (1837), "allocated this silver to request fourth-rank imperial patent for three generations: grandfather Guoxi Gong also granted Chaoyi Daifu (another record says Zhongxian Daifu, example-granted prefecture magistrate), father Guanghui Gong granted Chaoyi Daifu (another record says Zhongxian Daifu), himself Zhizhi Gong also requested example-granted Chaoyi Daifu." "By early Tongzhi, used person (i.e., Pijian) father De Lin Gong (suspected should be 'Deqi Gong') name to request three-generation fifth-rank patent. Grandfather (i.e., Lingxun) granted, father (i.e., Deqi) example-granted (Fengzheng) Daifu" (note: three generations mentioned but only two listed; the earlier generation Zhizhi had already received patent). This time the money came from Lingxun's very capable widow Mrs. Ye. After receiving the patent, "in Tongzhi years hung patent plaque in clan hall (i.e., Shide Hall), and Chongde Hall also hung patent plaque. Held clan regulation cakes, whole clan regulations, sea cucumber banquet at noon, shark-fin banquet in evening, all ten tables. All invited to eat." Pijian himself also "in the 20th year of Guangxu donated in Hubei-Hunan relief, example-added blue feather Fengzheng Daifu, prefecture magistrate title, according to provincial regulations, successively donated county assistant, assigned to Jiangxi试用 county assistant." Deqi was also "candidate Buliwensheng student," and his brother Depei was "candidate salt tax ambassador, Jiangxi候补 inspector."

The "Eight Families" also had several "Daifu." One was the 90th generation businessman Lingzhong of the sixth branch. A colored portrait commemorating his patent as Fengzheng Daifu still survives, with the full patent text from the third month of the 18th year of Guangxu (1892) respectfully written on it. His son Decheng was also Fengzheng Daifu with prefecture magistrate title; the "Eight Families" ancestor, 89th generation Zhaoshu, was Fengzheng Daifu, all patented through Decheng.

Wealthy and idle parasitic life was highly corrosive. In the late Qing and Republican eras, Guanlu Village's local life changed. Some dissolute people were unrestrained, gambling, smoking opium, visiting prostitutes. There were many gambling dens. In the northwest corner of the village, the "Six Families" Wang Lisheng (Laijiu)'s home was once an opium den. Wang Piyu of the "Eight Families," who moved to Bao Village, was a Green Gang leader; in the 1940s he seized several shops at the village entrance and opened an inn, gambling and harboring prostitutes, and once plotted to murder a merchant for money. One li away in Hongtian Village, near Jiewu Bridge, were two large courtyards, local name "Xia Weigiang," one an opium den, the other housing a Qingyin troupe. Qingyin troupes were local opera troupes, summoned to perform at celebrations, also prostituting — both performer and prostitute. On the evening of the 13th day of the 12th month in the 8th year of the Republic (1919), Pijian wrote in his notebook: "...His second branch (91st generation Depei, Deqi's brother) has not a cent, all lost and gone, shows the local saying 'oil dry fire out,' passed away! Moved-in goods, expired pawn tickets over a hundred, calculating several hundred yuan. Exchanged for gold leaves total one or two jin. There were expired tickets exchanged for gold. Keeping now prices high, could be called a wealthy family. Truly regrettable. This is rare, rare. Recorded. Kuiluan's family goods, clothes, jewelry, pure gold leaves could be called first in Yi County, also ruined. Pity, pity! Truly not a few." The decline of these families was not due to business setbacks or accidents, but the corruption of sons who enjoyed unearned wealth.

1995

Postscript

During our investigation in Guanlu Village from autumn 1994 to spring 1995, there were still two carved hardwood opium beds. Villagers told us that when digging house foundations or turning vegetable plots, opium paraphernalia was often found. We collected one piece. Mr. Wang Zuwu said his maternal grandfather gambled away the family fortune in one night, and his mother was still addicted to gambling. Mr. Wang Yayun of the "Three Families" said: "The decline of branches like the 'Three Families' and 'Six Families' was mainly due to descendants' corruption. The 'Eight Families' descendants were more disciplined, not even smokers, hence prosperous."
