初到黄土高原

几年来，我们一直在南方的乡村里工作，那里自古农业经济发达，有些村落甚至早已有了繁荣的商业和手工业。文化教育水平也比较高，"进士第""大夫第"到处可见，祠堂门前曾经竖立过一对对的桅杆。那些村落大多是单姓的血缘村落。过去宗族组织完整，很有效地管理着村民的社会生活，宗法家长制的观念因而渗透到生活的各个方面。那样的村落，往往有明确的格局，有水口，有中心和副中心，有合理的街道网和给水排水系统，等等。建筑类型相当多，形成了一个与复杂的农村生活相对应的乡土建筑系统。各种建筑物的形制比较成熟而稳定，住宅的形制多种多样。它们的质量很高，能够满足社会的和家庭的生活需要，工艺讲究，装饰精致，形式和谐而多活泼的变化。从村落的整体到雕饰的题材，都反映出封建宗法制度的意识形态，文化含量非常丰富。

但南方的乡土建筑毕竟只不过是中国乡土建筑极为有限的一部分。我们当然不敢奢望在广袤的中国大地上东南西北选取足够多的典型村落来做研究，但我们希望稍稍扩大一些选题的范围，以开阔我们的眼界，活跃我们的思维，这样能把工作做得更好一点。恰好，有朋友问我们，能不能研究一个西北黄土高原上的窑洞村落，陕西长武十里铺。我们立刻就同意了。

黄土高原是中华文明的发源地之一，曾经是中国政治中心的所在地。那里发生过许多对中华民族的命运有重大影响的事件。然而，长期以来，那里又是全国最最贫穷的地区之一。

黄土高原是黄土沟壑区，塬蹙沟深，天高风紧，自然风光阔大雄伟而粗犷，特色非常鲜明强烈。

黄土高原上的乡风民俗，同样也是特色非常鲜明强烈。且不说婚丧嫁娶、年时节下，便是那震天动地的腰鼓，嘹亮高亢的民歌，饱含着人们理想和愿望的剪纸和炕围画，也早已远近闻名。

这些对我们都是诱惑。

窑洞，或许不免过于简单，但是，据说现在还有将近一亿人住在窑洞里。他们的生活怎么样？听说窑洞冬暖夏凉，是真的吗？

去，一定要去！

一决定了要去，便有点儿迫不及待。我们打算1996年春节之前去，在村子里过节，跟乡亲们一起玩社火，吃他们的蒸馍、面花。但是，在西安工作了几十年的朋友们告诉我们，我们要去的地方，大雪封山，交通十分困难而危险。我们还坚持要去。过几天，他们打来电话，那儿非常贫穷，年节本来就没有多少活动，加上这几年社会的大变动，民俗已经所剩无几了，去了也看不到什么。我们有点动摇了。再过几天，他们又来了电话，说，村民们根本没有多余的铺盖可供我们睡觉，我们不可能在村里住下。我们泄气了。最后，他们认真打听了之后，建议说，春天里去，近年来新栽的苹果树开了花，云霞一片，那时处处可以见到男婚女嫁，鼓乐骈阗，何况清明节还有伐树、扫墓之类的活动，这些都是冬天里没有的。于是，我们改变了主意：4月里去。

4月1日，清明节前三天，我们从北京出发。2日，从西安乘汽车去长武，渡渭河，经咸阳、醴泉、乾县，来到泾河一条支流的河谷里，便是彬县（旧豳县）。这一路每一处地方，都在中国历史上占一个位置，文化遗址一个接着一个。我们被一种巨大的历史感浸透了心灵，默默沉思着，望着车窗外的变化。醴泉县境内，几十公里的路边都是苹果园，夹杂着葡萄园，一望无垠，可惜枝条都还是空的。武则天的乾陵就在公路边上，恢宏有大气魄。从这里开始，公路两边就迤逦都是窑洞和窑院了。泾河支流的河谷深而且宽，我们在东岸，远远望见西岸高高的陡崖上，一层层厚厚的积雪，便预感到那边将是一个生活严酷的地方。汽车艰难地下了坡，过了河，又艰难地上了坡，眼前便是黄土高原。塬上景色开阔，无边无际，碧蓝的天滚滚圆，边上没有丝毫缺口。但是，一忽儿在左，一忽儿在右，突然就能见到深不可测的大沟，几百米宽。沟壁直上直下，却有些浅色的线贴在陡壁上盘旋，细细一看，那竟是人们踩出来的小径。有几处，公路两边都是沟，路就在一条刀脊般的土梁上走。我们看惯了南方农村的山峦，把天空咬得破破碎碎，猛然觉得这里的山峦是虚的，而且倒着朝下长，留下一个完整的天，像糕饼模子，很别致有趣。

离开北京的时候，榆叶梅的花骨朵已经红了，而这里麦子刚刚返青，还蔫蔫的没有精神。积雪一道一道的，像梳子梳着麦垄。远处隐隐有了树影，便到了长武城，正赶上集市，灰不溜秋的街上一堆堆鲜艳的塑料制品照得人眼花，卖烤饼的炉子漾出的香气，老远就能闻到。到县城建设局转了一圈，就直奔十里铺村所在的丁家乡。我们向乡长提出来要到农家住，乡长说，天很冷，窑洞里没有闲着的暖炕，又缺铺少盖，水也金贵，不好住。到农家吃呢？乡长也觉得为难，说，只有油泼辣子和去年腌下的咸菜，日子多了怕也不行。于是，我们就只好在公路边上做过路司机买卖的小店里安顿了下来，好在离十里铺村头不过一百多米。

十里铺村是个细长条，沿道沟延伸三里多路。道沟六米多深，十来米宽。一条直路穿过去，两侧一个挨一个的窑院。窑院前脸不是原土壁就是夯土墙，一副很原始的黄土沟面貌。只有稀稀落落几个近来新造的砖房和门楼，给它一点生气。

窑院和窑院的间隙，土壁上有些用镢头粗粗刨出来的踏步，农民们扛着锄头曲曲折折走上塬面去。塬面一马平川，能看到天边，却看不见人家，只看见从沟里冒出来的杨树梢，听见地底下传出来的人声。走近地坑的边缘，往下一看，窑院里演出着家庭生活的各种场景，梨树和桃树孕了花骨朵，小小的，还没有变色。

村子没有一定的结构和布局，随地势形成，散而无序。只在中段有一座村民委员会办公室，原本是三仙庙，新盖了五间砖瓦房。旁边有一间小小的卫生站，十平方米大小，卫生员常常不在，吊着锁。小学校倒有两座，有一座是在过去的大车店窑院里造的，几座砖瓦房，很整齐。院子种些花木，一下课，老师们便把院子扫得净光亮堂。村路也很干净，家家每天都出来打扫一段，清一清水沟。

路两旁密密种着杨树。我们到的第三天是清明节，那天伐了许多树，邻村也在伐树。我们觉得奇怪，打听了一下，说是杨树遭了虫灾，是一种蛾子，幼虫把树干蛀空了。仔细一看，要砍伐的树，树身上都刮去了一小块皮，白茬上贴着一张红纸条，写着"树神回避"四个字。当地的风尚，年年砍树必在清明节，红纸条提前几天贴上，以免伤了树神，万一伤了，以后再栽树就难了。虽然树的所有权是私人的，但传统的习惯，"村民公约"上也写着，谁砍一棵树，就必须补种一棵，以保持村里总有树木。今年要补栽的是楸树、槐树，不像杨树那样容易招虫子。

这真是个好习惯，树木给村子带来了生气。我们看到，许多还健康的树上，挂着小小的秋千，小学校一放学，活蹦乱跳的孩子们便抢着悠荡起来，有大姐姐在旁边帮着推的，便特别欢势。村人们告诉我们，这荡秋千也是清明节的一个习俗。不过从前不挂在树上，而是在窑院里搭个架子。因为秋千主要是女孩子玩的，穷乡野村里，规矩不多，不过女孩子还是不能在大路边上太疯了。本领大的女孩子，秋千荡得高高的，墙外也能看得见。"墙里秋千墙外道，墙外行人、墙里佳人笑"，或许是这种情景。

家家的门虚掩着，推开进去，窑院都收拾得很整洁，而且宽敞亮堂，纵横足有十几米，高高的黄土削壁，脚下三五孔窑洞刻出浑圆的轮廓，窑垴子上的门窗还有些细棂和亮色，看起来很大方。土壁上挂着浑圆的蒸笼盖子，是麦秸编成辫子再盘成的，旁边一嘟噜一嘟噜挂着深红的辣椒和金黄的玉米，下面蹲着几只山羊。难怪画家们很喜欢画这些东西，它们自有一种憨厚的风味。

日子住长了，我们对这条几里长的沟和窑院也真生出了喜爱的心情。

让我们喜爱的主要原因是那些与黄土地一样朴实憨厚的村人们。他们把我们当好朋友来接待，我们走进任何一家，主人都先喝住狗，把我们请进屋，上炕。虽然已经是4月上旬，高原上还是寒气袭人，又逢连阴天，老年人都盘在炕上，下面生火，上面盖着棉被。我们三个教师，被他们称为"两个老汉一个姨"，算是上了岁数的，要到暖炕上坐。学生们则坐在炕沿上。大娘打开箱子盖，摸出去年的大红枣来分给我们，不吃不行。到了饭口儿上，说什么也得坐下来吃几口馍。家里有绣品、香囊什么的，只要我们开口，有时甚至没有开口，她们都会高高兴兴地说："拿去罢，我们再做。"乾隆《重修长武县志叙》里，知县樊士锋说"民虽贫，有醇朴而无机诈，跻堂称觥之风当未泯也"，到现在依旧如此。

十里铺在这一带算是比较富的，从宝鸡来的公路正好在村边与西安至兰州的公路相会。人们见闻多一点，便有几家舍得花钱叫孩子读中学。知识开通，谋生的路子随之宽阔，早些年就有人到彬（豳）县的煤矿和电力公司工作，近年来出去打工的人不少，挣了些钱，回来种苹果和烟草，收益很好。有一些人攒钱买拖拉机，跑近途运输，最不济的也知道打一眼机井，家里老人坐在井边按电钮卖水，一吨能卖二元五角钱。还有少数高中毕业生，会搞经营，到地广人稀的甘肃租地，在当地雇工耕种，一年只过去几次，秋后收入便相当可观。至于那些跟村里当权人有点关系的，便可以到公路边上弄块地皮开饭铺、旅社，赚过路人的钱。因此，十里铺村里这几年造了些新房子。

邻近不靠大路的村子，有一些境况可就差多了。不但新房子很少，窑洞也很破旧。春节才过了一个多月，处处见不到春联、门神的痕迹。不过，那些最穷困人家住的、大沟壑边上的单孔靠崖窑，没有路、没有水的，大多已经废弃，许多人已经搬到了村里，改善了生活。我们在直谷堡、陶林堡、斜坡村、裕头村找到了一些那样的窑洞，叫"一炷香"，简直是挖在绝壁上。我们战战兢兢攀援过去，眼前脚下是望不见尽头的大深沟，不觉心惊胆战，真弄不明白当年的住户，老人和孩子，怎么在这里生活。在斜坡村和裕头村，我们都见到一些侏儒，尤其是斜坡村的几位更加畸形，这都是上一代人或几代人因为贫穷而不得不近亲结婚，以致留下后患。有一天，我们在斜坡村，进了一眼破破烂烂的窑洞，女主人显然很局促不安，看我们亲亲热热坐下，她便到厨窑里端来了一碗面片汤，怯生生地抱歉说没有什么好吃的。我们立即接过来大口吞下肚去，肚子里的酸楚却不是那只缺口的青花碗盛得下的。

但是，在窑洞门头上斗格中题着的生活格言里，常常可以见到一句"忍为高"或"能忍是福"。我们所住的旅社，有一间餐室，墙上挂着一面祝贺开业的镜子，刻着四个大字："知足常乐"。更教我们触目惊心感慨不已的，是公路边许多村头破墙上刷着的广告："抽帝王烟，过皇上瘾。"帝王烟是当地制造的一种劣质土烟，所以叫"帝王牌"，是因为陕西关中八百里秦川曾经是十一朝都城所在。

我们天天都记得我们最初的愿望，巴不得能遇上个把民俗活动，看到剪纸、皮影、炕围画，最好还听见青年男女们对唱山歌。但是，确实，这一带过去太穷，而且多是杂姓村，所以民俗活动很少。十里铺只有正月十五日晚上的社火，由爱玩的青年人临时凑合起来，踩着高跷，扮成各种戏文角色，挨家挨户去送喜，也就是到窑院里转转，唱几段秦腔。有些人家把火锅送到三仙庙里，闹社火的人完了事便蹲在庙里饱吃一顿。春节，据说以前有狮子和龙灯，现在则用几辆拖拉机后斗拼成戏台，由农民自己演些秦腔小戏。面花过去做的，这些年不做了。剪纸、炕围画也没有见着，不过我们终于访到了一位剪纸能手，还有一位熟悉许多民歌的老太太。在二十几天的日子里，有几起婚丧红白事，大都很简单，而且相当现代化了，有"领导同志讲话"之类的节目。我们在十里铺和邻近的村子里，塬上的、沟坎上的，现实生活中几乎找不到历史的遗迹。宣统《长武县志·跋》说："长武自古豳地，读《豳风·七月》，先圣之德泽，民风之忠厚，咸于是乎哉。而代远年湮，流风余韵，罕有存者。古今之不相及非细故矣！"公刘啊，古公亶父啊，扶苏啊，除了县博物馆长，老百姓是听都没有听到过。有些人连自己祖父的名讳都不知道。

不过，也许我们能解释一个中国美术史里的有趣现象，这里的年轻女子，不论是比较富裕的村子里还是穷村里的，几乎个个都长着肥大而鲜红的脸蛋，跟唐代仕女画和陶俑上的一模一样。唐代皇族起于陇西，离长武不远，当年皇族的妇女大概就是这样，以至于影响到了有唐一代的审美理念，反映到了美术品上。这也许是秦陇少数民族的脸型。美术史家在研究室里百思不得其解的问题，到现场去看一看便可以明白。但愿我们是对的。

再有一点，这里的人把黄土塬上经千百年人踏车辗而成的道沟叫作"胡同"。元代的蒙古人正是从这一带跃马扬鞭冲到无定河边，建成大都城的，所以，北京的巷子都叫"胡同"。这也是不少学者考据的课题，我们在十里铺轻而易举地弄明白了。

1996年夏
sections.content_en:
First Visit to the Loess Plateau

For several years, we had been working in southern villages, where agricultural economy had been developed since ancient times, and some villages even had prosperous commerce and handicrafts early on. Cultural and educational levels were relatively high; "jinshi mansions" and "daifu mansions" could be seen everywhere, and pairs of masts once stood before ancestral halls. Those villages were mostly single-surname blood-relation villages. In the past, clan organizations were complete and effectively managed villagers' social life, so the concept of patriarchal clan system permeated all aspects of life. Such villages often had clear layouts, with water mouths, centers and sub-centers, reasonable street networks, and water supply and drainage systems, etc. There were quite many building types, forming a vernacular architecture system corresponding to complex rural life. The forms of various buildings were relatively mature and stable, and residential forms were diverse. Their quality was high, able to meet social and family living needs, with refined craftsmanship, exquisite decoration, and harmonious yet lively varied forms. From the overall village to decorative themes, all reflected the ideology of the feudal patriarchal clan system, with very rich cultural content.

But southern vernacular architecture was, after all, only a very limited part of Chinese vernacular architecture. Of course we dared not hope to select enough typical villages from east, west, south, and north across the vast Chinese land for research, but we hoped to slightly expand the scope of topics to broaden our horizons and enliven our thinking, so we could do better work. Coincidentally, a friend asked if we could study a cave-dwelling village on the northwest Loess Plateau, Shilipu in Changwu, Shaanxi. We immediately agreed.

The Loess Plateau is one of the birthplaces of Chinese civilization and was once the location of China's political center. Many events with major impacts on the fate of the Chinese nation occurred there. Yet, for a long time, it has also been one of the poorest regions in the country.

The Loess Plateau is a loess gully region, with tablelands compressed and gullies deep, high skies and strong winds; the natural scenery is vast, majestic, and rugged, with very distinct and intense characteristics.

The local customs and folkways on the Loess Plateau are equally distinct and intense. Not to mention weddings, funerals, and festivals — even the earth-shaking waist drums, the loud and resonant folk songs, and the paper-cuts and kang wall paintings full of people's ideals and aspirations have long been famous far and wide.

These were all temptations to us.

Cave dwellings, perhaps inevitably too simple, but reportedly nearly one hundred million people still live in them. What is their life like? I heard cave dwellings are warm in winter and cool in summer — is that true?

Go, we must go!

Once we decided to go, we were somewhat impatient. We planned to go before the 1996 Spring Festival, spending the holiday in the village, playing shehuo (folk festivities) with the villagers, eating their steamed buns and flower-shaped buns. But friends who had worked in Xi'an for decades told us that the place we were going to would be snow-blocked, with very difficult and dangerous transportation. We still insisted on going. A few days later, they called saying it was very poor there, with few activities during the festival anyway, and with the great social changes of recent years, folk customs had almost disappeared, so we wouldn't see much. We wavered a bit. A few more days later, they called again saying villagers simply didn't have extra bedding for us to sleep on, so we couldn't stay in the village. We were discouraged. Finally, after careful inquiry, they suggested going in spring — the newly planted apple trees would be blooming like clouds, and weddings with music and festivities could be seen everywhere, not to mention tree-felling and tomb-sweeping during Qingming Festival, activities absent in winter. So we changed our plan: go in April.

On April 1, three days before Qingming Festival, we departed Beijing. On the 2nd, we took a bus from Xi'an to Changwu, crossing the Wei River, passing through Xianyang, Liquan, and Qianxian, arriving at the valley of a tributary of the Jing River — Bin County (old Bin County). Every place along this route held a place in Chinese history, with cultural sites one after another. Our souls were permeated by a tremendous sense of history; we silently meditated, watching the changes outside the window. In Liquan County, dozens of kilometers of roadside were apple orchards, interspersed with vineyards, boundless, though unfortunately the branches were still bare. Wu Zetian's Qianling Mausoleum was right by the highway, grand and imposing. From here on, cave dwellings and cave courtyards stretched along both sides of the road. The valley of the Jing River tributary was deep and wide; we were on the east bank, and from afar saw thick layers of snow on the high steep cliffs of the west bank, sensing that life there would be harsh. The bus laboriously descended the slope, crossed the river, and laboriously climbed again — before us was the Loess Plateau. The tableland scenery was open, boundless, the deep blue sky perfectly round, not a gap at the edges. But now on the left, now on the right, suddenly unfathomable great gullies appeared, hundreds of meters wide. The gully walls were vertical, yet some light-colored lines coiled on the steep cliffs; looking closely, they turned out to be paths trodden by people. In several places, the road was flanked by gullies on both sides, running on a knife-ridge earth beam. Accustomed to southern village mountains that bit the sky into pieces, we suddenly felt the mountains here were illusory, growing downward instead, leaving a complete sky like a pastry mold — quite unique and interesting.

When we left Beijing, the buds of flowering almond had already turned red, but here the wheat had just turned green, still listless. Snow lay in strips, like combs raking the wheat rows. Distant tree shadows faintly appeared, and we reached Changwu City, just in time for the market. On the gray streets, piles of bright plastic goods dazzled the eyes, and the aroma from baked cake stalls could be smelled from afar. After a stop at the county construction bureau, we went directly to Dingjia Township where Shilipu Village was located. We asked the township head if we could stay with farmers; he said it was very cold, with no idle warm kangs in cave dwellings, lacking bedding, and water was precious — hard to stay. As for eating at farmers' homes? The township head also found it difficult, saying there was only oil-sprinkled chili and last year's pickled vegetables, which wouldn't do for many days. So we had to settle at a small shop by the highway serving passing drivers, fortunately only a hundred meters from the head of Shilipu Village.

Shilipu Village is a long narrow strip, extending over three li along a road gully. The gully is over six meters deep and ten meters wide. A straight road runs through it, with cave courtyards one after another on both sides. The front faces of the cave courtyards are either original earth walls or rammed earth walls, presenting a very primitive loess gully appearance. Only a few recently built brick houses and gate towers sparsely give it some vitality.

Between cave courtyards, there are roughly hewn steps on the earth walls, and farmers carrying hoes zigzag up to the tableland. The tableland is flat as a board, with the horizon visible but no households — only the tops of poplar trees rising from the gullies, and voices heard from underground. Approaching the edge of a sunken courtyard, looking down, various scenes of family life unfold in the cave courtyard; pear and peach trees have formed small buds, not yet changed color.

The village has no fixed structure or layout, formed according to terrain, scattered and disordered. Only in the middle section is there a village committee office, originally the Three Immortals Temple, with five newly built brick-tile rooms. Beside it is a small health station, about ten square meters, where the health worker is often absent, with a lock hanging. There are two primary schools; one was built in the courtyard of a former cart shop, with several neat brick-tile houses. Flowers and trees are planted in the yard, and after school, teachers sweep the yard spotless. Village roads are also clean; every family comes out daily to sweep a section and clear the drainage ditch.

Poplar trees are densely planted along both sides of the road. The third day after our arrival was Qingming Festival, and many trees were felled that day, as in neighboring villages. We found it strange and inquired — it turned out poplars had suffered insect damage from a type of moth whose larvae hollowed out the trunks. Looking closely, the trees to be felled had a patch of bark scraped off, with a red paper strip on the white wood reading "Tree God, Avoid." Local custom requires tree-felling always on Qingming Festival, with red paper strips attached a few days in advance to avoid offending the tree god; if offended, future tree planting would be difficult. Although tree ownership is private, traditional custom — also written in the "village covenant" — requires whoever cuts a tree to plant one, to ensure the village always has trees. This year's replacements are catalpa and locust trees, less prone to insects than poplars.

This is truly a good custom; trees bring vitality to the village. We saw small swings hanging on many healthy trees; as soon as school let out, lively children scrambled to swing, with older sisters pushing nearby, making it especially joyful. Villagers told us swinging is also a Qingming custom. But in the past, swings weren't hung on trees but on frames built in cave courtyards. Because swings were mainly for girls, and in poor remote villages rules were few, girls still shouldn't be too wild by the roadside. Skilled girls swung high, visible outside the walls. "Inside the wall, swings; outside, the road; outside, passersby; inside, beauties laugh" — perhaps this was the scene.

Every family's door was left ajar; pushing in, the cave courtyards were all tidy, spacious and bright, over ten meters across, with high loess cliffs, three to five cave dwellings carved at the base with rounded contours, and the doors and windows on the cave tops had some fine lattice and bright colors, looking quite elegant. On the earth walls hung round steamer covers, braided from wheat straw and coiled; beside them hung clusters of deep red chilies and golden corn, with a few goats squatting below. No wonder painters love painting these things — they have a simple and honest charm of their own.

After living there for some time, we truly grew fond of this several-li-long gully and its cave courtyards.

The main reason for our fondness was the villagers, as simple and honest as the loess land. They received us as good friends; entering any home, the master would first call off the dog, invite us in, and onto the kang. Although it was early April, the plateau was still cold, and with overcast days, elderly people sat cross-legged on the kang, with fire below and quilts above. We three teachers, called "two old men and an aunt" by them, considered elderly, were asked to sit on the warm kang. Students sat on the kang edge. The aunt opened a trunk lid and took out last year's big red dates to distribute — we had to eat them. At mealtime, we had to sit down and eat a few buns no matter what. If there were embroidery, sachets, etc., as long as we expressed interest, sometimes even without asking, they would happily say: "Take it, we'll make more." In the Qianlong "Preface to Revised Changwu County Annals," county magistrate Fan Shifeng wrote: "Although the people are poor, they are honest and guileless, and the custom of toasting at gatherings has not vanished" — this remains true today.

Shilipu is relatively wealthy in this area; the highway from Baoji meets the Xi'an-Lanzhou highway right by the village. People are a bit more worldly, and several families are willing to spend money sending children to middle school. With knowledge opening up, livelihood paths broadened; some went to work in coal mines and power companies in Bin County years ago, and in recent years many have gone out to work, earning money to plant apples and tobacco at home with good returns. Some saved money to buy tractors for short-haul transport; even the least capable knew to drill a motorized well, with elderly family sitting by the well pressing buttons to sell water at 2.5 yuan per ton. A few high school graduates, good at business, rent land in sparsely populated Gansu, hire local labor, going there only a few times a year, with considerable income after autumn. As for those with connections to village authorities, they could get land by the highway to open restaurants and inns, earning money from passersby. Therefore, Shilipu Village has built some new houses in recent years.

Neighboring villages not on major roads have much worse conditions. Not only are new houses rare, but cave dwellings are also dilapidated. Over a month after Spring Festival, no traces of spring couplets or door gods could be seen anywhere. However, the single cliff caves where the poorest families lived — on the edges of great gullies, without roads or water — have mostly been abandoned, and many people have moved into the village, improving their lives. We found some such caves in Zhigubao, Taolinbao, Xiepo Village, and Yutou Village, called "one stick of incense," simply dug into sheer cliffs. We climbed over tremblingly, with unfathomable deep gullies before and below, feeling terrified — truly incomprehensible how former residents, elderly and children, lived there. In Xiepo and Yutou villages, we saw several dwarfs, especially several in Xiepo more deformed — all due to previous generations having to marry close relatives because of poverty, leaving consequences. One day in Xiepo Village, entering a dilapidated cave dwelling, the hostess was clearly ill at ease; seeing us sit down warmly, she went to the kitchen cave and brought a bowl of noodle soup, timidly apologizing that there was nothing good to eat. We immediately took it and gulped it down, but the bitterness in our stomachs was more than that chipped blue-and-white bowl could hold.

However, on the lintel grids of cave dwellings, life mottos often included "Endurance is noble" or "Being able to endure is blessing." The inn where we stayed had a dining room with a congratulatory mirror on the wall engraved with four large characters: "Contentment brings happiness." What struck us even more, causing endless emotion, were advertisements painted on broken walls at village heads by the highway: "Smoke Emperor Wang cigarettes, experience the emperor's pleasure." Emperor Wang cigarettes were a locally made low-quality native tobacco, called "Emperor Wang brand" because the 800-li Qinchuan in Shaanxi was once the capital of eleven dynasties.

We daily remembered our original wish, longing to encounter some folk activity, see paper-cuts, shadow puppetry, kang wall paintings, and ideally hear young men and women singing folk songs in antiphony. But indeed, this region was too poor in the past, and mostly multi-surname villages, so folk activities were few. Shilipu only had shehuo on the evening of the 15th day of the first lunar month, improvised by playful young people on stilts, dressed as various opera characters, going door to door to deliver blessings — that is, circling in cave courtyards and singing a few passages of Qinqiang opera. Some families sent hot pots to the Three Immortals Temple, and after the shehuo, participants squatted in the temple for a full meal. For Spring Festival, reportedly there used to be lion and dragon dances, but now several tractors' rear beds are joined into a stage, with farmers performing short Qinqiang plays themselves. Flower-shaped buns used to be made, but not in recent years. We didn't see paper-cuts or kang wall paintings, though we finally found a skilled paper-cutter and an old woman familiar with many folk songs. In over twenty days, there were several weddings and funerals, mostly simple and quite modernized, with programs like "leading comrade's speech." In Shilipu and neighboring villages, on tablelands and gully edges, historical traces were almost absent from real life. The Xuantong "Changwu County Annals · Postscript" says: "Changwu was ancient Bin territory; reading 'Bin Feng · Seventh Month,' the former sages' virtues and the people's honesty are all there. But as time passes, lingering customs rarely survive. The difference between past and present is no small matter!" Gong Liu, Gugong Danfu, Fusu — except for the county museum director, ordinary people have never even heard of them. Some don't even know their own grandfather's name.

However, perhaps we can explain an interesting phenomenon in Chinese art history: the young women here, whether in relatively wealthy or poor villages, almost all have plump, bright red cheeks, exactly like those in Tang dynasty court lady paintings and pottery figurines. The Tang imperial family originated from Longxi, not far from Changwu; imperial women of that time probably looked like this, influencing the aesthetic ideals of the entire Tang dynasty and reflecting in artworks. This may be the facial type of Qin-Long ethnic minorities. A problem art historians puzzle over in their studies can be understood by a visit to the field. We hope we are right.

Another point: local people call the road gullies on the loess tableland, formed over centuries by people and carts, "hutong." The Mongols of the Yuan dynasty precisely rode from this region to the Wuding River and built Dadu (Beijing), so Beijing's alleys are all called "hutong." This is also a subject of scholarly research, which we easily understood in Shilipu.

Summer 1996

sections.name: 婺源掠影
sections.content_zh:
婺源掠影

婺源县现在位于江西省的东北部，北界安徽，东邻浙江，是个"鸡鸣三省醒"的地方。不过，半个多世纪之前，它长期是徽州六邑之一，与歙县、黟县、绩溪、祁门、休宁同属一个徽州文化圈。

婺源辖地大部分原在休宁境内，小部分原在江西东平，唐开元二十四年（736）地方不靖，应缙绅之请于二十八年（740）设县，隶于歙州，县治初在今清华镇，后因军人跋扈，移治至弦高镇（今紫阳镇）。县境应婺女星分野，所以水称婺水，县称婺源。

由于一千多年来同为一个行政区划，所以婺源和徽属其余五邑一起，共同创造了光辉的徽州文化，也一起以"徽商"的名义，参与了明末至清的中国商业资本的大发展。婺源的历史和文化与整个徽州的历史和文化是一致的。

不过，由于地理条件的不同，婺源的历史和文化与其他五邑也有一些差别。在婺源东北方，与休宁、祁门之间，有大鄣山和浙岭。春秋时，它们是吴、楚两国的疆界。其余五邑为吴地，婺源为楚地，宋人权邦彦过浙岭有诗，"巍峨俯吴中，盘结亘楚尾"。岭脊至今尚存高一点七米的石碑一座，刻阴文隶书"吴楚分源"四字，是康熙年间立的。

以这两道山为分水岭，婺源和祁门县的水系归鄱阳湖入长江，其余诸邑的由新安江下钱塘江。水系不同，所接触的外界便不同，尤其在商业资本发展过程中，水路的影响更加显著。所以，婺源的文化，与其余诸邑相比，大同之中有小异。在建筑方面更如此。婺源是皖南（徽州）建筑文化圈中的一个亚文化圈。

徽州山多地少，耕不能自给，男子不得不外出"经营四方"。康熙《徽州府志》录明末汪伟奏疏："徽州介万山之中，地狭人稠，耕三不赡一，即丰年亦仰食江楚。……天下之民寄命于农，徽民寄命于商。而商之通于徽者，取道有二，一从饶州、鄱、浮，一从浙省杭、严，皆壤地相邻，溪流一线，小舟如叶，鱼贯尾衔，昼夜不息。"寄命于商的结果是到明代嘉靖以后，"徽商遍天下"，至有天下"无徽不成镇"之说。光绪《两淮盐法志·列传》统计，自嘉靖至乾隆，扬州客籍商人之著名者八十人，徽商占六十，其余山西、陕西各十人。《两浙盐法志》则称，明清两代，浙江著名盐商三十五人，其中徽籍者二十八。

经营有成的，引亲荐友，徽州外出的人越来越多。明王世贞《龠州山人四部稿》中"赠程君五十序"说："徽俗十三在邑，十七在天下。"万历间歙人汪道昆《太函集》"阜成篇"也说，徽州"业贾者什七八"。

这些外出的人，有当帮工、店员、管账、代理人的，一些长袖善舞的成了富商。万历间谢肇淛《五杂俎》写道："富室之称雄者，江南则推新安，江北则推山右。新安大贾，渔盐为业，藏镪有至百万者，更有积赀达千万者。""其余二三十万者则中贾耳。"明末清初人魏禧也说："徽州富甲江南。"

徽商经营，主要是盐业、典当、木材和茶叶，其中木、茶是乡土产品，长期稳定，成为徽州商人主要的经营项目。《古今图书集成·草木典》说："大抵新安之木，松、杉为多，必栽始成材，民勤于栽植。"徽州木商，以婺源人为多，乾隆《婺源县志》说"婺源贾者率贩木"。早在南宋，建设临安宫殿和百官府邸园池，大多采用徽木。明代万历年间修坤宁、乾清二宫，婺源木商王元俊为御商，供应木材。天启修大内，崇祯造皇陵，木材也都靠徽商供应。茶业的历史也很悠久，陆羽《茶经》卷下所列茶叶产地即有宣州、歙州。注云：歙州茶"生婺源山谷"。茶业很早就对徽州经济有很大影响。唐歙州司马张途《祁门县新修阊门溪记》里说："邑之编籍民五千四百余户，其疆境亦不为小。山多而田少，水清而地沃，山且植茗，高下无遗土。千里之内，业于茶者七八矣。由是给衣食，供赋役，悉恃此。"（见《文苑英华》卷八一三）婺源的绿茶专供海外，清初从广州出口，太平军战争之后，改由上海出口。

在徽属六邑中，婺源的自然条件尤其困难。虽丰林木，而诛求无极，终有尽期。嘉靖《婺源县志·序》说：

夫婺源之为县也，山砠而弗车，水激而弗舟，故其民终岁勤动，弗获宁宇，此一疚也。地狭而弗原，土薄而弗圳，厥入既纤，仰给邻境五岭，其东北八十四滩，其西南率二而致一，此又一疚也。田苦不足，并种于山，迟其效于数十年之后，虽博犹约也。迩来诛材督檄交下，破斧缺斨，势不可极，其几童矣，此又一疚也。

又过了一百多年，到光绪县志中，不但枫香、松木"今绝少"，由于"贩木筏者皆取杉木于江右，而婺源多童。培植孔艰，戕害甚易，亦几无杉筏矣"。所以婺源木商多到云南、贵州、四川、湖南、浙西等地采伐贩运。木商虽富，婺源的乡土经济却失去了气血。

徽商对全国的经济发展都起了良好的推动作用，却无力改变徽州不利的农业生产条件。

早期的工商业者，远远没有摆脱封建宗法制度，他们在族规和传统的束缚下，把眷属留在农村老家，把在外面积攒的钱财带回来，无田地可买，就用来建造祠堂、庙宇、牌坊、文阁、住宅、园林、书院、学塾、道路、桥梁、亭子、义冢等等，甚至连官署、城池、文庙、学宫、试院、考棚等的修建也由他们捐资，以致徽州城市和农村的建筑环境达到很高的水平。但另一方面，却减缓了资本的积累增殖，阻滞了徽商进一步的发展。因此，到清代晚期，更现代化的工商业资本在沿海兴起之后，徽商就退坡了。

两晋之前，徽州土著以山越人为主，"唐黄巢之乱，中原衣冠避地于此后，或去或留，俗益尚文雅"（宋罗愿《新安志》）。至今徽州还有不少村落是唐末避乱而来的人建立的。他们带来的中原雅言文化到宋代而大盛。那时先后出了大理学家程氏兄弟和朱熹，所以徽州一向以"程朱阙里"自许。朱熹祖居婺源城内，后称"文公阙里"，他父亲游宦福建时生熹，后来熹多次返乡扫墓和讲学，在婺源影响很大。《新安文献志》甚至说徽州人"非朱子之传不敢言，非朱子之家礼不敢行"。虽然十分夸张，但理教的严酷在徽州是显而易见的，而尤以婺源为最烈。明末天启《婺源县志》桐城何如宠撰序说：

新生聚之庶，财赋人物之盛，甲于天下，诸属邑之所同也。而婺独弦歌礼乐，有邹鲁风。君子食才，小人食力，读父书而明高曾之南亩，无迁异物焉。

康熙《婺源县志》通判署县事蒋灿撰序也说："婺于新安称名邑……而又有紫阳夫子笃生其间，故其人往往淳朴温粹，蹈礼义而被诗书。"

除了大理学家之外，徽州也多文化名人。其中婺源籍的就有宋代的朱弁、胡伸、程洵、王炎、滕璘，元代的胡炳文，明代的詹希源、汪鋐、潘潢、余懋衡、何震，清代则有江永、汪绂、齐彦槐等人。据《婺源风物录》统计，自宋至清，婺源有著作一千二百七十五部刊刻行世，选入《四库全书》的有一百七十五部。

婺源的县学建立很早，宋仁宗庆历四年（1044）诏天下郡县建学，婺源县很快就建立了学宫，后来成为徽属六邑中最大的。婺源科名虽不及歙县和休宁，在宋代仍有较高成就。

但是，明代晚期以后，虽然清代初年还出了江永、戴震这样著名的学者，徽州的雅言文化，总体上是江河日下，就科名说，婺源在宋代有进士三百一十六人，明代一百一十三人，清代只有八十七人了。康熙《婺源县志》知县张绶撰序说："顾同一儒雅也，科名阀阅昔则盛而今则衰；同一愿朴也，忠孝廉节昔则多而今则少。"同志蒋灿的序慨叹婺源科名之衰：

曩者明中叶时，英贤鹊起，甲第蝉联，钟鼎旂常之伟伐，志乘不绝书。而今则世历二纪，春秋两闱，告隽者指才一二屈。名元鼎甲，皆发祥于寓公，此邦怀瑾握瑜之彦，率以牖下老，尚得有人文乎？

他对这现象的解释是百姓烧石灰坏了县城学宫龙脉。

余尝闻婺人言其县治学宫之龙，皆鼻祖于大鄣山，由水岩、石城、历角子尖再聚而后渡脉于重台石，至大小船槽二峡乃大发皇。……顾其石理缜密，可熔为灰，射利者争趋焉。地脉由此受创。

严令禁烧石灰，从明代晚期就开始了，但利之所在，杜绝实难，开山烧灰者依旧，一直到清朝中叶，这场"保龙"之争还没有了结。风水迷信徒然扼杀经济的发展，而无补于雅言文化的衰退。

雅言文化衰落的真实原因恰恰在于徽商的繁荣。徽州的人口外流并且人才转向商业，学术和科名自然会失去过去的辉煌。顾炎武在《肇域志》中说徽州，"贾人娶妇数月则外出，或数十年，至有父子邂逅不相识者"。而徽州人一般在二十一二岁娶妻。明万历间次辅歙人许国（1527—1596）父亲是茶商，他在给母亲写的行状里说："先府君贾吴中，率三数年或八九年一归。归席未暖复出。"这种情况一直延续到清末。近人胡适在《四十自述》中写得最明白：

我们徽州人通常是在十一二岁便到城市里去学生意，最初多半是在自家长辈或亲戚的店铺里当学徒。在历时三年的学徒期间，他们是没有薪金的。其后稍有报酬，直至学徒期满。至二十一二岁时，他们可以享有带薪婚假三个月，还乡结婚。婚假期满，他们又只身返回原来的店铺，继续经商。自此以后，他们每三年便有三个月的带薪假期，返乡探亲。所以徽州人有句土语，叫作"一世夫妻三年半"。

既然"十室九商，商必外出"，一是人才外流，二是人才转向商业，则徽州学术、科名的没落就不可避免了。

另一方面，就在学术、科名不景气的情况下，施于十一二岁之前的儿童的初级蒙学却大大发达起来，也就是文化大大地普及了。这是因为，经商比之农耕，需要更多的读、写、运算等能力和应对修养，徽商富有之后，回馈故里，除了修建学宫和少数书院之外，便是建立大量的社学、祠学、私塾等等，并且资助族中子弟读书。所以《休宁县志》里说，明清两朝，"自井邑、田野以至远山深谷，居民之处，莫不有学、有师、有书史之藏"。嘉靖《婺源县志》则说本邑"十户之村，不废诵读"。徽州六邑，在康熙年间共有社学四百六十二所，其中婺源有一百四十所。此外当然还有大量的祠塾和私塾等等。初等教育的普及，推动了社会一般文化水平的提高。

明代晚期，由于商业资本的发展，在一些城镇，市井文化繁盛起来。徽商往来于这些城镇，熟悉市井文化，自然会把它带到故乡去。市井文化的一个重要特点是重新辨正"士农工商"的四民观，也就是为商人争社会地位。嘉靖进士汪尚宁，在为徽商汪远写的《像赞》（见明隆庆刻本休宁《汪氏统宗谱》）里说：

古者四民不分，故傅岩鱼盐中，良弼师保寓焉，贾何后于士哉？……故业儒服贾各随其矩，而事道亦相为通。人之自律其身，亦何艰于业哉？

这位作者官至都察院右副都御史，竟如此直接地批判传统儒家的四民观。到清末，翰林许承尧著《歙事闲谭》，径直说："商居四民之末，徽俗殊不然。"可见新的四民观在徽州已经确立。

市井文化的另一个特点是炫富。乾隆《婺源县志》知府何达善"序"说到歙县、休宁的人文："歙休多巨贾，豪于财，好言礼文，以富相耀，虽多散处吴楚间而家于乡者半亦习奢尚气。"这种文化特点已经由徽商带回到故乡来了。

市井文化开拓了新的视野，改变了人们的价值观，在一些方面突破了理学的束缚。男女情爱、商贾辛劳、市民生活都进了他们的兴趣领域，成了戏剧、版画、建筑装饰等的重要题材。

市井文化在徽州的主要代表是戏剧和雕版印刷。它们促进了市井文化向雅言文化渗透，也向民俗文化渗透，给它们以新的题材和思想。

市井文化的发展也改变了农村的风尚习惯。顾炎武在《天下郡国利病书》中引《歙县风土论》说，早在明代正德末、嘉靖初，"商贾既多，土田不重……纷华染矣，靡汰臻矣"，指出风俗之变确为"商贾既多"。康熙丁未进士张英撰《恒产琐言》中说："天下惟山右新安人善于贸易，彼性至悭吝。"到清末许承尧著《歙事闲谭》则说，徽人的生活"比者亦渐增饰矣"！

大批徽商眷属住在农村，过着寄生性的富裕而悠闲的生活，大大促进了民俗文化的繁荣。社火、灯会、狮子、拜月、酬神、傩舞、傩戏等等都很热闹，四季不断。与手工业经济相结合的则有木雕、石雕、砖雕、雕砚、墨模、盆景、刻书等等，也都是为富裕人家服务的。

民俗文化中还有医卜星相。风水堪舆术在徽州很盛行，尤其是婺源县。《中国风水》一书里统计了明清时代的风水名家，共计二十六人，徽籍者十二人，而婺源占九人。游朝宗、游克敬、江仕从等三人还参加过明初天寿山陵地的勘察，受到褒奖。堪舆风水对徽属各邑的聚落和建筑的一些方面很有影响。

学术、科名成绩下降，初级教育普及，民俗文化繁荣，市井文化兴起，这就是明清时期包括婺源在内的徽州文化的一般情况。

婺源，乃至徽州各地，就在这样的经济、文化背景下建造了大量的村落。既有建筑，也有园林。

徽人因农耕不能自给，不得已外出经营。不论是稍有裕蓄还是致富巨万，都会在宗族势力和传统习俗的约束下回馈故里，从事兴造。由于婺源的农村建设主要靠徽商的回馈，而徽商又主要出自农业不能自给的穷困山区，所以，婺源的北乡和东乡，山高谷深，而村落很漂亮；西乡多平川，农业尚可活口，村落反倒逊色。

然而，稍加考察，可见从明晚期到清晚期，三百年上下的徽州乡土建设史，是一部徽州人民不屈不挠，顽强地与命运抗争的悲壮的史诗。

嘉靖进士汪道昆《太函集》中《阜成篇》说："新安多世家强盛，其居室大抵务壮丽。"又说："春秋肸飨之典所在多有，而吾郡为盛郡……其中若寝、若祠、若庙者无虑数十百千。"到了明清易代之际，遭到一次大破坏。光绪《婺源县志·建置志》引康熙《县志》中张绶所写的"跋"说："婺邑草创于开元，历宋元明而规模大备，鼎革之初，半遭焚毁。修葺未毕闽变又复见告。故今之公署、城垣、泮宫、营垒往往多创建也。"数十年之后，徽州从废墟中重建。该《建置志》又引康熙"邑志"蒋灿文："今民家作室，犹必高其垣墉，敞其堂室，邃其房闼，易其道路。其他宾祭之所，讲习之堂，水旱潴泄之具，莫不次第备兴。"不料这一次重建到太平军战争时又一次遭到更加酷烈的破坏。婺源是太平军战争最长期反复的地区之一。从咸丰五年（1855）太平军犯婺源，到同治元年（1862）左宗棠入婺源，其间"焚民居三十余家""焚杀甚众""焚县治及民居数百家""民居焚毁殆尽"之类的记载，在县志中连篇累牍。曾国藩上同治奏折说："徽池宁国等属，黄茅白骨，或竟日不逢一人。"（《奏稿》卷二一）"皖南及江南各属，市人肉以相食，或数十里野无耕种，村无炊烟。"（《奏稿》卷二四）这里当然有为邀功而夸大的成分，但太平军侍王李世贤在同治二年（1863）一封致部下信中也说到了"众兄弟杀人放火"的事实。（见《太平天国史料译丛》，33—34页）另一方面，官军的焚掠杀戮甚至更加残酷。战争亲历者李圭在《思痛记》中说："官军败贼及克复贼所据城池后，其烧杀劫夺之惨，实较贼为尤甚，此不可不知也。"又说："至官军一面，则溃败后之虏掠，或战胜后之焚杀，尤属耳不忍闻，目不忍睹，其惨毒实较贼又有过之无不及。"道光五年（1825），祁门人口四十七万零二百七十九，到同治十年（1871）只有十万零二百四十九，减少百分之七十九之多。黟县人口，嘉庆十五年（1810）为二十四万六千四百七十八，同治六年（1867）为十五万五千四百五十五，减少百分之三十七。歙县人口，道光年间（1821—1850）为六十一万七千一百一十一，同治年间（1862—1874）为三十万九千六百零四，减少百分之五十。绩溪人口，嘉庆九年（1804）为十九万三千一百六十一，宣统二年（1910）为九万三千零三十七，减少百分之五十二。婺源情况必大致如此。

经过这样惨重的破坏，到了清末，翰林许承尧著《歙事闲谭》里写道：徽州"乡村如星列棋布，凡五里十里，遥望粉墙矗矗，鸳瓦鳞鳞，棹楔峥嵘，鸱吻耸拔，宛如城廓，殊足观也"。徽州人又一次从废墟中重建了家乡。

虽然徽州地理偏僻，风俗近古，但屡经变故，明代遗构已经寥寥无几，很足惋惜。然而，到清代末年，乡土建设的光辉成就，则是徽州人民旺盛的生命力、坚毅的意志力的纪念碑，能使人肃然感奋不已。

乡土建筑的几毁几兴，都靠乡人自力，徽商捐输。康熙《徽州府志》总纂、休宁人赵吉士在府志《尚义》门前题记中说：

吾乡之人，俭而好礼，吝啬而负气。其丰厚之夫，家资累万，尝垂老不御绢帛。敝衣结鹑，出门千里，履草屩，襆被自携焉。……然急公趋义，或输边储，或建官廨，或筑城隍，或赈饥恤难，或学田、道路、山桥、水堰之属，且输金千万而不惜。甚至赤贫之士，黾勉积蓄十数年而一旦倾囊为之。

县志、府志里，上自县署、学宫、城墙，下至茶亭、板桥，莫不由商而致富的或农而有志的出资出力修建。有一些事迹非常动人。

可惜，徽商虽然有力兴建一些房屋，却无力改变徽州不利于农业的自然条件。因此，在徽州出现了一个奇异的对比，正如康熙《婺源县志》张绶的"序"所说，"其土田瘠硗而迫隘，其都聚稠密而整齐"。所以，在小农经济还占主导地位的时代，一旦商业受挫，这些乡土建设不但难以为继，连维修已有的房屋都不可能做到，村子就难免败落。

徽州的村落，几兴几踬，到20世纪中叶，一场激烈的社会动荡，终于结束了私营商业的历史。徽商故乡的农村失去了外来的经济支援，一落千丈。同时，一向管理着血缘村落的公众事务的宗族组织被粉碎。数百年来处于下层的"伙计""客户"，一向靠租佃和为富户服务为生的"佃仆"，翻身掌握了政权。新的当权者缺少必要的文化素养，对原来的村落建设既不理解，也没有感情，甚至会有点憎恶。因此，村落的公共设施和公共建筑遭到破坏，传统的有关维护村落的完整、整齐、卫生的制度也被废除。等到"文化大革命"一发动，这种破坏就空前酷烈。以致我们现在所见的婺源村落，都不过是劫后残余。

Glimpses of Wuyuan

Wuyuan County is now located in the northeast of Jiangxi Province, bordering Anhui to the north and Zhejiang to the east — a place where "a rooster's crow wakes three provinces." However, over half a century ago, it was long one of the six counties of Huizhou, belonging to the same Huizhou cultural circle as Shexian, Yixian, Jixi, Qimen, and Xiuning.

Most of Wuyuan's territory was originally within Xiuning, with a small part in Dongping, Jiangxi. In the 24th year of Tang Kaiyuan (736), due to local unrest, the county was established in the 28th year (740) at the request of local gentry, under Shezhou. The county seat was initially at today's Qinghua Town, later moved to Xiangao Town (today's Ziyang Town) due to military insubordination. The county territory corresponds to the Wunü star constellation, so the river is called Wu River and the county Wuyuan.

Having shared the same administrative division for over a thousand years, Wuyuan, together with the other five Huizhou counties, jointly created the brilliant Huizhou culture and participated, under the name of "Huizhou merchants," in the great development of Chinese commercial capital from the late Ming to the Qing dynasty. Wuyuan's history and culture are consistent with those of Huizhou as a whole.

However, due to geographical differences, Wuyuan's history and culture also differ somewhat from the other five counties. To Wuyuan's northeast, between it and Xiuning and Qimen, lie the Dazhang Mountains and Zhe Ridge. In the Spring and Autumn period, these formed the border between Wu and Chu states. The other five counties were Wu territory, while Wuyuan was Chu territory. Song dynasty poet Quan Bangyan wrote of crossing Zhe Ridge: "Towering over Wu, stretching to Chu's tail." A 1.7-meter stone stele still stands on the ridge, carved in clerical script with "Wu-Chu Divide," erected during the Kangxi period.

With these two mountain ranges as watersheds, Wuyuan and Qimen's water systems flow into Poyang Lake and then the Yangtze, while the other counties' waters flow via the Xin'an River to the Qiantang River. Different water systems meant different external contacts, especially significant in commercial capital development where water transport mattered. Thus, Wuyuan's culture, compared to other counties, has minor differences within major similarities — especially in architecture. Wuyuan is a sub-cultural circle within the southern Anhui (Huizhou) architectural cultural circle.

Huizhou has many mountains and little arable land; farming cannot sustain itself, so men had to go out to "do business everywhere." Kangxi's "Huizhou Prefecture Annals" records a late Ming memorial by Wang Wei: "Huizhou lies among ten thousand mountains, narrow land with dense population, farming yields less than a third of needs, even in good years it relies on Jiang and Chu for food. … The people of the world depend on farming, Huizhou people depend on commerce. And commerce to Huizhou has two routes: one from Raozhou, Po, Fu; one from Zhejiang's Hang, Yan — all adjacent, with narrow streams, small boats like leaves, following one after another, day and night without ceasing." The result of depending on commerce was that after the Ming Jiajing period, "Huizhou merchants spread everywhere," giving rise to the saying "no Huizhou merchants, no town." Guangxu's "Lianghuai Salt Law Annals · Biographies" statistics show that from Jiajing to Qianlong, of 80 famous non-native merchants in Yangzhou, 60 were Huizhou merchants, with Shanxi and Shaanxi having 10 each. "Liangzhe Salt Law Annals" states that in Ming and Qing, of 35 famous Zhejiang salt merchants, 28 were Huizhou natives.

Successful merchants brought relatives and friends, and more and more Huizhou people went out. Ming Wang Shizhen's "Yuezhou Shanren Sibugao" in "Preface to Cheng Jun's Fiftieth Birthday" says: "Huizhou custom: thirteen in the county, seventeen in the world." Wanli period Shexian native Wang Daokun's "Taihan Ji" "Fucheng Chapter" also says Huizhou "seven or eight out of ten are merchants."

Those who went out worked as helpers, clerks, accountants, agents; some skilled ones became wealthy merchants. Wanli period Xie Zhaozhe's "Wuzazu" wrote: "Among wealthy households, the south promotes Xin'an, the north promotes Shanxi. Xin'an's great merchants deal in fish and salt, with hoarded silver reaching millions, some tens of millions." "Those with two or three hundred thousand are medium merchants." Late Ming early Qing Wei Xi also said: "Huizhou is the wealthiest in Jiangnan."

Huizhou merchants mainly dealt in salt, pawnbroking, timber, and tea — timber and tea being local products, long-term stable, becoming their main business. "Gujin Tushu Jicheng · Caomu Dian" says: "Generally Xin'an's timber is mostly pine and fir, must be planted to mature, people diligently plant." Huizhou timber merchants were mostly Wuyuan people; Qianlong's "Wuyuan County Annals" says "Wuyuan merchants mostly trade timber." As early as Southern Song, construction of Lin'an palaces and government gardens mostly used Huizhou timber. In Ming Wanli, repairing Kunning and Qianqing palaces, Wuyuan timber merchant Wang Yuanjun was imperial supplier. Tianqi palace repairs and Chongqing imperial mausoleum construction also relied on Huizhou merchants. Tea has a long history; Lu Yu's "Tea Classic" lists Xuanzhou and Shezhou as tea-producing areas, noting Shezhou tea "grows in Wuyuan valleys." Tea greatly influenced Huizhou economy early on. Tang Shezhou Sima Zhang Tu's "Qimen County Newly Repaired Changmen Stream Record" says: "The county has over 5,400 registered households, territory not small. Many mountains, little farmland, clear water fertile soil, mountains planted with tea, no land wasted. Within a thousand li, seven or eight out of ten work in tea. Food, clothing, taxes all depend on it." (See "Wenyuan Yinghua" vol. 813) Wuyuan green tea was exclusively for export, initially from Guangzhou in early Qing, then from Shanghai after the Taiping Rebellion.

Among the six Huizhou counties, Wuyuan's natural conditions were especially difficult. Though rich in forests, relentless exploitation had limits. Jiajing's "Wuyuan County Annals · Preface" says:

Wuyuan as a county: mountainous without carts, rapid waters without boats, so people work year-round without rest — one hardship. Narrow land without plains, thin soil without irrigation, yields meager, relying on neighboring five ridges; northeast has 84 shoals, southwest requires two trips for one result — another hardship. Farmland insufficient, planting on mountains, effects delayed decades, though broad still meager. Recently timber-cutting orders come one after another, axes broken, situation extreme, mountains nearly bare — another hardship.

Over a hundred years later, in Guangxu county annals, not only maple and pine "now extremely rare," but because "timber rafters all take fir from Jiangxi, Wuyuan is mostly bare. Cultivation difficult, destruction easy, almost no fir rafts left." So Wuyuan timber merchants went to Yunnan, Guizhou, Sichuan, Hunan, western Zhejiang to log and trade. Though timber merchants grew rich, Wuyuan's local economy lost its vitality.

Huizhou merchants promoted national economic development, but could not change Huizhou's unfavorable agricultural conditions.

Early industrial and commercial merchants, far from escaping feudal patriarchal systems, kept families in rural homes under clan rules and traditions, bringing accumulated wealth back. With no farmland to buy, they built ancestral halls, temples, memorial arches, literary pavilions, residences, gardens, academies, schools, roads, bridges, pavilions, charity cemeteries — even government offices, city walls, Confucian temples, schools, examination halls were funded by them, raising Huizhou's urban and rural architectural environment to high levels. But on the other hand, this slowed capital accumulation and hindered further merchant development. Thus, by late Qing, when more modern industrial and commercial capital rose along the coast, Huizhou merchants declined.

Before the Two Jin dynasties, Huizhou's natives were mainly Shanyue people. "After Tang Huang Chao's rebellion, Central Plains scholars took refuge here, some leaving some staying, customs increasingly refined" (Song Luo Yuan's "Xin'an Annals"). Many Huizhou villages were founded by those fleeing late Tang chaos. They brought Central Plains scholarly culture that flourished in Song, producing great Neo-Confucianists Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi, so Huizhou prided itself as "Cheng-Zhu's hometown." Zhu Xi's ancestral home was in Wuyuan city, later called "Wengong's hometown"; his father, serving in Fujian, gave birth to Xi, who later returned many times to sweep graves and lecture, greatly influencing Wuyuan. "Xin'an Literature Annals" even says Huizhou people "dare not speak without Zhu Xi's tradition, dare not act without Zhu Xi's family rites." Though exaggerated, the severity of Neo-Confucian teaching in Huizhou is obvious, especially in Wuyuan. Late Ming Tianqi "Wuyuan County Annals" preface by Tongcheng He Ruchong says:

The abundance of population, wealth, and talent is foremost under heaven, common to all counties. But Wuyuan alone has stringed instruments and rites, with Zou-Lu style. Gentlemen value talent, commoners value labor, reading fathers' books and knowing ancestors' fields, no foreign things.

Kangxi "Wuyuan County Annals" preface by Tongpan (acting magistrate) Jiang Can also says: "Wuyuan is a famous county in Xin'an … with Master Ziyang born here, so its people are often simple and gentle, following rites and immersed in books."

Besides great Neo-Confucianists, Huizhou produced many cultural figures. Wuyuan natives include Song's Zhu Bian, Hu Shen, Cheng Xun, Wang Yan, Teng Lin; Yuan's Hu Bingwen; Ming's Zhan Xiyuan, Wang Hong, Pan Huang, Yu Maoheng, He Zhen; Qing's Jiang Yong, Wang Fu, Qi Yanhuai. According to "Wuyuan Scenery Records," from Song to Qing, Wuyuan had 1,275 published works, 175 selected into "Siku Quanshu."

Wuyuan's county school was established early; in Song Renzong Qingli 4th year (1044), the emperor ordered all counties to build schools, and Wuyuan soon established a school, later the largest among six Huizhou counties. Though Wuyuan's examination success didn't match Shexian and Xiuning, it achieved highly in Song.

However, after late Ming, though early Qing still produced famous scholars like Jiang Yong and Dai Zhen, Huizhou's scholarly culture generally declined. In examination success, Wuyuan had 316 jinshi in Song, 113 in Ming, only 87 in Qing. Kangxi "Wuyuan County Annals" preface by Magistrate Zhang Shou says: "Though equally scholarly, examination success was then prosperous now declining; though equally simple, loyalty and filial piety were then many now few." Fellow preface by Jiang Can laments Wuyuan's decline:

In mid-Ming, talents arose like magpies, examination success continuous, great achievements recorded in annals. Now two generations later, in spring and autumn examinations, only one or two succeed. Top graduates all from outsiders; local talents with jade in hand grow old at home — is there still culture?

His explanation was that people burning lime damaged the county school's "dragon vein."

I've heard Wuyuan people say the county school's dragon originates from Dazhang Mountain, via Shuiyan, Shicheng, Lijiaozijian, gathering again at Chongtaishi, then greatly flourishing at Dachuan and Xiaochuan gorges. … Its stone is fine, can be melted into lime, profit-seekers rush there. The earth's vein is thus damaged.

Strict bans on lime burning began in late Ming, but with profit at stake, enforcement was difficult; mountain burning continued, and this "dragon protection" dispute lasted until mid-Qing. Fengxi superstition merely stifled economic development without helping scholarly culture's decline.

The real cause of scholarly decline was precisely Huizhou merchants' prosperity. With population outflow and talent转向 commerce, academic and examination success naturally lost past glory. Gu Yanwu's "Zhaoyu Zhi" says of Huizhou: "Merchants marry and go out for months, sometimes decades, even father and son meeting without recognizing each other." Huizhou people generally married at 21-22. Ming Wanli Grand Secretary Shexian native Xu Guo (1527-1596), whose father was a tea merchant, wrote in his mother's biography: "My father did business in Wuzhong, returning every three or eight or nine years. Hardly settled before leaving again." This continued until late Qing. Modern Hu Shi wrote most clearly in "My Forty Years":

We Huizhou people usually go to cities to learn business at 11 or 12, initially as apprentices in relatives' shops. During three-year apprenticeship, no salary. Then small pay until completion. At 21-22, they get three months paid marriage leave to return home and marry. After marriage, they return alone to continue business. Thereafter, every three years they get three months paid leave to visit home. So Huizhou has a saying: "a lifetime of marriage, three and a half years."

Since "nine out of ten rooms are merchants, merchants must go out" — first talent outflow, second talent转向 commerce — Huizhou's academic and examination decline was inevitable.

On the other hand, while academic and examination success declined, primary education for children before 11-12 greatly developed, meaning culture greatly spread. This was because commerce, compared to farming, required more reading, writing, calculation, and social skills. After growing rich, Huizhou merchants, besides building schools and academies, established many community schools, clan schools, private schools, and funded clan children's education. So "Xiuning County Annals" says in Ming and Qing, "from towns and fields to remote mountains and valleys, wherever people live, there are schools, teachers, and books." Jiajing "Wuyuan County Annals" says the county "even villages of ten households don't abandon reading." The six Huizhou counties had 462 community schools in Kangxi, 140 in Wuyuan. Plus many clan and private schools. Primary education普及 raised general cultural levels.

In late Ming, due to commercial capital development, urban culture flourished in some towns. Huizhou merchants, familiar with urban culture, naturally brought it home. An important feature of urban culture was re-evaluating the "scholar-farmer-artisan-merchant" hierarchy, asserting merchants' social status. Jiajing jinshi Wang Shangning, in "Portrait Eulogy" for Huizhou merchant Wang Yuan (Ming Longqing edition Xiuning "Wang Clan Genealogy") wrote:

In ancient times the four occupations weren't separated, so among salt and fish merchants were great ministers and teachers — why should merchants rank after scholars? … Thus scholarship and commerce each follow their rules, and the Way connects them. A person's self-discipline, what difficulty in occupation?

This author, reaching Censorate Vice Censor-in-Chief, so directly criticized traditional Confucian hierarchy. By late Qing, Hanlin Xu Chengyao's "Sheshi Xiantan" plainly said: "Merchants rank last among four occupations, but Huizhou custom is different."可见 new hierarchy was established in Huizhou.

Another feature of urban culture was flaunting wealth. Qianlong "Wuyuan County Annals" preface by Prefect He Dashan says of Shexian and Xiuning: "She and Xiu have many great merchants, proud of wealth, fond of rites and culture, showing off wealth; though many live in Wu and Chu, those at home are also extravagant and ambitious." This cultural feature was brought home by Huizhou merchants.

Urban culture opened new horizons, changed values, breaking Neo-Confucian constraints in some ways. Love between men and women, merchant hardship, urban life entered their interests, becoming important themes in drama, woodblock prints, architectural decoration.

Urban culture's main representatives in Huizhou were drama and woodblock printing. They promoted urban culture's penetration into both scholarly and folk culture, giving them new themes and ideas.

Urban culture also changed rural customs. Gu Yanwu's "Tianxia Junguo Libingshu" quotes "Shexian Fengtu Lun" saying as early as Ming Zhengde-Jiajing, "with many merchants, farmland not valued … luxury染, extravagance reached," noting custom change确为 "many merchants." Kangxi Dingwei jinshi Zhang Ying's "Hengchan Suoyan" says: "Only Shanxi and Xin'an people are good at trade, their nature most stingy." By late Qing Xu Chengyao's "Sheshi Xiantan" says Huizhou people's lives "are increasingly decorated"!

Large numbers of Huizhou merchant families lived in rural areas, leading parasitic wealthy leisurely lives, greatly promoting folk culture prosperity. Shehuo, lantern festivals, lion dances, moon worship, god offerings, Nuo dances, Nuo dramas were all lively, year-round. Combined with handicraft economy were wood carving, stone carving, brick carving, inkstone carving, ink molds, bonsai, book engraving — all serving wealthy families.

Folk culture also included medicine, divination, astrology. Fengshui (geomancy) was very popular in Huizhou, especially Wuyuan. "Chinese Fengshui" statistics show 26 famous Ming-Qing fengshui masters, 12 Huizhou natives, 9 from Wuyuan. You Chaozong, You Kejing, Jiang Shicong even participated in early Ming Tianshou Mountain mausoleum site survey, receiving praise. Fengshui influenced settlement and architecture in Huizhou counties.

Academic and examination decline, primary education普及, folk culture prosperity, urban culture rise — this was the general situation of Huizhou culture including Wuyuan in Ming-Qing.

Wuyuan, and Huizhou generally, built numerous villages under such economic and cultural backgrounds — both architecture and gardens.

Huizhou people, unable to sustain themselves by farming, had to go out to do business. Whether modestly well-off or extremely wealthy, under clan power and traditional customs they回馈 hometown with construction. Since Wuyuan's rural construction mainly relied on Huizhou merchants'回馈, and merchants mainly came from agriculturally unable poor mountain areas, Wuyuan's north and east townships, with high mountains and deep valleys, have beautiful villages; west townships, with plains and viable agriculture, have less impressive villages.

However, close examination reveals that from late Ming to late Qing, three centuries of Huizhou rural construction history is an epic of Huizhou people's unyielding, tenacious struggle against fate.

Jiajing jinshi Wang Daokun's "Taihan Ji" "Fucheng Chapter" says: "Xin'an has many powerful families, their residences generally strive for magnificence." Also: "Spring and autumn sacrifice ceremonies everywhere, our county most prosperous … among them bedrooms, ancestral halls, temples number in the tens of hundreds." At the Ming-Qing transition, great destruction occurred. Guangxu "Wuyuan County Annals · Construction" quotes Kangxi "County Annals" Zhang Shou's postscript: "Wuyuan founded in Kaiyuan, through Song Yuan Ming规模 complete, at dynasty change half burned. Repairs unfinished before Fujian rebellion again. So today's government offices, city walls, school, barracks are mostly newly built." Decades later, Huizhou rebuilt from ruins. The "Construction" also quotes Kangxi county annals Jiang Can: "Today people building homes still must high walls, spacious halls, deep rooms, good roads. Other guest-sacrifice places, lecture halls, water storage-drainage facilities, all built in order." Unexpectedly, this reconstruction suffered even more severe destruction during the Taiping Rebellion. Wuyuan was one of the longest-contested areas. From Xianfeng 5 (1855) Taiping troops entering Wuyuan to Tongzhi 1 (1862) Zuo Zongtang entering, records of "burning 30+ homes," "killing many," "burning county office and hundreds of homes," "homes completely burned" fill the county annals. Zeng Guofan's Tongzhi memorial says: "Hui, Chi, Ningguo etc., yellow grass white bones, sometimes no one seen all day." ("Memorials" vol. 21) "Southern Anhui and Jiangnan, people eating human flesh, sometimes tens of li no farming, villages no smoke." ("Memorials" vol. 24) Though exaggerated for merit, Taiping Prince Li Shixian's 1863 letter to subordinates also mentions "brothers killing and setting fires." (See "Taiping Heavenly Kingdom Historical Materials Translation," pp. 33-34) On the other hand, government troops' burning and killing were even crueler. War survivor Li Gui's "Sitong Ji" says: "After government troops defeat rebels and recapture cities, their burning, killing, looting is actually worse than rebels — this must be known." Also: "As for government troops, looting after defeat or burning after victory, especially unbearable to hear and see, their cruelty surpasses rebels." In Daoguang 5 (1825), Qimen population 470,279; by Tongzhi 10 (1871) only 100,249, a 79% decrease. Yixian population: Jiaqing 15 (1810) 246,478; Tongzhi 6 (1867) 155,455, 37% decrease. Shexian population: Daoguang (1821-1850) 617,111; Tongzhi (1862-1874) 309,604, 50% decrease. Jixi population: Jiaqing 9 (1804) 193,161; Xuantong 2 (1910) 93,037, 52% decrease. Wuyuan's situation must be similar.

After such severe destruction, by late Qing, Hanlin Xu Chengyao's "Sheshi Xiantan" wrote: Huizhou "villages like stars on a chessboard, every five or ten li, from afar white walls standing, mandarin duck tiles overlapping, gate towers towering, owl ornaments rising, like city walls, quite a sight." Huizhou people once again rebuilt their hometown from ruins.

Though Huizhou is geographically remote with ancient customs, after repeated upheavals, Ming dynasty structures are few, regrettably. However, by late Qing, the brilliant achievements of rural construction are monuments to Huizhou people's vigorous vitality and firm will, inspiring awe and admiration.

Rural architecture's repeated destruction and revival all relied on local self-reliance and Huizhou merchants' donations. Kangxi "Huizhou Prefecture Annals" chief compiler, Xiuning native Zhao Jishi, wrote in the preface to "Shangyi" (Righteous Deeds):

Our townspeople are frugal and fond of rites, stingy yet spirited. Wealthy men with accumulated wealth often don't wear silk in old age. Worn clothes, traveling a thousand li in straw sandals, carrying their own bedding. … Yet for public good — border supplies, government offices, city walls, famine relief, school land, roads, mountain bridges, water dams — they donate millions without regret. Even the poor, saving for over a decade, give all at once.

County and prefecture annals record everything from county offices, schools, city walls to tea pavilions and small bridges, all built by wealthy merchants or aspiring farmers. Some stories are very moving.

Unfortunately, though Huizhou merchants could build houses, they couldn't change Huizhou's unfavorable agricultural natural conditions. Thus, a strange contrast appeared in Huizhou, as Kangxi "Wuyuan County Annals" Zhang Shou's preface says: "its farmland barren and narrow, its settlements dense and orderly." So, in the era of small-scale peasant economy dominance, once commerce suffered setbacks, these rural constructions not only couldn't continue, but even maintaining existing houses became impossible, and villages inevitably declined.

Huizhou villages, repeatedly rising and falling, by mid-20th century, a fierce social upheaval finally ended private commerce history. Huizhou merchants' hometown rural areas lost external economic support, plummeting. Meanwhile, clan organizations that had managed blood-relation village public affairs were shattered. For centuries lower-class "helpers," "clients," and "tenant servants" who lived by renting and serving wealthy families rose to power. New rulers lacked necessary cultural素养, neither understanding nor feeling for original village construction, even somewhat resentful. Thus, village public facilities and buildings were destroyed, traditional systems for maintaining village integrity, order, and hygiene abolished. When the Cultural Revolution began, destruction was unprecedentedly severe. So the Wuyuan villages we see today are but remnants after catastrophe.

sections.name: 清华彩虹
sections.content_zh:
清华彩虹

从建筑的角度看，清华镇最值得骄傲的是它的两座桥，一座是西头的彩虹桥，通景德镇的大路所经，一座是东北角的聚星桥，通徽州府的大路所经，都是石墩木梁的风雨桥，另外至少还有四条板凳桥。1985年，修通了往沱川的公路，造了一座钢筋水泥的公路桥之后，就拆了聚星桥，板凳桥也不再架设，现在只剩下彩虹桥了。彩虹桥在村西将近一百米，在婺水向北环弯的地方，走向东西。它长一百四十米，有四个石砌的桥墩，五个桥洞。桥墩横长十三点八米，宽七米，迎上流作分水（燕嘴）。桥洞跨度大小不等，在十二米上下。每洞架四根大木梁，上面密铺木枋，形成桥面。桥上造廊，两坡顶。位于洞上的段落跨度小，只有四点五米，墩上的段落跨度大，有十一点五米，左右都凸出。因此墩上的和桥上的廊子结构分开，各自独立。而且墩上的廊，屋脊明显高于洞上的，外观轮廓有起有伏，产生了节奏感。桥内的空间也因宽窄的变化而产生了节奏感。墩上的廊，向北的凸出比较大，形成完整的小空间，摆着石桌石凳。桥的两侧通长设栏杆凳，倚栏眺望，南面正对锦屏似的五老峰和云雾缭绕的茱岭。东北烟波连天，渔舟在板桥下悠然漂过，左岸层层山岗，右岸竹丛掩映着村落，白粉墙在青翠的竹叶间闪闪而出。走到桥西端，前面山岗顶上，"文化大革命"前曾经巍然矗立着十几米高的文笔。东端第二个桥墩的南端，也就是它的燕嘴上，有过一座经幢，它北面的凸间里，有一座神橱，供着三个神位，正中是"治水有功大禹王"，左右两侧分别是"募化僧人胡济祥"和"创始理首胡永班"。楹联"两水夹明镜，双桥落彩虹"，摘自李白的诗，横批"长虹卧波"。楹联大约并非原制。这个桥墩在1983年被洪水冲垮，1986年8月修复，神橱是重建的，木构的小建筑，有翘得很高的翼角，挂落做成水波和红太阳。经幢在"文化大革命"时被拆除了，现在在村里古街西部的转弯处，原仁德堂遗址边，离通往彩虹桥的小巷口（也许是古方头巷）大约三十米，地上横躺着一段残损了的经幢，灰白色大理石的，八边形，直径五十厘米左右，每面相间刻着"南无阿弥陀佛"六个字和一个佛龛。很可能，这就是原来桥墩上那个经幢的残石。

彩虹桥东端南侧，水边有一块石矶，摩岩刻"小西湖"三字，传说是明代嘉靖年间吴派篆刻家文彭和徽派篆刻家何震到这里赏玩山水时题下的，有款。嘉庆二十二年（1817）婺源知县觉罗长庚（满人）曾重刻加深。矶上另有一首刻诗是齐彦槐写的："睢阳庙外一灯孤，五老峰前飞夜乌。绝好荷花无一柄，月明空照小西湖。"仿佛对眼前景致很有点凄凉的感慨。

所以，彩虹桥头有一副楹联，写的是："胜地著华川爱此间长桥卧波五峰立极；治时兴古镇尝当年文彭篆字彦槐对诗。"桥廊建筑十分简洁，做法和去甲路村中途的凉亭以及思溪村的风雨桥相同。构件方正平直，斩截整齐，结构和构造全部简单明了，榫卯搭接一清二楚，没有多余的东西，完全合乎严谨而简洁的理性要求。施工制作也都经济方便。同时，每个构件本身的长、宽、厚尺寸之间，构件与构件之间，以及构件与整体之间，配合得非常和谐匀称。这个桥廊建筑的结构美，完全不同于婺源县住宅和宗祠之类中常见的装饰美。宗祠中虽然也可以见到很动人的结构美，但它们总还有装饰，还有刻意的加工，而彩虹桥则是纯粹的素净白描，天然自如。在一个惯于往建筑上堆砌装饰的地区，同时在桥梁和凉亭上还有这样一种工艺传统，或许是因为有两种工匠，造房子的和造桥的。不过这只是猜测，并没有有力的证据。

彩虹桥离清华镇居民生活区比较远，所以没有成为日常的交往中心。据说到了炎热的夏季，许多居民到桥上乘凉避暑，晚风吹来，带着水上的清爽气，消去一身汗热。没有蚊虫，只见萤火飘忽，一明一灭，蒲扇不举，烟斗不燃，老人们半睡半醒，喃喃着含糊的话。这时月上东山，水中闪烁着鱼鳞似的银光，丝丝波影，像颤动的水藻。这就是清华八景之一"藻潭浸月"。

桥的东端，守桥人小屋的墙上嵌着一块1986年刻的石碑，碑文说桥始建于唐代。《婺源风物录》说它始建于宋代。但《清华胡氏仁德堂世谱》和乾隆《婺源县志》都分明记载它建于清代乾隆年间。《世谱》说：

彩虹桥在方头溪，原胡仁德孙建木桥，乾隆庚寅，德公裔宏鸿，即林坑巷庵僧济祥与里人永班募捐，创建石垛，架亭设茶其上，至今并设祀祭之。

这济祥和永班的神位就在桥上大禹神位的左右。乾隆《婺源县志·义行》记得更加生动：

胡班（按：无永字），清华人，家于里之方头溪。溪当两源之冲，架木桥通行旅，山雨暴涨，则患叵测。班故贫，幼负贩供亲甘旨。尝夏月桥圮，阻不得归，誓成此桥，以济众危。自是修葺绋缡、视如己急。遇霜雪夜，辄披衣起，扫除之。如是者历二十六年。既又议易木以石，众皆首肯，推为部署，中遭洪水冲决，复督其成。

本志并说胡班是乾隆时人。《世谱》中说的胡仁德，是胡从政（1379—1458）、胡礼道（1385—1457）兄弟二人的合称，他们热心乡土建设，可能有人把胡仁德误认为仁德堂始祖胡学了。

清华镇东北下市的聚星桥，走向为西南至东北，《世谱》也有记载：

聚星桥，京省通津。五显庙头陀隐谷募建，后车田洪宗益独建三垛，余皆陆续而成。吴楚舟楫俱集于此。今架亭设茶于桥上。乾隆甲子五月大水倾，重圮重修。光绪年间又复修。

这篇记没有说明初建年代。乾隆甲子为乾隆九年（1744），则始建时也可能是乾隆初。家谱方志，往往记载不清，尤其于年代不很在意。又说"今架亭设茶于桥上"，《世谱》编于道光戊戌（1838），或许亭是道光年间造的。从《世谱》中的八景图上看，聚星桥和彩虹桥一样。因为迟到1985年才拆毁，所以镇上人记忆犹新，也能确认它与彩虹桥是一样的。

聚星桥南连古街东端的关圣庙，对岸便是如意寺。右侧浙水注入婺水处是八景之一的"双河晚钓"。

《世谱》中另记一座丁字桥："相传岳武穆布丁字阵于此，故名。原为京省通津，后改造石垛建亭桥于五显庙前，此桥只为居民渡处。"

五显庙在下市，也就是古街东端，建于明晚期，后改为关圣庙。八景图上，关圣庙前除聚星桥外，西侧另有一木桥，或许就是丁字桥。这段文字没有写清楚，可以理解为"石垛建亭"的桥与"此桥"不是同一道桥，则一为聚星桥，一为丁字桥。
sections.content_en:
Qinghua Rainbow

From an architectural perspective, what Qinghua Town is most proud of are its two bridges: one is Caihong (Rainbow) Bridge at the west end, on the main road to Jingdezhen; the other is Juxing (Gathering Stars) Bridge at the northeast corner, on the main road to Huizhou Prefecture. Both are stone-pier wooden-beam covered bridges, plus at least four plank bridges. In 1985, after the highway to Tuochuan was built and a reinforced concrete highway bridge was constructed, Juxing Bridge was demolished, and plank bridges were no longer built — now only Caihong Bridge remains. Caihong Bridge is about 100 meters west of the village, where the Wu River bends northward, running east-west. It is 140 meters long, with four stone piers and five spans. The piers are 13.8 meters long horizontally and 7 meters wide, with pointed upstream ends (swallow mouths) as water dividers. Span widths vary, around 12 meters. Each span has four large wooden beams, closely laid with wooden planks forming the deck. A corridor is built on the bridge with a double-slope roof. Sections over spans have small spans of only 4.5 meters; sections over piers have large spans of 11.5 meters, protruding on both sides. Thus the corridors over piers and over spans are structurally separate and independent. Moreover, the roof ridges of pier corridors are明显 higher than span corridors, creating a rhythmic undulating silhouette. The interior space also has rhythm from width variations. The pier corridor's north protrusion is larger, forming a complete small space with stone tables and benches. Both sides of the bridge have long railings with benches; leaning on the railing, south faces the screen-like Wulao (Five Elders) Peak and cloud-wreathed Zhu Ridge. Northeast, misty waves reach the sky, fishing boats drift leisurely under plank bridges; left bank has layered hills, right bank has bamboo groves shading villages, with white walls glinting through green bamboo leaves. At the west end, on the hilltop before, before the Cultural Revolution stood a towering 10+ meter writing brush (wenbi). At the south end of the second pier from the east — its swallow mouth — once stood a Buddhist pillar (jingchuang); in its north protrusion was a shrine with three deity positions: center "Great Yu King, Meritorious in Water Control," left and right "Monk Hu Jixiang who solicited donations" and "Founder Manager Hu Yongban." The couplet "Two waters embrace a bright mirror, twin bridges fall like rainbows" is from Li Bai's poem, with horizontal inscription "Long rainbow lying on waves." The couplet is probably not original. This pier was washed away by flood in 1983, repaired in August 1986; the shrine was rebuilt as a small wooden structure with high upturned eaves and hanging decorations shaped as water waves and red suns. The jingchuang was demolished during the Cultural Revolution; now at the turn of the western part of the old street, by the former Rende Hall site, about 30 meters from the alley mouth to Caihong Bridge (perhaps ancient Fangtou Alley), lies a damaged section of jingchuang on the ground — gray-white marble, octagonal, about 50 cm diameter, with alternating faces carved with "Namo Amitabha" and a Buddhist niche. Very likely this is the remnant of the original pier's jingchuang.

South of the east end of Caihong Bridge, by the water, is a rock outcrop with cliff carving "Small West Lake" three characters, legend says carved by Wu school seal carver Wen Peng and Huizhou school seal carver He Zhen during Ming Jiajing when they came to enjoy the scenery, with signatures. In Jiaqing 22nd year (1817), Wuyuan Magistrate Jueluo Changgeng (Manchu) had it re-carved and deepened. On the rock is another carved poem by Qi Yanhuai: "Outside Suiyang Temple one lamp lonely, before Wulao Peak night crows fly. Perfect lotus flowers not one stem, bright moon empty shines on Small West Lake." As if feeling somewhat desolate about the scenery.

So at Caihong Bridge head there is a couplet: "Famous place Huachuan loves this long bridge lying on waves, five peaks stand supreme; prosperous times revive old town, recall Wen Peng's seal characters and Yanhuai's matching poems." The bridge corridor architecture is very simple, with methods same as the pavilion on the way to Jialu Village and the covered bridge in Sixi Village. Components are square and straight, neatly cut, structure and construction all simple and clear, mortise-and-tenon joints plainly visible, nothing superfluous, fully meeting rigorous and concise rational requirements. Construction is economical and convenient. At the same time, each component's length, width, thickness dimensions, between components, and between components and whole, are harmoniously and proportionately coordinated. The structural beauty of this bridge corridor is completely different from the decorative beauty common in Wuyuan residences and ancestral halls. Though ancestral halls also have moving structural beauty, they always have decoration and deliberate refinement, while Caihong Bridge is pure plain line drawing, natural and effortless. In a region accustomed to piling decoration on architecture, simultaneously having such craft tradition in bridges and pavilions — perhaps because there were two types of craftsmen: house builders and bridge builders. But this is only speculation, without strong evidence.

Caihong Bridge is relatively far from Qinghua Town's residential area, so it didn't become a daily social center. It is said that in hot summer, many residents go to the bridge to cool off; evening breeze brings fresh air from water, dispelling sweat heat. No mosquitoes, only fireflies flickering, on and off; palm fans not raised, pipes not lit; elderly people half-asleep, murmuring indistinct words. Then moon rises over east mountain, water glints with fish-scale silver light, thread-like wave shadows like trembling water plants. This is one of Qinghua's Eight Scenes: "Algae Pond Soaking Moon."

At the east end of the bridge, on the wall of the bridge-keeper's hut, is embedded a 1986 stone stele saying the bridge was first built in Tang dynasty. "Wuyuan Scenery Records" says it was first built in Song dynasty. But "Qinghua Hu Clan Rende Hall Genealogy" and Qianlong "Wuyuan County Annals" clearly record it built in Qing Qianlong period. The Genealogy says:

Caihong Bridge is at Fangtou Stream, originally Hu Rende's grandson built wooden bridge; Qianlong Gengyin (1770), descendant Honghong,即 monk Jixiang of Linkeng Lane and local Yongban solicited donations, created stone piers, built pavilion and served tea on it,至今 and set up sacrificial worship.

The deity positions of Jixiang and Yongban are on the left and right of Great Yu's position on the bridge. Qianlong "Wuyuan County Annals · Righteous Deeds" records more vividly:

Hu Ban (note: no Yong character), Qinghua person, lived at Fangtou Stream. The stream is at the confluence of two sources, wooden bridge for travelers; when mountain rains rise, danger unpredictable. Ban was poor, from young peddled to provide parents good food. Once in summer bridge collapsed, blocked from returning home, vowed to complete this bridge to save people from danger. From then on repaired ropes, treated as own urgency. On frost and snow nights, would get up dressed to clear snow. Thus for 26 years. Then proposed replacing wood with stone, all agreed, pushed him as manager; midway washed away by flood, again supervised completion.

The annals also say Hu Ban was a Qianlong period person. The "Hu Rende" in Genealogy is the combined name of brothers Hu Congzheng (1379-1458) and Hu Lidao (1385-1457), who were enthusiastic about local construction; possibly someone mistook Hu Rende for Rende Hall founder Hu Xue.

Juxing Bridge at northeast lower market of Qinghua Town, running southwest to northeast, is also recorded in Genealogy:

Juxing Bridge, capital-province thoroughfare. Wuxian Temple monk Yingu solicited construction, later Chetian Hong Zongyi alone built three piers, rest completed successively. Wu and Chu boats all gather here. Now pavilion and tea on bridge. Qianlong Jiazi (1744) May flood collapsed, rebuilt. Guangxu period repaired again.

This record doesn't specify initial construction year. Qianlong Jiazi is 1744, so initial construction may also be early Qianlong. Genealogies and local annals often record unclearly, especially not caring about dates. It also says "now pavilion and tea on bridge"; the Genealogy was compiled in Daoguang Wuxu (1838), perhaps the pavilion was built in Daoguang. From the Eight Scenes illustrations in Genealogy, Juxing Bridge looks the same as Caihong Bridge. Since it was only demolished in 1985, townspeople remember it well and confirm it was the same as Caihong Bridge.

Juxing Bridge south connects to Guansheng (Guan Yu) Temple at east end of old street; opposite bank is Ruyi Temple. Where Zhe Stream flows into Wu River on the right is one of Eight Scenes: "Double River Evening Fishing."

The Genealogy also records a Dingzi (T-shaped) Bridge: "Legend says Yue Wumu (Yue Fei) arranged a T-shaped battle array here, hence name. Originally capital-province thoroughfare, later rebuilt as stone-pier pavilion bridge before Wuxian Temple, this bridge only for residents crossing."

Wuxian Temple is at lower market, i.e., east end of old street, built in late Ming, later changed to Guansheng Temple. On the Eight Scenes illustration, besides Juxing Bridge before Guansheng Temple, there is another wooden bridge on the west side, perhaps Dingzi Bridge. This text is not clear; can be understood that the "stone-pier pavilion" bridge and "this bridge" are not the same — one is Juxing Bridge, one is Dingzi Bridge.

sections.name: 芙蓉村
sections.content_zh:
芙蓉村

青青的山上耸立起三块悬岩。乡人们说，它们像一朵芙蓉花，于是，山下便有了芙蓉村。芙蓉峰是一朵水芙蓉，村中央便开了一方水池，可可儿地把芙蓉峰倒映在池里。山川秀丽，必有俊彦，芙蓉村年轻人牛角挂书，亦耕亦读，出过几位进士，大宗祠里还挂着一块金龙盘边的状元匾。村人说，南宋时候，小小的芙蓉村有"十八金带"，便是同时有十八个人在临安当京官。于是，又有人说芙蓉峰像纱帽，村前的小溪像袍带，没有好风水，哪里来的功名富贵呢？

但是，"读圣贤书，所学何事"，无非是"孔曰成仁，孟曰取义"。有了知识，当了官，就承担了庄严的社会责任。南宋末年，元兵南下，咸淳元年（1265）进士陈虞之响应文天祥，起兵勤王，率领全村义士八百多人据守芙蓉峰三整年，全部殉难。山下离离蔓草丛中，散乱着几块残破的青石，那儿曾是陈虞之的墓。

元兵把芙蓉村荡为平地。芙蓉花年年都开，不久之后，陈氏后人又重建了一座新的芙蓉村，像芙蓉花一样，素雅而充满了清新的生气。

废墟上重建新村，容易整齐。遗存至今的芙蓉村，平面是个长方形，占地十四点三公顷。一圈寨墙，都用大块蛮石砌筑。墙上有铳眼，那时的人们还没有忘记祖先英勇的自卫战斗。西门外碧绿的农田一直铺到青山脚下，农夫们"晨兴理荒秽，带月荷锄归"，斗笠蓑衣，从寨门出出进进，用汗珠养育禾苗。南门外一条小溪，水色澄碧，奔流不息。妇女们提着鹅兜，领着孩子，到溪边洗衣，把鲜艳的色彩和款款的谈笑声一起溶进水里，闪闪烁烁。村人们心疼妇女和孩子，怕暴雨淋，怕骄阳晒，给他们在一旁造了一座凉亭，亭子里的三官大帝，笑眯眯坐着，也被青春的场景陶醉。东门是村子的正门，村里官多，正门就得有点儿官气。两层楼阁，画栋雕梁，檐下斗栱把象鼻形的下昂挑出老远。进门右手边是陈氏大宗祠，形制完备。左手边是乐台，每逢祭祀或者节庆大事，有乐队吹吹打打迎接贵宾进村。

一条宽宽的主街，从东门笔直向西，正对芙蓉峰，有个优雅的名字叫如意街。街的中段，就是洋溢着恬美气息的芙蓉池。池中央有座芙蓉亭。玲珑的重檐亭子高高挑起翼角，又像一朵盛开的芙蓉花。它背后天际舒展着芙蓉峰，峰和亭的影子又在芙蓉池里重叠。汲水浣纱的妇女，像芙蓉花一样美丽，给芙蓉池镶了一道彩色缤纷的花边。芙蓉亭里，整天坐着些老年人，默默相视，沉浸在几十年的友谊里。他们交谈些传说轶闻、农事年景，都轻声细语，为的是怕扰乱了隔墙飞过来的读书声。墙那边便是芙蓉书院，那里教化过精通翰墨经史的进士举人，也教化过为民族舍生忘死的志士仁人。哎，低声些，让那琅琅书声飘得更远，飘满全村。

全村各个角落又有启蒙的初级学塾。宗族规定，要厚待老师，要资助学子。学塾里栽花种竹，房舍精洁，给读书郎一个文明的环境，涵养性情。村子西北角上，康熙年间造的司马第的学塾，漏空花墙后，假山小池，俨然一座园林。

如意街南北，小巷纵横，铺着卵石，被几百年先人们的足迹磨得圆润，细雨轻洇，闪出柔和的光泽。巷子里有井，姑娘们担水走过，履声在小巷里回响，清脆，却静悄悄。小巷曲折，到处可以见到竹树掩映，短篱矮墙遮不住宽敞的院落，向巷里行人亮出主人的家居生活。是晒谷，是磨粉，是打年糕，还有孩子们在廊下数着雏燕，数不清了，便一头扑向母亲的怀里。行人隔着矮墙头上的菊花，问主人，新酒熟了没有？

小小的住宅，自然灵活，无规无矩，不受拘束。屋顶微微翘曲，轻盈舒展，它随时会振翅飞去吗？不会，它留恋着村里的人们呐！几片粉壁，勾勒出原木，随弯就曲，依然挺拔有力；衬托出蛮石，刚毅浑厚，像为国捐躯者的气血凝成。楠溪江的山水陶冶出了楠溪江人这么朴实又这么精致，这么豪放又这么强悍的审美情趣。

小巷转角处，有一口池塘。塘岸的百日红，累累垂向水面，像少女们对镜梳妆。在楠溪江青山绿水之间吟出中国第一批山水诗的谢灵运，思念弟弟，写下"池塘生春草，园柳变鸣禽"的千古名句。南宋诗人"永嘉四灵"之一的赵师秀则写道："清明时节家家雨，青草池塘处处蛙。有约不来过夜半，闲敲棋子落灯花。"原来一方小池，竟可以有这么深的感情寄托。

楠溪江人是有感情的，任何人见到他们被阳光烤成紫铜色的胸膛，就会知道它的宽阔，感到它的坦诚。于是就能理解，只有他们，才会建造出那么安宁静谧，那么祥和温馨的村落。

楠溪江人是有感情的，任何人只要来到这里，然后挥挥手离开这里，就会想到，倘然不幸国破家亡的时候，他们必会慷慨赴难，义无反顾，留下千古英名。于是也就能理解，只有他们才会在离离草丛中让芙蓉峰下的芙蓉村再像芙蓉花绽放开去……

芙蓉峰上的义士也罢，纱帽岩下的官宦也罢，他们，都是这个村落的子弟。普普通通的村民养育了他们，便养育了民族的文化和精神。

芙蓉峰是永恒的。
sections.content_en:
Furong (Hibiscus) Village

On the green mountain stand three towering overhanging rocks. Villagers say they look like a hibiscus flower, so below the mountain there is Furong Village. Furong Peak is a water hibiscus, and in the center of the village opens a square pond, perfectly reflecting Furong Peak. Beautiful mountains and rivers必然 produce talented people; young people in Furong Village hung books on ox horns, farming and studying, producing several jinshi, and the great ancestral hall still hangs a zhuangyuan (top scholar) plaque with golden dragon border. Villagers say that in Southern Song, small Furong Village had "eighteen gold belts" — meaning eighteen people simultaneously serving as capital officials in Lin'an. So some say Furong Peak looks like an official's gauze hat, and the stream before the village like an official's robe belt — without good fengshui, where would official success and wealth come from?

But "reading sages' books, what does one learn?" — nothing but "Confucius says achieving benevolence, Mencius says choosing righteousness." With knowledge and official position, one assumes solemn social responsibility. In late Southern Song, when Yuan troops advanced south, Chen Yuzhi, jinshi of Xianchun 1st year (1265), responded to Wen Tianxiang, raised troops to serve the king, leading over 800 village righteous men to defend Furong Peak for three full years, all dying martyrs. Among the lush grass below the mountain, scattered broken bluestones mark where Chen Yuzhi's tomb once was.

Yuan troops razed Furong Village to the ground. Hibiscus flowers bloom every year; before long, Chen descendants rebuilt a new Furong Village, like a hibiscus flower — elegant and full of fresh vitality.

Rebuilding a new village on ruins makes it easy to be orderly. The surviving Furong Village has a rectangular plan, covering 14.3 hectares. A ring of village walls, all built with large rough stones. The walls have gun ports — people then hadn't forgotten their ancestors' heroic self-defense battle. West of the west gate, green farmland stretches to the green mountain foot; farmers "rise at dawn to clear weeds, return with moon carrying hoes," in bamboo hats and straw raincoats, going in and out through the village gate, nurturing seedlings with sweat. South of the south gate, a small stream with clear blue water flows endlessly. Women carrying goose-shaped baskets, leading children, go to the stream to wash clothes, dissolving bright colors and gentle laughter into the water, sparkling. Villagers, caring for women and children, fearing rain and sun, built a pavilion beside it; the Three Officials Emperor inside sits smiling, also intoxicated by the youthful scene. The east gate is the village's main gate; with many officials in the village, the main gate must have official dignity. Two-story pavilion, painted beams and carved rafters, under-eave dougong (bracket sets) extend elephant-nose-shaped lower angled beams far. Entering, right side is Chen Great Ancestral Hall, complete in form. Left side is a music stage; whenever sacrifices or festivals, a band plays to welcome distinguished guests into the village.

A wide main street runs straight west from the east gate, facing Furong Peak, with an elegant name: Ruyi (As-You-Wish) Street. The middle section of the street is the Furong Pool, full of tranquil beauty. In the center of the pool stands Furong Pavilion. The exquisite double-eaved pavilion has high upturned corners, like a blooming hibiscus flower. Behind it, Furong Peak stretches across the sky; peak and pavilion shadows overlap in Furong Pool. Women drawing water and washing silk, beautiful as hibiscus flowers, frame Furong Pool with a colorful border. In Furong Pavilion, elderly people sit all day, silently looking at each other, immersed in decades of friendship. They talk of legends and anecdotes, farming and harvests, all in soft voices — for fear of disturbing the sound of reading flying over the wall. Beyond the wall is Furong Academy, which educated jinshi and juren skilled in calligraphy and classics, and also educated righteous men who sacrificed their lives for the nation. Ah, lower your voice, let the sound of reading float farther, filling the whole village.

In every corner of the village are primary schools for启蒙. The clan stipulated to treat teachers well and support students. Schools planted flowers and bamboo, with clean rooms, giving scholars a civilized environment to cultivate temperament. At the village's northwest corner, the school of Sima Di (Sima Residence) built in Kangxi period, behind openwork flower walls, has rockery and small pond, just like a garden.

North and south of Ruyi Street, alleys crisscross, paved with cobblestones, worn round by centuries of ancestors' footprints; in light drizzle, they shine with soft luster. There are wells in alleys; young women carrying water pass, their footsteps echoing in the alley, crisp yet quiet. Alleys wind, with bamboo and trees everywhere; short hedges and low walls cannot hide spacious courtyards, revealing the master's home life to passersby. Drying grain, grinding flour, pounding New Year cakes, and children counting baby swallows under the eaves — when they can't count anymore, they throw themselves into mother's arms. Passersby, over the chrysanthemums on the low wall, ask the master: is the new wine ready?

Small residences are natural and flexible, without rigid rules, unrestrained. Roofs curve slightly upward, light and graceful — will they flap wings and fly away any moment? No, they are attached to the village people! A few white walls outline original timber, following curves yet still upright and powerful; setting off rough stones, resolute and浑厚, like condensed blood of those who died for the country. The mountains and waters of Nanxi River have cultivated Nanxi River people's aesthetic taste — so simple yet so refined, so bold yet so strong.

At an alley corner, there is a pond. Crape myrtle on the pond bank hangs heavily toward the water, like young girls grooming at a mirror. Xie Lingyun, who composed China's first landscape poems among Nanxi River's green mountains and clear waters, missing his brother, wrote the eternal line: "The pond gives birth to spring grass, garden willows change singing birds." Southern Song poet Zhao Shixiu, one of the "Four Spirits of Yongjia," wrote: "Qingming season, rain in every home; green grass ponds, frogs everywhere. Appointment not kept past midnight, idly tapping chess pieces, lamp flowers fall." It turns out a small pond can hold such deep emotional sustenance.

Nanxi River people are emotional; anyone seeing their sun-baked bronze chests will know their breadth and feel their sincerity. Then one can understand: only they could build such peaceful, quiet, auspicious and warm villages.

Nanxi River people are emotional; anyone who comes here, then waves and leaves, will think: if unfortunately the country falls and family perishes, they will surely go to disaster generously, without hesitation, leaving eternal fame. Then one can understand: only they would let Furong Village under Furong Peak bloom again like a hibiscus flower among the lush grass…

Whether righteous men on Furong Peak or officials under the Gauze Hat Rock, they are all this village's children. Ordinary villagers raised them, and thus raised the nation's culture and spirit.

Furong Peak is eternal.

sections.name: 到张壁村去
sections.content_zh:
到张壁村去

1998年11月4日，我们一大早从北京乘长途公共汽车出发，六个多小时后到达太原，立即换乘一辆中型汽车，沿汾河左岸南下，经过太谷、祁县、平遥这几个以晋商"大院"闻名的城市，来到介休。这大体是从北京到西安去的古道，一路上有许多故事，讲的大都是庚子年清廷仓惶出奔，受到开票号的大商人的资助和平常小老百姓箪食壶浆的呵护。这是一个富庶的地方，公路两侧的田地平平展展，一眼望不到边。在纯农业时代，山西有个民谣，唱的是：

凑凑付付汾河湾，
凑凑付付晋东南，
哭哭啼啼吕梁山，
死也不出雁门关。

汾河湾就是这晋中盆地。人们传说，晋中盆地在远古时候是个大湖，叫晋阳湖。湖水浩渺，却没有土地。大禹治水的时候，劈开了南端的灵石口（又名雀鼠谷），把水放了出去，湖底就变成了肥沃的田野，世世代代的居民们从此欢欢喜喜。

立冬过了，秋庄稼已经收拾干净，农地里空空荡荡，反衬着公路上的忙忙碌碌。来往的车辆，大多是运煤的。煤是山西的主要矿产资源，公路边一座接一座的工厂，大都和煤有关，不是发电厂就是炼焦厂，一支支烟囱把天空喷得乌七八糟。工厂附近，树木房舍朦朦胧胧，浓浓的硫磺味呛得我们憋气。一些过去"凑凑付付""哭哭啼啼"甚至"死也不去"的地区，指望着靠煤矿摆脱贫困，也过上"欢欢喜喜"的好日子，他们做的第一件事却是运出煤来，把本来欢欢喜喜的地方熏黑。

盆地到了头，远远看到山影子了，我们就到了介休。车子驶进一条岔路，溯龙凤河左岸上行。龙凤河是汾河的支流，只有五十六公里长，发源于绵山东侧，向西北流来。龙凤河流域是黄土沟壑地区，地形破碎，公路两边零乱起来。车子渐渐走出了烟雾，前面层层叠叠的山岭渐渐清晰，那是太行山。一个塔尖从小山包后冒出来，绕过山包，便来到塔下。龙凤河在这里遇到突出的岩角，转折了一下，塔就立在这岩角上。这里原有一个小小的石鼻庵，塔是庵堂的，叫凌空塔，乡民们叫它姑姑塔，因为传说在尼姑庵里修行的是唐王朝的一位皇太姑。但《介休县志》说它造于雍正十年（1732），乾隆四十三年（1778）维修。它高九级，三十八米，是龙凤村的地标。

过了塔不远，到了龙凤村。龙凤村是乡政府所在地，张壁村属于龙凤乡。在乡政府门前问了问路，车子在中学校的球场前拐弯，上了机耕道，跌跌撞撞，扬起一天灰土。正逢中学散学，我们截了三个回张壁村去的女孩子上车，请她们带路。路在黄土丘陵和沟壑之间盘过来又绕过去，越走越高，女孩子指着前方的高山说，那就是绵山。

绵山，喔嗬！那可是一座大大有名的山。春秋时期，晋国公子重耳为避祸去国，周游列国十九年，困窘的时候，随从侍臣介子推曾经割身上的肉煮给他吃。公元前636年，重耳回国即位为晋文公，当年的随从大都被重用，大约是介子推的真本事不大，没有得到一官半职，于是发牢骚回家奉母隐居绵山。晋文公觉得有损自己的名声，派人召他，他不从，文公设计放火烧山，企图逼他出来。不料母子二人脾性倔得古怪，也可能是烟火迷了眼睛，竟死心眼儿抱住一棵老树不放，被活活烧死。由于历代统治者提倡"割肉啖君"式的愚忠，知识分子又标榜"不可再辱"的风骨，所以介子推就成了一种伦理价值的典范，受人尊崇。他遇难的日子，清明节前三天，被定为寒食节，家家不得举火。

这座绵山距介休县城二十公里，张壁村离绵山还有五公里，在绵山北麓的黄土台地上。据清代嘉庆《介休县志》，介休的得名是"因晋文公绵上旌介子"。不过这个论断有点儿疑问。介休是一个古县，春秋时称邬县，韩、魏、赵三家分晋之后属魏国，秦代置县，称为界休，两汉依旧，到晋代才改为介休。所以介休是不是因介子推而得名，还很难说。而且晋南又另有几处绵山，都争传当年晋文公放火的故事，历来没有定论。

我们随小女孩的手指往山上看，当然没有看到焦木枯树。只见眼前一带土冈，稀稀落落长着几棵杨树、槐树，不料车子向右一偏猛然停下，土冈后面露出一段青砖城墙，我们已经到了城门口。抬头看看，券门洞上的石匾刻着"德星聚"三个字，这便是张壁村北门外瓮城的东门了。城头上有一座庙，脊兽顶着滚圆的夕阳，火红的，正冉冉下沉。

进了瓮城东门，右手便是二郎庙的大院子，村民委员会设在庙里。吃过饭，天早已全黑，我们被分开到几处住宿，有的住在农家，有的住在北门内三孔旧窑洞里，那是过去给守卫北门的更夫们住的，叫更窑。也有住在三大士殿的偏屋里的。虽然介休纬度比北京低不少，但地势高，张壁村的海拔超过一千米，所以天气很冷。我们住的房子都有火炕。从第一个晚上起，我们就跟火炕斗争起来，有时候，热得不得了，烧糊了炕席，有时候冰冷，冻得缩成一团，睡不成觉。也有时候火口冒出浓烟，熏得眼泪流淌满面。跟火炕的斗争，我们是败绩累累，后来成了我们对张壁村有趣的回忆之一。

画图和吃饭在二郎庙的大殿里。几位大婶大嫂给我们蒸馍、煮饭。我们要吃土豆、白薯和玉茭面，大婶们咯咯笑，说那都是喂猪的东西。年轻一点儿的大嫂甚至不会蒸窝头、贴饼子。家家都养鸡，但人们只吃鸡蛋而不会料理鸡只，我们中有一个自封为"总务长"的人，夸下海口要教会大婶们做红绕鸡块。第二天一大早，村长就在大喇叭里宣布了这条"好消息"，不料待她们挤满了二郎庙的厨房，却找不到"总务长"了，村长又拿出大喇叭广播找人，"总务长"再也没有现身，有人说，看见他清早搭一辆交通摩托车走了，带着行李包。我们很记挂，大婶大嫂们现在是不是还不会料理鸡只。

我们在张壁村的第一次亮相失败了，但后来的学术工作却很成功，或许可以补偿大婶大嫂们当时的失望。
sections.content_en:
Going to Zhangbi Village

On November 4, 1998, we departed Beijing early morning by long-distance bus, arriving in Taiyuan over six hours later, immediately transferring to a mid-size bus, heading south along the left bank of the Fen River, passing through Taigu, Qi County, and Pingyao — cities famous for Shanxi merchants' "grand courtyards" — arriving in Jiexiu. This is roughly the ancient road from Beijing to Xi'an; along the way are many stories, mostly about the Qing court's hasty flight in the Gengzi year (1900), aided by major merchants who ran piaohao (remittance banks) and ordinary people with food and drink. This is a prosperous region; farmland on both sides of the highway is flat and endless. In the purely agricultural era, Shanxi had a folk song:

Barely getting by, Fen River bend,
Barely getting by, southeast Shanxi,
Crying and weeping, Lüliang Mountains,
Rather die than leave Yanmen Pass.

The Fen River bend is this Jinzhong Basin. Legend says the Jinzhong Basin was a great lake in ancient times, called Jinyang Lake. The lake was vast but had no land. When Great Yu controlled the floods, he split open the Lingshi Pass (also called Queshu Valley) at the southern end, releasing the water; the lake bottom became fertile fields, and generations of residents have lived happily ever since.

After Lidong (Start of Winter), autumn crops had been harvested, farmland empty, contrasting with the busy highway. Most passing vehicles transported coal.
