Coal is Shanxi's main mineral resource; factories lined the highway, mostly related to coal — power plants or coking plants, chimneys spewing filth into the sky. Near factories, trees and houses were hazy, strong sulfur smell choking us. Some regions that were once "barely getting by," "crying and weeping," or even "rather die than go," hoping to escape poverty through coal mines and live "happily," their first act was to ship out coal, blackening the originally happy places.

At the end of the basin, mountain shadows appeared in the distance, and we reached Jiexiu. The bus turned onto a side road, going upstream along the left bank of the Longfeng River. The Longfeng River is a tributary of the Fen River, only 56 km long, originating east of Mian Mountain, flowing northwest. The Longfeng River basin is a loess gully region with broken terrain; both sides of the road became disordered. The bus gradually emerged from the smog; layered mountain ridges ahead became clearer — that was the Taihang Mountains. A pagoda spire appeared behind a small hill; rounding the hill, we arrived at the pagoda. The Longfeng River here meets a protruding rock corner and turns; the pagoda stands on this rock corner. Originally there was a small Shibi Nunnery here; the pagoda belonged to the nunnery, called Lingkong Pagoda, villagers call it Auntie Pagoda, because legend says the nun who practiced here was an imperial aunt of the Tang dynasty. But "Jiexiu County Annals" says it was built in Yongzheng 10th year (1732), repaired in Qianlong 43rd year (1778). It is nine stories high, 38 meters, a landmark of Longfeng Village.

Not far past the pagoda, we reached Longfeng Village. Longfeng Village is the township government seat; Zhangbi Village belongs to Longfeng Township. After asking directions at the township government, the bus turned at the middle school playground, onto a tractor road, bumping along, raising clouds of dust. Just as school let out, we stopped three girls returning to Zhangbi Village and asked them to guide us. The road wound between loess hills and gullies, climbing higher; the girls pointed to the high mountain ahead and said that was Mian Mountain.

Mian Mountain, oh! That is a very famous mountain. In the Spring and Autumn period, Jin prince Chong'er fled the country to avoid disaster, traveling among states for 19 years; in times of hardship, his attendant Jie Zitui once cut flesh from his own thigh and cooked it for him. In 636 BC, Chong'er returned and became Duke Wen of Jin; most former attendants were重用, but perhaps Jie Zitui's real abilities were limited, he received no official position, so he complained and went home to serve his mother, living in seclusion on Mian Mountain. Duke Wen felt this harmed his reputation, sent people to summon him, but he refused; the duke designed to set fire to the mountain, trying to force him out. Unexpectedly, mother and son were stubbornly odd, or perhaps smoke blinded them, they foolishly clung to an old tree and were burned alive. Because successive rulers promoted "cutting flesh to feed the lord" type of blind loyalty, and intellectuals flaunted the spirit of "cannot be humiliated again," Jie Zitui became a model of ethical value, revered by people. The day of his death, three days before Qingming Festival, was designated Cold Food Festival, when no household may light a fire.

This Mian Mountain is 20 km from Jiexiu county town; Zhangbi Village is another 5 km from Mian Mountain, on the loess terrace at the northern foot of Mian Mountain. According to Qing Jiaqing "Jiexiu County Annals," Jiexiu got its name "because Duke Wen of Jin honored Jie Zitui at Mian." But this assertion is somewhat questionable. Jiexiu is an ancient county, called Wu County in Spring and Autumn, belonging to Wei after the three families divided Jin; Qin established the county as Jiexiu (界休), Han dynasty continued, only in Jin dynasty changed to Jiexiu (介休). So whether Jiexiu is named after Jie Zitui is hard to say. Moreover, there are several other Mian Mountains in southern Shanxi, all claiming the story of Duke Wen setting fire, historically inconclusive.

We looked up the mountain following the girls' fingers, of course seeing no charred wood or withered trees. Only a stretch of earth mounds before us, with a few scattered poplars and locust trees; unexpectedly the bus turned right and stopped suddenly — behind the earth mound appeared a section of blue-brick city wall, we had arrived at the city gate. Looking up, the stone plaque above the arched gate reads "De Xing Ju" (Gathering of Virtuous Stars); this is the east gate of the outer barbican (wengcheng) outside Zhangbi Village's north gate. On the city wall stands a temple, its ridge ornaments topped by the round setting sun, fiery red, slowly sinking.

Entering the barbican east gate, on the right is the large courtyard of Erlang Temple, where the village committee is located. After dinner, it was already completely dark; we were split up to several accommodations — some stayed with farmers, some in three old cave dwellings inside the north gate, which used to house night watchmen guarding the north gate, called watchman caves. Some stayed in side rooms of the Three Great Masters Hall. Although Jiexiu's latitude is much lower than Beijing's, the terrain is high; Zhangbi Village's altitude exceeds 1,000 meters, so the weather was very cold. The houses we stayed in all had heated kangs. From the first night, we struggled with the heated kangs — sometimes unbearably hot, burning the kang mat; sometimes freezing cold, huddling into a ball, unable to sleep. Sometimes the fire mouth belched thick smoke, stinging eyes to tears. Our struggle with the heated kangs was a series of defeats, later becoming one of our interesting memories of Zhangbi Village.

Drawing and eating took place in the main hall of Erlang Temple. Several aunts and sisters-in-law steamed buns and cooked rice for us. We asked for potatoes, sweet potatoes, and cornmeal; the aunts giggled, saying those were pig feed. Younger sisters-in-law couldn't even steam corn bread or bake flat cakes. Every family raised chickens, but people only ate eggs and didn't know how to cook chicken; one of us, self-styled "General Affairs Manager," boasted he would teach the aunts to make braised chicken chunks. Early next morning, the village chief announced this "good news" on the loudspeaker; unexpectedly when they crowded into Erlang Temple's kitchen, the "General Affairs Manager" was nowhere to be found. The village chief used the loudspeaker again to search, but the "General Affairs Manager" never appeared; someone said they saw him leave early morning on a motorcycle taxi, with his luggage. We often wonder whether the aunts and sisters-in-law still don't know how to cook chicken.

Our first appearance in Zhangbi Village failed, but our later academic work was very successful, perhaps compensating for the disappointment of the aunts and sisters-in-law at that time.

key_terms.en: De Xing Ju (Gathering of Virtuous Stars)

sections.name: 重回楠溪江
sections.content_zh:
重回楠溪江

十三年前，1989年，我们到楠溪江流域做乡土建筑研究，工作范围在中游地区，连续在那里奔跑了三年。研究成果在台湾和大陆出版之后，引起过一些读者的兴趣。事隔十年，永嘉的朋友们又邀我们到上游村落做一些工作。

楠溪江是瓯江的支流，瓯江是浙江省南部最大的一条江，干流由西而东，从仙霞岭经枫岭流到雁荡山，最后在温州注入东海。楠溪江在瓯江北岸，由北向南流，汇注瓯江的地方离瓯江的入海口已经不远了，潮水涨落，一直影响到它中游的沙头镇。楠溪江干流全长一百四十五公里，流域面积两千七百四十二平方公里，这便是现今整个永嘉县的辖境。

楠溪江的文明史从下游逐渐向上游发展，经过西晋末年和北宋末年的两次中原衣冠南渡，尤其是五代十国时南闽王氏内乱导致的生民北迁，下游和中游已经人口密集，村聚相望。这些移民，文化水平比较高，很快就使楠溪江中下游村落成为农业经济繁荣的人文荟萃之地。经过他们一代又一代的经营，村落的发育比较充分，除了住宅之外，宗祠、庙宇、书院、亭阁、戏台、牌坊、寨墙、堤岸、水渠之类，凡古代农耕社会所应该有的各类建筑，都已经完备，甚至还有规模不小的园林。到清代晚期，少数几个大一点的镇子上，商业街也已经初步成形。

不过，楠溪江下游隔江对面城市经济发达的温州，古老的村落早已没有了。上游呢？我们在关于中游村落的研究报告里写道："上游的村子比较贫穷，村落的发育程度低，建筑类型少，规划也不大严谨。"因此，我们的第一次工作就把范围限定在中游。中游村落文化蕴涵的丰厚，布局结构的优美，建筑风格的雅致朴实，给我们的研究成果以很现成的光彩。

当时我们对上游村落的评价大体上是正确的，除了昆阳、潘坑、碧莲等几个集镇相当繁华之外，上游山区里大都是些很小的村子，有一些甚至只有"篱落三四处，野屋五六家"而已。宗祠、庙宇，偶然在几个村子里可以见到，大多规模很小，体制也不完备。不过，我们对上游聚落其实很早就发生了兴趣。1991年，中游聚落的研究到了尾声，最后的一幕便是我和当时的硕士研究生舒楠为了证实楠溪江建筑风格的边界，在烈日直晒之下，冒着四十摄氏度出头的高温，步行翻过四道山岭，到张家岸、白岩、佳溪和岩龙去过。带路的是一位复员军人，岩头金姓一族，名字里有一个豹字，他拿出军人豹子般过硬的本事来，翻山越岭如履平地，把舒楠累得中了暑，我的旧布鞋双双掉了底，迈一步响两声"噼啪"。虽然相当艰苦，那一趟却很使我们兴奋。那些聚落，挂在山坡上，谷底流淌着澄澈透明的溪水，哗哗地响。轻巧的木屋，错错落落地层叠在一起，透过轻雾般的炊烟，好像是一片仙山楼阁。有几个小村，溪水环绕，须得踏着长长的石步进去。有几个村子连钉步都没有，岸边停着小小的竹筏，行人要上筏子，自己撑篙，或者攀着一根架在两岸之间的篾丝缆绳，才能慢慢渡过去。那些村子，即使不在人间之外，仿佛也不在人间之中。凑巧天气多变，偶然有白云缭绕在檐头，灵动幻化，看得我们心迷神摇，不觉就盼望着巫山神女也会在这里飘飘然走将出来。

村舍素雅，大多也有一定的矩度，因地势起伏而稍作自由变化，粗看上去仿佛随宜而生，随兴而长，只求与自然相亲而不受人为的拘束。构架完全是用木材撑起来的。往往用大块蛮石垒砌基座和底层外墙，有光有影，体积感很强，仿佛出自雕塑家之手。但越往山里走，砖石的砌筑部分就越少，到了深林区，有些房子就只剩下一副轻巧的木架子和薄薄的一层板壁了。这样的房子，冬季怎么御寒呢？山风很硬啊！问一问山民才知道，这些房子，看上去那么空灵，就因为四面有一圈外廊，每年秋收之后，檐柱间穿上几根横木，把脱过粒的稻草一把一把地搭到横木上，便形成了防风保温的屏障。房子里一冬天都生火盆，烧的是老树兜，火苗虽然不旺，能保昼夜温和。到来年春天，阳气回暖，便逐渐把挂着的稻草一把把揪下来烧灶火。气温一天天升高，稻草的屏障一天天稀落，到天气热了，稻草也烧光了，房子四面八方都透风，凉快得很。这样一年一个轮回，冬暖夏爽，设想得非常巧妙，或许这也是一种生态建筑设计。我曾经在书本上看到过，两三万里路之外的意大利农村里，有这样的农舍，很佩服它们的巧妙，到了楠溪江上游，才知道原来中外劳动者在这件事上都同样聪明，想到一起去了。

楠溪江流域是个国家级的风景区，中游的山水比较柔美，河谷宽，山势缓，波光闪闪，挎着鹅兜到埠头去浣洗的村姑，只要一蹲下在水边，就融进到自然景色里去了。上游则不然，峡谷紧窄，溪流湍急，山坡陡而郁郁森森长满了树木和毛竹，在这样的图画里，最合适的是再画上一个袒露着紫红色胸膛，挑着沉重的担子翻山越岭的男子汉。南北朝时候刘宋诗人谢灵运曾经当过永嘉太守，他写的诗《登石门最高顶》有句："疏峰抗高馆，对岭临回溪。长林罗户穴，积石拥阶基。连岩觉路塞，密竹使径迷。"石门在楠溪江上游，那里连绵的山岩把路堵塞了，密匝匝的竹林遮蔽了小径，打开屋门便是森林，岩石一直崛突到台阶下。那种风光既雄浑又苍凉。

上游山民谋生艰难，远不如中游那样水丰土腴，衣食有余，所以读书科举的成绩不像中游那样出色。但也不是一片荒芜。溪口戴氏，宋代出了几位重要的大学者，不过它处于上游中游之间，且不去说它。科名不断的潘坑、昆阳、碧莲等都是集镇，也姑且不提。远在县境西北林区里的岩龙村，没有几户人家，却有一座建了戏台的祠堂，大门前还立着一对狮子，族里出过一位进士。这个小村，在我和舒楠访问之前几天才通了电，当年的读书郎，临窗夜读，未必会囊萤映雪，那么，是燃着竹篾还是燃着油灯？是桕子油还是桐油？在全国各地农村，不论多么偏僻，多么穷困，我们几乎都可以见到大一统的中华典籍文化鲜明的存在。但是，纵然这样，我还是朦胧地意识到，荒僻、闭塞、过着自然生活的山村，必定有过和中游有明显差异的带着点儿野性的民俗文化。它会反映在物质和精神生活的一切方面，包括房舍和村落。而且也意识到，这种民俗文化正在迅速消失，当前已经所存无几，我们将在不久之后便永远失去它们。

所以，我们那时并没有完全排斥到楠溪江上游去研究几个村子。何况，即使是最贫穷落后的山村，也代表中国农耕时代乡土聚落的一种或几种类型，我们要写出中国农业聚落完整的谱系，当然不能没有它们。于是，2001年春季，我应邀到泰顺去，便先到温州，在瓯北雇一辆出租汽车到了上游的林坑、黄南和上坳三个村落。它们的景观大不同于中游的任何一座村落，更自然、更开放、更亲切，也更具诗情画意，而且建筑风格和岩龙、佳溪相比又有异趣。这次访问大大激起了我的热忱，回到北京便向凤凰电视台"寻找远去的家园"摄制组建议，请他们去拍摄这三个村子。这年夏天，他们终于去了。一到林坑，摄制组的全体朋友被出奇秀丽的景色震住了，他们拉起手，排成一个圆圈，齐声高呼，感谢我把他们带到那里。愉快地拍完片子之后，8月31日我离开温州。9月2日，摄制组的航拍大师赵群力先生不幸在林坑附近因飞机失事而殉职。这件意外事故引起了很大的震动，林坑人怀着山民们最真诚、最强烈的感情纪念他，要给他建一座纪念馆，永嘉县的领导人也决意用保护林坑等三个村子来纪念这位杰出人物。于是，我们接受了邀请，在2002年深秋到了林坑住下，以它和黄南、上坳为起点，着手我们的楠溪江上游乡土建筑研究。
sections.content_en:
Returning to Nanxi River

Thirteen years ago, in 1989, we went to the Nanxi River basin to study vernacular architecture, working in the middle reaches, running there continuously for three years. After our research results were published in Taiwan and mainland China, they aroused some reader interest. Ten years later, friends in Yongjia invited us again to do some work on upper-reach villages.

Nanxi River is a tributary of the Ou River, the largest river in southern Zhejiang Province; the main stream flows west to east, from Xianxia Ridge through Fengling to Yandang Mountain, finally emptying into the East China Sea at Wenzhou. Nanxi River is on the north bank of Ou River, flowing north to south; where it joins Ou River is not far from Ou River's mouth, and tides affect it as far as Shatou Town in the middle reaches. Nanxi River main stream is 145 km long, with a drainage area of 2,742 square km — this is the entire jurisdiction of today's Yongjia County.

Nanxi River's civilization developed gradually from lower to upper reaches. After two Central Plains scholar migrations — late Western Jin and late Northern Song — especially the northward migration caused by the Wang clan civil war in Southern Fujian during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, the lower and middle reaches became densely populated, with villages facing each other. These immigrants, with relatively high cultural levels, quickly made Nanxi River's middle and lower villages prosperous agricultural economy and cultural gathering places. Through generations of management, villages developed fully; besides residences, ancestral halls, temples, academies, pavilions, stages, memorial arches, village walls, embankments, water channels — all building types ancient agrarian society should have — were complete, even with sizable gardens. By late Qing, commercial streets had初步 formed in a few larger towns.

However, across the river from Nanxi River's lower reaches is economically developed Wenzhou, where ancient villages are long gone. What about the upper reaches? In our research report on middle-reach villages, we wrote: "Upper-reach villages are relatively poor, village development degree is low, building types are few, planning is not very rigorous." Therefore, our first work was limited to the middle reaches. The rich cultural connotation, beautiful layout structure, and elegant yet simple architectural style of middle-reach villages gave our research results ready-made brilliance.

Our evaluation of upper-reach villages at that time was generally correct. Except for fairly prosperous market towns like Kunyang, Pankeng, and Bilian, upper-reach mountain areas were mostly very small villages, some with only "three or four fences, five or six wild houses." Ancestral halls and temples could occasionally be seen in a few villages, mostly small in scale and incomplete in system. However, we had actually long been interested in upper-reach settlements. In 1991, as middle-reach settlement research neared its end, the final episode was me and then-master's student Shu Nan, to verify the boundary of Nanxi River architectural style, under scorching sun, braving over 40°C heat, walking over four mountain ridges to Zhangjia'an, Baiyan, Jiaxi, and Yanlong. Our guide was a demobilized soldier, of the Jin clan from Yantou, with "bao" (leopard) in his name; he showed soldier-leopard toughness, climbing mountains like flat ground, exhausting Shu Nan to heatstroke, and my old cloth shoes both lost their soles, making "pit-pat" sounds with each step. Though quite arduous, that trip excited us greatly. Those settlements, hanging on hillsides, with clear transparent streams gurgling in the valleys. Light wooden houses, scattered and layered, through mist-like cooking smoke, looked like immortal mountain pavilions. A few small villages, surrounded by streams, required stepping on long stone stepping-stones to enter. Some villages had no stepping-stones at all; small bamboo rafts waited at the bank, travelers had to board and pole themselves, or grab a bamboo cable strung between banks, to slowly cross. Those villages, even if not beyond the human world, seemed not within it either. Coincidentally the weather was changeable, occasionally white clouds coiled around eaves, dynamic and transforming, making us enchanted, unconsciously hoping that the Wushan goddess would also float out here.

Village houses were elegant, mostly with certain order, varying freely with terrain起伏, at first glance seeming to grow naturally and spontaneously, only seeking intimacy with nature without artificial constraint. The framework was entirely supported by timber. Often large rough stones were used for foundations and ground-floor outer walls, with light and shadow, strong volumetric sense, as if by a sculptor's hand. But deeper into the mountains, brick and stone masonry decreased; in deep forest areas, some houses were left with only a light wooden frame and thin plank walls. How could such houses keep warm in winter? Mountain winds are harsh! Asking mountain people, we learned these houses, looking so ethereal, because they have a一圈 outer corridor; after autumn harvest each year, horizontal beams are placed between eave columns, and threshed rice straw is hung bunch by bunch on the beams, forming windproof and insulating barriers. Inside the house, fire basins burn all winter, using old tree roots; though flames are not strong, they maintain day and night warmth. Come next spring, as yang energy warms, the hanging straw is gradually pulled down to fuel kitchen stoves. As temperature rises day by day, the straw barrier thins; when hot weather comes, straw is burned up, and the house is ventilated on all sides, very cool. Thus one cycle per year, warm in winter and cool in summer, ingeniously conceived — perhaps this is a type of ecological architectural design. I had read in books that Italian rural areas, twenty or thirty thousand li away, had such farmhouses, admiring their ingenuity; coming to Nanxi River upper reaches, I learned that Chinese and foreign laborers were equally clever in this matter, thinking alike.

Nanxi River basin is a national scenic area. Middle-reach landscapes are softer: wide valleys, gentle mountains, sparkling waves; village girls carrying goose-shaped baskets to wash at the docks, once squatting by water, merge into natural scenery. Upper reaches are different: narrow gorges, rapid streams, steep slopes densely covered with trees and bamboo; in such a picture, the most fitting addition is a man with bare purplish-red chest, carrying heavy loads over mountains. During the Northern and Southern Dynasties, Liu Song poet Xie Lingyun served as Yongja Prefect; his poem "Climbing the Highest Peak of Shimen" has lines: "Sparse peaks support tall lodges, facing ridges above winding streams. Long forests line doorways, piled stones embrace steps. Continuous rocks seem to block the road, dense bamboo make paths confusing." Shimen is in Nanxi River upper reaches, where continuous mountain rocks block roads, dense bamboo groves shade paths, opening the door reveals forest, rocks jut right to the steps. That scenery is both majestic and desolate.

Upper-reach mountain people struggled for livelihood, far less than middle reaches with fertile land and surplus food and clothing, so their examination success was not as outstanding. But not entirely barren. Xikou Dai clan produced several important Song dynasty scholars, though it lies between upper and middle reaches, let's not discuss it. Pankeng, Kunyang, Bilian with continuous examination success are market towns, also let's set aside. Far in the northwest forest area, Yanlong Village, with few households, had an ancestral hall with a stage, and a pair of stone lions before the gate; the clan produced a jinshi. This small village only got electricity a few days before Shu Nan and I visited;当年的 scholars reading by window at night, perhaps not catching fireflies or reflecting snow, then — did they burn bamboo strips or oil lamps? Tallow oil or tung oil? In rural areas nationwide, no matter how remote or poor, we can almost see the distinct existence of unified Chinese classical culture. But even so, I vaguely realized that remote, isolated, naturally-living mountain villages must have had folk culture with明显 differences from middle reaches, with a touch of wildness. It would reflect in all aspects of material and spiritual life, including houses and villages. And I also realized this folk culture was rapidly disappearing, now barely remaining; we would soon lose them forever.

So we didn't completely reject studying a few villages in Nanxi River upper reaches. Moreover, even the poorest and most backward mountain villages represent one or several types of Chinese agrarian-era vernacular settlements; to write a complete genealogy of Chinese agricultural settlements, we certainly cannot do without them. Thus, in spring 2001, invited to Taishun, I first went to Wenzhou, hired a taxi at Oubei, and went to three upper-reach villages: Linkeng, Huangnan, and Shang'ao. Their landscapes were very different from any middle-reach village — more natural, more open, more intimate, more poetic, and architectural style differed from Yanlong and Jiaxi. This visit greatly aroused my enthusiasm; back in Beijing I suggested to Phoenix TV's "Searching for Vanishing Homelands" film crew to shoot these three villages. That summer, they finally went. Upon arriving at Linkeng, all crew friends were stunned by the extraordinarily beautiful scenery; they joined hands in a circle, shouting in unison, thanking me for bringing them there. After happily filming, I left Wenzhou on August 31. On September 2, the crew's aerial photography master Mr. Zhao Qunli unfortunately died in a plane crash near Linkeng. This accident caused great shock; Linkeng people, with mountain people's most sincere and strongest feelings, commemorated him, wanting to build a memorial hall; Yongjia County leaders also decided to protect Linkeng and other two villages to commemorate this outstanding figure. So we accepted the invitation, went to live in Linkeng in late autumn 2002, using it, Huangnan, and Shang'ao as starting points, beginning our Nanxi River upper-reach vernacular architecture research.

sections.name: 曲径通幽处
sections.content_zh:
曲径通幽处

林坑、上坳、黄南三村在永嘉县治上塘镇以北大约八十公里，楠溪江主流大楠溪的上游，接近源头了。从这三个村子向北走，十几里路，便上了分水岭，过去就是仙居县。三个村相距很近，从林坑到上坳步行只要十分钟，到黄南半小时就可以了。

它们现在同属黄南乡，过去属五十二都。这里自古以来就是林区。谢灵运有一首诗叫《从斤竹涧越岭溪行》，据光绪《永嘉县志》，斤竹涧就在五十二都。诗是这样写的：

猿鸣诚知曙，谷幽光未显。
岩下云方合，花上露犹泫。
逶迤傍隈隩，迢递陟陉岘。
过涧既厉急，登栈亦陵缅。
川渚屡经复，乘流玩回转。
苹萍泛沉深，菰蒲冒清浅。
企石挹飞泉，攀林摘叶卷。
想见山阿人，薜萝若在眼。
……

写的是山高谷深，草深林密，溪涧回环，野兽出没，而且洪莽未辟，路人还要登临栈道才得通行。2002年11月，我们来到理只村（古名里崔），海拔虽然只有四百米，但东望海拔一千二百多米的四海山林场，峰峦一层层一直叠到天边，竹木森森，两条谷底里溪水如带，泛着白光，奔流到我们脚下相会。那气势雄伟得惊心动魄，或许当年谢灵运见到的，就是这样的风光。

到楠溪江上游去的交通一向很艰难，都靠在盘旋的山路上步行，直到1991年才修成了一条很窄的从永嘉到仙居去的砂石公路，通过林坑、上坳和黄南。那年我们乘着三个轮子的"蹦蹦车"到上坳南邻李家坑去测绘一座风雨桥，还是这条公路的早期旅客。现在这条路正在改造，叫作四十一号省道，是一条战备路。

2001年春3月，我初次到林坑去，在瓯北码头乘了一辆出租小轿车，逆流而上，穿过整个楠溪江中游。芙蓉村、岩头村、苍坡村，这些十年前工作过的村子，一一在左手边掠过。右手边蜿蜒着清澈的江水，时时有茂密的滩林把它渲染得生气勃勃。钻过渡头村西北的山洞，公路过桥到了江东，河谷渐渐窄了，于是一丛丛杜鹃花就从山坡坡上向车子扑来。到了上游和中游交界的溪口村，我下车去看了一看，这是在宋代出过几位大理学家的村子，十年前我们曾在这里工作，现在旧貌彻底换了新颜，连当年戴氏族人引为无限荣光的存放皇帝诏书的圣旨门也改造成了贴白瓷砖的小楼。一时兴味索然，上车继续往北。大约三个小时罢，到了黄南口。这里是大楠溪上游两条溪流的交点，东侧的是黄山溪，西侧的是黄南溪。靠近交点，黄山溪上架着一条五跨石拱桥。过了桥，沿黄山溪北岸走，公路绕过一个山岬，正在改造的公路在这里打了一条隧道，还没有衬砌，不能走车。往前走，便是有一座风雨桥的李家坑。这是一座古村，"屋舍俨然"，不过老房子比十年前我们在这里测绘的时候更破烂了。新房子布局很杂乱，已经堵到了桥头，它们一般比老房子质量高，但农村的新房基地归土地管理部门划拨，不是"见缝插针"利用老村里的空地，就是干脆"拆旧建新"，利用老房基地，因此，根本不可能考虑整体的规划，老村破坏了，新村也乱七八糟。这是到处都有的现象，我只有叹息，像见到老朋友患了不治之症。

过了李家坑，黄南溪的山光水色变了样，山谷更窄了，山坡更陡了，溪里出现了一处处倔强的礁石，冒着白花的浅滩，碧绿的深潭。水声哗哗，回荡在两岸的石壁间。穿过一个峡口，再转一个弯，眼界忽然开阔，溪对岸绵延着一带房子，有高高的蛮石墙护着。墙后，房屋画出错错落落的天际线。几堵山墙上，原木构架在白粉壁衬托下勾出轻巧的图案，薄薄的屋坡和腰檐飘扬得老远，屋脊那一道楠溪江建筑特有的曲线，那么柔和，那么微妙。这小小的村子，看上一眼，人心就会软下来，感到生活的亲切。这就是上坳村。

溪这边，正对着上坳村，有一个小小的山口，车子左转弯往里一拐，从这时候起，我就成了那个捕鱼为业的武陵人了。山谷幽深，路右边一条小溪，缘溪而行，听水声哗哗啦啦。对岸，紧贴着溪水，陡然耸立起一堵几十米高的崖壁，挂满了藤蔓薜荔，长满了苔藓蕨薇，苍劲突兀，森气逼人。这崖壁叫"大肚崖"，很有林区山民声口的特色。这段小溪就叫"崖下溪"，也是顺口而来。我立刻就感到这些名称和中游"芙蓉崖""五鶒溪"那种由读书人咬嚼出来的雅号的鲜明对比。崖壁尽处，小小一座庙宇站立在临溪的一座高台上，这便是林坑的小水口了。狭窄的小水口把路逼得绕一个弯。前面只见群山簇聚的一个深谷，估计林坑村就要到了，我默默念着"只在此山中，云深不知处"。进了小水口，怀着对大自然的敬意下了车，大约走了百十来步，山峦忽然稍稍后退，让出一个小小的盆地，迎面一个长满了参天大树的小山包，抢前一步挤进盆地，把它分为两岔。岔里各有一条湍急的小溪奔腾在大大小小的礁石间，激起浪花飞沫，滋润得空气清爽新鲜。站在两条小溪的汇合处，抬头四望，我先是一惊，立刻就兴奋起来，眼前是仙山楼阁，循周遭山坡一层层参差重叠上去，构架玲珑，轩廊空阔。但它们梁前翩跹着紫燕，檐头缭绕着炊烟，分明是农户人家。衣衫鲜艳的孩子们趴在美人靠上，呼唤着溪边大石上蹲着洗衣的姐姐和妈妈。也许是太清秀了，洁白的鸭子围着她们浮来浮去，不肯离开。四面轻盈通透的楼台前，老人们闲闲地坐着，抽烟，轻声聊天。这不就是"黄发垂髫，并怡然自乐"吗？

这儿是林坑，这儿是"秦人旧舍"。沉淀在我心底的"桃花源情结"，一下子苏醒过来了，这正是一千多年来中国读书人朝暮渴望的田园。

现在，它在谢灵运歌吟过的奇丽环境中展陈在面前，山水之美和田园之情，那么和谐地结合在一起。陶渊明的桃花源是虚构的，作为安抚"池鱼"和"羁鸟"们的梦。我眼前的林坑，这一幅醉人的图画，也会掩盖着历史的和现实的种种矛盾，但我不愿去触动它，我需要休息、放松，我需要幻想中的宁静和安详。

这个在中国知识分子心理中因袭了一千多年的重担，也同样压在乡野文人的心中，渗透到农耕文明里去。我们曾经有许多次，看到宗谱里族内高人逸士的小传中常用的赞辞"足不践城市，身不入公门"，赋予这种闲云野鹤般的自由生活以一种道德价值。也曾经多次看到，在长长的龙骨水车上，一节一个字，写着"五日一风，十日一雨，帝力于我何有哉"，只要风调雨顺，五谷丰登，"化外之民"就什么都不在乎了。这是一种生活和心态上的满足，而"知足常乐"，就是所谓"农家乐"。
sections.content_en:
Winding Path to Secluded Place

Linkeng, Shang'ao, and Huangnan villages are about 80 km north of Shangtang Town, the county seat of Yongjia, in the upper reaches of the Great Nanxi River (main stream of Nanxi River), near its source. Going north from these three villages for over ten li, one reaches the watershed, beyond which is Xianju County. The three villages are close together; walking from Linkeng to Shang'ao takes only ten minutes, to Huangnan half an hour.

They now belong to Huangnan Township, formerly to the 52nd District (du). This has been forest area since ancient times. Xie Lingyun has a poem called "Crossing Ridges and Following Streams from Jinzhu Gully"; according to Guangxu "Yongjia County Annals," Jinzhu Gully is in the 52nd District. The poem reads:

Monkeys cry indeed knowing dawn, valley deep light not yet shown.
Below rocks clouds just gather, on flowers dew still glistens.
Winding along hidden bends, far ascending steep ridges.
Crossing gullies both swift and urgent, climbing plank roads also remote.
River islets repeatedly twist, riding currents playing with turns.
Duckweed floats in deep depths, wild rice rises in clear shallows.
Standing on rocks drawing flying springs, climbing forests picking curled leaves.
Imagining the person in the mountain hollow, climbing vines seem before eyes.
……

It describes high mountains and deep valleys, dense grass and forests, winding streams, wild beasts, and untamed wilderness, where travelers must climb plank roads to pass. In November 2002, we came to Lizhi Village (ancient name Li Cui), altitude only 400 meters, but looking east at the 1,200+ meter Sihai Mountain Forest Farm, peaks layer upon layer to the horizon, dense bamboo and trees, two valley streams like ribbons, gleaming white, rushing to meet at our feet. The momentum is breathtakingly majestic; perhaps what Xie Lingyun saw was such scenery.

Transportation to Nanxi River upper reaches has always been difficult, relying on walking along winding mountain paths; only in 1991 was a narrow gravel road from Yongjia to Xianju built, passing through Linkeng, Shang'ao, and Huangnan. That year we rode a three-wheeled "bouncing car" to Lijiakeng, south of Shang'ao, to survey a covered bridge — we were early travelers on this road. Now this road is being upgraded, called Provincial Highway No. 41, a strategic road.

In March 2001, on my first trip to Linkeng, I took a taxi from Oubei Wharf, going upstream through the entire middle reaches of Nanxi River. Furong Village, Yantou Village, Cangpo Village — these villages where we worked ten years ago — passed by on the left. On the right, clear river wound, with dense shoal forests making it vibrant. Through the cave northwest of Dutou Village, the road crossed the bridge to the east bank, the valley gradually narrowed, and clusters of azaleas rushed toward the car from the slopes. At Xikou Village, the boundary between upper and middle reaches, I got off to look — a village that produced several great Neo-Confucianists in Song dynasty, where we worked ten years ago. Now its old appearance completely changed; even the Shengzhi Gate, where the Dai clan proudly stored imperial edicts, was rebuilt into a small building with white ceramic tiles. Momentarily disheartened, I got back in and continued north. About three hours later, I reached Huangnankou. Here two upper-reach streams of Great Nanxi meet: east is Huangshan Stream, west is Huangnan Stream. Near the confluence, a five-span stone arch bridge spans Huangshan Stream. Crossing the bridge, along the north bank of Huangshan Stream, the road rounds a headland; the road being upgraded has a tunnel here, not yet lined, impassable. Going forward is Lijiakeng with a covered bridge. This is an ancient village, "houses neatly arranged," but old houses are more dilapidated than when we surveyed them ten years ago. New houses are chaotically laid out, already blocking the bridgehead; they are generally higher quality than old houses, but rural new housing plots are allocated by land management departments — either "squeezing into gaps" using empty land in old villages, or simply "tearing down old to build new" on old house sites — therefore overall planning is impossible; old villages destroyed, new villages messy. This phenomenon is everywhere; I can only sigh, like seeing an old friend with an incurable disease.

Past Lijiakeng, Huangnan Stream's scenery changes: valley narrower, slopes steeper, stubborn reefs appear in the stream, white-capped shallows, emerald green deep pools. Water rushes, echoing between stone banks. Through a gorge, around a bend, the view suddenly opens; across the stream stretches a row of houses, protected by high rough-stone walls. Behind the walls, houses form a jagged skyline. On several gable walls, original timber frameworks draw light patterns against white plaster walls; thin roof slopes and waist eaves extend far, the roof ridge curve characteristic of Nanxi River architecture, so soft, so subtle. This small village, at a glance, softens the heart, feeling the warmth of life. This is Shang'ao Village.

On this side of the stream, facing Shang'ao, is a small mountain pass; the car turns left in, and from this moment, I became that Wuling fisherman. Valley deep, a small stream on the right of the road, following it, hearing water gurgle. On the opposite bank, close to the water, abruptly rises a tens-of-meters-high cliff, covered with vines and climbing figs, moss and ferns, rugged and towering, awe-inspiring. This cliff is called "Big Belly Cliff," very much in the forest mountain people's colloquial style. This stream section is called "Below-Cliff Stream," also named casually. I immediately felt the contrast between these names and the elegant names of middle reaches like "Furong Cliff" and "Wuchi Stream," chewed over by scholars. At the cliff's end, a small temple stands on a high platform by the stream — this is Linkeng's small water mouth (shuikou). The narrow water mouth forces the road to bend. Ahead is only a deep valley clustered with mountains; estimating Linkeng Village near, I silently recited "only in this mountain, clouds deep unknown." Entering the small water mouth, with respect for nature I got off the car, walking about a hundred steps; mountains suddenly receded slightly, making a small basin; ahead, a small hill covered with towering trees pushed forward into the basin, dividing it into two branches. Each branch has a rapid stream rushing among large and small reefs,激起 spray and foam, making air fresh and clean. Standing at the confluence of the two streams, looking around, I was first startled, then immediately excited — before me were immortal mountain pavilions, layered unevenly up the surrounding slopes, with exquisite frameworks and spacious verandas. But purple swallows flit before their beams, cooking smoke curls from their eaves — clearly they are farmhouses. Colorfully dressed children lean on beauty rails (meirenkao), calling to sisters and mothers squatting on large rocks by the stream washing clothes. Perhaps too elegant, white ducks float around them, unwilling to leave. Before light and airy buildings on all sides, elderly people sit leisurely, smoking, chatting softly. Isn't this "yellow-haired and垂髫, all happy and content"?

This is Linkeng, this is "the old dwelling of Qin people." The "Peach Blossom Spring complex" settled in my heart suddenly awakened — this is exactly the countryside Chinese scholars have longed for day and night for over a thousand years.

Now it unfolds before me in the extraordinary environment Xie Lingyun sang of; beauty of mountains and waters and feeling of countryside combine so harmoniously. Tao Yuanming's Peach Blossom Spring was fictional, a dream to comfort "pond fish" and "caged birds." The Linkeng before my eyes, this intoxicating picture, may also hide various historical and现实 contradictions, but I don't want to touch them; I need rest, relaxation, I need imagined peace and serenity.

This burden inherited in Chinese intellectuals' psychology for over a thousand years also weighs on rural scholars' hearts, penetrating into agrarian civilization. We have many times seen in genealogies, in short biographies of clan recluses, the common praise "feet never tread cities, body never enter government gates,"赋予 this free wandering life a moral value. We have also many times seen on long dragon-bone waterwheels, one character per section, reading "wind every five days, rain every ten days, what has the emperor's power to do with me" — as long as favorable weather and abundant harvest, "people beyond civilization" care about nothing. This is a satisfaction in life and mindset, and "contentment brings happiness" is the so-called "peasant joy."

sections.name: 俞源村
sections.content_zh:
俞源村

1997年春天，我们做完了浙江省武义县郭洞村的调查、测绘工作，秋天到江西省乐安县的流坑村做村落的保护规划，1998年春天，又回到武义，这回的研究对象是俞源村。

俞源和郭洞一样，位置在一条山沟里，青山重重，绿水处处，风景非常优美。1949年以前，它的居民有不少是农业社会里的成功者，虽然山高沟窄，却在沟外平原里拥有大量肥沃的土地，经济很富裕，所以华堂丽屋，整齐可观。两个村子相距只有几十里，不到一小时的车程，风尚习俗并没有差别。我们的乡土建筑研究工作，每做一个课题，首先就得写出它的特点，而不是去重复地写那些到处都差不多的概括过的共性。这是我们工作的难处，也是我们工作的价值所在，我们之所以要在村子里一次住二十来天，还要去几次，就是为了抓住它的特点。这不只是那种浮面上一眼看得出来的特点，更是隐藏在深处的历史文化特点以及它们在环境、村落和建筑上的表现。这是我们的追求，虽然绝大多数村子的历史和民俗文化都早已模糊不清，我们常常感到失落，却仍然坚持着这样的追求。但要寻找俞源与郭洞的差别特点，可不容易。

俞源和郭洞的不同之处在于，郭洞的山沟非常偏僻，只有一个人的出入口，小小的村子躲在里面，宁静自得，仿佛连炊烟都只会笔直地升起。参天古树下的水口村门，把岁月都锁住了。说不定这里就是武陵捕鱼人无意中来过而又再也找不到了的地方。俞源的山沟却有大路通过，山场广阔，溪流又多少能起一点运输作用，俞源人利用这些条件，大都经商致富。这就给村子带来一些新的特点：它的宗法家族制比较弱，没有形成强有力的房派，因此没有建造大小房派的支祠，虽然也以房派的居住团块作为村落的结构单元，但没有支祠作为单元的中心而只有香火堂；而且它的房地产买卖没有受到房派的严格管制，所以各房派的后裔居住得比较杂乱；它的一些富商家大宅的规模显得浮夸；它们的大木作和小木作都很华丽。俞源村的过境大路两侧有一些店铺和作坊，甚至有一般农业村落没有的歇栈，晚期还有些公用设施。俞源人文化心理也比较开放，很早就有书院、赏玩风景的园亭，甚至还有迎宾馆。

但俞源人的商业活动还远远比不上我们工作过的兰溪诸葛村的居民。他们主要经营山货土产，自己拥有山场土地，赚了钱再来买山买地，资本没有脱离土地，身份也没有脱离地主，因此他们更多地依赖乡土，崇拜自然，市井文化几乎没有萌生。他们中虽然开始有人弃儒从商，但不敢像诸葛氏那样对重仕轻商的传统观念挑战，家谱里给大富人立传，总要说本来可以轻取功名，迫于不得已才去"理家"。俞源人发了财之后赶紧买一个贡生当当，好在家门前和祠堂门前立一棵桅杆。他们的豪宅有一股土财主气，规模很大，甚至很壮观，远远超过了普通农业村落的住宅，但它们都是支系的集合住宅，小家庭的私密性很少，居住质量不高，没有诸葛村的商人住宅那么大小得体、精致、安逸。俞源住宅的装饰雕刻，一方面很少见到农业时代耕读文化的"笔墨纸砚""琴棋书画"之类的题材；一方面也还没有像诸葛村那样处处可见聚宝盆、刘海戏金蟾、古老钱串之类。在俞源村，对财富的热切追求和炫耀，最强烈地表现在种种风水传说上，也就是对地理环境的自然崇拜上。在诸葛村，风水几乎只关系到最古老的宗法制时代的传统，主要是人口繁衍，而作为"商战之雄"，则靠的是"善操奇赢"，从不附会于风水。俞源村也没有形成一地的商业中心，只有几家小店铺和歇栈，供应本村的财主们和过往路人。

俞源村还有一个特点，就是它的鲜明的浪漫主义色彩。早在明代初年，就有些俞氏族人的先祖们爱壮游天下，交结四方豪杰。一去数年，北至燕赵秦晋，遍访名士贵胄，并且吟诗作画为记，留在宗谱。他们在家乡竟造了一所迎玩楼，拨田二百亩资用，作为招待宾客的场所。大约是这种性格的表现之一，俞源村，里里外外，几乎处处有故事、有神话，连它的种种风水之说也都故事化、神话化了。我们还从来没有见过一个村子有这么多有趣的故事和神话，笼罩在浓浓的浪漫主义气氛之中。故事和神话当然没有多少直接的历史真实性，但它们有感情的真实性，反映着村民的愿望、心理和信念，因此归根到底，它们也折射着历史的真实。只要善于理解，这些故事和神话对认识俞源村都很有价值，它们是民俗文化重要的一部分。

一个商业活动，一个浪漫主义色彩，我们在写作俞源村的研究报告的时候，抓住这样两个特点。但在环境、村落、建筑中的反映都很微妙，很难把握。我们希望读者们能知道我们的用心。

我们的乡土建筑研究，已经干了将近十年了。十年来，我们都是以聚落整体做研究对象，越做越知道，工作中最困难的是认识对象的特点，抓住特点，写出特点。这当然也是最重要的。只有一个个村落的独特性，才能汇合成中国乡土建筑的丰富性和生动性。匆匆做一般化的概括，只会把研究工作引向很狭窄的死胡同，而且很容易会有虚假和谬误。

在俞源村，我们住在洞主庙的圆梦楼里。窗外淌着两条山涧水，深夜躺在床上，听水声哗哗啦啦，奔流不息。山涧水从泉眼里滴出，从树根下渗出，它们不舍昼夜匆匆赶去的地方是钱塘江口，在那里它们投入掀天动地的钱塘大潮。它们在大潮里汹涌，卷起在高高的浪尖上，映着太阳飞溅，闪出自己灿烂的光彩。

2001年
sections.content_en:
Yuyuan Village

In spring 1997, we completed investigation and survey of Guodong Village in Wuyi County, Zhejiang Province; in autumn we went to Liukeng Village in Le'an County, Jiangxi Province to do village conservation planning; in spring 1998, we returned to Wuyi, this time the research object was Yuyuan Village.

Yuyuan, like Guodong, is located in a mountain valley, with green mountains layer upon layer and clear waters everywhere, scenery very beautiful. Before 1949, many of its residents were successful in agricultural society; though mountains high and valley narrow, they owned large amounts of fertile land in the plains outside the valley, economy very prosperous, so grand halls and beautiful houses, neat and impressive. The two villages are only几十 li apart, less than an hour's drive, with no difference in customs. Our vernacular architecture research, for each project, must first write out its characteristics, rather than repeatedly writing common generalizations found everywhere. This is the difficulty of our work, and also its value; the reason we stay in a village for over twenty days at a time, and visit several times, is to grasp its characteristics. Not only surface characteristics visible at a glance, but deeper historical and cultural characteristics and their expression in environment, village, and architecture. This is our pursuit; though most villages' history and folk culture have long been blurred, we often feel lost, yet persist in this pursuit. But finding the differing characteristics between Yuyuan and Guodong is not easy.

The difference between Yuyuan and Guodong is that Guodong's valley is very remote, with only one-person entrance, the small village hidden inside, tranquil and self-contained, as if even cooking smoke only rises straight. The water-mouth village gate under towering ancient trees locks away the years. Perhaps this is the place the Wuling fisherman accidentally visited and could never find again. Yuyuan's valley, however, has a main road passing through, vast mountain fields, and streams that can serve some transport function; Yuyuan people, using these conditions, mostly became wealthy through commerce. This brought new characteristics to the village: its patriarchal clan system was relatively weak, no strong lineage branches (fangpai) formed, so no branch ancestral halls (zhici) of various sizes were built; though lineage-branch residential blocks served as village structural units, there were no branch halls as unit centers, only incense halls; and its real estate transactions were not strictly controlled by lineage branches, so descendants of various branches lived relatively chaotically; some wealthy merchant mansions had exaggerated scale; their major and minor carpentry were both ornate. Along the transit road in Yuyuan Village were some shops and workshops, even inns (xiezhan) not found in ordinary agricultural villages, and in late period some public facilities. Yuyuan people's cultural psychology was also relatively open; early on there were academies, garden pavilions for enjoying scenery, even a guest house (yingbinguan).

But Yuyuan people's commercial activity was far less than that of Lanxi Zhuge Village residents we had worked on. They mainly dealt in mountain products and local goods, owning their own mountain fields and land; after making money, they bought more mountains and land — capital never脱离 land, status never脱离 landlord, so they relied more on native land, worshipped nature, and urban culture (shijing wenhua) hardly emerged. Though some began to abandon scholarship for commerce, they didn't dare challenge the traditional concept of valuing officialdom over commerce like the Zhuge clan; in genealogies, biographies of the very wealthy always say they could have easily earned academic honors, but were forced by necessity to "manage family affairs." After getting rich, Yuyuan people quickly bought a gongsheng (tribute student) title, so they could erect a mast before their home and ancestral hall. Their mansions had a rustic landlord air, large scale, even impressive, far exceeding ordinary agricultural village residences, but they were collective residences of branch lineages, with little privacy for small families, low residential quality, not as appropriately sized, refined, and comfortable as Zhuge Village's merchant residences. Yuyuan residences' decorative carvings: on one hand, rarely seen are agricultural-era farming-reading culture themes like "brush, ink, paper, inkstone" or "qin, qi, book, painting"; on the other hand, not yet like Zhuge Village where treasure basins, Liu Hai playing with golden toad, ancient coin strings are everywhere. In Yuyuan Village, the eager pursuit and display of wealth is most strongly expressed in various fengshui legends, i.e., nature worship of geographical environment. In Zhuge Village, fengshui almost only relates to the oldest patriarchal-era tradition, mainly population propagation; as "heroes of commercial warfare," they relied on "skillful speculation," never attaching to fengshui. Yuyuan Village also didn't form a local commercial center, only a few small shops and inns, serving the village's wealthy and passing travelers.

Yuyuan Village has another characteristic: its distinct romanticism. As early as early Ming, some Yu clan ancestors loved to travel widely, making friends with heroes everywhere. Gone for years, north to Yan-Zhao-Qin-Jin, visiting famous scholars and nobles, and composing poetry and paintings as records, kept in the clan genealogy. At home they even built a Yingwan (Welcome-Play) Tower, allocating 200 mu of farmland for expenses, as a place to entertain guests. Perhaps as one expression of this character, Yuyuan Village, inside and out, almost everywhere has stories and myths; even its various fengshui tales are storified and mythologized. We have never seen a village with so many interesting stories and myths, shrouded in thick romanticist atmosphere. Stories and myths of course have little direct historical authenticity, but they have emotional authenticity, reflecting villagers' desires, psychology, and beliefs; therefore ultimately, they also refract historical truth. As long as one is good at understanding, these stories and myths are valuable for understanding Yuyuan Village; they are an important part of folk culture.

One: commercial activity; two: romanticist color — when writing the Yuyuan Village research report, we grasped these two characteristics. But their reflection in environment, village, and architecture is very subtle, hard to把握. We hope readers can understand our intention.

Our vernacular architecture research has been going on for nearly ten years. For ten years, we have taken settlements as a whole as research objects; the more we do, the more we know that the most difficult part of the work is recognizing the object's characteristics, grasping characteristics, writing characteristics. This is of course also the most important. Only the uniqueness of individual villages can converge into the richness and vividness of Chinese vernacular architecture. Hastily making generalizations will only lead research into a narrow dead end, and easily produce falsehood and error.

In Yuyuan Village, we stayed in the Yuanmeng (Dream-Fulfilling) Tower of Dongzhu Temple. Outside the window flow two mountain streams; lying in bed late at night, listening to water gurgling, rushing endlessly. Mountain stream water drips from spring eyes, seeps from under tree roots; the place they rush to day and night is the Qiantang River mouth, where they投入 the earth-shaking Qiantang tidal bore. They surge in the great tide, curling on high wave crests, splashing in the sun, flashing their own brilliant radiance.

2001

sections.name: 九龙山下人家
sections.name_en: Families at the Foot of Jiulong Mountain
sections.content_zh:
九龙山下人家

俞源村现在位于浙江省中部的武义县。它原属宣平县，宣平在武义之南，但它在县境北缘，与武义县贴邻。1958年4月，宣平县并入武义县后，它就在武义县的中部了。宣平县是明朝景泰二年（1451）平定了一次银矿工人暴动后，为了加强弹压，于次年从丽水县划出设置的，俞源村却至迟在南宋末年已经有了居民，所以它最初属丽水县。

直到1927年以前，武义属金华，是婺州地界；宣平属丽水，是处州地界。处州也叫括州，因为它在括苍山区。婺州属钱塘江水系，处州属瓯江水系，武义和宣平分属两个水系，以樊岭、清风岭、大黄岭、少妃岭、大殿岭一线为分水岭。但俞源却在清风岭、大黄岭的北麓，它的溪水经丽阳川（今名武义江）入婺江、兰江，经富春江而达钱塘江。俞源和武义两个县的联系因此早就很密切，风尚习俗也相近。

俞源过去是宣平县两个最大的村子之一，20世纪中叶已经有大约三百户人家，现在人口早过了两千。它能够发展成为一座人烟稠密而富庶的聚落，自有一些特殊的条件。

俞源南靠宣平的大山区，它位于一个狭窄的山坳里，水田不多，但山区物产丰富，很利于多种经营。有一首山歌唱道：

种田不如种山场，
种起苞谷当口粮，
种起番薯养猪娘，
种起棉花做衣裳，
种起靛青落富阳，
种起杉树造屋做栋梁，
住在高山上，风吹荫荫凉。

多种经营萌生了以贩运为主的早期商业，这便是俞源潜在的优势之一。它在山脚之下，避免了山上的各种困难，而向北出它所在的山坳不远便是广阔而富饶的金华盆地南端的武义平原，水田十分肥沃，这又是它的潜在优势之一。

俞源也沾上交通方便的利。它位于从武义到宣平的大路上，也便是从婺州到处州的大路上。从婺州到杭州可经钱塘江通舟楫，从处州到温州则可直下瓯江，也通舟楫。因此，古时杭州和温州之间的官私交通都走这条路，也便是都经过俞源。俞源北距武义城四十五里，南距宣平城也是四十五里，正是赶脚人一天路程的中点。加上它正处在山地和平野的交会点上，自然是一个歇歇气，换一双草鞋，吃一顿竹筒饭的好场所。俞源又是地方性小水运的起点。它身边的俞川溪将近二十米宽，虽因多急弯，不足以通舟楫，甚至不通竹筏，但可以在旺水季节流放短木材，乡人叫作"赶羊"。赶下去十几里，到乌溪桥便可以编排外运。别的山货也能从那里经武义江直下钱塘江。俞源得了水陆转运和山货汇集的便利，所以很早就有小歇栈和小商店，村民的性格也比较开放。

单纯依靠山场，依靠官路和小溪，俞源人还是不可能富起来的。他们更重要的是依靠从迁来之始便有的社会和文化优势。大约从明代起，俞源村的主姓便是俞姓，俞姓的始迁祖俞德是南宋末年的松阳县儒学教谕。他有文化，也有比较多的社会联系，爱游历，眼界开阔，重视子子孙孙的教育。到元代末年，俞氏在当地就成了望族。俞源村的第二大姓是李姓，明初始迁祖李彦兴的叔父是一位进士，当过御史。弘治《俞源李氏重修谱序》说李彦兴"读书乐善，仗义丰财"，一到俞源，便娶了当时已经声望很高的俞氏的女儿为妻。李氏也很快成了当地的望族。正是这种社会和文化的优势，使他们能抓住交通和资源的潜在优势，至迟从明代晚期起便经营贩运，再以所得广置田产。他们的田产起初在山坳北口外的村子里，后来扩展到整个武义平原各处，极盛时连金华、宣平郊区都有他们的田产，建起田庄。俞源很快便胜过了远近很大范围里文化教育水平比较低的纯农业村落。在那个宗法制度时代，血缘网络的作用之下，俞源村的俞、李二姓都有七八成的住户经商，并且拥有大量水田。普遍的富裕促进了整个村子的发达，终于烟灶稠密，成了大村。俞源人很狂傲地诌了一句话："金村、荷漾、溪口，不值俞源金狗。"金狗是清代嘉庆、道光年间本村大财主俞志俊的绰号。金村、荷漾、溪口都是武义的大村。

俞源的自然形势大有利于它形成一个内聚性很强的村落。它四面环山，谷地狭窄，只有南、北两个曲折的出口。南面的出口是崎岖的上山路。北面的出口有一座不高的凤凰山遮挡。由武义平原过来，左右的群山渐渐逼近，绕过凤凰山角，突然就进了四面被山围住的俞源。这样的环境，能够强化宗族成员的认同心理，给村人以有力的安全感。村民称这个地形为"口袋形"，把村子的兴旺归因于它，说它只能往里装财宝，不会往外流失。这样的风水传说，反映出萌芽状态的商业活动还没有冲破村人对生养他们的土地的依恋。

俞源村的山水风光是非常美的。周遭的山，千形万状，有雄奇的，有秀丽的，有峻峭的，有浑厚的，重重叠叠，一层又一层，愈远愈高。几道深沟幽谷，切进群山中去，引出溪水，在岩石上左冲右突，跌扑而下，溅成白花，哗哗地响。当年山上满布浓密的混交森林，四季变换着颜色。水中有鱼，天上有鸟，林子里奔窜着野兽，万类都在这里享受着生命的愉悦。明代初年苏伯衡为俞源人写的《皆山楼记》描绘得很生动：俞源"介于群山之中，其地方广数里，山联络无间断。其溪折行山罅间，首尾皆自高趋下，初于山隙处遥遥望见，是为瀑布。其田皆垦山址为之，累石以为畔岸，高高百丈，秩若阶级。其路皆侧径，绿崖悬蹬，临流如曳练，隐见木末。其民居多负山，而因山以为垣墉，散处凡数百家。族大而望于乡者曰俞氏"（见《俞源俞氏宗谱》）。俞、李二姓的宗谱里都说他们的始迁祖是因为爱这里的风景之美而迁来定居的。大约在元末明初，俞源就有了"八景"和"十景"，累世题咏不绝。村民们热爱这片栖居之地，几百年来给几乎所有的山、崖、洞、石，所有的溪、潭、井、泉，都编了引人入胜的神话故事和传说，使他们的生活环境充满了浪漫的诗意。大多数的神话故事和沉香劈山救母有关，周围的山水木石都因沉香的勇敢善良、因他与龙王和二郎神的英勇的战斗而生气勃勃。作为俞源村"发脉之山"的九龙山，传说本来是东海龙宫，沉香用宝葫芦吸干了东海水，龙宫变成了九龙山。九龙山伸向俞源的一脉就叫龙宫山。

村民们也把俞源的富庶归因于当地的山水。这便有了大量的风水堪舆的说法。比如说：东面的九龙山是青龙，东溪水碧；西面的雪峰山是黄龙，西溪水浑。两条溪在村边合流，"清水冲浑水，浑水混清水，代代出财主"。俞姓的大宗祠就造在两溪合流之处。俞源大约是风水堪舆的传说最多也最神奇的村落之一，几乎所有的传说，都在解释和夸耀俞源的富庶。因为相传俞氏第五代俞涞的儿子、孙子都和明代开国功臣刘基（伯温）友善，这件事成了俞氏后代的骄傲，所以这些风水传说又常常和刘基发生关系。

可惜，现在和美丽的神话故事有关的以及和神异的风水传说有关的许多东西都遭到了破坏。在一个科学昌明的时代，这些神话和传说不免都显得幼稚甚至荒诞，但是，它们所映照出来的那些宗法时代农民们的理想和愿望，他们单纯的、近乎天真的自负，是很可爱的，而且具有认识的价值。它们本来可以像林花山鸟一样永远装点着河山，使河山富有灵气。

然而，现在俞源四周的山上连林木鸟兽都已经稀少了。1958年大炼钢铁的"全民运动"中，整山整坡的树木砍了去烧土高炉，连几百年的古老香樟树也一样烧成了灰，把好端端的农具甚至饭锅炼成了废铁渣。武义有一首新民歌唱道：

山中树木都砍走，
山坑冷坞断水流，
一心炼铁火焰高，
哪怕畲山剃光头。（见《武义县歌谣卷》1989年）

山上没有了树木，涵养不了水分，青龙也变成了黄龙，两条溪水都浑了，而且雨少了就旱，雨多了就暴发山洪。1960年，赶上全国性的大灾荒，号召开山自救，更彻底地破坏了自然植被。于是，1961年，一场大雨，俞源村里水深一米，浸塌房屋两幢，一座木桥和两座石板桥被冲走，村北溪流下游的堤坝大部冲塌。生态的破坏，到现在还没有动手去恢复，却恢复了过去的老迷信，年年到东南方沉香显过灵的龙潭去祈求龙王保祐。村后向阳的锦屏山上，只见新坟累累，光秃秃不见绿色。清明时节，满山细竹竿挑着的"蟒纸"，在东风中轻灵地卷扬飞动，烧剩的纸灰，高高飘起，悄悄撒落在村庄人家。村人们现在把锦屏山叫作大坟山，忘记了它过去美丽的名字。当然更没有人知道"金屏红旭"曾是宗谱中记载着的《俞川十咏》之一。俞缪的诗这样写着："红日光从海峤腾，重重瑞气霭金屏。景添晓色山川胜，千古钟英此地灵。"金屏就是锦屏，那景色可就全变了。

俞源人过去拥有的大量农田在20世纪50年代初期的改革中失去了大半。以后，竹木砍光了，硬炭烧不成了，靛青淘汰了，苎麻也不种了。新建的武义到宣平的汽车路从村北几里路外的宋村转弯，不再经过俞源，它成了交通的盲肠。俞源人赖以致富的资源和交通优势都不再存在。过去全宣平县数一数二的富村俞源，成了贫困村。幸而近年重新有了转机，不少年轻人外出打工，收入不错，甚至有人自己买十几个座位的中型客车，专跑武义、王宅，一天能赚几十块钱。听说现在孩子们读书成绩都很好，或许俞姓人、李姓人的书香传统还能重新振兴俞源。但青龙也还得及早唤回！
sections.content_en:
People Below Nine Dragons Mountain

Yuyuan Village is now located in Wuyi County, central Zhejiang Province. It originally belonged to Xuanping County, which was south of Wuyi, but Yuyuan was at the northern edge of Xuanping, adjacent to Wuyi County. In April 1958, after Xuanping County was merged into Wuyi County, it became central Wuyi County. Xuanping County was established in the second year of Ming Jingtai (1451), after suppressing a silver miners' uprising, to strengthen control, carved out from Lishui County the following year; but Yuyuan Village had residents as early as late Southern Song, so it originally belonged to Lishui County.

Until 1927, Wuyi belonged to Jinhua, Wuzhou territory; Xuanping belonged to Lishui, Chuzhou territory. Chuzhou was also called Kuozhou, because it was in the Kuocang mountain area. Wuzhou belonged to Qiantang River system, Chuzhou to Ou River system; Wuyi and Xuanping belonged to two water systems, with Fan Ridge, Qingfeng Ridge, Dahuang Ridge, Shaofei Ridge, and Dadian Ridge as the watershed. But Yuyuan was at the northern foot of Qingfeng and Dahuang Ridges; its stream flows through Liyangchuan (now Wuyi River) into Wu River, Lan River, via Fuchun River to Qiantang River. Thus Yuyuan and Wuyi counties had long been closely connected, with similar customs.

Yuyuan was formerly one of the two largest villages in Xuanping County; by mid-20th century it had about 300 households, now population over 2,000. It could develop into a densely populated and prosperous settlement due to special conditions.

Yuyuan is backed by Xuanping's large mountain area to the south, located in a narrow mountain hollow with little paddy field, but rich mountain products, favorable for diversified farming. A folk song sings:

Farming is not as good as mountain fields,
Plant corn for staple food,
Plant sweet potatoes to raise sows,
Plant cotton for clothes,
Plant indigo to sell in Fuyang,
Plant fir trees to build houses as beams,
Living on high mountains, wind blows cool shade.

Diversified farming spawned early commerce centered on trafficking, one of Yuyuan's potential advantages. It is at the mountain foot, avoiding mountain difficulties, and north out of its hollow not far is the broad and fertile Wuyi Plain at the southern end of Jinhua Basin, with very fertile paddy fields — another potential advantage.

Yuyuan also benefited from convenient transportation. It was on the main road from Wuyi to Xuanping, i.e., from Wuzhou to Chuzhou. From Wuzhou to Hangzhou, boats navigated via Qiantang River; from Chuzhou to Wenzhou, boats went straight down Ou River. Thus ancient official and private traffic between Hangzhou and Wenzhou took this road, passing through Yuyuan. Yuyuan is 45 li north of Wuyi city, 45 li south of Xuanping city — exactly the midpoint of a porter's one-day journey. Plus it is at the junction of mountains and plains, naturally a good place to rest, change straw sandals, eat a bamboo-tube meal. Yuyuan was also the starting point of local small water transport. Its nearby Yuchuan Stream is nearly 20 meters wide; though with many sharp bends, not navigable by boats or even bamboo rafts, short timber could be floated downstream in high-water season, locally called "driving sheep." Floating over ten li to Wuxi Bridge, it could be rafted for transport. Other mountain products also went from there via Wuyi River straight down Qiantang River. Yuyuan gained convenience of land-water transshipment and mountain product collection, so early on it had small inns and shops, and villagers' character was relatively open.

Relying solely on mountain fields, official roads, and streams, Yuyuan people still couldn't get rich. More importantly, they relied on social and cultural advantages from the time of settlement. From about Ming dynasty, the main surname of Yuyuan Village was Yu; the founding ancestor Yu De was a Confucian school instructor in Songyang County in late Southern Song. He was cultured, had many social connections, loved travel, broad-minded, valued descendants' education. By late Yuan, Yu clan became a prominent local family. The second largest surname was Li; the Ming founding ancestor Li Yanxing's uncle was a jinshi, served as censor. Hongzhi "Yuyuan Li Clan Genealogy Preface" says Li Yanxing "loved reading and goodness, upheld justice and was generous"; upon arriving at Yuyuan, he married the daughter of the already prestigious Yu clan. Li clan also quickly became prominent locally. It was these social and cultural advantages that enabled them to seize potential transportation and resource advantages, operating trafficking at least from late Ming, then using proceeds to buy extensive farmland. Their farmland initially was in villages north of the hollow mouth, later expanded throughout Wuyi Plain, at peak even in Jinhua and Xuanping suburbs, building manors. Yuyuan soon surpassed purely agricultural villages with lower cultural education levels over a wide area. In that patriarchal era, under blood-relation network作用, 70-80% of Yu and Li households in Yuyuan did business and owned large amounts of paddy field. Universal prosperity promoted the whole village's development, finally becoming a large village with dense households. Yuyuan people arrogantly coined a saying: "Jin Village, Heyang, Xikou, not worth Yuyuan's Golden Dog." Golden Dog was the nickname of Yu Zhijun, a wealthy local landlord in Qing Jiaqing-Daoguang period. Jin Village, Heyang, Xikou were all large Wuyi villages.

Yuyuan's natural terrain greatly favored forming a strongly cohesive village. It is surrounded by mountains, with a narrow valley, only two winding exits — south and north. The south exit is a rugged mountain path. The north exit is blocked by a low Fenghuang (Phoenix) Mountain. Coming from Wuyi Plain, mountains on both sides gradually close in; rounding the Phoenix Mountain corner, one suddenly enters Yuyuan, surrounded by mountains. Such environment strengthens clan members' identity and gives villagers a strong sense of security. Villagers call this terrain "pocket-shaped," attributing the village's prosperity to it, saying it can only hold treasure inside, not let it flow out. Such fengshui legends reflect that budding commercial activity hadn't yet broken villagers' attachment to the land that nurtured them.

Yuyuan Village's mountain-water scenery is very beautiful. Surrounding mountains, in countless shapes — majestic, graceful, steep,浑厚 — layer upon layer, farther and higher. Several deep valleys cut into the mountains,引出 streams, dashing left and right over rocks, plunging down, splashing white flowers, roaring. Once mountains were covered with dense mixed forests, changing colors with seasons. Fish in water, birds in sky, beasts in forests — all enjoyed life's pleasure here. Early Ming Su Boheng wrote vividly in "Jieshan Tower Record" for Yuyuan people: Yuyuan "among mountains, its place several li wide, mountains connected without break. Its stream winds through mountain gaps, head and tail both from high to low; first seen from mountain gap afar, it is a waterfall. Its fields are reclaimed on mountain slopes, stone piled as banks, high up a hundred zhang, orderly as steps. Its roads are narrow paths, along cliffs and hanging steps, by stream like pulled silk, glimpsed through treetops. Its residences mostly back mountains, using mountains as walls, scattered several hundred households. The large clan prominent in the district is the Yu clan" (see "Yuyuan Yu Clan Genealogy"). Both Yu and Li clan genealogies say their founding ancestors settled here because they loved the scenic beauty. Around late Yuan-early Ming, Yuyuan had "Eight Scenes" and "Ten Scenes," with generations of poetry. Villagers loved their dwelling place; over centuries, they wove fascinating myths and legends for almost every mountain, cliff, cave, rock, stream, pool, well, spring, filling their living environment with romantic poetry. Most myths relate to Chen Xiang splitting mountains to save his mother; surrounding mountains, waters, trees, rocks became vibrant through Chen Xiang's bravery and kindness, and his heroic battles with Dragon King and Erlang Shen. As Yuyuan's "origin mountain," Nine Dragons Mountain was legendarily the East Sea Dragon Palace; Chen Xiang used a treasure gourd to suck dry the East Sea, and the Dragon Palace became Nine Dragons Mountain. The ridge extending toward Yuyuan is called Dragon Palace Mountain.

Villagers also attributed Yuyuan's prosperity to local mountains and waters. This gave rise to numerous fengshui geomancy sayings. For example: the east Nine Dragons Mountain is Azure Dragon, east stream water green; the west Xuefeng Mountain is Yellow Dragon, west stream water muddy. The two streams merge at the village edge: "clear water strikes muddy water, muddy water mixes clear water, generations produce wealthy men." The Yu clan's great ancestral hall was built at the confluence. Yuyuan is perhaps one of the villages with the most and most miraculous fengshui legends; almost all legends explain and boast Yuyuan's prosperity. Because legend says Yu Lai's (5th generation Yu) sons and grandsons were friends with Ming founding merit minister Liu Ji (Bowen), this became Yu descendants' pride, so these fengshui legends often relate to Liu Ji.

Unfortunately, many things related to beautiful myths and miraculous fengshui legends have now been destroyed. In an age of advanced science, these myths and legends inevitably seem naive or even absurd, but the ideals and aspirations of patriarchal-era farmers they reflect, their simple, almost innocent self-satisfaction, are lovely and have cognitive value. They could have adorned mountains and rivers forever like forests, flowers, birds, and beasts, giving them spiritual vitality.

However, now even trees, birds, and beasts on Yuyuan's surrounding mountains are scarce. In the 1958 "all-people movement" of backyard steelmaking, entire mountain slopes of trees were cut for earthen blast furnaces; even centuries-old camphor trees were burned to ash, and good farm tools甚至 cooking pots were smelted into scrap iron. Wuyi has a new folk song:

Mountain trees all cut away,
Mountain hollows cold, streams stop flowing,
Wholeheartedly smelting iron, flames high,
Even She mountains shaved bald. (See "Wuyi County Folk Songs Volume" 1989)

Without trees on mountains, water couldn't be conserved; Azure Dragon became Yellow Dragon, both streams turned muddy; less rain brought drought, more rain brought flash floods. In 1960, during the nationwide great famine, "opening mountains for self-rescue" was called for, further destroying natural vegetation. Thus in 1961, a heavy rain flooded Yuyuan Village one meter deep, collapsing two houses, washing away one wooden bridge and two stone slab bridges, and most embankments downstream of the north stream were breached. Ecological destruction hasn't been restored yet, but old superstitions have revived — yearly going to the Dragon Pool in the southeast where Chen Xiang manifested spirit to pray for Dragon King's blessing. On the sunny Jinping Mountain behind the village, only new graves pile up, bare without green. At Qingming, thin bamboo poles across the mountain carry "python paper," lightly swirling in the east wind; burned paper ash rises high, quietly falling on village homes. Villagers now call Jinping Mountain "Big Grave Mountain," forgetting its beautiful old name. Of course no one knows that "Golden Screen Red Sunrise" was one of the "Ten Chants of Yuchuan" recorded in the genealogy. Yu Miao's poem reads: "Red sunlight rises from sea cape, layers of auspicious mist veil golden screen. Scene adds dawn color, mountains and rivers superb, through ages nurturing talent this place divine." Golden Screen is Jinping — that scenery has completely changed.

The large farmland Yuyuan people once owned was mostly lost in the early 1950s reforms. Afterwards, bamboo and timber were cut bare, charcoal couldn't be made, indigo was淘汰, ramie no longer planted. The new Wuyi-Xuanping highway turns at Song Village, several li north of the village, no longer passing Yuyuan — it became a transportation dead end. The resources and transportation advantages Yuyuan people relied on for wealth no longer exist. Yuyuan, once one of the top two wealthy villages in all Xuanping County, became a poor village. Fortunately, recent years have brought a turnaround; many young people go out to work with good income, some even buy 10+ seat mid-size buses running Wuyi-Wangzhai, earning几十 yuan a day. I hear children now do well in school; perhaps the scholarly tradition of Yu and Li clans can revive Yuyuan. But the Azure Dragon must also be called back soon!

key_terms.en: Chen Xiang splitting mountain to save mother

sections.name: 苍坡村
sections.content_zh:
苍坡村

都说乡土建筑是一本乡土生活和乡土文化的历史书。乡民们想些什么，做些什么，村落和房舍就记录下什么。

楠溪江村边的路亭里、村中的水阁里，美人靠上靠着的是些满脸风霜的老年人，他们把楠溪江人的遗闻逸事一遍又一遍絮说，一代又一代流传了下来。这些遗闻逸事，在乡土建筑这本历史书上都能读到。田夫野老最爱说的故事里，有几则发生在小小的苍坡村。

苍坡村的东面和南面，平展展几百亩水田。秋熟时节，夕阳下，橙红色的稻叶像遍地的火焰，一直烧到苍坡村寨墙下。村子的西面和北面，层层叠叠的山峦，青绿色，倒像汹涌的海浪。这村子，初建于五代后周显德二年（955）。

溪水从西北来，快快活活流进苍坡村，曲曲折折在小巷里流过，把清凉和洁净送到家家户户。流到村子东南角，寨墙加高加厚，把水拦蓄成两个大大的池子，一个在东，叫东池，一个在西，叫西池。

村子的正门开在南寨墙上，两个池子之间，偏一点儿西。传说苍坡村跟南面的霞美村有世仇，各自在风水上斗法。苍坡村的正门前辟了两亩来大的一泓半月形的水池，抵挡霞美村施过来的煞气。池里荷叶田田，池边蒹葭苍苍，衬托着质朴而雄壮的寨门。那寨门，结构刚健，显出乡民的性格。

一进寨门，便打开了历史书，左边一页是西池，右边一页是东池。夹在两页之间的，是李氏大宗祠。传统农业时代，宗祠照管着村民生活的一切方面。它最关心的两件事，一是聚亲睦族，一是科甲连登，事关生存和发展。

那西池一页，记载的是半耕亦半读的生活理想，祠规教导："耕为本务，读可荣身"。耕读的理想，要风水来寄托。

村子的西方有一座山，三个尖尖的山峰，齐齐地并肩而立。村人说，那是笔架。西池宽阔，村人说，那是砚池。笔架山正巧倒映在砚池中，村人说，那是"文笔蘸墨"，权把笔架当作笔尖。真正的笔在西池北岸，村子的主街，它又平又直，正对笔架山，就叫笔街。砚池北岸还有小小一方空地，躺着三根几米长的石条，便是墨锭。其中一根已经研磨过，端头有一点儿斜。笔街以北，展开村子的建筑区，几条巷子，把它划成竖格，那不是笺纸又是什么？

笔墨纸砚，文房四宝，一一都齐全了。年轻的读书人啊，你们还缺什么？缺的只是你坐下来，静心息虑，刻苦攻读了。"朝为田舍郎，暮登天子堂"，这样的机会，只等你自己去抓紧。前辈们成功的榜样，你们不是已经看到了吗？三退巷和儿间巷里整整齐齐的大宅子，便是"书中自有黄金屋"的明证。

再看东池那一页历史。东池不宽，南北向倒有一百几十米长。北头有一座水月堂，南头是兼作拦水坝用的寨墙。墙上立着一座望兄亭。水月堂和望兄亭都说着同样的故事，两个故事，一个发生在北宋末年，一个在南宋初年。

水月堂的故事略略有点儿叫人凄然神伤。徽宗时候，苍坡八世祖李霞溪任迪功郎，他哥哥李锦溪任成忠郎，兄弟友好，情深意切。李锦溪在宣和二年（1120）随童贯征辽，不幸战死沙场，为国捐躯。李霞溪心碎肠断，不能再在汴京当官，就辞去职务，回归故里。这时候东、西两池已经形成，他便在东池北头水中央造了这座水月堂，住在里面，日夜思念兄长，"寄兴觞咏，以终老焉"。

望兄亭的故事有点儿浪漫。南宋高宗时候，七世祖李秋山、李嘉木两兄弟感情深笃。建炎二年（1128），李秋山迁徙到东面两里路外的方巷村。弟弟每天一早就站在寨墙上向东远望，等待哥哥踏着田间的卵石路走来，"会桃李之芳园，叙天伦之乐事"。晚上，弟弟送哥哥到方巷，哥哥再回送弟弟到小溪边。弟弟进了苍坡村，先到寨墙上摇一摇灯笼，哥哥见了才放心回家休息。天长日久，弟弟在寨墙上造了望兄亭，哥哥在小溪边造了送弟阁。两座亭子遥遥相望，一模一样。望兄亭上的对联，写的是："礼重人伦明古训；亭传佳话继家风。"这古训、这家风，就是告诫子弟，家族内部，大家要相亲相爱。宗族的内聚力是宗族兴旺发达的基本条件。

西池东池，两页书写的是农业社会中关系宗族命运最重要的两件大事。

还有第二件大事，那便是敬祀神明。大宗祠的东南侧，西池东池之间的中缝里，十世祖李伯钧于南宋孝宗淳熙七年（1180）造了一座仁济庙，庙里供的是平水圣王周凯。他是西晋人，能治水患，屡显神异，唐时封为平水显应公，宋时加爵护国仁济王。水是农业的命脉，在农业社会中，管水的神总会受到特殊的尊崇，不论是兴水利的还是平水害的。或许因为他是水神，所以让他的庙三面临水，东面是东池，西面是东西两池之间的一个小池，南面则是连通东西池的一道渠水。临水的三面都用敞廊，设美人靠。人也亲水，庙也亲水，异常的轻灵妩媚。庙里的院落，竟也是一池水，种着莲花，清香四溢。庙融进了园林里，人性化了。人性化正是乡土神灵的特色，他们用慈爱的心，抚慰人们的痛苦，给人们以生活的希望。
sections.content_en:
Cangpo Village

It is said that vernacular architecture is a history book of rural life and rural culture. What villagers think and do, villages and houses record.

In roadside pavilions by Nanxi River villages and in water pavilions within villages, on beauty rails (meirenkao) lean weather-beaten elderly people, who recount Nanxi River people's anecdotes over and over, passing them down generation after generation. These anecdotes can all be read in the history book of vernacular architecture. Among the stories farmers and old folks love most, several took place in small Cangpo Village.

East and south of Cangpo Village, hundreds of mu of flat paddy fields stretch out. In autumn harvest season, under the setting sun, orange-red rice leaves look like flames everywhere, burning right up to Cangpo's village wall. West and north of the village, layered mountains, blue-green, resemble surging ocean waves. This village was first built in the second year of Later Zhou Xiande (955).

Stream water comes from the northwest, cheerfully flowing into Cangpo Village, winding through alleys, bringing coolness and cleanliness to every household. Flowing to the village's southeast corner, the village wall is raised and thickened, damming the water into two large pools — one east, called East Pool; one west, called West Pool.

The village's main gate is on the south wall, between the two pools, slightly west. Legend says Cangpo Village had a generations-long feud with Xiamai Village to the south, each fighting in fengshui. Before Cangpo's main gate, a two-mu crescent-shaped pool was dug to deflect the evil qi from Xiamai Village. Lotus leaves fill the pool, reeds grow by the banks, setting off the simple and majestic village gate. The gate, with its robust structure, reveals villagers' character.

Entering the gate opens the history book: left page is West Pool, right page is East Pool. Between the two pages stands the Li Great Ancestral Hall. In traditional agricultural society, the ancestral hall oversaw all aspects of village life. Its two greatest concerns were: uniting the clan, and continuous examination success — matters of survival and development.

The West Pool page records the ideal of half-farming half-studying; clan rules teach: "Farming is the fundamental task, studying can glorify oneself." The farming-reading ideal is entrusted to fengshui.

West of the village is a mountain with three sharp peaks, standing side by side evenly. Villagers say that is a brush rest (bijia). West Pool is broad; villagers say that is an inkstone (yanchi). The brush-rest mountain happens to reflect in the inkstone pool; villagers say that is "writing brush dipping ink," treating the brush rest as the brush tip. The real brush is north of West Pool — the village's main street, flat and straight, facing the brush-rest mountain, called Brush Street (Bijie). North of the inkstone pool is a small open space with three several-meter-long stone bars lying there — those are ink ingots (moding). One has been ground, with a slanted end. North of Brush Street, the village's building area展开, with several alleys dividing it into vertical grids — what are those if not writing paper?

Brush, ink, paper, inkstone — the four treasures of the study, all complete. Young scholars, what do you still lack? Only that you sit down, calm your mind, and study diligently. "Morning a farmer's son, evening in the emperor's hall" — such opportunity waits only for you to seize it. Haven't you already seen the examples of successful predecessors? The neat large mansions in Santui Lane and Erjian Lane are proof that "in books there is a golden house."

Now look at the East Pool page of history. East Pool is not wide, but north-south it is over 100 meters long. At the north end is Shuiyue (Water-Moon) Hall; at the south end is the village wall doubling as a dam. On the wall stands Wangxiong (Gazing-at-Brother) Pavilion. Both Shuiyue Hall and Wangxiong Pavilion tell similar stories — one from late Northern Song, one from early Southern Song.

The Shuiyue Hall story is somewhat poignant. During Huizong's reign, Cangpo's 8th-generation ancestor Li Xaxi served as Digonglang; his brother Li Jinxi served as Chengzhonglang; the brothers were close and affectionate. Li Jinxi, in Xuanhe 2nd year (1120), accompanied Tong Guan on the campaign against Liao, unfortunately dying in battle, sacrificing for the country. Li Xaxi was heartbroken, unable to continue serving in Bianjing, so he resigned and returned home. By then East and West Pools had formed; he built this Shuiyue Hall in the middle of the water at the north end of East Pool, living inside, day and night missing his brother, "finding solace in wine and poetry, to end his days there."

The Wangxiong Pavilion story is somewhat romantic. During Southern Song Gaozong's reign, 7th-generation ancestors Li Qiushan and Li Jiamu were deeply affectionate brothers. In Jianyan 2nd year (1128), Li Qiushan moved to Fangxiang Village, two li east. Every morning the younger brother stood on the village wall gazing east, waiting for his brother to walk along the field cobblestone path, "meeting in the peach-plum fragrant garden, recounting the joy of family ties." In the evening, the younger brother escorted the older to Fangxiang, then the older escorted the younger back to the stream. The younger, entering Cangpo, first went to the wall to wave a lantern; the older, seeing it, went home reassured. Over time, the younger built Wangxiong Pavilion on the wall, and the older built Songdi (Seeing-Off-Brother) Pavilion by the stream. The two pavilions face each other from afar, identical. The couplet on Wangxiong Pavilion reads: "Rites value human relations, clarifying ancient teachings; pavilion passes佳话, continuing family tradition." This ancient teaching, this family tradition, admonishes descendants: within the clan, all must love one another. Clan cohesion is the basic condition for clan prosperity.

West Pool and East Pool, two pages recording the two most important matters for clan fate in agricultural society.

There is also the second major matter: worshipping deities. Southeast of the great ancestral hall, in the gap between West and East Pools, 10th-generation ancestor Li Bojun built Renji Temple in Southern Song Xiaozong Chunxi 7th year (1180), enshrining Pingshui (Peaceful-Water) Holy King Zhou Kai. He was a Western Jin person, able to control floods, repeatedly showing divine miracles; Tang dynasty enfeoffed him as Pingshui Xianying Duke, Song dynasty added title Huguo Renji King. Water is the lifeline of agriculture; in agricultural society, water gods always receive special reverence, whether they promote water benefits or quell water disasters. Perhaps because he is a water god, his temple is surrounded by water on three sides: east is East Pool, west is a small pool between East and West Pools, south is a channel connecting the two pools. The three water-facing sides use open corridors with beauty rails. People love water, the temple loves water — exceptionally light and graceful. The temple's courtyard is also a pool of water, planted with lotus, fragrance filling the air. The temple merges into the garden, humanized. Humanization is precisely the characteristic of rural deities; with loving hearts, they soothe people's suffering and give them hope for life.

sections.name: 岩头村
sections.content_zh:
岩头村

火热的太阳底下，一队破衣烂衫的人，各挑一副沉重的大筐，紧捣脚步，走进岩头村的东门，献义门。这些是脚夫，他们给老板从乐清挑盐到缙云去卖，路过岩头，这楠溪江中游最大的村落（占地十八点五公顷），江西岸唯一有商店的村落。它创建于南宋初年，或说初建于元代延祐年间。

进献义门，向南一拐，便是一条三百米长的商业街。街东一溜店铺，店面前搭出厦廊，覆盖着整条街。脚夫们放下盐担，斜倚到街西的美人靠上，点一袋烟，吹一身风。美人靠外，一带长湖，莲花莲叶，一直铺开到远远的对岸，岸边粉壁青瓦，闪闪像鳞片。缕缕的炊烟升起，微风送过来苦味的柴香，叫脚夫们仿佛感到灶头的温馨，渐渐退尽了汗珠。这长湖叫丽水湖，是岩头村十八胜景之一，这街，叫丽水街。街廊上有一副对联，写的是："萍风碧漾观鱼栏；柳浪翠泛闻莺廊。"又观鱼又闻莺，这里难道是商业街吗，歇在美人靠下的人是为了可怜的几个脚钱奔走在艰险山路上吗？怎么不是呢？那分明是七十二间小店，柜台上陈列着烟草、煤油、洋布、食盐、火柴，还有几罐浸着杨梅的烧酒，深深的紫红色。

献义门这头，丽水湖的北岸，有一座茶馆，泡一杯土茶，跟过往的人谈谈各路异闻奇事，很能解乏，但要花几个钱，脚夫们不去。他们顺弯弯的丽水街南下，到尽头，是乘风亭。亭子里有泡着暑药的凉茶，有备足了柴草的锅灶，脚夫们可以免费喝茶、点火，把随身带来装着糙米和霉干菜的竹筒往锅里一煮，一忽儿香气飘出，竹筒饭便熟了。亭子的柱子上挂着一串一串金黄色的草靴，行路人翻过脚底板看看，鞋底磨穿了，取下一双来换上，也不必付钱。亭里有一副对联，写道："茶待多情客；饭留有义人。"善心的主人称辛苦的过客为多情和有义的人，问饥问渴，多么仁厚。他们温暖的关怀，叫为生计奔波的人懂得了乡情，认识了乡亲。

丽水街本来是一段兼作拦水坝的寨墙，叫作长绛。丽水湖便是由它拦蓄而成的。嘉靖年间金氏桂林公建设岩头村水利工程时候筑成。初时河绛上作为子弟们演习骑射的场所，以防萎弱，而且事关全村风水，规定"只许种树莳花与建亭亭点缀风景而已，不与筑屋经商"。后来，骑射荒废了，河绛成了道路，"挑盐过缙云，不一天分银"，从乐清来的盐贩络绎不绝，以至"民元以来，商业日渐发达，四处商贩云集，市场扩大"，河绛一带，终于"悉已筑为商店"，"风水迷梦，今则破除之矣"。

挑脚的人从乘风亭南侧出村，丽水街到亭子结束。河绛在这里转向西走，兼作岩头村的南寨墙，又拦蓄成了镇南湖和进宦湖，形成楠溪江中游村落中最大的公共园林。乘风亭前三跨的石板桥，叫丽水桥，造于嘉靖三十七年（1558），是丽水湖和这个风景区的分界线。一棵古老的大樟树，远远伸出枝丫，俯身爱护着它。

公共园林包括河绛、琴屿以及琴屿南北两侧的镇南湖和进宦湖，西端还有一座小小的汤山。河绛上古木参天，荫蔽着一座接官亭，又叫花亭，造型很别致。琴屿上满种木芙蓉，粉的、白的，还有朝粉暮白的，夏秋两季，开得热热闹闹，像锦云一片。琴屿西头，汤山东麓，造一座塔湖庙，庙门外搭着个戏台。庙右手是森秀轩，桂林公的书斋，轩后小院里凿一方右军池，流水潺潺。庙左手是文昌阁，面对不大的智水湖。阁后，汤山顶上，立一座灰白大理石的文峰塔。汤山北麓，是祭祀桂林公的专祠水亭祠。这公共园林是在乡文人的活动场所。他们在里面读书、吟咏、作画、垂钓，涵养性情，欣赏四野里大自然的蓬勃生机。

专祀桂林公的水亭祠，本来是桂林公造的书院，和文峰塔、文昌阁呼应。楠溪江下游任何一个村落，都决不怠慢读书，何况岩头金氏这样的大族。村人们到现在还口传宋代大学者叶适。

曾在岩头读书，说起来很觉得光彩。更光彩的是岩头村北门仁道门口金氏大宗祠前的进士牌楼，是明世宗赐给大理寺左寺右寺副、端州知府金昭的。牌楼八米多高，少年读书郎，吃力地抬头仰视，心中会涌起多少羡慕，多少憧憬？从北门进来的那条南北主街，便叫进士街。

进士街南头，横街的丁字路口，把角两家店铺，外檐装修很华丽，村民叫它们苏式店面。商业刚刚萌芽，行旅稍有往来，岩头村的建筑风格就开始走向多样化，显见得眼界宽了，心思便也活了。

横街向南，有四条直街，街上曾有连排十几座三进大宅，传说也是桂林公主持统一建造的。太平军战争的时候，世仇枫林镇告发岩头村勾结"长毛"，官兵来烧了这一大片。后来在老基址上造了些小房子，它们的墙脚还砌着大宅的残石，可以想见当年的豪华。

大宅最多的是浚水街。七米多宽的街，二米多宽的水渠。水渠从村北二里左右的五溪引来，进村子西北角，形成上花园，以后分前浚、后浚，前浚向东，又形成下花园，并且分支流经大半个村子，从北头注入丽水湖。后浚顺村子西部的浚水街南下，在水亭祠西南角汇合汤山北麓从西来的水渠，注入塔湖庙风景区的几个湖里。这是由元代日新公开始，明代桂林公扩大并且完成的引水工程的主体，是楠溪江中游最大、最成功的水利工程，快五百年了，现在还滋润着全村人的生活。
sections.content_en:
Yantou Village

Under the scorching sun, a line of ragged people, each carrying a heavy large basket, hurried steps, entering Yantou Village's east gate, Xianyi Gate. These are porters, carrying salt from Yueqing to sell in Jinyun for their bosses, passing through Yantou — the largest village in the middle reaches of Nanxi River (covering 18.5 hectares), the only village with shops on the west bank of the river. It was founded in early Southern Song, or some say in Yuan Yanyou period.

Entering Xianyi Gate, turning south, is a 300-meter commercial street. East side is a row of shops, with covered verandas extending from storefronts, covering the entire street. Porters put down their salt loads, lean against the beauty rails (meirenkao) on the west side, light a pipe of tobacco, let the wind blow over them. Beyond the beauty rails, a long lake stretches, with lotus leaves and flowers, extending to the far opposite bank, where white walls and blue tiles glint like fish scales. Wisps of cooking smoke rise, breeze carries the bitter aroma of firewood, making porters feel the warmth of a kitchen, gradually sweating off. This long lake is called Lishui Lake, one of Yantou Village's Eighteen Scenes; this street is called Lishui Street. On the street corridor is a couplet: "Duckweed wind, green ripples, fish-watching rail; willow waves, emerald泛, oriole-hearing corridor." Watching fish and hearing orioles — is this really a commercial street? Are those resting under beauty rails people struggling on dangerous mountain paths for pitiful porter wages? How could it not be? Those are clearly 72 small shops, counters displaying tobacco, kerosene, foreign cloth, salt, matches, and several jars of烧酒 soaked with bayberries, deep purplish-red.

At the Xianyi Gate end, north bank of Lishui Lake, is a teahouse — a cup of local tea, chatting with passersby about strange tales from various roads, very refreshing, but costs money, so porters don't go. They follow the winding Lishui Street south to the end, where is Chengfeng (Riding-the-Wind) Pavilion. In the pavilion are herbal cooling tea for summer, and stoves with plenty of firewood; porters can drink tea and light fires for free, putting their bamboo tubes of brown rice and pickled vegetables into the pot to cook — soon aroma wafts out, bamboo-tube rice is done. On the pavilion pillars hang strings of golden straw sandals; travelers check their soles, if worn through, take a pair to change into, no payment needed. In the pavilion is a couplet: "Tea awaits sentimental guests; rice留 for righteous people." Kind hosts call hardworking passersby sentimental and righteous, asking about hunger and thirst — how benevolent. Their warm care makes people struggling for livelihood understand village affection and know their fellow villagers.

Lishui Street was originally a section of village wall doubling as a dam, called Changjiang (Long Embankment). Lishui Lake was formed by its damming. It was built during Jiajing period when Jin Guilin (Guilin Gong) constructed Yantou Village's water conservancy project. Initially, the river embankment was a place for village youths to practice horse riding and archery, to prevent weakness, and it concerned the village's fengshui, stipulating "only planting trees, flowers, and building pavilions to adorn scenery, no building houses or doing business." Later, horse riding and archery fell into disuse, the embankment became a road; "carrying salt to Jinyun, earning silver in less than a day" — salt merchants from Yueqing came continuously, so that "since the Republic, commerce gradually developed, merchants gathered from everywhere, market expanded," and the embankment area finally "all built into shops," "the fengshui迷梦, now broken."

Porters exit the village from the south side of Chengfeng Pavilion; Lishui Street ends at the pavilion. The embankment here turns west, doubling as Yantou Village's south wall, and dams up Zhennan Lake and Jinhuan Lake, forming the largest public garden in Nanxi River middle-reach villages. The three-span stone slab bridge before Chengfeng Pavilion is called Lishui Bridge, built in Jiajing 37th year (1558), the boundary between Lishui Lake and this scenic area. An ancient large camphor tree, branches extending far, leans over to protect it.

The public garden includes the river embankment, Qinyu (Lute Isle), and Zhennan Lake and Jinhuan Lake on both north and south sides of Qinyu, with a small Tang Mountain at the west end. Ancient trees tower on the embankment, shading a Jieguan (Receiving-Official) Pavilion, also called Flower Pavilion, with a distinctive shape. Qinyu is planted with cotton roses — pink, white, and those pink in morning turning white at dusk — blooming lively in summer and autumn, like a sheet of brocade clouds. At the west end of Qinyu, at the eastern foot of Tang Mountain, stands Tahu (Pagoda-Lake) Temple, with a stage built outside the temple gate. To the temple's right is Senxuan Studio, Guilin Gong's study; behind the studio, a small courtyard has a Youjun (Right Army) Pool with flowing water. To the temple's left is Wenchang (Literary Prosperity) Pavilion, facing the small Zhishui Lake. Behind the pavilion, on Tang Mountain top, stands a Wenfeng (Literary Peak) Pagoda of gray-white marble. At the northern foot of Tang Mountain is Shuiting (Water-Pavilion) Shrine, dedicated to Guilin Gong. This public garden was the activity place for local literati. They read, chanted poetry, painted, fished there, cultivating temperament, appreciating the vibrant life of nature in all directions.

Shuiting Shrine, dedicated to Guilin Gong, was originally the academy Guilin Gong built, echoing Wenfeng Pagoda and Wenchang Pavilion. No village in lower Nanxi River ever neglected reading, let alone a great clan like Yantou's Jin clan. Villagers still orally pass down that Song dynasty great scholar Ye Shi.

Once studied in Yantou — speaking of it brings pride. More pride is the jinshi (presented scholar) archway before the Jin Great Ancestral Hall at the north gate Rendao Gate entrance, bestowed by Ming Shizong to Jin Zhao, Left Assistant of the Court of Judicial Review and Duanzhou Prefect. The archway is over 8 meters high; young students, straining to look up, would feel how much admiration, how much longing? The north-south main street entering from the north gate is called Jinshi (Presented Scholar) Street.

At the south end of Jinshi Street, at the T-junction of the cross street, the two corner shops have ornate exterior eaves decoration; villagers call them Su-style storefronts. Commerce just sprouting, travelers coming and going, Yantou Village's architectural style began to diversify — clearly broadened horizons, lively minds.

South of the cross street are four straight streets, where once stood over a dozen consecutive three-courtyard grand mansions, legend says also uniformly built under Guilin Gong's direction. During the Taiping Rebellion, the feudally hostile Fenglin Town reported Yantou Village colluding with "Long Hair" (Taipings); government troops came and burned this whole area. Later small houses were built on the old foundations; their wall bases still use remnant stones from the grand mansions, one can imagine the luxury of that time.

The most grand mansions are on Junshui (Dredging-Water) Street. Over 7 meters wide street, over 2 meters wide water channel. The channel draws water from Wuxi Stream, about two li north of the village, entering the village's northwest corner, forming Upper Garden, then dividing into Front Dredge and Rear Dredge; Front Dredge goes east, forming Lower Garden, and branches flow through most of the village, entering Lishui Lake from the north end. Rear Dredge goes south along Junshui Street in the village's west, at the southwest corner of Shuiting Shrine merges with the channel coming west from the northern foot of Tang Mountain, then flows into the several lakes of the Tahu Temple scenic area. This is the main body of the water-diversion project started by Yuan dynasty Rixin Gong and expanded and completed by Ming dynasty Guilin Gong — the largest and most successful water conservancy project in Nanxi River middle reaches, nearly 500 years old, still nourishing the whole village's life today.

sections.name: 蓬溪村
sections.content_zh:
蓬溪村

当过永嘉太守，在楠溪江写下中国最早一曲山水诗的谢灵运，于南朝宋文帝元嘉十年（433）在广州遇害之后，他的次子扶柩回永嘉，建墓于温州城内飞霞洞侧，并定居在温州城里。后来，"诜五五公游楠溪，见鹤阳之胜，又自郡城迁居鹤阳"，时间在北宋。鹤阳村在楠溪江中游东北、鹤盛溪畔。子孙繁衍，逐渐分出新村，沿鹤盛溪的有鹤盛、鹤湾、东皋和蓬溪等。在整个楠溪江流域，谢氏村落有二十多个。东皋和蓬溪大约建村于南宋。谢氏的总祠在鹤阳，那里供奉着谢灵运的神主。

楠溪江村落的选址看重风景，或许因为脉管中流着康乐公的血，谢氏村落都在山水最美处，其中尤其是鹤阳和蓬溪。楠溪江村落的选址又看重安全，鹤阳和蓬溪也是道路险阻，很难进入。楠溪江房舍多用蛮石原木，本性、本形、本色，经几片粉壁勾勒衬托，如画如塑。鹤阳和东皋，在竹树掩映中，这样宛自天然的房舍像谢灵运的诗一样清新。

鹤阳、东皋两村，都要走过鹤盛溪上长长的矴步才能到达。东皋村寨门前的矴步，全长一百二十一米，二百一十一步。矴步又叫过水明梁，一步一块母矴，隔六七步，有一块母矴旁边附一块子矴，便于对面行人避让。楠溪江民风淳厚，乡民习惯，矴步上，男让女，长让幼，空手让挑担，轻担让重担，夏季山洪过后，整修矴步，全村男女老少一齐踊跃，溪滩上人影穿梭，号子声和着水声，沉重中透着欢快。溪边小亭里，石碑上刻着一次次的整修，出钱出力，琐屑必录，叫人们永远记得公益事业的高尚。

蓬溪村的形势最险固。它在一个袋形盆地里，四围高山重重，只有北面缺口，却又被鹤盛溪封住。先人们凿山开路，在溪西绝壁上架起一里多长的栈道，村子才能出入。小心翼翼走过栈道，村口叫霞港头，鹤盛溪在这里一个反弯，霞港头正对弓背，好在岩体坚牢，不怕冲刷。不过，为了更加可靠，霞港头上造了一幢关帝庙。关帝降妖伏魔，镇灾禳祸，楠溪江各村的水口大都有他的香火。和各村的关帝庙一样，蓬溪的这一座也是大庇各路神仙、老爷娘娘，数十尊泥塑木雕，济济一堂，甚至有孙悟空在场。乡民们无论有什么困苦，什么请求，什么愿望，都可以来叩头烧香。说是"有祷必应"，不知谁来验证。溪边一棵巨大的老樟树，千枝万叶，像云盖一样遮蔽住庙前的广场。广场上逢年过节演戏，舞龙，是全年仅有的娱乐，点缀日出而作、日落而息的宁静单调的生活。

绕过霞港头，山坡几座小祠堂，都已残破。一座亭子，玲珑轻俏，位于高台上，这是康乐亭。康乐公的肖像已经现代化了，他昂首向天，神情孤傲，或许正是这种性格，使他在广州被杀。康乐亭是蓬溪年轻人的聚会之地，从朝到暮，甩纸牌的噼啪声不断，他们大概已经不知道祖先曾是一位伟大的诗人，更不知道他在流连山水的时候，也写过"未厌青春好，已睹朱明移。戚戚感物叹，星星白发垂"这样的诗句。

康乐亭前一条主街，从北向南，笔直。街西建筑区，街东便是广阔的潴湖，山水所汇。这是"水聚天心"。湖中央螺髻青碧，小岛一座，美丽的名字叫凤凰屿。岛外东南方层叠的群山上有圆锥形高峰，那便是文笔峰，正在巽位。街西的谢家祠堂，存著堂，正对着它。文笔峰倒映在潴湖中，形成"笔入砚池"的风水，大有利于发荣科甲。虽有好风水，蓬溪谢氏文运并不发达。谢家子弟，空负了桃源仙境。近几十年里，山林伐尽，泥沙俱下，潴湖已经淤成了稻田。

早在谢氏未来之前，蓬溪已有李姓人居住。南宋时候，出了一位李时靖，咸淳元年（1265）进士，传说还是状元，故宅北侧辟了一条不到百米的又平又直又宽的街，铺砌得很精致，便叫状元街。《永嘉县志》里记载，朱熹在浙江东路常平盐茶公事任上，曾经到楠溪江访问几位大学者，其中就有李时靖。所以蓬溪村有几处传说是朱熹的遗迹，一处是村口船崖上摩崖石刻"钓台"两个字和一首诗："观鱼胜濠上，把钓超渭阳。严子如来此，定忘富春江。"1985年炸开悬崖筑公路的时候全毁掉了。一处是凤凰屿南麓的两块大石壁上的刻字，"把钓"和"索觞"，字迹拙劣，是年久蚀损后重新剔过的。最后一处是一座住宅砖门头上的"近云山舍"四个字。山舍是清代晚期造的，据说这家人把手迹代代留传了下来，不过，刻上门头之后却把原件丢失了。江南各地，口传为朱熹的题字很多，大都是伪托，蓬溪村的也不大可能是真迹。不过，乡民们谨谨慎慎地珍视它们，以它们为荣，心中对文化的尊崇之情却是非常认真的。

蓬溪村的住宅多内向，院落谨严，三合或者四合，两层，有腰檐。相传为李时靖故居的，非常简朴，单层，四面板壁，檐口低矮，用方形木墩为柱础，看来久经风霜。村里有几幢大型住宅，其中一幢造于明代，传说当年它主人的表弟在这里宅里住过，后来任南国子监祭酒，写文章提到过它。这幢大宅，屡经修缮，布局已乱，大致是主体七开间，三进两院，左右各自有跨院。整个大约有七十多间房间。重要的特点是，两进院落都是水池，前院中央有甬路，水池一分为二，后院则是整个一方大池。内向的住宅外，村景不免沉闷一些。

鹤阳和东皋，还有蓬溪，都有许多住宅，木石天然本色，加工无非用双手，它们带着生命原有的气质，与天地间一切生命相亲和。它们布局外向，就像乡民一样坦诚，使陌生人走进村子，便感到亲切，自信能够受到主人欢迎。这便是楠溪江的性格。
