2007年冬
sections.content_en:
Pengxi Village

Xie Lingyun, who served as Yongjia Prefect and wrote China's earliest landscape poetry in Nanxi River, after being killed in Guangzhou in the 10th year of Liu Song Wen Di Yuanjia (433), his second son escorted the coffin back to Yongjia, built a tomb beside Feixia Cave in Wenzhou city, and settled in Wenzhou. Later, "Shen Wuwugong traveled to Nanxi River, saw the beauty of Heyang, and moved from the prefecture city to Heyang," in the Northern Song. Heyang Village is in the northeast of Nanxi River middle reaches, by Hesheng Stream. Descendants multiplied, gradually branching into new villages; along Hesheng Stream are Hesheng, Hewan, Donggao, and Pengxi. In the entire Nanxi River basin, there are over twenty Xie clan villages. Donggao and Pengxi were probably founded in Southern Song. The Xie clan's main ancestral hall is in Heyang, where Xie Lingyun's spirit tablet is enshrined.

Nanxi River village site selection values scenery; perhaps because Kangle Gong's (Xie Lingyun's) blood flows in their veins, Xie clan villages are all in the most beautiful landscapes, especially Heyang and Pengxi. Nanxi River village site selection also values safety; Heyang and Pengxi are also difficult to access with dangerous roads. Nanxi River houses mostly use rough stone and raw timber, with their nature, form, and color, outlined and set off by a few white plaster walls, like paintings and sculptures. Heyang and Donggao, amid bamboo and trees, have such naturally graceful houses as fresh as Xie Lingyun's poetry.

Both Heyang and Donggao villages require crossing long stepping-stones (dingbu) over Hesheng Stream to reach. The stepping-stones before Donggao Village gate are 121 meters long, 211 steps. Stepping-stones are also called "water-crossing bright beams"; one step is one "mother stone," every six or seven steps, a "mother stone" has an attached "child stone" beside it for pedestrians to yield to each other. Nanxi River people are honest and kind; villagers' custom on stepping-stones: men yield to women, elders yield to children, empty-handed yield to burdened, light loads yield to heavy loads. After summer floods, repairing stepping-stones, the whole village — men, women, old, young — enthusiastically joins; figures shuttle on the stream beach, work songs mingle with water sounds, heavy yet joyful. In a small pavilion by the stream, stone steles record each repair — money given, labor contributed, every detail recorded, so people forever remember the nobility of public welfare.

Pengxi Village's terrain is the most strategically secure. It is in a bag-shaped basin, surrounded by layered high mountains, with only a northern gap, which is sealed by Hesheng Stream. Ancestors chiseled mountains to open roads, building a over-one-li-long plank road on the west cliff by the stream, so the village could be accessed. Carefully crossing the plank road, the village entrance is called Xiagangtou; Hesheng Stream makes a reverse bend here, Xiagangtou faces the bow's back, fortunately the rock body is solid, not afraid of erosion. However, for greater reliability, a Guandi (Guan Yu) Temple was built at Xiagangtou. Guan Yu subdues demons and disasters, and most Nanxi River villages' water mouths (shuikou) have his incense. Like other villages' Guandi Temples, Pengxi's also shelters various gods, lords and ladies — dozens of clay and wood carvings, gathered together, even Sun Wukong present. Villagers, whatever hardship, request, or wish, can come to kowtow and burn incense. Said to be "every prayer answered," who knows who verifies. By the stream, a huge old camphor tree, with countless branches and leaves, covers the square before the temple like a cloud canopy. On the square, during festivals, operas are performed and dragon dances held — the only entertainment all year, adorning the quiet, monotonous life of rising at sunrise and resting at sunset.

Rounding Xiagangtou, several small ancestral halls on the slope are all dilapidated. A pavilion, exquisite and light, on a high platform, is Kangle Pavilion. Kangle Gong's portrait has been modernized; he holds his head high toward the sky, with a孤傲 expression — perhaps正是 this character caused him to be killed in Guangzhou. Kangle Pavilion is a gathering place for Pengxi young people; from morning to evening, the snapping of card games continues; they probably no longer know their ancestor was a great poet, nor that when wandering among mountains and waters, he also wrote lines like "Not yet tired of youth's beauty, already seeing summer's red move. Sorrowfully sensing things and sighing, starry white hair hangs down."

Before Kangle Pavilion, a main street runs north to south, straight. West of the street is the building area; east of the street is the broad Zhuhu (Stored-Water) Lake, where mountains and waters converge. This is "water gathering at the heart of heaven." In the lake center, a small island with a spiral green peak, beautifully named Phoenix Isle. Beyond the island to the southeast, layered mountains have a conical high peak — that is Wenbi (Writing-Brush) Peak, exactly in the xun (southeast) position. West of the street, the Xie clan ancestral hall, Cunzhu Hall, faces it directly. Wenbi Peak reflects in Zhuhu Lake, forming the fengshui of "brush entering inkstone pool," greatly beneficial for examination success. Despite good fengshui, Pengxi Xie clan's literary fortune was not prosperous. Xie clan youths, in vain possessed a Peach Blossom Spring paradise. In recent decades, mountains and forests were cut bare, silt and sand came down, and Zhuhu Lake has silted into rice fields.

Long before the Xie clan arrived, Pengxi already had Li clan residents. In Southern Song, a Li Shijing emerged, jinshi of Xianchun 1st year (1265), legend says even zhuangyuan (top scholar); north of his former residence, a less-than-100-meter street, flat, straight, and wide, exquisitely paved, was called Zhuangyuan (Top-Scholar) Street. "Yongjia County Annals" records that Zhu Xi, while serving as Commissioner of Salt and Tea in Eastern Zhejiang, once visited several great scholars in Nanxi River, including Li Shijing. So Pengxi Village has several sites传说 to be Zhu Xi's relics: one is cliff carving "Diaotai (Fishing Platform)" and a poem on the boat cliff at the village entrance: "Watching fish surpasses Hao River, fishing surpasses Weiyang. If Master Yan came here, he'd forget Fuchun River." All destroyed when the cliff was blasted for a highway in 1985. One is carvings on two large stone walls at the southern foot of Phoenix Isle: "Bafish (Fishing)" and "Suoshang (Seeking Wine)," with clumsy characters, re-carved after long erosion. The last is four characters "Jinyun Shanshe (Near-Cloud Mountain Retreat)" on a residential brick gatehead. The mountain retreat was built in late Qing;据说 the family passed down the handwriting for generations, but after carving it on the gatehead, the original was lost. In Jiangnan, many places orally claim Zhu Xi's calligraphy, mostly forged; Pengxi's is unlikely authentic either. However, villagers carefully and cautiously treasure them, taking pride in them — their reverence for culture in their hearts is very sincere.

Pengxi Village's residences are mostly inward-facing, with strict courtyards — three-sided or four-sided, two stories, with waist eaves. The residence传说 to be Li Shijing's former home is very simple: single story, four-sided plank walls, low eaves, using square wooden blocks as column bases, looking weathered. The village has several large residences; one built in Ming dynasty, legend says its owner's cousin once stayed here, later becoming Director of the Southern Guozijian (Imperial Academy), and mentioned it in writing. This large mansion, repeatedly renovated, layout now disordered, roughly has a main body of seven bays, three halls and two courtyards, with side courtyards on left and right. Altogether about seventy rooms. The important feature is that both courtyards are pools: the front courtyard has a central path, dividing the pool in two; the rear courtyard is one entire large pool. Beyond the inward-facing residences, the village scenery is inevitably somewhat dull.

Heyang, Donggao, and Pengxi all have many residences, with wood and stone in natural colors, worked only by hand, carrying life's original temperament, in harmony with all life between heaven and earth. Their layouts are outward-facing, as honest as villagers, making strangers entering the village feel亲切, confident of being welcomed by the hosts. This is the character of Nanxi River.

Winter 2007

sections.name: 楼下村掠影
sections.content_zh:
楼下村掠影

我们在楼下村的工作其实还包含着另一个自然村，南山村。南山村在楼下村的东南，两村之间相距不过几十米，这间隙里还散布着几幢零星的房子，以致不留心就看不出这是两个村子。作为两村的界线的，是一条曲曲折折的山水沟，在高处大致是由西向东流，然后下了陡坡，向北流，穿过垟田，到鲤屿西北角跟自东面垟头村来的另一条大沟汇合，成了真正的溪。这山水沟大约只有一米宽，两边长着茂草，几乎把它遮住。我们来来回回走了许多趟，经乡人提醒才意识到它。

南山村的地势比楼下村高，房屋少得多，分布比较零散，而且质量和规模也明显不如楼下的。

楼下村和南山村一起，从西到东，总长大约五百三十米，最宽处在楼下村，大约三百五十米。有三条主要村路从西到东贯穿全村，大体循等高线走，但上面两条，在中段登高像一道岭。有些断断续续的短路连接它们，坡度很陡。

楼下村的水口在西北端，我们天天早晨从狮峰寺来便经水口入村。水口的上手山坡以前本有一大片树林，前些年被伐光，建了小学校。现在只剩下一棵大榕树，小学校的围墙本来正好要通过它的位置，但绕它转了半圈，把它隔在墙外，保护得很好，教人看了欢喜，觉得学校毕竟是个传播文明的地方。

水口的下手山坡是一座"仙宫"，供着各种神灵。它背对水口，从它的后墙根进村，路分两支，一支向左下陡坡顺"仙宫"的东南墙走向村政府前，最低的一条村路就从这里开始。另一支向右走大约一百多米来到刘氏宗祠左前角，又分岔，一支绕到宗祠背后再转向东南走，这就是最高的一条村路。另一支到宗祠的右前方向右上坡，再分岔。继续向右的一支，与最高的村路相接，在这个接合点向上走一段路便是王氏宗祠，向左偏一点便向东南走去的一支逐渐散乱。最高的那条村路，一下坡，在楼下村与南山村之间，有一座单间的"翠竹湖宫"，模样和名字一样可爱。再向前走，到南山村中央，向北一拐，下了陡坡。在那一拐的怀抱里，有一座"五显神庙"，村民们叫它"众厅"。中间那条村路在散乱了之后，一条小支岔走出楼下村，那里有一座属于南山村的"宫"。

最低处的那条村路，西端有几家店铺。排板门，一开间至三开间不等。铺面大多是旧有的，1949年以前，那里有杂货店、水产店和染布作坊等，商业比现在还多一些，是柏柱垟里唯一的"商业街"，更繁华的便是十七里外的溪柄街了。50年代初，社会大变动之后，店铺停业了，只有一家供销合作社门市部。近十来年，才恢复了几家店铺，供销社门市部也造了一座砖木结构四开间的新房子。小店卖油盐酱醋、糕饼糖果、火柴香烟、甘蔗甜橙和小学生的笔墨纸张。有两家小店在角落立着个冰箱，存着些海杂鱼。营业的时候，卸下门板，在门前搭个摊子，就把杂鱼、海带、鲜菇之类摊在上面卖。

居然有两家药店，卖药的懂得一点皮毛医道，能向农民推荐用药。我们中的一位患了感冒，咳嗽，去买药，对症的药的有效期已经过了十年了。我们问老板，这药怎么能治病，他满不在乎地一笑，说："农民嘛，就这样！"宋人陈宓写了一篇《惠民药局记》，里面说：福建"俗信巫尚鬼，市绝无药，有则低价以贸州之滞腐不售者，贫人利其廉，间服不瘳，则淫巫之说益信。于是，有病不药，不天阏幸矣。诗曰：'蓝水秋来八九月，芒花山瘴一齐发，时人信巫纸多烧，病不求医命自活。'呜呼，兽且有医，而忍吾赤子诞于巫、累于贾哉"？现在"低价以贸州之滞腐不售"之药，仍在继续，青牛山上的"五谷仙宫"里还有人烧香摇签求药方。这一千年的岁月悠悠，某些世事却未必有根本的改变。

有一位药店老板兼写对联、斗方之类出卖，常有墨迹淋漓的作品铺在街上晾干。内容抄自一本《楹联大全》，虽是近出，却依旧是陈词滥调。

供销社的商品多一点，日用品比较齐全，还有农药、化肥、柴油和农用塑料薄膜。

顺这条街向前走，有几十米的一段，右边为拓宽街面而拆掉了一些老店铺，现在补上了红砖墙。有一幢大型住宅也被拆掉了一角，这一角正是一个地窖所在。地窖已经暴露，被填平了。我们丈量了痕迹，深一百八十厘米，当年大约是贮藏些什么值钱东西的。

街的东南口上，有一座小小的单开间的庙，供着土地公公和"泗洲文佛"，是楼下村的。在刘氏宗祠左前方十来米还有同样的一座，天天都有一伙人蹲在里面打纸牌。

最低的街，地形最平，几乎没有起伏，曲折也不大，两侧密排着房屋。上面两条，地形高低起伏剧烈，道路左拐右弯，房屋稀稀落落，间隔很大，有些完整地展现出轮廓优美、山墙飘逸的侧面。空地上点缀着一些椿树和棕榈树，挺拔而清秀。这一部分的景观寥廓、明朗并富有变化，跟我们在浙西、皖南和赣北见到的基本上以小巷组成的村落大不相同，使我们感到很舒畅。

视野最开阔的是楼下村的刘氏宗祠和王氏宗祠。它们都在高坎上，王氏宗祠居全村的最高处。宗祠前面有很大的空场，从门前远望，青青的马上山像屏风一样展开。我们从鲤屿背上看村子，两个宗祠清晰地呈现在重重叠叠的瓦顶之上。楼下村水口边的"仙宫"，右侧也有一个大空场，这里是举行崇祀仪式的地方。宗祠和"仙宫"，是全村的几个公共活动中心，位置适当，而且有足够的面积。现在，王氏宗祠已经被改成初中校舍，门厅戏台被拆掉，享堂明间放着两张乒乓球桌，次间加了夹层，上面是教师住宅，下面是办公室。原来院落的右侧造了两层的教室楼，整齐而亮堂，女孩子们穿着红红绿绿的花衫，课间休息时挤在走廊上看男孩子们在下面打篮球，洋溢着活泼的生气。刘氏宗祠锁着大门，里面已经租给人家育菇苗，前面的空场上正晒着新谷，一片金黄。"仙宫"的院子和右侧的空场也都用来晒新谷，甚至戏台上都晾着谷子！

三十幢左右的大型住宅分布在三条村路的中段，越往下越多，在最低的那条路的北侧，垟田的边缘上，有十二幢大型住宅，分前后两排，一幢挨着一幢，又和路南的四幢接连成一大片。在这一片住宅区里走，两侧长长的、高高的夯土墙，淡淡的土黄色，斑驳粗粝，沉闷而苍老，仿佛隐藏着许多故事。只有几个披檐门头，斜看过去，也不见出色。有一天，为了测量，我们爬到了位于巷子尽头的一幢大宅子的阁楼上，推窗一望，意外的景色把我们惊呆了。那些住宅，好一派壮丽气象。轻巧而体形丰富多变的山墙，两端尖尖的高翘的脊尾，向上升腾的火形屏风墙，白粉壁映衬着栗色的木构架，一层又一层，远远铺开过去。在飘飘洒洒的屋顶下，往昔的富丽豪华依然可以清晰地想见。抬头遥望四周触天的山峦，我们禁不住要问，在这个荒僻的山地里，怎么会有这样的一个村子？

中小型的住宅很少，零散在高处的两条村路上下，年代大都比较晚近，有些甚至是新造的。

楼下村所有的房子，也包括宗祠和"仙宫"，一律朝向东偏北大约十五度。只有泗洲佛的小庙朝向东略偏南。东偏北有马上山的两个锥形山峰，一个便是狮峰寺的朝山，八百二十五米高的，另一个在它的东南，稍稍矮一些。有些房子正对着前者，有些对着后者，相差小小一个夹角，不到五度。背后则对着西南的笔架山。前面两个锥形山峰并列，也像一座笔架，乡民因此把马上山叫作"前笔架山"，把笔架山叫作"后笔架山"。面对笔架，大有利于文运，许多大宅子都把它写进大门门联，例如："此处文峰容架笔；吾家世业本传经。""鲤屿祥辉昭户宇；笔峰爽气起人文。"为了喜兴，柏柱垟过去就叫双峰乡。

南山村的房子，一部分也面对前笔架山，但背后便不可能对后笔架山了；另一部分则向西面对后笔架山，背后是东方的群山，山峰参差，笼统叫作"八仙山"。有一天，我们访问村中被叫作"寻龙先生"的风水师郑成祥（1930年生）。他的口音我们一点也听不懂，我们的话他也听不懂，只好找一位高年级小学生当翻译。才说了几句，小学生便败下阵来，于是请来了小学老师。她也不大听得懂风水师玄奥的学问，翻译非常困难。我们彼此猜谜语，笑话百出。堵在房门口和窗外的男女老少嘻嘻哈哈，觉得好玩，有时候也插嘴帮忙翻译几句，越译越乱。断断续续，我们听明白了老风水师解释的南山村在各方面都落后于楼下村的原因：南山村的风水原来非常好，远远好过楼下村的，因此宋代出了一个进士，叫"郑武成"。他到朝中做官，带走了风水。他再也没有回来，南山村从此衰败了。

风水之说固然荒诞不经，但"郑武成"却引起了我们的大兴趣。回来之后，在《福安县志》上寻找了几遍，原来，不是郑武成，而是郑虎臣，不是进士，而是"会稽尉"，生于宋嘉定十二年（1219）。奸佞贾似道远谪南荒，郑虎臣自请为押行官，到了清漳县城外木绵庵中，郑虎臣杀了贾似道，自缚请死。《福安县志·山川》记："狮峰在县南四十里……其下为柏柱村，宋郑虎臣居此。"《古迹》又记："会稽尉郑虎臣墓，在柏柱阳（应为垟）头村，康熙五十年……准立墓道碑。道光五年重修。"重修时建祠。柏柱村指的就是南山村，阳头村就是垟头村，在南山村东二里，祠、墓今存。那篇《重建柏柱仙宫募捐倡议书》里写着"虎臣祠流芳千古"，指的就是这座墓祠，我们当时没有注意。福安又有三贤祠，祀本邑历史贤士，除郑虎臣外，有唐神龙二年（706）进士、开元中曾任左补阙兼太子侍读的薛令之。还有南宋末年的谢翱均以清廉闻，他的老家得名为廉村；谢是著名的义士，文天祥的追随者。明李东阳有诗咏郑虎臣杀贾似道事："君王不诛监押诛，父仇国愤一时摅。监押虽死名不灭，元城使者空呕血。"郑虎臣墓祠内有相传为文天祥撰的对联："作正气人都为名教肩任；到成仁处总缘大义认真。"联和诗都歌颂了郑虎臣的大义正气。南山村，这个衰落而洋溢着浓重慵懒气氛的山村，原来有过这样的一位义士，真是难以想象。教我们深深觉得遗憾的是，我们在南山村工作了好多日子，竟没有一个人向我们提起这位英雄，他的一位识字能文当寻龙先生的子孙竟连他的名字都写错了，而且还埋怨他带走了风水。

不过，村民外迁，会带走风水福气的说法，至今在乡民中还很当真。就在我们工作期间，有一位楼下村王姓的女儿出嫁到山背后的松萝村去。我们追着花轿照相。轿子抬到刘氏宗祠左前方的路口，那里设着一只香案，新娘下轿拜了两拜，留下了一些钱，才上轿接着赶路。我们打听这叫什么仪式，正在收拾香案的老人说，这是为了叫新娘留下楼下村的风水福气，不要带走。"嫁出去的女儿泼出去的水"，这种防范真够绝情的。

1995年冬
sections.content_en:
Glimpses of Louxia Village

Our work in Lousia Village actually included another natural village, Nanshan Village. Nanshan Village is southeast of Lousia Village, only a few dozen meters apart; several scattered houses in the gap make it hard to notice they are two villages. The boundary between them is a winding mountain gully, flowing roughly west to east at higher ground, then down a steep slope northward, through farmland, meeting another large gully from Yangtou Village to the east at the northwest corner of Liyu, forming a true stream. This mountain gully is only about one meter wide, with lush grass on both sides almost covering it. We walked back and forth many times, only realizing it after villagers reminded us.

Nanshan Village's terrain is higher than Lousia's, with far fewer houses, more scattered distribution, and clearly inferior quality and scale.

Lousia and Nanshan together, from west to east, total about 530 meters long; the widest part is at Lousia, about 350 meters. Three main village roads run west to east through the whole village, roughly following contour lines, but the upper two rise like a ridge in the middle section. Some intermittent short roads connect them, with steep slopes.

Lousia Village's water mouth (shuikou) is at the northwest end; we entered the village through it every morning from Shifeng Temple. The upper slope of the water mouth once had a large forest, cut down years ago to build a primary school. Now only one large banyan tree remains; the school's wall, which would have passed right through its position, instead curved half a circle around it, keeping it outside the wall, well protected — a joy to see, making one feel school is after all a place spreading civilization.

The lower slope of the water mouth is a "Xian Palace" (immortal palace), enshrining various deities. It faces away from the water mouth; from its back wall, entering the village, the road splits into two: one goes left down a steep slope along the palace's southeast wall to before the village government, where the lowest village road begins. The other goes right about 100+ meters to the left front corner of the Liu Ancestral Hall, then splits again — one goes behind the hall then southeast, the highest village road. The other goes right and uphill from the hall's right front, then splits again. The branch continuing right connects to the highest road; from this junction, going up a stretch is the Wang Ancestral Hall; the branch going slightly left then southeast gradually becomes scattered. The highest road, going downhill, between Lousia and Nanshan, has a single-room "Cuizhu Lake Palace," as lovely as its name. Further on, to Nanshan Village center, turning north, down a steep slope. In the embrace of that turn is a "Wuxian (Five Manifestations) Temple," villagers call it "Zhongting" (Public Hall). After the middle road becomes scattered, a small branch exits Lousia Village, where there is a "palace" belonging to Nanshan.

The lowest village road has several shops at its west end. Sliding plank doors, one to three bays wide. Most storefronts are old; before 1949, there were general stores, aquatic product shops, dye workshops, etc. — more commerce than now, the only "commercial street" in Baizhuyang; the more prosperous one was Xibing Street, seventeen li away. In the early 1950s, after great social changes, shops closed, only one supply and marketing cooperative remained. In recent ten years, several shops have recovered; the cooperative also built a new four-bay brick-wood building. Small shops sell oil, salt, soy sauce, vinegar, cakes, candy, matches, cigarettes, sugarcane, sweet oranges, and students' brush, ink, paper. Two small shops have refrigerators in corners, storing some sea fish. During business hours, removing door panels, setting up stalls in front, displaying fish, kelp, fresh mushrooms for sale.

Surprisingly there are two pharmacies; the sellers know a little superficial medicine, can recommend drugs to farmers. One of us caught a cold with cough, went to buy medicine; the appropriate drug had expired ten years ago. We asked the boss how this medicine could cure; he smiled carelessly: "Farmers, that's how it is!" Song dynasty Chen Mi wrote "Huimin Pharmacy Record," saying: Fujian "custom believes in shamans and ghosts, markets have no medicine; if any, sold cheap as stale unsold goods from prefectures; poor people favor the cheap, sometimes taking without cure, then shaman beliefs grow stronger. Thus, sick without medicine, not dying young is luck. The poem says: 'Blue water comes in autumn eighth-ninth month, awn flowers and mountain miasma break out together; people burn shaman paper more, sickness doesn't seek doctor, life lives on its own.' Alas, even beasts have doctors, yet our innocent children are deceived by shamans and exploited by merchants?" Now "cheap stale unsold goods" medicine continues; in the "Wugu Xian Palace" on Qingniu Mountain, people still burn incense and shake lots for prescriptions. A thousand years pass, yet some things may not have fundamentally changed.

One pharmacy boss also writes couplets and square calligraphy for sale; often ink-dripping works spread on the street to dry. Content copied from a "Complete Couplets Collection," though recent publication, still clichés.

The cooperative has more goods, daily necessities fairly complete, plus pesticides, fertilizer, diesel, and agricultural plastic film.

Following this street forward, for several tens of meters, the right side had some old shops demolished to widen the street, now patched with red brick walls. One large residence also had a corner demolished — that corner was a cellar. The cellar was exposed and filled in. We measured the痕迹, 180 cm deep, probably used to store valuables in old times.

At the southeast end of the street, a small single-room temple, enshrining Tudi Gong (Earth God) and "Sizhou Wenfo," belongs to Lousia Village. About ten meters left front of Liu Ancestral Hall is another similar one, where every day a group of people squat inside playing cards.

The lowest street has the flattest terrain, almost no起伏, little winding, with houses densely lined on both sides. The upper two roads have剧烈 terrain起伏, roads wind left and right, houses sparse with large intervals; some fully display elegant silhouettes and graceful gable walls. Open spaces are dotted with toon and palm trees, tall and graceful. This part's landscape is open, bright, and varied, very different from the alley-based villages we saw in western Zhejiang, southern Anhui, and northern Jiangxi, making us feel comfortable.

The widest views are from Lousia's Liu Ancestral Hall and Wang Ancestral Hall. Both are on high terraces; Wang Ancestral Hall is at the village's highest point. Large open squares before the halls; from the doors, the green Mashang Mountain unfolds like a screen. Looking at the village from Liyu Ridge, the two ancestral halls clearly appear above layers of tile roofs. The "Xian Palace" by Lousia's water mouth also has a large open square on its right, where worship ceremonies are held. Ancestral halls and "Xian Palace" are the village's several public activity centers, appropriately located with sufficient area. Now, Wang Ancestral Hall has been converted to a junior high school; the entrance hall and stage were demolished; the main hall's central bay has two ping-pong tables, side bays have added mezzanines — teacher housing above, office below. A two-story classroom building was built on the right side of the original courtyard, neat and bright; girls in colorful blouses crowd the corridor during breaks watching boys play basketball below, full of lively vitality. Liu Ancestral Hall is locked, inside rented to someone for mushroom cultivation; the front square is drying new grain,一片 golden. The "Xian Palace" courtyard and right square are also used to dry new grain — even the stage has grain spread on it!

About thirty large residences are distributed in the middle sections of the three village roads, more numerous lower down; on the north side of the lowest road, at the edge of farmland, are twelve large residences in two rows, one next to another, connecting with four south-of-road residences into a large block. Walking through this residential area, the long, high rammed-earth walls on both sides, pale yellow, mottled and coarse, gloomy and aged, seem to hide many stories. Only a few eaves porches over doorways, seen obliquely, don't look outstanding. One day, for measurement, we climbed to the attic of a large mansion at the end of an alley; pushing open the window, the unexpected view stunned us. Those residences — what a magnificent sight. Light and richly varied gable walls, pointed high-rising ridge ends at both ends, upward-surging fire-shaped screen walls, white plaster walls set off chestnut timber frames, layer upon layer, spreading far. Under the flowing roofs, past wealth and luxury can still be clearly imagined. Looking up at the sky-touching mountains all around, we couldn't help asking: in this remote mountain area, how could there be such a village?

Small and medium residences are few, scattered along the upper two roads, mostly of later date, some even newly built.

All houses in Lousia, including ancestral halls and "Xian Palace," uniformly face about 15 degrees east of north. Only the small Sizhou Buddha temple faces slightly east of south. East-north has Mashang Mountain's two conical peaks — one is Shifeng Temple's facing mountain, 825 meters high; the other southeast of it, slightly shorter. Some houses face the former, some the latter, differing by a small angle less than five degrees. Behind them faces the southwest Bijia (Brush-Rest) Mountain. The two front conical peaks side by side also look like a brush rest; villagers therefore call Mashang Mountain "Front Brush-Rest Mountain" and Bijia Mountain "Rear Brush-Rest Mountain." Facing a brush rest greatly benefits literary fortune; many large mansions include it in their gate couplets, e.g.: "Here literary peak holds brush; our family tradition passes classics." "Liyu auspicious light shines on doors; brush peak refreshing air raises culture." For auspiciousness, Baizhuyang was formerly called Shuangfeng (Twin Peaks) Township.

Nanshan Village's houses, some also face Front Brush-Rest Mountain, but behind cannot face Rear Brush-Rest Mountain; others face west toward Rear Brush-Rest Mountain, behind are eastern mountains with varied peaks, generally called "Eight Immortals Mountain." One day, we visited the village's fengshui master called "Xunlong (Dragon-Seeking)先生" Zheng Chengxiang (born 1930). We couldn't understand his accent at all, and he couldn't understand ours, so we found a senior primary student as translator. After a few sentences, the student gave up, so the primary school teacher came. She also couldn't understand the fengshui master's esoteric learning, translation very difficult. We guessed riddles at each other, jokes abounded. Men, women, old, young堵 at door and window laughing, finding it fun, sometimes interrupting to help translate a few sentences, the more translated the more confused. Intermittently, we understood the old fengshui master's explanation of why Nanshan Village lags behind Lousia in all aspects: Nanshan's fengshui was originally very good, far better than Lousia's, so in Song dynasty it produced a jinshi called "Zheng Wucheng." He went to court to be an official, taking the fengshui away. He never returned, and Nanshan Village declined ever since.

Fengshui theories are of course absurd, but "Zheng Wucheng" aroused our great interest. After returning, searching "Fu'an County Annals" repeatedly, it turned out not Zheng Wucheng but Zheng Huchen, not a jinshi but "Kuaiji Commandant," born in Song Jiading 12th year (1219). The treacherous Jia Sidao was exiled to the southern wilderness; Zheng Huchen volunteered as escort; at Mumian Cottage outside Qingzhang city, Zheng Huchen killed Jia Sidao, then bound himself to request death. "Fu'an County Annals · Mountains and Rivers" records: "Shifeng is 40 li south of the county … below is Baizhu Village, where Song Zheng Huchen lived." "Historic Sites" also records: "Kuaiji Commandant Zheng Huchen's tomb, at Baizhuyang (should be垟) Tou Village, Kangxi 50th year … approved to erect tomb path stele. Daoguang 5th year rebuilt." A shrine was built during reconstruction. Baizhu Village refers to Nanshan Village, Yangtou Village is垟头 Village, two li east of Nanshan; shrine and tomb exist today. That "Reconstruction of Baizhu Xian Palace Fundraising Proposal" wrote "Huchen Shrine's fragrance lasts through ages," referring to this tomb shrine — we didn't notice at the time. Fu'an also has a Three Worthies Shrine, honoring local historical worthies: besides Zheng Huchen, Tang Shenlong 2nd year (706) jinshi, Kaiyuan period Zuo Buque and Crown Prince Reader Xue Lingzhi. And late Southern Song Xie Ao, known for integrity — his hometown named Liancun (Honest Village); Xie was a famous righteous scholar, follower of Wen Tianxiang. Ming Li Dongyang has a poem about Zheng Huchen killing Jia Sidao: "The sovereign doesn't execute, the escort does; father's revenge and national anger vented at once. Though the escort dies, his name never dies; the Yuancheng messenger merely vomits blood in vain." Inside Zheng Huchen's tomb shrine is a couplet attributed to Wen Tianxiang: "Being an upright person, all shoulder moral teachings; at the moment of dying for righteousness, all take great justice seriously." Both couplet and poem praise Zheng Huchen's righteousness. Nanshan Village, this declining mountain village full of heavy lazy atmosphere, once had such a righteous man — truly unimaginable. What we deeply regret is that working in Nanshan for many days, no one mentioned this hero to us; one of his literate descendants, the fengshui master, even wrote his name wrong, and complained he took away the fengshui.

However, the belief that villagers moving away takes fengshui fortune is still taken seriously by villagers. During our work, a Lousia Wang family's daughter married to Songluo Village behind the mountain. We chased the bridal sedan to photograph. The sedan was carried to the intersection left front of Liu Ancestral Hall, where an incense table was set; the bride got out, bowed twice, left some money, then got back in to continue. We asked what ceremony this was; the old man收拾 the incense table said it was to make the bride leave Lousia's fengshui fortune behind, not take it away. "A married daughter is like spilled water" — this precaution is truly heartless.

Winter 1995

sections.name: 狮峰寺一日
sections.content_zh:
狮峰寺一日

晨前四点半，我们在钟声和木鱼声中醒来，"罗衾不耐五更寒"，蜷缩在盖不住双脚的短小被窝里等待天亮。到窗帘上朦朦胧胧影出疏棂，阶前放生池里鱼儿的泼剌声渐渐紧密，我们起床，洗漱。和尚师父们散了早课，嘴里嘟囔着匆匆走回禅室。跟他们打过招呼，我们便轻轻推开了庙门。

庙门对面一排壁立的高山，隐隐被天空衬出坚硬锋利的轮廓，山脚却消失在静静的一抹浅蓝色的烟雾里。烟雾又衬出一溜小丘冈浑圆柔和的轮廓。从门前高高的台阶往下走，正前方笔架山峰尖上忽然闪出明亮的金色，它捕捉到了扑过来的第一绺阳光。小小的盆地醒来了。

踏着弯弯曲曲的石子路向东走去。右边坡上一层层梯地种着的茶树正盛开花朵。左边坡下，是一片又一片的茉莉田；不是花季，花朵却也不少。茶香和着花香，熏得我们神清气爽。一群群的雏鸭迎面过来，准备到收割了的稻田里去过富足的日子，我们恭敬地肃立在小路的边边上，谦卑地向它们微笑致意，它们却惊慌失措，嘎嘎叫着，乱作一团。待牧鸭人小心翼翼把它们哄过去，我们才继续往前走。转过一个山脚，上几层小坡，前面一棵大榕树和几丛水竹的剪影，勾勒出疏疏密密一幅铁锈的图画。水竹丛中隐隐呈现一座庙宇，尖尖的檐角高高挑起，刺破了薄雾。薄雾漫射着晨光，给图画罩上似梦似幻的恍惚迷离。这是村子的水口，也便是村口，后面躺着宁静的山村。

走进图画，小学校的大门已经打开，时间还早，只有零零落落几个女孩子，衣着鲜艳，款款来到。教师宿舍的窗里，早起的灯光还没有熄灭，有几个学生在拍门。我们从门前过去，不远，来到一个空场边上，这时候，东方山顶上散发出一片片鱼鳞般的红云，漫涌过来，越过头顶。刹那间，阳光打到了场子边长长一带金黄色的墙上，灿烂光明，照着"中山世裔"四个大字，这是刘氏宗祠前的影壁。

我们在宗祠右侧一座小小的农家吃早餐，甜甜的番薯稀粥，大大的碗。一阵阵穿堂风吹来，有点儿冷。吃饱了，身子暖和过来，大家分头到村里挨家挨户去做我们的工作。有的绘图，有的量尺寸，有的拍照，有的缠住老人家问东问西，问古问今，听不懂话，手脚一起参加解释，时不时因为发觉了误会而哈哈大笑。累了半天，中午再回到这家吃午饭，有绵软的大芋头，偶然还有滑溜溜的三寸来长的龙头鱼。

四周围山高，太阳出来得迟，隐去得却早。两点半钟，山影便遮到了村边。不到三点半，整个盆地笼罩在影子里了，只有东边的重重山峦，在斜阳下像波浪起伏奔腾，又像一幅迎风翻卷的绿色绸子。到它们也变成了阴沉的紫色，我们便走回寺庙去。依然是那条氤氲着茶香和花香的碎石小路，依然是一群一群的雏鸭，它们吃得饱饱的回来，又跟我们狭路相逢。为了躲闪我们，几只贪吃太多的，身子过重，一不小心，便扭伤了脚。牧鸭人把伤鸭倒提起来走，鸭子挣扎着，大叫大嚷，明天早晨，也许不会再见到它们了，我们觉得有点儿遗憾。

转过山脚，斜望寺庙，山门和大殿顺着山坡展开又庄重又玲珑的身姿。它后院那株高高的柏树下，是我们借住的禅房。斋堂的炊烟袅袅升起，送来温暖的情意。和尚师父正在晚课，柔和的诵经声缠绕着低沉的鼓声，迎我们踏进山门。

这是广化禅寺，一座初创于唐代的古刹，乡人们都叫它狮峰寺，说是它背后的大山好像一头狮子。我们在庙里吃晚餐，园子里采来的佛手瓜鲜甜脆嫩，香菇真有山野的清香。晚餐后，在小院的堂屋里整理我们一天的工作所得，核查在彼此都不大听得懂的一问一答里所得的调查记录，计划明天的工作。有不少收获使我们高兴，也有不少困扰使我们犯愁、失望。于是相互说些宽心的话，歇一夜再想办法。小院里的四季桂送来浓浓的甜香，灯光下，影影绰绰可以见到鱼池边秋菊金灿灿的花瓣上，露珠已经凝结成霜，闪闪发亮。

八点半，响起了沉闷的笃笃声，那是住持师父用棒槌敲打门槛，通知全寺的人熄灯睡觉。我们在禅房里躺下，夜寒凛冽，辗转等待着入睡。

没有青灯黄卷，却有暮鼓晨钟，二十来天，就这样在福建省福安市的楼下村工作。我们是贪婪的文化探宝者，在这红尘万丈的年月，竟来到这个群山环抱的小小村落，寻觅当年蓬首跣足的先人们，披荆斩棘，在这荒僻的山地建设家园的历史痕迹。

入睡前，我们默诵着明代邑人孙瑶的《狮峰寺》："晓发狮峰寺，岚光远近浮。竹交荒径合，石绣古苔幽。海气朝随雨，松风夜到楼。褰裳问闽俗，喜见万家秋。"（见光绪《福安县志·古迹》）此情此景，与我们的工作生活多么相合。

睡意上来了，盼一个好梦！

1995年冬
sections.content_en:
A Day at Shifeng Temple

At 4:30 before dawn, we woke to the sound of bells and wooden fish (muyu). "Silk quilt cannot endure the fifth watch cold" — curled up in short quilts that couldn't cover our feet, waiting for daylight. When faint window lattice shadows appeared on the curtains, and the splashing of fish in the release pond before the steps grew denser, we got up and washed. The monks finished morning prayers, muttering as they hurried back to their cells. After greeting them, we gently pushed open the temple gate.

Opposite the temple gate, a row of sheer high mountains, faintly outlined against the sky with hard, sharp contours, their foothills disappearing in a quiet layer of light blue mist. The mist又 outlined a row of small hills with round, soft contours. Walking down the high steps before the gate, directly ahead, the peak of Bijia (Brush-Rest) Mountain suddenly flashed bright gold — it caught the first ray of sunlight rushing over. The small basin woke up.

Walking east along the winding cobblestone path. On the right slope, terraced fields planted with tea bushes were in full bloom. On the left slope below, field after field of jasmine; not flowering season, yet quite a few blossoms. Tea fragrance mixed with flower fragrance, refreshing us. Flocks of ducklings came toward us, heading to the harvested rice fields for a rich day; we respectfully stood aside on the path edge, humbly smiling at them, but they panicked, quacking, in chaos. After the duckherd carefully herded them past, we continued. Rounding a foot of the mountain, climbing a few small slopes, ahead the silhouette of a large banyan tree and clumps of water bamboo outlined a sparse-dense iron-rust picture. Among the water bamboo, a temple faintly appeared, its sharp eave corners high and upturned, piercing the thin mist. The mist diffused morning light, casting a dreamlike, trance-like veil over the picture. This was the village's water mouth (shuikou), also the village entrance; behind lay the quiet mountain village.

Entering the picture, the primary school gate was already open; still early, only a few scattered girls, brightly dressed, gracefully arriving. In the teachers' dormitory windows, early lights hadn't gone out; a few students were knocking on doors. We passed the gate, not far, came to an open square; at this moment, from the eastern mountain top, fish-scale-like red clouds spread, surging over our heads. In an instant, sunlight hit the long golden-yellow wall by the square, brilliant and bright, illuminating the four large characters "Zhongshan Shiyi" (Descendants of Zhongshan) — this was the screen wall before the Liu Ancestral Hall.

We ate breakfast at a small farmhouse right of the ancestral hall — sweet sweet potato porridge, in large bowls. Drafts blew through, a bit cold. After eating, bodies warmed up, we split up to go door to door doing our work. Some drew plans, some measured dimensions, some took photos, some pestered elderly people with questions, old and new; not understanding the dialect, using hands and feet to explain, occasionally bursting into laughter upon realizing misunderstandings. Tired after half a day, at noon we returned to this house for lunch — soft large taro, occasionally slippery three-inch-long dragon-head fish.

Surrounded by high mountains, the sun rose late and set early. At 2:30, mountain shadows reached the village edge. Before 3:30, the entire basin was in shadow; only the eastern layered mountains, in setting sun, looked like surging waves, or a green silk scroll fluttering in wind. When they too turned gloomy purple, we walked back to the temple. Still the碎石 path氤氲 with tea and flower fragrance, still flocks of ducklings, returning full-fed, again meeting us on the narrow path. To dodge us, a few that had eaten too much, too heavy, accidentally sprained their feet. The duckherd carried the injured ducks upside down; they struggled, quacking loudly; tomorrow morning, perhaps we won't see them again — we felt a bit regretful.

Rounding the mountain foot, looking斜 at the temple, the mountain gate and main hall spread along the slope with dignified yet graceful form. Under the tall cypress tree in its backyard was our borrowed cell. Smoke from the dining hall curled up, bringing warm affection. The monks were at evening prayers; soft chanting wrapped around low drumbeats, welcoming us through the mountain gate.

This is Guanghua Chan Temple, an ancient temple first founded in Tang dynasty; villagers call it Shifeng (Lion Peak) Temple, saying the mountain behind looks like a lion. We ate dinner at the temple — chayote from the garden, sweet and crisp; shiitake mushrooms truly had mountain wilderness fragrance. After dinner, in the small courtyard's main room, we整理 the day's work, checking survey records obtained through mutually barely understood Q&A, planning tomorrow's work. Many gains made us happy, many puzzles made us anxious and disappointed. So we said comforting words to each other, rest a night then think of solutions. The courtyard's four-season osmanthus sent thick sweet fragrance; in lamplight, faintly visible on the golden chrysanthemum petals by the fish pond, dew had condensed into frost, sparkling.

At 8:30, a dull thock-thock sounded — the abbot striking the threshold with a mallet,通知 everyone to lights out. We lay down in the cell; night cold piercing, tossing and turning waiting for sleep.

No green lamp and yellow scrolls, but evening drums and morning bells — for over twenty days, working thus in Louxia Village, Fu'an City, Fujian Province. We are greedy cultural treasure-hunters; in this age of towering mortal dust, we came to this small village surrounded by mountains, seeking the historical traces of ancestors who, with unkempt hair and bare feet, braved brambles and thorns to build homes in this remote mountain land.

Before sleep, we silently recited Ming dynasty local Sun Yao's "Shifeng Temple": "Dawn departing Shifeng Temple, mountain mist floats near and far. Bamboo crosses wild paths joining, stone embroidered with ancient moss serene. Sea air follows rain at dawn, pine wind reaches the tower at night. Lifting garments to ask Min customs, glad to see ten thousand homes' autumn." (See Guangxu "Fu'an County Annals · Historic Sites") This scene and feeling, how well it matches our working life.

Sleepiness comes, hoping for a good dream!

Winter 1995

sections.name: 岭南的暖冬
sections.content_zh:
岭南的暖冬

1996年清明时节，我们在陕西研究窑洞。一向荒旱的黄土高原上，偏偏下着缠绵的雨，不肯放一天晴，冻得我们瑟瑟发抖，双手青紫。这一年初冬，我们又到广东梅县，研究客家村落，却是满目青葱，到处有花。北京盆栽的一品红，在这里长得比房子还高，连片成林。和风丽日之下，整天在田野里走，一身的舒泰。南宋诗人杨万里到了梅县，写过一首诗道："一路谁栽十里梅，下临溪水恰齐开。此行便是无官事，只为梅花也合来。"我们没有遇见梅花开，但风光处处，随时都觉得该来这一趟。

人情也一样温暖。我们两个教师乘飞机到了汕头，已经是黄昏时刻，一打听住宿，普普通通的招待所都贵得吓人，便给梅州市土建学会侯歆芳秘书长打了个电话，问他能不能午夜到火车站接我们，如果可以，我们便不在汕头过夜了。侯秘书长一口答应。车到梅县，他和梅州市建筑设计院谢汉涛院长在车站迎着，把我们送到旅店，安顿下来，还吃了一餐广式夜宵。从此侯秘书长便为我们忙得不可开交。第二天，早上七点半出发，就带我们到四乡八村转了一天去选点，把梅州市比较完整的古老村落看了个遍。汽车司机徐师傅说："我早就认定侨乡村最好。"侨乡村是行政村，下属寺前排、高田和塘肚三个自然村。我们也这样认定。于是，隔天，由副秘书长陈震云陪着，会齐了江苏美术出版社《老房子》图集的摄影兼编辑李玉祥，细细地看了看侨乡村，选定了第一批要测绘的房屋。傍晚回到市里，侯秘书长把侨乡村的旧图抱出来，随我们挑选了几份。我们向他提出，要地方志，要万分之一的军用地形图，要什么什么资料等等，他都一一答应。

第三天一早，陈副秘书长陪我们到了侨乡村所属的南口镇，找到镇长。镇长以各种各样的理由反对我们住进农家，在农家吃饭。没有办法，只好暂时听他的。近午时分，六个学生来到，他们是乘火车到龙川再乘长途汽车来的，由侯秘书长在汽车站接到送来镇上。于是，一行人边打听边走，到了街上供销社的小旅店住下。侯、陈两位，尝了我们的伙食，摸了我们的床铺，虽然对我们的"艰苦"十分关切，但觉得还可以放心，才回市里去。

午饭后立即带学生了解村子，分配任务。次日一早动手工作，干了不久，听见村民传说，有人找我们。我们赶到村口，原来是侯秘书长，送来了新编的梅州志。我们还来不及道谢，他便说"怕你们有急用"。过一天，他亲自送来了万分之一的军用地形图，再过两天，又亲自送来了草图纸，这是学生们从学校动身的时候忘记带了的。有一天晚上，我们正在制图，陈副秘书长和市建筑设计院的丘权润总建筑师还驱车来看望，殷切关切我们的工作和食宿。这以后，便又是请侯秘书买火车票、汽车票，麻烦得不得了，最后还劳谢汉涛院长送我们上了赴江西的火车。

市土建学会和建筑设计院的朋友们对我们的支持，不但热情、及时，而且非常有效。我们东奔西跑地到各处工作，深深体会到，有没有这样的支持，对工作的关系很大。而这种支持并非到处都有。我们很感谢梅州市的这些朋友们。

村子里也有好师友。寺前排村的潘若珍、潘振峰姐弟，塘肚村的潘应耿，都给了我们许多帮助。潘应耿熟知侨乡村的历史、掌故和潘氏谱系，带着我们一幢一幢地跑遍了塘肚村的所有房屋，介绍它们的来历。还长期借了一部新修的族谱给我们用。潘振峰不大熟悉历史，但是熟悉村里镇上的许多人，带我们找到老泥水工黄海珠师傅和地理师潘淦兆先生，帮我们借来一些乡土文献。尤其难得的是，他居然对建筑向来很有兴趣，给我们揭开了阴沟转折处的秘密。他的姐姐潘若珍则是我们学生们最好的大嫂，工作开始之后不几天便在她家吃午饭。

黄海珠师傅从曾祖父起便是泥水世家，四代人在侨乡村造了好几幢大房子，他给我们讲了不少客家围龙屋的做法，我们大大受益。

此外还有很多朋友。当年四块大洋买来给主人端茶点烟现在儿孙满堂有了自己小洋楼的丫环，七十年前抱着公鸡拜堂一辈子没有见过丈夫的"屯家婆"，50年代初怀着满腔热情回国参加建设而后来却遭际困苦以致儿子跳楼成了残废的华侨，退休在家养花莳草天天上街买报纸看完了便议论天下大事的小学校长，儿子在深圳发了大财给她造了几十个房间的三层洋楼一个人孤零零住着的老妈妈，七八十岁整天扎堆在老人协会里打麻将的"天上的事知道一半，地下的事全知道"的活史书们，每天挺着腰板纹丝不动坐在池塘边钓鱼却从来不见他钓起一尾的前任公社主任，老远就打招呼走到身边拉住了一定要说几遍她在台湾有多少房子多少店铺的回乡休息的老板娘，穿上袈裟念经脱下袈裟杀鸡剖鱼有妻有子闲来聚一屋子人打牌喝酒唱流行歌曲的和尚。还有那些小学生，一到礼拜天，就带着我们当向导，我们端起相机对准他们，便一哄而散；我们给建筑物拍照，他们却装鬼脸抢着上镜头。所有的朋友都对我们非常和善，知道了我们住在供销社的旅店里，村民们便邀我们到家里去吃去住，但因为我们已经在小旅店布置好了画图设施，不便再搬，没有去。学生们为没有在农家吃住而遗憾万分。但我们几乎挨门挨户享受了友情，吃遍了家家又香又甜的柚子。偶然闯进了柚子林，不把肚子吃得溜圆便不让出来。临回来的时候，朋友们送来的柚子堆起老高，我们塞满了行囊，只能带走一小部分。

可惜，我们在村里却常常要耐渴。东奔西跑，我们需要的是牛饮，但村里朋友们把我们当金丝雀，端出一盘跟茉莉花茶朵差不多大小的细瓷杯子，斟上可能很贵重的香茶，只够我们把舌头尖润一润。要解渴，还得到公路边上的小饭铺里去，先灌足一肚子水，再要一碗面。边吃边越过茂密的凤尾竹林遥望三星山，想几百年前永发公的寡妻陈婆太挑着两个年幼的孩子回兴宁娘家去，仆仆风尘，薄暮时分到小店投宿，凄惶艰难中得人指点，在三星寨落户，这才有了眼前富足的侨乡村。小饭铺的地点，据说正位于她投宿的小店，前面的公路上奔驰着开往兴宁的客车。唉，千古兴亡，岂只是帝王们的家事！

有点儿尴尬的事还是应该记下。一件是，感谢镇长先生的安排，我们所住的供销社小旅店，也是镇上叫花子们住宿的地方。我们白天看见他们在集市上乞讨，晚上隔着一层薄板壁听着他们打呼噜。我们睡的床铺咯吱咯吱地响，黏滑的被褥已经分辨不出原来的颜色，那大概都是他们留下的"雪泥鸿爪"。三个礼拜，不但没有洗过一次澡，连洗脸都只能马马虎虎，因为唯一的一只水龙头装在不分男女的厕所里，一个人在打水，背后就会有人肆无忌惮地解急。旅店里偶然会有一些莫明其妙的闲汉来住，喝醉了酒，满嘴胡说，推我们的房门，偏偏房门连个插闩都没有，只好用一根筷子别住。夜半想起镇长先生说的，街上治安不错，我们才勉强睡了觉。承包这个小旅店的老板过去是农机站的技术人员，农机站工作辛苦，收入少，散了伙。他白天做肉丸子卖，晚上就跟老婆打架，一个打，一个骂，打声很脆亮，骂声很高亢，总要闹上个把钟头，也有一直闹到天亮的日子。但我们仍然高高兴兴地坚持到把工作做完，学生们没有发牢骚，反倒觉得挺有意思。

另一件是，我们找到了村民委员会，查看村里的基本资料。会计先生拿出1995年的年度报告，一看，里面有条有理地记载着各种数字：人口、户数、田亩、各项生产、人均收入等等，要什么有什么，足有厚厚的一大本。我们高兴得不得了，赶快掏出笔记本来要抄录。会计先生淡淡一笑，说：抄了有什么用，全是假的，是我自己坐在这房间里编出来的。问他为什么，他说：这种年报嘛，年年做，做了送上去，绝不会有人看。我们合上笔记本，想，我们偏偏来看，真傻出水平来了。长吁了一口气，谢谢他的诚实，否则难免又要骗了别人。

1996年冬
sections.content_en:
Warm Winter in Lingnan

During Qingming 1996, we were studying cave dwellings in Shaanxi. On the usually arid Loess Plateau, it偏偏 rained continuously, refusing to clear for a day, freezing us shivering with hands blue-purple. In early winter that year, we went to Meixian, Guangdong, to study Hakka villages — instead, everywhere green, flowers everywhere. Beijing's potted poinsettia grew taller than houses here, forming forests. Under gentle wind and bright sun, walking in fields all day, body at ease. Southern Song poet Yang Wanli, coming to Meixian, wrote a poem: "Along the road who planted ten li of plum blossoms, below by streams blooming all at once. This trip even without official business, just for plum blossoms one should come." We didn't see plum blossoms, but scenery everywhere made us feel this trip was worthwhile at any moment.

Human warmth was the same. We two teachers flew to Shantou, already dusk; asking about lodging, even ordinary guesthouses were shockingly expensive, so we called Hou Xinfang, Secretary-General of Meizhou Civil Construction Society, asking if he could meet us at the train station at midnight; if so, we wouldn't stay in Shantou. Secretary Hou readily agreed. Arriving at Meixian, he and Xie Hantao, Director of Meizhou Architectural Design Institute, greeted us at the station, took us to the hotel, settled us in, and even had a Cantonese late-night snack. From then on, Secretary Hou was忙得不可开交 for us. Next day, departing at 7:30 a.m., he took us around villages all day to select a site, showing us all the relatively complete ancient villages in Meizhou. The bus driver Master Xu said: "I've long decided Qiaoxiang Village is the best." Qiaoxiang Village is an administrative village, with three natural villages: Siqianpai, Gaotian, and Tangdu. We agreed. So the next day, accompanied by Deputy Secretary-General Chen Zhenyun, meeting Li Yuxiang, photographer and editor of Jiangsu Fine Arts Publishing House's "Old Houses" album, we carefully examined Qiaoxiang Village and selected the first batch of houses to survey. Returning to the city in evening, Secretary Hou brought out old maps of Qiaoxiang Village, letting us choose several. We asked him for local gazetteers, 1:10,000 military topographic maps, various materials — he promised everything.

Early third day, Deputy Secretary Chen accompanied us to Nankou Town, which Qiaoxiang Village belongs to, to find the town mayor. The mayor opposed our staying and eating with farmers with various reasons. No choice, we temporarily followed his advice. Around noon, six students arrived — they had taken train to Longchuan then long-distance bus, picked up by Secretary Hou at the bus station and brought to town. So our group, asking directions as we walked, went to the supply and marketing cooperative's small inn on the street to stay. Hou and Chen, tasting our food, touching our beds, though very concerned about our "hardship," felt reassured enough, then returned to the city.

After lunch we immediately took students to understand the village and assign tasks. Next morning we started work; not long after, villagers said someone was looking for us. We rushed to the village entrance — it was Secretary Hou, delivering the newly compiled Meizhou Gazetteer. Before we could thank him, he said "afraid you need it urgently." A day later, he personally delivered the 1:10,000 military topographic map; two days later, personally delivered drafting paper, which students had forgotten to bring from school. One evening, while we were drafting, Deputy Secretary Chen and Chief Architect Qiu Quanrun of the city architectural design institute drove to visit, earnestly concerned about our work and lodging. After that, it was asking Secretary Hou to buy train and bus tickets, endlessly troublesome; finally Director Xie Hantao even saw us onto the train to Jiangxi.

The support from friends at the city Civil Construction Society and Architectural Design Institute was not only enthusiastic and timely, but very effective. Working everywhere, we deeply felt that having such support matters greatly to work. And such support is not everywhere. We are very grateful to these friends in Meizhou.

The village also had good teachers and friends. Pan Ruozhen and Pan Zhenfeng siblings in Siqianpai Village, Pan Yinggeng in Tangdu Village, all gave us much help. Pan Yinggeng knew Qiaoxiang Village's history, anecdotes, and Pan clan genealogy well, taking us through every house in Tangdu Village, explaining their origins. He also lent us a newly revised clan genealogy long-term. Pan Zhenfeng didn't know much history, but knew many people in village and town, taking us to find old plasterer Master Huang Haizhu and geomancer Master Pan Ganzhao, helping us borrow some local documents. Especially rare, he had long been interested in architecture, revealing to us the secret of drainage channel turns. His sister Pan Ruozhen was the best "sister-in-law" for our students; a few days after work began, we ate lunch at her house.

Master Huang Haizhu came from a plasterer family since his great-grandfather; four generations built several large houses in Qiaoxiang Village. He told us much about Hakka weilongwu (enclosed dragon house) construction methods, greatly benefiting us.

Besides, there were many friends. The maidservant bought for four silver dollars to serve tea and light cigarettes for the master, now with grandchildren and her own small Western-style house; the "Tunjiapo" who married a rooster seventy years ago and never saw her husband; the overseas Chinese who returned with enthusiasm in early 1950s to participate in construction but later suffered hardship, his son jumping from a building becoming disabled; the retired primary school principal who grows flowers at home, buys newspapers every day, and discusses world affairs after reading; the old mother whose son made a fortune in Shenzhen and built her a three-story Western-style house with dozens of rooms, living alone; the 70-80 year olds who gather all day at the Elderly Association playing mahjong — "living history books" who "know half of heaven's affairs, all of earth's"; the former commune director who sits straight and motionless by the pond fishing every day but never catches a thing; the returned-resting landlady who greets from afar, grabs you when close, insisting on telling repeatedly how many houses and shops she has in Taiwan; the monk who wears kasaya to chant, takes it off to kill chickens and gut fish, has a wife and children, and gathers a roomful to play cards, drink, and sing pop songs when free. And the primary school students — every Sunday they guide us; when we aim cameras at them, they scatter in a rush; when we photograph buildings, they make faces and抢 the镜头. All friends were very kind to us; knowing we stayed at the supply cooperative inn, villagers invited us to eat and stay at their homes, but since we had set up drafting facilities at the inn, inconvenient to move, we didn't go. Students regretted not staying with farmers greatly. But we almost door to door enjoyed friendship, eating every family's fragrant sweet pomelos. Occasionally闯入 pomelo groves, not letting us leave until bellies full. Before returning, friends sent pomelos piled high; we stuffed our bags, could only take a small part.

Unfortunately, we often had to endure thirst in the village. Running around, we needed to drink like oxen, but village friends treated us like canaries — bringing out tiny porcelain cups about the size of jasmine tea flowers, pouring possibly precious fragrant tea, only enough to moisten the tip of the tongue. To quench thirst, we had to go to small eateries by the highway, first filling up on water, then ordering a bowl of noodles. Eating while looking past dense phoenix bamboo groves at Sanxing Mountain, thinking how hundreds of years ago, Yongfa Gong's widow Chen Potai carried two young children back to her natal home in Xingning, travel-worn, at dusk seeking lodging at a small shop, in distress and hardship getting guidance, settling at Sanxingzhai — thus才有 the prosperous Qiaoxiang Village before us. The small eatery's location,据说 is exactly where she lodged; on the highway in front, buses to Xingning speed by. Alas, the rise and fall of millennia, is it only the emperors' family affair!

Some awkward things should still be recorded. One: thanks to Mayor's arrangement, the supply cooperative inn we stayed at was also where town beggars lodged. We saw them begging at the market by day, at night hearing them snore through a thin board wall. Our beds creaked, sticky bedding no longer distinguishable in original color — probably their "snow泥鸿爪" left behind. Three weeks, not only no bath, even face-washing was perfunctory, because the only faucet was in the unisex toilet; while one person fetched water, behind someone would relieve themselves without restraint. Occasionally some inexplicable idlers stayed at the inn, drunk, talking nonsense, pushing our door —偏偏 the door had no bolt, so we used a chopstick to bar it. At midnight, remembering the mayor said street治安 was good, we勉强 slept. The inn boss was formerly a technician at the agricultural machinery station; the station, hard work low pay, disbanded. He makes meatballs by day, fights with his wife at night — one hits, one scolds, hitting sound crisp, scolding voice loud, always闹 an hour or so, sometimes until dawn. But we still happily persisted until work done; students didn't complain,反而 found it quite interesting.

Another: we found the village committee to check basic village data. The accountant brought out the 1995 annual report — inside, orderly recorded various figures: population, households, farmland, production, per capita income, etc., whatever you wanted, a thick book. We were delighted, quickly taking out notebooks to copy. The accountant smiled faintly and said: what's the use of copying, it's all fake, I made it up sitting in this room. Asked why, he said: these annual reports, made every year, sent up, no one ever reads. We closed notebooks, thinking: we偏偏 came to look, really foolish to a professional level. Sighed deeply, thanked his honesty — otherwise we might have deceived others.

Winter 1996

sections.name: 洞主庙
sections.content_zh:
洞主庙

俞源村唯一保存下来的庙宇是洞主庙，或者叫洞主殿，位于村东南以外二百来米的龙宫山尽端，大致朝西。同治《宣平县志》载："龙宫山洞主庙，在县东北四十里俞源，祀清源妙道真君，祈梦甚灵。每岁元旦起，七八日内每日一二百人不等，婺郡人为最多。如立春在先年腊底则少逊。"这是一座以祈梦灵验而名闻婺、括两州的庙。武义晚清名士何德润（道光十八年生，宣统三年卒）写过一篇《圆梦史志》，说："龙宫洞主庙，祈梦甚灵，武义项秉谦尝寄宿焉。梦胆瓶，插萱花六枝，觉而言之，其友顾倬标曰：萱、宣也；瓶，平也。六年秩满，君其司铎是邑乎？项年少气盛，意勿屑也。后顾以孝廉捷南宫，而项以拔贡为宣平教官，竟以先兆。"

洞主庙为祈梦人在北部造了一个三层的"圆梦楼"，正名是清幽阁，供他们宿夜。1983年恢复洞主庙香火后，每年农历六月二十六日洞主老爷生日前夜，求梦的人不但睡满了圆梦楼庙内大殿、偏殿、前厅和廊下，连庙外沿东溪北岸的道路上都睡满了人。村民家里则忙于招待各地来的亲朋们。嫁出去的女儿归宁，还会带来亲家母。四乡有些人凭《周公解梦》之类的几本术数书来摆摊给人解梦，收入很可观。平日则由"庙祝"解释，他也解释神签，总是说些好话，抚慰人心，或者鼓励年轻人上进。

洞主庙庙会期间，俞氏宗祠内演三天四夜的社戏。通宵达旦，四面八方的邻村人也都赶来看戏。那期间也会有许多做小买卖的和设赌局的。

洞主庙虽然香火兴旺，但它的主神是谁却说法纷纭。一种比较正宗的说法是战国时代秦国在四川灌县建都江堰的李冰。李冰在全国普遍被尊为治水的神，俞源和附近许多山区村落常受山洪之苦，因此多建李冰庙，俞源凤凰山口也早有颜姓人造的李冰庙。现存洞主庙中道光二十五年（1845）的石碑《洞主殿碑记》说："社庙之事无村无之，醵赀置产莫不专奉一神以祈黄茂而祝乌邪。俞源洞主庙则祀清源妙道真君，与我武二郎同，亦即二郎也。世俗不悉其详，猥以小说家所谓二郎神者当之，误矣！案秦李冰为灌令，开灌口堰，蜀人受其惠，罔弗祀二郎者。冰行二，故曰二郎。或曰，堰之成，冰次子实以死勤事，故祀之，当时称通济王，至宋封真人，而其祀遂遍天下。俞源之庙祀即始南宋，迄今六百有余岁矣。"碑文是住持道人郑萃灿和徒弟祝太义写的，文理不很通顺，但有几点很明确。一、这是庙，又为了镇水；二、庙初建于南宋；三、庙祀清源妙道真君，这位真君是李冰，叫二郎，但碑文又用"或曰"说庙也可能是奉祀李冰的次子的，他才是二郎，而且也会治水。于是就回到了究竟奉祀什么人的问题。宣平和武义的普通百姓又提出了第二个问题：宣平人把这座洞主庙叫作香子庙，武义人叫它沉香庙。沉香是二郎神杨戬的妹妹华英三圣母与书生刘彦昌的私生子。他母亲因失贞被二郎神镇在山下，沉香七岁时经霹雳大仙传授武艺和仙术，先战败龙王，取来法宝，然后大战杨戬，劈开山头救出了母亲。洞主庙为祀他而建。可以作为这个说法的佐证的是：一、大殿正中奉祀的"三姓社主"的木雕像是个七岁的孩子；二、从祖先传下规矩，村中演戏不许演"沉香救母"这一出；三、俞源村四面八方的山山水水，从九龙山、龙宫山、龙潭、仙云山、棋盘石、石佛冈，直到不大的山洞、岩石等等，有数不清的沉香战龙王的神迹，村人们到现在说起来还绘声绘色，非常生动；四、沉香用宝葫芦吸干海水降服了龙王，他也能镇水。

考证清源妙道真君的称号，也有几种说法。道光二十五年（1845）的《洞主殿碑记》说清源妙道真君就是李冰。《三教源流搜神大全》说："清源妙道真君，姓赵名昱，从道士李钰隐青城山，隋炀帝知其贤，起为嘉州太守。"后来赵昱率七圣制伏了春夏为水患的老蛟，"民感其德，立庙于灌江口，奉祀焉，俗曰灌口二郎。（唐）太宗封为神勇大将军。明皇幸蜀，加封赤城王。宋真宗朝……追尊圣号曰清源妙道真君"。这位赵昱，在灌口有祀，与李冰相邻，又叫二郎，而且也制伏了水患，加上真正封为清源妙道真君，那么，他也可能是这位洞主老爷。但乡民仍旧不服气，故事说，沉香打败了娘舅杨戬，劈山救出母亲之后，杨戬转而怜爱他，把一面写着"清源妙道真君"的旗帜送给了他。这旗帜本来是杨戬自己的，清源妙道真君是他的称号。他就是李冰的次子，叫杨二郎。沉香得了杨戬的旗号，便称清源妙道真君。于是传说中便有四个"二郎"，即沉香、赵昱、李冰次子和杨戬，而李二郎可能就是杨二郎。

至于祈梦灵验，乡民也和学者持不同意见。学者说，南宋大诗人陆游有一首诗，题目为《淳熙元年夜宿伏龙观圆梦梦见李冰驾百丈鲸鲵从天而降醒后所赋诗》。伏龙观就是都江堰的李冰庙，可见李冰与祈梦早有瓜葛。乡民们则说，洞主庙是应梦而建的。南宋时，一位住在山锦里的朱村老人梦见一个七岁小孩，在龙岩山洞中龙潭的水面上来回奔跑，并且闻到了沉香木的香味。第二天绝早，老人赶到龙潭边，看到一块沉香木在水面漂荡。他捞起沉香木，聚村民解梦，都认为是沉香子显圣，因为龙岩山洞就发源于九龙山，而九龙山是沉香战败龙王后从龙宫变来的，沉香就在山上成神。于是村民便把老人住的山叫梦山，就是现在的小祠堂山。在龙潭边造了祭祀沉香的洞主庙，神像和神牌便用龙潭中捞出来的那块沉香木做的。初建的庙很小，元代时，俞氏三世祖俞至刚才在现在的位置重建了新庙，原来的神像和神牌也搬了过来。可惜神像在"文化大革命"时被毁掉，神牌几年前被人偷走了。因为洞主庙是沉香托梦而建的，所以，它也成了人们祈梦的地方。

乡民们又说，俞源洞主庙每年举行两次庙会，一次在农历正月十三，连上灯节；一次在六月二十六，是洞主老爷生日。原来二郎神杨戬的生日和沉香相同，都是六月二十五日。但武义城里有座二郎庙，俞源和县城同一天举行庙会的话，香客和小贩等杂色人都忙不过来，经过协调，俞源的庙会推迟一天，这叫作"甥让舅"，可见洞主庙祭祀的确实是沉香。但是，据一般神话传说，六月二十六是李冰的生日，武义的戏班却以正月十二为二郎神的生日，那么，洞主庙正月十三的庙会才是"甥让舅"让出来的。乡民的说法可能有一点小差错。

如果二郎神杨戬就是李冰的次子，那么，加上沉香，本是三代一家人。只有赵昱是李冰的同行和邻居。至于为什么叫"洞主"，已经没有人追究了。

尽管有一块道光年间的石碑，不管怎么说，村民们偏爱沉香。他小小年纪，拜霹雳大仙为师学武艺，斗败龙王取宝，又打败封建卫道士亲娘舅杨戬，劈山救出忠于爱情的母亲，这浪漫得很的故事太动人了。据说，沉香大战龙王的时候，用细腰葫芦吸干了海水，龙王才不得不投降，所以俞源村人至今还用细腰葫芦装酒和水，葫芦外面用细篾丝编上非常精致的套子，下地、出门都背上。葫芦里的酒、水，口味甘甜，长期不变质。这种葫芦是俞源村的特产，家家户户的檐下都挂着几个还没有编套子的，等待干透了再加工。俞源住宅的门窗格扇上，雕花以拐子龙为主，这和当年沉香所擒的龙王本来是霹雳大仙的拐杖变的或许有点关系。

本来洞主庙的主神"三姓社主"神像是老人梦见的七岁的孩童，乡民都叫他洞主老爷。砸毁之后，现在新雕的一个却是四十来岁老农的模样，乡人们很不满意，打算另雕一个。

大殿上除了"三姓社主"沉香之外，神仙菩萨杂乱无序，表现出农民神谱的功利主义特色。沉香居于明间中央，左次间供梦神和夏禹王，传说以前夏禹王的位子供的是李冰，是从水口颜氏的李冰庙搬来的，前几年重修洞主庙的时候，觉得禹王治水的能耐比李冰大，所以改塑了禹王；左梢间供天廷中守护天门的周将军、唐将军、葛将军，是从雪峰庵搬来的；右次间供财神和五谷神，是从慈姑堂搬来的；右梢间则供周文王夫妇，据说他们多子多孙，可以帮人多得子息。此外，左手跨院是观音堂，正中供观音，左边文昌帝君，右边关公大帝，是文武二圣。右手跨院是土地堂，供土地公公和土地婆婆。这些神仙菩萨的专业关怀，足可涵盖农村生活的一切方面。

据道光二十五年（1845）的《洞主殿碑记》记载，庙产香火田是乾隆癸巳年（1773）由永谐、永隆、长发"三班香会"和"会长"李嵩萃捐置的。李嵩萃居于很重要的地位。这件事也有故事。洞主庙本来是俞氏三世祖至刚重建的，没有李氏的份。乾隆年间，拔贡俞启元的次女琪与李嵩萃的第四子君荣订亲，俞琪要求的陪嫁，便是让李氏共有洞主庙。于是两姓协商，俞姓提出，以后每十年一次的"开光"，沉香的全身金箔和龙袍以及每年擎台阁时抬神牌的三十二个人的素面点心由李姓出，则洞主庙可以两姓共有。当时正发财得红火的李嵩萃一口应承了下来，于是俞琪和李君荣于乾隆壬寅（1782）结婚。从此俞源村也添了一个风俗，凡娶亲的，都要先去洞主庙进香，供熟猪头、熟鸡和利市香烛。虽然李姓出钱是事实，这个小女子讨嫁妆和睦两姓的可爱的故事却有疑问。洞主庙里有一块石碑，刻着《台阁碑志》，说"擎台阁始自清咸丰"，那就比李嵩萃晚了许多年。不过这块碑是1993年腊月在擎台阁被迫停止了四十四年之后重新恢复的时候立的，它所说的也只凭大家的传闻，未必可靠。至于从什么时候起，沉香成了俞、李、董"三姓社主"，现在更没有人说得清了。

1998年夏
sections.content_en:
Dongzhu Temple

The only surviving temple in Yuyuan Village is Dongzhu Temple, also called Dongzhu Hall, located at the end of Longgong Mountain about 200 meters southeast of the village, roughly facing west. Tongzhi "Xuanping County Annals" records: "Longgong Mountain Dongzhu Temple, 40 li northeast of the county at Yuyuan, enshrines Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun, dream-praying very efficacious. Every year from New Year's Day, for seven or eight days, 100-200 people daily, most from Wujun. If Lichun falls in late previous year, slightly fewer." This was a temple famous for dream-praying efficacy in both Wu and Kuo prefectures. He Derun, a late Qing scholar of Wuyi (born Daoguang 18th year, died Xuantong 3rd year), wrote "Dream Interpretation History Records": "Longgong Dongzhu Temple, dream-praying very efficacious; Wuyi's Xiang Bingqian once lodged there. Dreamed of a gall vase with six daylily branches; upon waking told it, his friend Gu Zhuobiao said: daylily = Xuan (Xuanping); vase = Ping (peace). After six years' term, will you be instructor there? Xiang was young and ambitious, disdained it. Later Gu passed the metropolitan exam as juren, while Xiang became Xuanping instructor as bagong — indeed the omen."

Dongzhu Temple built a three-story "Dream-Fulfilling Tower" for dream-prayers in the north, properly named Qingyou Pavilion, for them to spend the night. After restoring Dongzhu Temple's incense in 1983, every year on lunar June 26th, the eve of Dongzhu Lord's birthday, dream-seekers not only fill the Dream-Fulfilling Tower, main hall, side halls, front hall and corridors, but even the road along the north bank of Dongxi outside the temple is full of sleepers. Villagers busy hosting relatives and friends from everywhere. Married daughters return home, bringing mothers-in-law. Some people from surrounding townships set up stalls interpreting dreams with books like "Zhou Gong's Dream Interpretation," income considerable. On ordinary days, the "temple keeper" explains, also interpreting divine lots, always saying good words, comforting hearts, or encouraging young people to progress.

During Dongzhu Temple fair, Yu Ancestral Hall stages three days and four nights of community opera. Through the night, people from neighboring villages all around come to watch. During that period there are also many small vendors and gambling stalls.

Though Dongzhu Temple's incense thrives, who its main deity is remains disputed. One more orthodox version is Li Bing, who built Dujiangyan in Guan County, Sichuan, during the Warring States Qin state. Li Bing is widely honored nationwide as a water-control god; Yuyuan and many nearby mountain villages often suffer flash floods, so many Li Bing temples were built; at Yuyuan's Fenghuang Mountain pass there was also an early Li Bing temple built by the Yan family. The existing Daoguang 25th year (1845) stele "Dongzhu Hall Stele Record" says: "Village temples exist in every village; pooling funds to acquire property, all dedicate to one god to pray for harvest and ward off evil. Yuyuan Dongzhu Temple enshrines Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun, same as our Wu Erlang, i.e., Erlang. Common people not knowing details, mistakenly take the novelist's so-called Erlang god as him. In Qin, Li Bing was magistrate of Guan, opened Guankou Weir, Shu people benefited, all worship Erlang. Bing was second son, hence called Erlang. Or: the weir's completion, Bing's second son actually died in service, hence worshiped, then called Tongji King, by Song封为 zhenren, and his worship spread nationwide. Yuyuan's temple worship began in Southern Song, now over 600 years." The stele text was written by presiding Daoist Zheng Cuican and disciple Zhu Taiyi, prose not very smooth, but several points clear: 1. This is a temple, also for water suppression; 2. Temple first built in Southern Song; 3. Temple enshrines Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun, this zhenjun is Li Bing, called Erlang, but the stele also uses "or says" that the temple may enshrine Li Bing's second son, who is Erlang, and also controls water. Thus returning to the question of who exactly is worshiped. Common people of Xuanping and Wuyi raised a second question: Xuanping people call this Dongzhu Temple Xiangzi Temple, Wuyi people call it Chenxiang Temple. Chenxiang is the illegitimate son of Erlang god Yang Jian's sister Huaying Sanshengmu and scholar Liu Yanchang. His mother, for losing chastity, was suppressed under a mountain by Yang Jian; at age seven, Chenxiang was taught martial arts and immortal arts by Pili Daxian, first defeated the Dragon King, obtained treasures, then battled Yang Jian, split the mountain to rescue his mother. Dongzhu Temple was built to worship him. Evidence for this version: 1. The wood statue of "Three-Surname Community Lord" enshrined in the main hall center is a seven-year-old child; 2. From ancestral rules, village opera may not perform "Chenxiang Rescues Mother"; 3. Yuyuan's mountains and waters all around — from Jiulong Mountain, Longgong Mountain, Longtan, Xianyun Mountain, Qipanshi, Shifogang, down to small caves and rocks — have countless miracles of Chenxiang battling the Dragon King, villagers still tell them vividly; 4. Chenxiang used a treasure gourd to suck dry seawater and subdue the Dragon King, he can also suppress water.

Researching the title Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun also has several versions. Daoguang 25th year (1845) "Dongzhu Hall Stele Record" says Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun is Li Bing. "Three Teachings Origin Searching Gods Complete" says: "Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun, surname Zhao name Yu, followed Daoist Li Yu to hide in Qingcheng Mountain; Emperor Yang of Sui, knowing his virtue, appointed him Jiazhou prefect." Later Zhao Yu led seven sages to subdue the old flood dragon causing spring-summer floods, "people grateful for his virtue, built temple at Guankou, worshiped, commonly called Guankou Erlang. (Tang) Taizong封为 Shenyong Great General. Minghuang visiting Shu,加封 Chicheng King. Song Zhenzong court … posthumous sacred title Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun." This Zhao Yu has worship at Guankou, adjacent to Li Bing, also called Erlang, and also subdued floods, plus actually封为 Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun — so he could also be this Dongzhu Lord. But villagers still不服气; story says, after Chenxiang defeated his uncle Yang Jian and split the mountain to rescue his mother, Yang Jian转而 pitied him, giving him a banner inscribed "Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun." This banner was originally Yang Jian's own; Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun was his title. He is Li Bing's second son, called Yang Erlang. Chenxiang, getting Yang Jian's banner, then called Qingyuan Miaodao Zhenjun. Thus legend has four "Erlangs": Chenxiang, Zhao Yu, Li Bing's second son, and Yang Jian — while Li Erlang may be Yang Erlang.

As for dream-praying efficacy, villagers and scholars disagree. Scholars say Southern Song great poet Lu You has a poem titled "Chunxi First Year, Night Lodging at Fulong Temple, Dreaming of Li Bing Riding a Hundred-Zhang Whale Descending from Heaven, Poem Composed Upon Waking." Fulong Temple is Dujiangyan's Li Bing Temple, showing Li Bing and dream-praying had early connections. Villagers say Dongzhu Temple was built because of a dream. In Southern Song, an old man from Zhu Village living in Shan Jinli dreamed a seven-year-old child running back and forth on the water surface of Longtan at Longyan Mountain Cave, and smelled agarwood fragrance. Early next morning, the old man rushed to Longtan, saw a piece of agarwood floating on the water. He捞起 the agarwood, gathered villagers to interpret the dream, all认为 it was Chenxiangzi manifesting holiness, because Longyan Mountain Cave originates from Jiulong Mountain, and Jiulong Mountain was transformed from the Dragon Palace after Chenxiang defeated the Dragon King, and Chenxiang became a god on the mountain. So villagers called the mountain where the old man lived Mengshan (Dream Mountain), now the Small Ancestral Hall Mountain. Built Dongzhu Temple by Longtan to worship Chenxiang; the statue and tablet were made from the agarwood捞 from Longtan. The initial temple was small; in Yuan dynasty, Yu clan's third ancestor Yu Zhigang rebuilt a new temple at the current location, moving the original statue and tablet. Unfortunately the statue was destroyed during the Cultural Revolution, and the tablet was stolen a few years ago. Because Dongzhu Temple was built because of Chenxiang's dream, it also became a place for people to pray for dreams.

Villagers also say Yuyuan Dongzhu Temple holds two fairs yearly: one on lunar January 13, connecting with the Lantern Festival; one on June 26, Dongzhu Lord's birthday. Originally Erlang god Yang Jian's birthday and Chenxiang's were the same, both June 25. But Wuyi city has an Erlang Temple; if Yuyuan and the city held fairs the same day, pilgrims and vendors would be too busy, so after coordination, Yuyuan's fair was postponed one day — this is called "nephew yields to uncle," showing Dongzhu Temple indeed worships Chenxiang. However, according to general myth, June 26 is Li Bing's birthday; Wuyi opera troupes take January 12 as Erlang's birthday, so Dongzhu Temple's January 13 fair is the one "nephew yields to uncle." Villagers' version may have a small error.

If Erlang god Yang Jian is Li Bing's second son, then plus Chenxiang, they are three generations of one family. Only Zhao Yu is Li Bing's colleague and neighbor. As for why called "Dongzhu" (Cave Master), no one pursues it anymore.

Despite a Daoguang-era stele, villagers prefer Chenxiang regardless. At a young age, he apprenticed to Pili Daxian to learn martial arts, defeated the Dragon King to take treasures, defeated his feudal moralist uncle Yang Jian, split the mountain to rescue his mother loyal to love — this very romantic story is too moving. It is said when Chenxiang battled the Dragon King, he used a narrow-waist gourd to suck dry seawater, forcing the Dragon King to surrender; so Yuyuan villagers to this day use narrow-waist gourds for wine and water, with exquisitely woven fine bamboo covers outside, carried when going to fields or out. The wine and water in the gourds taste sweet, don't spoil long-term. This gourd is Yuyuan's specialty; every household's eaves hang several without covers yet, waiting to dry before processing. On Yuyuan residences' door and window lattice panels, carvings feature "拐子龙" (curved dragon) mainly — perhaps related to the Dragon King Chenxiang captured originally being Pili Daxian's crutch transformed.

Originally the main deity "Three-Surname Community Lord" statue was the seven-year-old child the old man dreamed of; villagers call him Dongzhu Lord. After destruction, the newly carved one now looks like a 40-something peasant, villagers very dissatisfied, planning to carve another.

Besides "Three-Surname Community Lord" Chenxiang in the main hall, gods and bodhisattvas are disorderly, showing the utilitarian character of peasant pantheons. Chenxiang occupies the central bay; left secondary bay enshrines Dream God and King Yu of Xia — legend says previously King Yu's position enshrined Li Bing, moved from Yan family's Li Bing Temple at the water mouth; when rebuilding Dongzhu Temple a few years ago, felt Yu's water-control ability greater than Li Bing's, so re-sculpted Yu; left end bay enshrines Zhou General, Tang General, Ge General guarding heaven's gate in the celestial court, moved from Xuefeng Nunnery; right secondary bay enshrines God of Wealth and Five Grains God, moved from Cigu Hall; right end bay enshrines King Wen of Zhou and his wife, said to have many descendants, can help people get more sons. Besides, left courtyard is Guanyin Hall, center enshrines Guanyin, left Wenchang Emperor, right Guan Gong Great Emperor — civil and martial sages. Right courtyard is Tudi (Earth God) Hall, enshrines Tudi Gong and Tudi Po. These gods' professional concerns cover all aspects of rural life.

According to Daoguang 25th year (1845) "Dongzhu Hall Stele Record," temple incense fields were donated in Qianlong Guisi year (1773) by Yongxie, Yonglong, Changfa "three-class incense associations" and "president" Li Songcui. Li Songcui held an important position. This also has a story. Dongzhu Temple was originally rebuilt by Yu clan's third ancestor Zhigang, no Li share. During Qianlong, bagong Yu Qiyuan's second daughter Qi was betrothed to Li Songcui's fourth son Junrong; Yu Qi's requested dowry was for the Li clan to co-own Dongzhu Temple. So the two clans negotiated; Yu proposed that for the decennial "consecration" (kaiguang), Chenxiang's full-body gold foil and dragon robe, plus the plain noodles and snacks for the 32 people carrying the divine tablet during the annual pavilion procession, be provided by the Li clan — then Dongzhu Temple could be co-owned by both clans. Li Songcui, then prospering in wealth, readily agreed; so Yu Qi and Li Junrong married in Qianliang Renyin (1782). From then Yuyuan added a custom: any bride must first go to Dongzhu Temple to offer incense, with cooked pig head, cooked chicken, and auspicious incense candles. Though Li clan paying is fact, this lovely story of a young woman negotiating dowry to harmonize two clans has doubts. Dongzhu Temple has a stele inscribed "Pavilion Stele Record," saying "pavilion processions began in Qing Xianfeng" — much later than Li Songcui. But this stele was erected in 1993 12th lunar month when pavilion processions were restored after being forced to stop for 44 years; what it says relies only on hearsay, not necessarily reliable. As for when Chenxiang became Yu, Li, Dong "Three-Surname Community Lord," now no one can say clearly.

Summer 1998

sections.name: 告别俞源村
sections.content_zh:
告别俞源村

终于要走了。天还是下着蒙蒙细雨。

俞氏大宗祠前，簇拥着男女老少新结识的朋友们。告别是不容易的。向他们一个一个地道谢，耳朵里轰轰响着一片"再来，再来"的喊声。抬头望望他们，一张张被太阳晒黑了被风吹糙了的脸上，流露着那么深沉的真诚。

车子缓缓开动了，三位老人家，二十多天来一直陪着我们工作的，跟在车子后面大步追着。跑在最前面的是七十七岁的耀宗先生，矮矮胖胖的身子，摇摇晃晃，脚下高高踢起泥浆水，哗哗飞溅。我们从车窗探出大半个身子，满嗓子喊"别跑了，别跑了"，他不顾，仍然竭力地跑。双眼紧盯着我们，眼珠子通红通红的。车子向右转了个弯，见不到朋友们了，我们的眼珠子也都红了。

十年以来，我们一次又一次地经历过这样的告别。半个世纪的急风骤雨，丝毫没有改变农民那种天生的厚道、淳朴和热情。但是，当我们深深沉醉在他们宽阔怀抱中的时候，我们也分明地感觉到，他们的情谊中有一种祈愿，一种诉求，一种对命运的怨望。我们总忘不了在每次研究报告的"后记"里写下对村子里父老乡亲的感谢，这是出自心底的话，但这显然不是他们所期望的。我们怀着对父老乡亲的真挚感情，力求把工作做得好一些，但这也显然不能满足他们的祈求。

有一种期望，我们好像难以比较从容地面对，那就是一个最普遍遇到的问题：古老的村子和古老的房屋真的能使村民们摆脱近乎无望的贫穷吗？因为近几年旅游业闹得红红火火，已经有几个古村落向游人开放，经济收入很可观，村民们不但多有耳闻，甚至有人去做过调查。他们热切地企盼我们能帮助他们也把古建筑变成摇钱树。我们坐在住家的廊檐下，村口的桥头上，商店的柜台前，跟他们细细商量。有几次，几位退休的老区长、老武装部长，夜里摸黑到我们寄居的洞主庙找我们，问我们到底心里对村子怎么评价，对它的开发前景有怎样的估计，要我们说一句真话。于是，除了细数村落的历史、文化价值，我们又不得不坦率地说出许多困难来。在当前条件下，古老村子能不能开发旅游，并不完全决定于它们的历史、文化和建筑价值，还要有许多其他条件。而且，以古老的村落为旅游资源，首先必须把它们认真地当作文化资源，在开发之前，先科学地保护它们。但保护一个古老的村落，会牵涉到很多很复杂的问题。要有正确的观念，要有完善的体制，要有特殊的政策，要有专项的经费，要对村民生活的现代化做出妥善的安排，要给村子经济的发展留有充分的余地，还要有便利的交通和服务设施，如此等等。这些问题都不是一个村子自己能解决的。在到俞源村之前，我们帮浙江省诸葛村和江西省流坑村做过保护规划。我们自己知道，那两个规划都没有解决长远维持和增强村子生命力的问题。好在短期内矛盾还不至十分尖锐，我们还可以有几年时间静观待变。这就是说，我们应该继续对那两个村子密切注意观察，以便分阶段修订和调整保护规划。但是，交出了规划，我们便断了和村子的关系，而且，一旦旅游业强有力地介入并且干扰了村子的保护，那么，任何规划都会变成废物。这种干扰在当前几乎是不可避免的。急功近利，这是整个社会的现状，旅游业目前仿佛只为获利而存在。旅游业是大大赚钱的，而保护古村是要大大花钱的，搞旅游的人因此腰板就比搞文化的硬，说起话来中气更足得多。就说这个俞源村里，1993年县文化局把洞主庙和俞氏大宗祠定为重点文物保护点；1997年夏天，旅游局长一进村，就指令把几百年来一向是白色的洞主庙刷成了红色。这当然是小事一桩，局长先生还打算大大突出刘伯温在俞源的种种事迹，虽然都不过是些没有什么根据的传说。我们并不一概摈弃传说，因为它们蕴含着村民的理想、追求和价值观念。但是要把传说一一落实到环境和建筑上，做些虚假伪冒的东西，这就太出格了。面对着迫切要求摆脱贫困的穷怕了的村民，我们心里火急火燎。我们是书呆子吗？我们对村民的困苦漠然无动于衷吗？我们的眼光真的那么长远，我们的思想真的那么全面吗？

于是，一种比较容易面对的村民的期望，也变得困难起来了，何况还有许多更难面对的问题，比如县长官要靠古村落拿"政绩"，而政绩的主要衡量标准是经济效益。

我们在俞源村的工作，得到武义县博物馆涂志刚馆长的有力支持。他给我们做好了很切实的安排，隔两三天就挤破破烂烂的公共汽车来看我们一趟。涂志刚是我们见到过的最敬业、最称职的博物馆长。他精通文物业务，从考古发掘到鉴定古建筑年代，说来头头是道。他带我们到城里、镇里、村里参观，在乱麻似的巷子里钻来钻去，毫不犹豫便能找到一幢古建筑，熟悉得就像在自己卧室里找一件外套一样。说起这幢古建筑的年代和特点，又像数他外套上的纽扣，而且充满了感情。说来奇怪，他原来竟是在军队的大学里学习最可怕的毁灭性兵器的。

在村子里全面照料我们的生活和工作的是俞耀宗先生。这是一位经历了许多坎坷却十分乐观的人。他曾经当过中小学教师，五十年前的学生至今还记得，全校的教师都穿长袍，独有他西装革履。他生性活泼，自己带过戏班子，在四乡游动演出，很有名气。20世纪中叶土地改革之后走了背运，甚至受过牢狱之灾。现在一个人住在洞主庙里，担任类似管理员的角色，用老话说大概相当于"庙祝"，还负责讲解神签和圆梦，每次可以收一块钱，七毛归旅游局，三毛归他。村里人爱跟他开玩笑，叫他"洞主老爷"。1998年春节，他还带领着本村的龙灯，走了四十多里路到县城去热闹了一番。

俞步升先生带着我们一户挨一户地做调查，而且反复不止一次，虽然承认很累，却总是笑眯眯的。俞氏宗谱、李氏宗谱、宣平县志都是他给我们去找来。他本来是林业局的干部，退休之后，热心于研究本村的历史，近几年来，写过长长短短各种文章，还搜集了五十多则传说故事。所有这些资料都用漂亮的小楷抄得整整齐齐，订成好几本，供我们任意使用。而我们确实引用了不少，构成了我们这篇研究报告的特色。有好几次，为了解决我们提出的问题，他来回跑几十里路，到外村去找了解情况的人一起讨论。他闲话很少，却常常一大早就到洞主庙来，悄悄给我们打扫厕所，他嫌别人扫不干净。

俞文清先生早年曾经扛着枪跨过鸭绿江，后来长期在外地当法官，退休回乡，自己对本村的历史不很熟悉，便帮我们找来他八十多岁的叔叔，讲了许多难得的情况。他去年知道我们打算来工作，特意替我们拍摄了一套今年正月十三村里擎台阁的照片，给我们保留了一盏龙头灯。电台一广播天要变凉，风要变硬，他就赶紧给我们送来新买的毛毯。

村长是耀宗先生的后台，也为我们忙前忙后，帮我们找各种民间工艺匠人和各种民俗用品。还找来几大幅难得保存下来的祖像和中堂字画给我们拍照。临别的时候，弄来了一大箱子的茶叶和茶籽油叫我们带着，还有三只用细篾编上精美套子的葫芦。

村民们家家都热情接待我们，协助我们。正逢清明前后，我们走到哪一家都得吃几颗清明馃子，糯米里掺进蒿草芽，碧绿碧绿的。有几位小姑娘跟我们的女学生成了姐妹，见面搂搂抱抱，天不亮就送来煮山芋、山芋粥。像我们在以前工作过的地方一样，村里的父老乡亲们使我们生活和工作得非常愉快。

我们将会尽可能地为俞源村的保护和发展做些什么。我们爱村子、爱村里的人，我们的朋友们。

1998年夏
sections.content_en:
Farewell to Yuyuan Village

Finally leaving. The sky still drizzling fine rain.

Before the Yu Great Ancestral Hall, clustered men, women, old, young — newly made friends. Farewell is not easy. Thanking them one by one, ears roaring with cries of "Come again, come again." Looking up at them, faces sun-darkened and wind-roughened, revealing such deep sincerity.

The car slowly started; three elderly men, who had accompanied our work for over twenty days, strode after it. Running at the front was 77-year-old Mr. Yaozong, short and plump, staggering, feet kicking up muddy water high, splashing. We leaned half our bodies out the window, shouting at the top of our lungs "Don't run, don't run" — he ignored us, still running with all his might. Eyes fixed on us, eyeballs red-red. The car turned right, friends out of sight, our eyeballs also turned red.

For ten years, we have experienced such farewells again and again. Half a century of tempest has not in the least changed farmers' innate kindness, simplicity, and warmth. But when deeply immersed in their broad embrace, we also clearly felt that in their friendship there is a prayer, a plea, a resentment toward fate. We never forget to write thanks to the village elders in the "postscript" of every research report — words from the heart, but clearly not what they expect. We hold sincere feelings for the elders, striving to do better work, but this clearly cannot satisfy their prayers.

There is one expectation we find hard to face calmly: the most commonly encountered question — can ancient villages and ancient houses truly free villagers from nearly hopeless poverty? Because in recent years tourism has boomed, several ancient villages have opened to tourists with considerable economic income; villagers have not only heard much, some have even gone to investigate. They eagerly hope we can help them turn ancient buildings into money trees. We sat under the eaves of our lodging, on the bridge at the village entrance, at shop counters, discussing carefully with them. Several times, retired old district chiefs and old armed forces ministers came at night to the Dongzhu Temple where we stayed, asking how we truly evaluated the village, what estimate we had of its development prospects, demanding we tell the truth. So, besides detailing the village's historical and cultural value, we had to frankly state many difficulties. Under current conditions, whether an ancient village can develop tourism does not depend entirely on its historical, cultural, and architectural value — many other conditions are needed. Moreover, using ancient villages as tourism resources, first they must be seriously treated as cultural resources, scientifically protected before development. But protecting an ancient village involves many complex issues. Correct concepts, complete systems, special policies, dedicated funding, proper arrangements for villagers' modernization of life, sufficient room for village economic development, convenient transportation and service facilities, and so on. None of these can be solved by one village alone. Before coming to Yuyuan, we helped make protection plans for Zhuge Village in Zhejiang and Liukeng Village in Jiangxi. We ourselves know those two plans did not solve the problem of long-term maintenance and enhancement of village vitality. Fortunately, in the short term contradictions are not yet very sharp, we still have a few years to observe changes. That is, we should continue closely observing those two villages to revise and adjust protection plans in stages. But once the plan is handed over, we sever relations with the village; and once tourism forcefully intervenes and interferes with village protection, any plan becomes waste. Such interference is currently almost inevitable. Seeking quick success and instant profit — this is the whole society's current state; tourism currently seems to exist only for profit. Tourism makes big money, while protecting ancient villages costs big money; so tourism people have stiffer backbones than culture people, speak with more confidence. Take this Yuyuan Village: in 1993 the county cultural bureau designated Dongzhu Temple and Yu Great Ancestral Hall as key cultural relic protection sites; in summer 1997, as soon as the tourism director entered the village, he ordered Dongzhu Temple — white for hundreds of years — painted red. This is of course a trivial matter; the director also plans to greatly highlight Liu Bowen's various deeds in Yuyuan, though they are nothing but baseless legends. We do not reject legends outright, because they contain villagers' ideals, pursuits, and values. But to implement legends one by one into environment and architecture, making fake and counterfeit things, that goes too far. Facing villagers who have long been poor and urgently demand escaping poverty, our hearts burn with anxiety. Are we bookworms? Are we indifferent to villagers' hardship? Is our vision really so far-sighted, our thinking really so comprehensive?

Thus, even villagers' expectations that are relatively easy to face become difficult; not to mention many harder-to-face problems, such as county officials wanting to use ancient villages for "political achievements," whose main measure is economic benefit.

Our work in Yuyuan received strong support from Tu Zhigang, Director of Wuyi County Museum. He made very practical arrangements for us, every two or three days挤 the dilapidated public bus to visit us. Tu Zhigang is the most dedicated and competent museum director we have ever met. He masters cultural relic business, from archaeological excavation to dating ancient buildings, speaking fluently. He took us to visit cities, towns, villages; in tangled alleys, drilling in and out, unhesitatingly finding an ancient building, as familiar as finding a coat in his own bedroom. Speaking of that building's age and features, like counting buttons on his coat, and full of emotion. Strangely, he originally studied the most fearsome destructive weapons at a military university.

Comprehensively taking care of our life and work in the village was Mr. Yu Yaozong. A man who experienced many setbacks yet remained very optimistic. He was once a primary and secondary school teacher; students from fifty years ago still remember that all school teachers wore long gowns, only he wore suit and leather shoes. By nature lively, he once led an opera troupe, touring performances in surrounding townships, quite famous. After land reform in mid-20th century he had bad luck, even suffered imprisonment. Now living alone in Dongzhu Temple, serving a role similar to caretaker — in old terms roughly "temple keeper" — also responsible for interpreting divine lots and dreams, earning one yuan each time, 70 cents to the tourism bureau, 30 cents to himself. Villagers love to joke with him, calling him "Dongzhu Lord." In Spring Festival 1998, he led the village's dragon lantern, walking over forty li to the county town for festivities.

Mr. Yu Busheng took us door to door doing surveys, repeatedly more than once; though admitting exhaustion, always smiling. Yu clan genealogy, Li clan genealogy, Xuanping County Annals — all he found for us. Originally a forestry bureau cadre, after retirement he enthusiastically studies village history; in recent years has written various articles long and short, also collected over fifty legends. All these materials neatly copied in beautiful small regular script, bound into several volumes, for our free use. And we indeed cited many, forming the特色 of our research report. Several times, to solve questions we raised, he ran dozens of li back and forth to other villages to find knowledgeable people for discussion. He talks little, but often arrives at Dongzhu Temple early in the morning, quietly cleaning our toilet — he thinks others don't clean it well.

Mr. Yu Wenqing in his early years shouldered a gun across the Yalu River, later served as a judge away from home for a long time; after retiring back to the village, not very familiar with local history himself, he helped us find his over-eighty-year-old uncle, who told many rare situations. Last year, knowing we planned to come work, he specially photographed a set of this year's January 13 village pavilion procession photos, preserving a dragon-head lantern for us. As soon as the radio broadcast weather turning cold, wind turning harsh, he hurriedly brought us newly bought blankets.

The village chief, Mr. Yaozong's backer, also busied himself for us, helping find various folk craftsmen and folk custom items. Also found several large rare preserved ancestor portraits and central hall calligraphy-paintings for us to photograph. At departure, got a big box of tea and tea-seed oil for us to take, plus three gourds with exquisitely woven fine bamboo covers.

Every villager warmly received and assisted us. Right around Qingming, whichever house we went to, we had to eat a few Qingming dumplings — glutinous rice mixed with mugwort sprouts, emerald green. Several young girls became sisters with our female students, hugging on meeting, before dawn bringing boiled sweet potatoes and sweet potato porridge. Like in places we worked before, the village elders made our life and work very pleasant.

We will do whatever we can for Yuyuan Village's protection and development. We love the village, love the people in it, our friends.

Summer 1998

sections.name: 从哥老会说起
sections.content_zh:
从哥老会说起

到福宝镇的头两天是半阴晴，一阵一阵的阳光。虽然早过了立冬，但天气又潮又闷，上一段台阶，身上就发黏。第三天下雨，空气反倒干爽了。我把龚在书老先生邀到小茶馆里，找一个靠街的桌子坐下，请他接着讲讲福宝镇过去的情况。龚在书年轻时是个刻字匠，后来在供销社工作，平日很留心镇上的事情，记得街上整整一百家店铺的营业项目、店主姓名和身份。龚先生大我一岁，七十四了，已经陪我在街上跑了两天，我们都有点儿疲累，趁雨天，就喝杯茶慢慢聊，当地话叫"摆龙门阵"。

老街上没有多少人。年轻的不是到外地打工去了，就是搬到白色溪以西的新区去了。留下的大多是老年人，加上几个侍候公公婆婆的媳妇和交给爷爷奶奶照顾的中小学生。一下雨，街上更加冷清，檐头的滴水打着地面，一声一声都听得分明。

骨头都酥软了，不想再谈什么枯燥而又难记的事和人。找些轻松有趣的话题，谈着谈着就谈到了哥老会，这可是四川特有的话题。没有想到，龚老先生自己就曾经是一个"袍哥"。袍哥就是哥老会成员。一提起袍哥，他来了兴致，把两只大拇指竖起来，右腕搁到左腕上，笑眯眯叫我看这个手势。我一发呆，他就解释说，这意思是"我是大爷，大爷就是舵把子"。接着把右手往上一挪，搁到左前臂中央，"这叫我是二爷"。再往上搁到臂弯，"我是三爷"。哥老会是流行于四川城乡的民间组织，分"仁、义、礼、智、信"五个堂口，每个堂口有大爷、二爷、三爷，以下是五牌、六牌、九牌、十牌。没有四牌、七牌和八牌。据说老早以前，什么地方有个四牌当了"叛徒"，所以就取消了四牌。七牌和八牌不知道为什么也没有了。大爷，舵把子，也叫大哥，是总当家；二爷不管事，但人品最能服人，又叫"圣贤"；三爷是"能人"，实际的管家，说话算数。五牌是三爷的帮手，六牌又是五牌的帮手。九牌是众多的普通成员，十牌是初加入的，又叫"老幺"。普通成员自报身份的方式是用右手拍拍左肩，老幺则是摸一下耳垂。

堂口的成员有身份的差别。仁号成员大多是"少爷"、"公帮"和"仕宦"，就是绅粮和公职人员；义号是"买卖客商"；礼号"刀刀枪枪"，就是小商小贩；智号则"猴猴囊囊"，都是些医卜星相、三教九流的人，龚在书先生叫他们"知识分子"。福宝没有信字号。信号的成员大多是苦力和乡农，"焦干二十四"，而福宝是个场镇。
