这个话题很有趣，老板娘端上两杯茶，就打横头坐下了。四川的城市和场镇里，最多的是茶馆，一家望到一家。小茶馆，一间店面，最多放三四张桌子，很平民化，常去坐坐摆龙门阵的都是些小买卖人和苦力。集市日子，乡里人挑一担菜到街上卖，换几个钱就进茶馆，不管认识不认识，八个人围一个方桌坐下，一杯茶，一碟胡豆，谈天说地，不到饭时不走。直到现在，茶馆仍然是四川场镇里的特殊景观，坐满了穿蓝色短衣、头缠白帕的男子汉，个个抽着烟杆，一屋子蓝色烟雾直往街上冒。茶馆的设备也很粗糙简陋，白木桌子，条凳，柜台上偶然有几碟豆腐干，买的人没有几个。人们来喝一杯茶，为的是享受一席社会交往的乐趣。

以前福宝老街的一百来家店铺里，有五家茶馆，其中一家是双开间，一家是三开间，规模之大算是少见的了。不过，自从20世纪80年代在白色溪对岸开辟了新区之后，老街居民不多，集市也搬走了，只剩下两家茶馆。一家是那三开间的老茶馆，过去叫天禄阁，1949年后换了老板，没有给茶馆起名字。另一家是单开间的，过去是卖糖果糕饼的京果店。两家的主管都是中年妇女，一面照应老人孩子，一面张罗顾客。其实也没有什么顾客，寥寥几个街坊邻里，进来坐坐，摆摆龙门阵，并不花钱喝茶。最常来的是几位老太太，凑在一起打纸牌。纸牌一寸来宽，三寸来长，叫作"大二"，是四川特有的，据说规则很简单，输赢数也不大，无非消磨时间。打一上午，只给老板娘五角钱。

一杯茶也是五角钱。端给龚老先生的是一只搪瓷杯，有几块圆形的黑疤。端给我的是一只盖杯，盖子缺了一个大口子。福宝本来是产茶叶的地方，春季收了新叶，放在石臼里用木杵捣成饼子，晾干了，运到宜宾去，在那里加工成沱茶，远销到云南、贵州。我们坐的这家茶馆，出门向右下几十步台阶有个巷子口，踅进去，一排房子都是捣茶叶的作坊。龚先生说，过去每到茶季，那里热闹得很。现在作坊早已经歇业，冷冷清清，住着几户人家。龚先生叫我喝一口茶，问我什么味道，我品不出来。他说，这叫"白茶"，不是茶树的嫩叶泡的，是用茶树的枝干，削成薄片，在砂锅里熬的。我一看，杯子里果然没有叶片。"白茶"是福宝的特产，说起来又会有许多清热解毒、活血化瘀之类的好处。

大约是因为下雨，打牌的老太太们没有来，四张茶桌，只有我们，连老板娘三个人，坐在一起接着聊天。我问龚老先生，哥老会是干什么的呢？为什么要加入哥老会？老先生说，加入哥老会是一种风气，街上的成年男子，如果不"海"（加入）袍哥，人家就觉得你不是个"打烂仗"（不安分守己）的人就是个"冬菇儿"（脑筋糊涂），不合群。所以街上一百个男人里至少有九十个是袍哥。好处嘛，也不好说，就是出门在外，"打流跑滩"，到当地相同的袍哥堂口里打个招呼，拜了码头，就可能少一点麻烦。福宝人从前外出打工或者跑买卖的多，向南挑担子翻山越岭到贵州遵义，向北顺大漕河进入长江，往下是重庆，往上是泸州、宜宾，溯沱江、岷江到成都也不远。出外谋生，总希望有人照应，遇到难事好有个依靠，这哥老会就是这样的组织。如果不拜码头，赌赢了钱也拿不回来，拜了码头，赢多少拿多少。

我曾听到，哥老会的兴起也许还有一个原因。明清之交，"八大王剿四川"，杀得白骨蔽野，土地荒芜。后来清兵入川，接着杀，四川土著所剩无几。天下大定之后，朝廷抛出了几条优惠政策，吸引外省人大量向四川移民，民间叫这件事为"湖广实四川"。这些人初来的时候，地广人稀，政府基层组织不全而且软弱无力，血缘的宗族和地缘的会馆因为人口密度不大还来不及形成。但社会是不能没有组织的，于是民间继承天地会的余绪就自发产生了互助组织哥老会，讲究江湖义气。最初团结成员的口号是"反清复明"，后来渐渐分化，分布在各地的组织有好有坏，有善有恶，性质和作用并不一致。

我问龚老先生，"海"袍哥，有没有烧香叩头，歃血盟誓之类的手续。他提了提精神，说："哪能没有？要找三个袍哥办手续。有讲究的哇，他们各有名堂，叫作'引''保''恩'。引是引见，保是保举，都要五牌以上的老袍哥担当。恩是恩准，就是大爷点头。""海"袍哥还要交五升米。不过，倒是没有什么会员证之类的东西。

哥老会既没有血缘关系又没有地缘关系，只讲求哥们儿义气，所以崇拜以义气传颂万代的刘、关、张三兄弟，每年旧历五月二十三日举行一次关圣人"单刀会"，隆重祭祀他们。龚老先生说，袍哥都遵守严格的规矩，凡犯了不孝父母、不敬尊长、欺侮妇女和乱伦等罪行的，都要"传查"，就是大爷、二爷、三爷坐堂审判犯人。轻的叩头认罪，或者开除，叫"搁袍哥"。重的判打板子甚至死刑。死刑很残酷，有一种叫"三刀六眼"，就是捅三个"透明窟窿"。还有挖坑自埋的刑罚。我读过李劼人和沙汀的小说，有些地方的哥老会有点儿黑，便带点挑衅的意思追问，哥老会就不做坏事了？龚先生显然不大爱说这个话题，讪讪一笑，说："差不多个个都是袍哥，还做得了什么坏事？"在一旁哼哼哈哈听了半天的老板娘忽然插话了："不做坏事？"声音有点儿激动，右手中指叩一下桌子，说："那老二不就是跟堂口勾结的？""老二"是土匪的别称，福宝镇二百多年里，受土匪的祸害可多了，不但抢，还要烧房子，所以直到现在，一提起土匪，许多人马上就来气。龚老先生怕老板娘上火，立刻笑笑，说："是的，是的，没有堂口掩护，当不了土匪。"刘家巷西口住着一个叫刘汉民的小地主，是礼号的大爷，国民党时候当剿匪大队长，其实跟土匪通声气。共产党来了，他上山当了土匪中队长。被捕以后，考虑到从前他曾经两度劝止土匪抢劫福宝，所以从轻发落，只判了三年刑。他家有一座碉楼，前几年拆掉了。"街上做生意，都要给舵把子交保护费，不交，就砸了，是不是啊？"老板娘紧追不放，又补上一句，"还有开鸦片烟馆，开妓院，开赌场。"龚先生说："那个嘛，不敢公开的。"老板娘不服气，指一指左边："那家长乐社，不是前堂卖茶开赌，后堂又吃（烟）又嫖！"长乐社离我们坐着的茶馆不远，在老街中央的坝子上，两间门面，是仁字号的茶馆。叫长乐社，是因为它组织川剧的"玩友"，也就是票友，在那里唱戏过瘾，有一把胡琴、一堂锣鼓的小小乐队伴奏。20世纪50年代，为了办卫生所，把这幢房子改造成了砖木混合结构的，现在卫生所搬到新区去了，房子空着，门脸上还留着个红十字。老板娘又把手往右边老街的南半段一指，说："那几家茶馆，义号的集贤居，礼号和智号的什么，还不是一样。"当年袍哥一个堂口开一家茶馆，这茶馆就是他们的"办事处"。除了烟、赌、嫖，还在茶馆里谈生意、斗地盘、贩卖人口、闹纠纷，有时候也调解纠纷，叫"吃讲茶"。

老先生说："天禄阁可不是袍哥的。"天禄阁老板叫刘秉仲，自称刘邦的后代，专爱结交区乡政府的文武小官吏，因此仿汉代皇家旧例，把茶馆取名为天禄阁。它就是老街南端十字路口那三间门面的茶馆，后院有一幢三开间的三层小楼，民国年间造的，是镇上唯一的砖楼，叫"逍遥宫"。那里是"五毒俱全"。龚老先生放低了声音说："那里的女人都是外地来的，街上的一个都没有。"

从避忌谈土匪、鸦片、赌博和妓女，到脱净本街妇女和卖淫的干系，龚老先生步步为营，力求回护福宝场的声誉。他实在是热爱他的家乡呀！

福宝是个场镇，又是个砦子。进砦子的街巷口上都有砦门，街中央坝子两头又有砦门，一共十道砦门。还有三座碉楼，两座在镇子的西侧边缘，一座在东侧边缘。防卫很严。绅粮和大店铺出钱养三四十个防兵，叫"门户练"。老先生说，小股土匪来，砦门上有动静，各家各户就紧闭门户，土匪不敢久留，往往抢一两家就走了。也发生过几次绑票，叫"拉肥猪"。老板娘又说了："甲子年那场火，烧掉了一大片房子。"甲子年大火，我来了只有三天，就听到好多次了，忙问是怎么回事。老先生回答："天禄阁的老板刘秉仲，是个大绅粮，甲子年，刻薄过一个雇工，为一点不清不楚的事把那雇工开除了。雇工就去当了土匪，结伙来抢场报仇。那天他火烧天禄阁，火蔓延开来。幸亏坝子的南砦门紧紧关闭，断了火路。可惜门外房子都烧了。"老板娘接着说："后来那一大段街都是王家人出钱修复的，政府答应王家人永远免税。"街上老人到现在计年还用干支法，六十年一轮回，对他们一生来说大概够用了，但说到古老事情就很麻烦。因为老先生说那场大火至今不到一百年，火场重建的时候他还看到上梁喝酒放炮，我算了一算，这个甲子是1924年，到现在八十四年了。老先生又讲了一个故事：甲子年的事件里，有一个土匪在仓惶逃走时把抢来的二十锭银子丢进张爷庙隔壁黄姓染坊的染池里，说："你姓黄，我也姓黄，送给你了罢。"后来黄老板靠这些银锭扩大了染坊，发了财。

谈袍哥谈到了土匪，又牵扯出许多有趣的话题来，都靠老板娘打岔。我们在别的地方调查，应对的都是男子，妇女不参与，不插嘴，问到她们，大都不知道多少情况。福宝街上的妇女可是不同，个个健谈，甚至抢着说话，知道的情况不比男人少。因为细心，记事比男子更具体。好像受教育水平也比男子高，男子说不清楚的话，她们会夺过笔在我的笔记本上写出来。还有一位退休的中学数学教师蹇有明，给我勾画过福宝镇环境的山形水势，有模有样，相当准确。

雨还没停，只听见滴滴答答响起一阵檐头水打在斗笠上的声音，进来一位穿黑衣黑裤的老人，矮矮的，臂弯里挎着个小竹篮。走到桌子边，掀开篮子上的塑料膜，轻声问："豆腐干，买不买？"福宝的豆腐干全县闻名，我前两天就听说过。一看，方方的豆腐干，焦黄色，巴掌那么大，只有碗沿那么厚。一块钱四片。"好，买两块钱的。"我把茶碗上缺了个大口的盖子翻过来，放上八块，三个人扯了嚼，很有筋道。老先生说，豆腐干是何沛霖、牟德荣两人做得最好，用火烤，加盐巴不加酱油。说到食品，福宝还有著名的酥饼。龚先生说："大绅粮皮家从外乡请来个厨师会做一手好酥饼，先用油炸，再用火烤。皮家摆酒席，最好吃的是酥饼。后来糕饼店都学会了，一到赶场的日子，满街都有卖的，甚至卖到重庆去。豆腐干也是满街卖，背着背篼来赶场的，大都会买上一小包。现在酥饼没有人做了，年轻人爱吃蛋糕什么的。豆腐干不如过去的香了。"老先生深深叹了一口气。下乡做调查，常常可以听到父老们这种"今不如昔"的叹息，我总是半信半疑，它包含着太多的怀旧伤感。青春时期接触过的一切，在老年人的记忆里，都和自己的青春一样，那么美好。不过，也确实有不少好东西，因为利薄，因为费工，因为需要特别耐心地制作，现在失去了。所以，我也陪着龚先生有点儿惆怅。我们已经失去的和将要失去的好东西确实是太多了。

卖豆腐干的老人并不急于做生意，搬个条凳在门槛边坐下，抬头望着雨珠歇气。年岁大了，凭老手艺做点豆腐干卖，不是为了谋衣谋食，而是一种习惯，一种对几十年生活的留恋。这条街上的老人们大概都有这样的心情，所以尽管老房子十分破败，仍然不肯随儿孙们搬到新区去。新区哪有这样的檐头水呢？清脆而有节律，伴着老朋友的话声，已经听了大半辈子了。街上的台阶，上上下下几十步，自己坐在妈妈背篼里的时候就熟悉了哇。赶场的日子，街上挤得踩了鞋都弯不下腰去提拔，从妈妈的脖颈边望出去，人头滚滚，多壮观，多繁盛哦。歇了一阵，老人提起小篮子，又向雨中走去，头也不回，撂下一句话，老板娘应答了一句，我都没有听懂。斗笠上淅沥的雨声渐渐远了，龚先生说："老朋友呀，"停一停，补一句，"越来越少了。"这样的心情弥漫在老街的空气里。我自己也是七十三岁的人了，对这种空气非常敏感。我们一起沉默了一会儿，眼神空空的。

斜对面杂货店的老板娘端起饭碗坐到街檐下了，我向龚先生提最后一个关于哥老会的问题：各地的哥老会，各个堂口，有统一的组织关系吗？有上下级领导吗？他回答，没有，都是独立的，遇到大事才互相支持。不过，有些地方的哥老会和堂口的舵把子声望高，号召力大，有点儿领袖人物的意思。民国初年，四川副都督夏之时，就是合江人，全县第一大爷。他的老婆叫董竹君，在上海创建了锦江饭店，前几年拍过她的传记电视剧，叫《世纪人生》，在福宝街拍过外景。还有一个合江县团总，叫裴雨皋，也是一个袍哥大爷。民国三十六年（1947），国民政府搞国民代表大会选举，合江的一位袍哥大爷何肃雍，就在六十九个哥老会舞刀弄枪的支持下当上了代表。看来袍哥不但和土匪勾结，也和官府勾结。老板娘突然高声说："还有那个范绍增呐。""什么人？""范绍增，你不晓得？就是哈儿司令啊！"老先生插话解释道："他叫范哈儿，重庆人，礼号大哥。一个有福气的人哦，凡事都能逢凶化吉。跟蒋介石也有交情。"老板娘接着说："当过师长，又当过司令，峨眉电视台拍过故事片，都是真事。"忽然一位妇女在我背后很兴奋地说："《傻儿师长》，就是在这条街上拍的嘛！"我一回头，看见一位挺精神的青年妇女，肩膀上还伸出一个孩子头来，那是站在背篼里的儿子。用背篼背孩子是四川的习惯，背篼是竹子编的，又硬又有弹性，孩子受到很有效的保护。篼的中段有个折，孩子可以站在篼里，也可以很舒服地坐在折上，自由自在，四面八方随意转身张望。站在地上，孩子身高不到大人的膝盖，一装到篼里背起，双眼就跟妈妈的一样齐，眼界忽然大开，一定很有趣。这位妇女大约是我们沉默的时候进来的，她接着说："火神庙前那段高台阶下，天禄阁对面，临时布置了一个豆花店，哈儿师长就是在那里把个大姑娘扛起走的。"我们都兴奋起来，老先生乐得直笑。

我很关心哥老会在土地改革中的命运。老先生说：没有什么，不再活动就没事了。有几个绅粮，是袍哥，打成地主，分掉了土地就当老百姓了。只有在旧政府里当过事的，要受群众监督，"就地改造"，其实也平常。几个当土匪的袍哥被镇压了，其中一个姓皮的，叫皮达才，有几十担租子，当过团总，又当过区长，是仁号的舵把子。皮达才有几间大房子，就在街中央"坝子"北端之外的西侧。房子后身有座碉楼，原来五层，前几年顶层朽了，拆掉之后剩了四层。

那背孩子的妇人急匆匆问老先生，看到娃儿他爷爷没有。老先生大概回答了一句"没有"，妇人刚要走，街上却踢踢踏踏过来了个满面红光的大高个儿，妇人一转身就闪了出去，带上他走了。鲜艳的上衣在湿漉漉的青石板路上映出几片跳动的红光。老板娘看着背景，轻轻赞叹："好女子哇！"

到了午饭时候了。老板娘伸伸懒腰，双手抵住桌子，慢慢站了起来。我扶着龚老先生告辞出来，老先生住在隔壁，向左一拐就到家。雨依旧不紧不慢地下着，屋面的出檐宽，檐溜水滴在檐阶之下，老先生家门口有一块干爽地。他余兴未尽，拉过小竹椅给我，要告诉我一些土匪的"切口"（黑话）。我刚坐下，他突然叫我一声"老腌"。我莫名其妙，他笑了起来，笑呛了气，待气顺了，说，贵州人和四川人，对朋友都有亲切的特殊叫法，把朋友的姓用多少有点关联的词来代替。"老腌"就是"陈"。姓罗的叫老响，姓薄的叫老飞，姓唐的叫老蜜，姓钟的叫老撞。姓杨的叫老咪，大约杨与羊谐音的缘故。姓杜的叫老撑，是从杜联想到肚，吃饱了就撑。姓刘的叫老顺，是先把刘谐音为柳，再从柳条联想到顺。姓古的叫老绷，是从古联想到鼓，再联想到绷。有一些叫法则无从推测，例如姓何的叫老灰，姓韦的叫老圈，姓曾的叫老板，姓王的叫老还。龚先生一口气说了二三十个姓的叫法。我问，这是土匪切口吗？"不是的。"他回答。他大女儿从合江城里来看他，正在洗菜，听到这里，嘟囔了一句说："不是土匪切口也是袍哥的黑话。"老先生连忙摆手："不是，不是！"

但他是要告诉我一些土匪切口的，我等着。他定了定神，终于开口了：土匪要抢场，就是抢集市，叫"赶混子"，或者"打混子"。抢绅粮家叫"打窑子"。米叫粉子，吃饭叫吊粉子，碗叫莲花，勺叫耍子，筷子叫划签，布叫闭子，衣服叫大衫，草鞋叫划勾。四川有一种用粗大的竹筒做的烟管，可以两个人同时吸烟，这叫"抬溜子"。因为他大女儿对"切口"和"黑话"之类表示出轻蔑的厌烦，老先生的兴致遭到打击，说了些就不再说了。我觉得可惜，看得出来，没有说痛快，他也觉得可惜，简直有点赍志不得伸的委屈。他不得不转变话题，便重新为袍哥说点好话。两眼一亮，说：咸丰十一年（1861），福宝天主教徒横行乡里，鱼肉百姓，袍哥李文定叫儿子成生带领街上青壮年，捣毁了教堂，平息了教祸。这段故事我在民国《合江县志》和1986年《合江县社会风土志》里也看到过，很有兴趣了解一下，但偷眼看见门里女儿已经掀开了锅盖，便起身告辞了。

我边走边沉思，这个福宝镇，大屋檐底下藏着多少带点儿神秘色彩的故事哦！

打开伞，窸窸窣窣，轻柔的细雨声仿佛给我的沉思笼上一层迷幻的情调。真有趣，我想。于是，我记起了李劼人《死水微澜》，天回镇的袍哥管事罗歪嘴，做皮肉生意的刘三金，烫猪毛和剥活狗皮的赌场，人人都能躺倒吞云吐雾的烟馆，原来在这里都曾经一模一样地存在过。难怪沙汀一回到四川的场镇上就能写出好作品，这里满地都是小说素材嘛！但我不是为写小说而来。
sections.content_en:
Starting from the Gelaohui (Elder Brothers Society)

The first two days in Fubao Town were half cloudy, with patches of sunlight. Though Lidong (Start of Winter) had long passed, the weather was damp and stuffy; climbing a flight of steps made one sticky. On the third day it rained, and the air反而 became dry and fresh. I invited old Mr. Gong Zaishu to a small teahouse, sat at a street-side table, and asked him to continue telling about Fubao's past. Gong Zaishu was a seal-engraver in his youth, later worked at the supply and marketing cooperative; always paying attention to town affairs, he remembered the business, owner names, and status of exactly one hundred shops on the street. Mr. Gong is one year older than me, seventy-four; he has accompanied me around the streets for two days, we are both a bit tired, so taking advantage of the rain, we drink tea and chat slowly — local dialect calls this "摆龙门阵" (chatting).

Few people on the old street. The young either went to work elsewhere or moved to the new district west of Baise Stream. Those remaining are mostly elderly, plus a few daughters-in-law serving parents-in-law, and primary/secondary students left in grandparents' care. When it rains, the street is even quieter; eaves dripping onto the ground, each drop clearly audible.

Bones gone soft, no longer wanting to discuss dry, hard-to-remember people and events. Finding light, interesting topics, we talked and talked and arrived at the Gelaohui — a uniquely Sichuan topic. Unexpectedly, old Mr. Gong himself was once a "Paoge" (robed brother). Paoge means Gelaohui member. At the mention of Paoge, he perked up, raised both thumbs, placed right wrist on left wrist, smilingly asking me to look at this gesture. I stared blankly; he explained: this means "I am Daye (Great Uncle), Daye is the Duobazi (helmsman)." Then moving right hand up to center of left forearm: "This means I am Erye (Second Uncle)." Moving further up to the elbow: "I am Sanye (Third Uncle)." The Gelaohui was a folk organization popular in Sichuan cities and countryside, divided into five "tangkou" (branches): Ren (Benevolence), Yi (Righteousness), Li (Propriety), Zhi (Wisdom), Xin (Trust). Each branch has Daye, Erye, Sanye, below them Wupai (5th card), Liupai (6th card), Jiupai (9th card), Shipai (10th card). No 4th, 7th, or 8th cards. It is said long ago, somewhere a 4th card became a "traitor," so 4th card was abolished. Why 7th and 8th cards disappeared is unknown. Daye, the Duobazi, also called Dage (Big Brother), is the overall head; Erye doesn't manage affairs but has the most respected character, also called "Sage"; Sanye is the "able man," actual manager, whose words count. Wupai is Sanye's helper, Liupai is Wupai's helper. Jiupai are the many ordinary members, Shipai are new joiners, also called "Laoyao" (youngest). Ordinary members identify themselves by patting left shoulder with right hand; Laoyao touches an earlobe.

Branch members have status differences. Ren-hao members are mostly "young masters," "public helpers," and "officials" — i.e., gentry and public servants; Yi-hao are "merchants and traders"; Li-hao "knives and guns" — small vendors; Zhi-hao "monkey-like" — fortune-tellers, doctors, astrologers, people of all walks; Gong Zaishu called them "intellectuals." Fubao has no Xin-hao. Xin-hao members are mostly laborers and peasants, "dry as a bone twenty-four," while Fubao is a market town.

This topic was interesting; the landlady brought two cups of tea and sat down crosswise. In Sichuan cities and market towns, teahouses are most numerous, one after another. Small teahouse, one storefront, at most three or four tables, very populist; regulars chatting are small traders and laborers. On market days, villagers carry vegetables to sell, earn some money then enter teahouse; whether acquainted or not, eight people sit around a square table, one cup tea, one plate broad beans, chatting, not leaving until mealtime. Even now, teahouses remain a special sight in Sichuan market towns — full of men in blue short jackets, white turbans, each smoking a pipe, a roomful of blue smoke billowing into the street. Teahouse equipment is rough and simple: plain wood tables, benches; counter occasionally has a few plates of dried tofu, few buyers. People come for a cup of tea, to enjoy a session of social interaction.

Previously, among Fubao old street's hundred-odd shops, there were five teahouses — one double-storefront, one triple-storefront, unusually large scale. However, since the 1980s when the new district was opened across Baise Stream, old street has few residents, market also moved away, only two teahouses left. One is the triple-storefront old teahouse, formerly called Tianlu Pavilion; after 1949 changed owner, no name given. The other is single-storefront, formerly a confectionery shop. Both managed by middle-aged women, caring for elderly and children while tending customers. Actually few customers — a handful of neighbors, coming in to sit, chat, not paying for tea. Most regulars are several old ladies, gathering to play cards. Cards one inch wide, three inches long, called "Da'er" (Big Two), unique to Sichuan; rules supposedly simple, stakes small, just passing time. Playing a whole morning, only pay the landlady fifty cents.

A cup of tea is also fifty cents. Served to old Mr. Gong is an enamel cup with several round black scars. Served to me is a lidded cup, lid missing a large chunk. Fubao originally produced tea; in spring, new leaves collected, pounded into cakes in stone mortars with wooden pestles, dried, transported to Yibin, processed into tuocha (compressed tea), sold as far as Yunnan and Guizhou. The teahouse we sit in — going out, right, down dozens of steps, there's an alley entrance; turning in, a row of houses are all tea-pounding workshops. Mr. Gong says, in tea season, it used to be bustling there. Now workshops long closed, desolate, housing a few families. Mr. Gong asks me to take a sip, what flavor? I can't tell. He says this is "white tea" — not brewed from tender tea leaves, but from tea tree branches, shaved thin, boiled in a clay pot. I look, indeed no leaves in the cup. "White tea" is Fubao specialty, supposedly has many benefits like clearing heat, detoxifying, activating blood circulation.

Probably because of rain, the card-playing old ladies didn't come; four tea tables, only us, plus landlady three people, sitting together chatting. I ask old Mr. Gong: what does the Gelaohui do? Why join? The old gentleman says joining Gelaohui was a custom; adult men on the street, if not "hai" (joined) Paoge, people thought you either a "打烂仗" (restless type) or a "冬菇儿" (muddlehead), not sociable. So of a hundred men on the street, at least ninety were Paoge. Benefits, hard to say — when away from home, "打流跑滩" (drifting), greeting the local Paoge branch, "拜码头" (paying respects at the wharf), might mean less trouble. Fubao people used to travel for work or trade: south, carrying loads over mountains to Zunyi, Guizhou; north, down Dacao River to Yangtze — downstream Chongqing, upstream Luzhou, Yibin, up Tuo and Min rivers to Chengdu not far. Making a living away, always hoping for someone to watch one's back, someone to rely on in difficulty — the Gelaohui was such an organization. If not paying respects at the wharf, even gambling winnings can't be taken back; after paying respects, win as much as you take.

I once heard the Gelaohui's rise may have another cause. At Ming-Qing transition, "Eight Kings exterminated Sichuan," killing until white bones covered fields, land barren. Then Qing troops entered Sichuan, continued killing; Sichuan natives few remaining. After the realm settled, the court offered several preferential policies, attracting large numbers of outsiders to migrate to Sichuan — folk call this "Huguang filling Sichuan." When these people first arrived, land vast people sparse, government grassroots organization incomplete and weak; blood-line clans and native-place guilds hadn't yet formed due to low population density. But society cannot exist without organization; so folk, inheriting remnants of the Tiandihui (Heaven and Earth Society), spontaneously formed mutual-aid organization Gelaohui, emphasizing jianghu (brotherhood) loyalty. Initially the slogan uniting members was "Overthrow Qing, restore Ming"; later gradually differentiated, organizations in various places good and bad, virtuous and evil, nature and role not uniform.

I ask old Mr. Gong: when "hai"-ing Paoge, were there procedures like burning incense, kowtowing, blood oath? He perks up: "How could there not be? Need three Paoge to handle procedures. There are distinctions, they have titles: 'Yin' (introduce), 'Bao' (recommend), 'En' (approve). Yin is introduction, Bao is recommendation, both must be Paoge of Wupai or above. En is approval — the Daye nods." "Hai"-ing Paoge also requires paying five sheng of rice. However, no membership cards or such.

Gelaohui has neither blood nor native-place ties, only brotherhood loyalty; so they worship Liu, Guan, Zhang three brothers whose righteousness was传颂 through ages; every lunar May 23rd holds a Guan Sage "Single Sword Meeting," solemnly sacrificing them. Old Mr. Gong says Paoge all follow strict rules; those committing crimes like unfilial to parents, disrespect to elders, bullying women, incest — all undergo "传查" (investigation): Daye, Erye, Sanye sit in court trying the offender. Minor: kowtow confession, or expulsion, called "搁袍哥" (shelving the robe). Major: beating with boards or even death penalty. Death penalty cruel — one called "三刀六眼" (three knives six eyes), stabbing three "transparent holes." Also punishment of digging pit and self-burial. I've read Li Jieren and Sha Ting novels, some places' Gelaohui somewhat dark; with a provocative tone I ask: doesn't the Gelaohui do bad things? Mr. Gong clearly dislikes this topic, smiles awkwardly: "Almost everyone is Paoge, what bad things can be done?" The landlady, who had been listening half-heartedly, suddenly interjects: "Not do bad things?" Voice somewhat agitated, right middle finger tapping the table: "That 'Lao Er' (bandit) — wasn't he in cahoots with the branch?" "Lao Er" is another name for bandits; Fubao Town over two hundred years suffered much from bandits — not only robbing, but burning houses; so even now, mentioning bandits, many get angry immediately. Old Mr. Gong, afraid landlady gets heated, immediately smiles: "Yes, yes, without branch protection, can't be a bandit." At west entrance of Liujia Lane lived a small landlord named Liu Hanmin, Li-hao Daye; under Kuomintang was bandit-suppression captain, actually in league with bandits. When Communists came, he went up the mountain as bandit squadron leader. After arrest, considering he had twice persuaded bandits not to rob Fubao, leniently sentenced to only three years. His family had a watchtower, demolished a few years ago. "Doing business on the street, all must pay protection fee to the Duobazi; if not, get smashed, right?" Landlady presses on, adding: "Also opium dens, brothels, gambling houses." Mr. Gong says: "That sort, couldn't be public." Landlady unconvinced, points left: "That Changle Society — wasn't front hall tea and gambling, back hall opium and whoring!" Changle Society not far from our teahouse, on the "bazi" (open square) in middle of old street, two storefronts, Ren-hao teahouse. Called Changle Society because it organized Sichuan opera "玩友" (amateur players), singing opera for fun, with a small band of one huqin and one set of gongs-drums. In 1950s, to set up a health clinic, this building was renovated to brick-wood structure; now clinic moved to new district, building empty, facade still bears a red cross. Landlady points right to south half of old street: "Those teahouses — Yi-hao Jixian Residence, Li-hao and Zhi-hao whatever — all the same." Back then each Paoge branch ran a teahouse, which was their "office." Besides opium, gambling, whoring, also discussed business, fought for territory, trafficked people, caused disputes; sometimes mediated disputes, called "吃讲茶" (eating mediation tea).

Old gentleman says: "Tianlu Pavilion was not Paoge's." Tianlu Pavilion owner named Liu Bingzhong, claiming descendant of Liu Bang, loved befriending minor civil and military officials of district government; thus following Han dynasty imperial precedent, named teahouse Tianlu Pavilion. It is the three-storefront teahouse at the crossroad south end of old street; backyard has a three-bay three-story small building, built in Republican era, the only brick building in town, called "Xiaoyao Palace" (Carefree Palace). There "all five poisons present." Old Mr. Gong lowers voice: "The women there were all from out of town, none from the street."

From avoiding talk of bandits, opium, gambling, prostitutes, to completely exonerating local women from prostitution, old Mr. Gong步步为营, striving to protect Fubao's reputation. He truly loves his hometown!

Fubao is a market town, also a fortified village (zhai). Alley entrances into the zhai all have zhai gates; both ends of the central bazi also have zhai gates — total ten zhai gates. Also three watchtowers (diaolou): two at west edge of town, one at east edge. Defense strict. Gentry and large shops paid for 30-40 defense soldiers, called "门户练" (gate-guards). Old gentleman says: small bandit bands come, zhai gates alert, every household closes doors; bandits dare not stay long, usually rob one or two families and leave. Also several kidnappings, called "拉肥猪" (pulling fat pigs). Landlady says again: "Jiazi year fire, burned a whole block of houses." Jiazi year fire — I've been here only three days, heard it many times; hurriedly ask what happened. Old gentleman answers: "Tianlu Pavilion owner Liu Bingzhong, a big gentry, in Jiazi year was harsh to a hired hand, fired him over some unclear matter. The hired hand became a bandit, gathered gang to rob the market for revenge. That day he set fire to Tianlu Pavilion, fire spread. Fortunately the south zhai gate of the bazi was tightly closed, cutting the fire path. Unfortunately houses outside the gate all burned." Landlady continues: "Later that whole block of street was rebuilt at Wang family's expense; government promised Wang family permanent tax exemption." Old people on street still count years by sexagenary cycle, sixty-year cycle — enough for their lifetime probably, but discussing old events gets complicated. Because old gentleman says the fire was less than a hundred years ago, and he saw beam-raising, drinking, firecrackers during reconstruction; I calculate — this Jiazi is 1924, now eighty-four years ago. Old gentleman tells another story: in the Jiazi incident, a bandit in panicked flight threw twenty silver ingots stolen into the dye vat of the Huang dye shop next to Zhangye Temple, saying: "Your surname Huang, mine also Huang, take them." Later Boss Huang used these ingots to expand the dye shop, made fortune.

Talking Paoge led to bandits, then pulled in many interesting topics, all thanks to landlady's interruptions. In other places we investigate, dealing with men only; women don't participate, don't interject; asking them, most know little. Fubao street women are different — all talkative, even抢 to speak, know no less than men. Because careful, remember details more specifically than men. Seems education level also higher than men; when men can't explain clearly, they snatch the pen and write in my notebook. Also a retired middle school math teacher named Jian Youming sketched Fubao's surrounding mountains and waters for me, quite model-like, fairly accurate.

Rain still not stopped; only hear patter of eaves water hitting a bamboo hat, then enters an old man in black clothes and pants, short, carrying a small bamboo basket on his arm. Walks to table, lifts plastic film on basket, softly asks: "Dried tofu, buy or not?" Fubao dried tofu famous county-wide; I heard about it two days ago. Look — square dried tofu, burnt yellow, palm-sized, only bowl-rim thick. One yuan four pieces. "Good, buy two yuan worth." I flip over the chipped lid of my tea cup, place eight pieces; three of us tear and chew, very chewy. Old gentleman says dried tofu best made by He Peilin and Mou Derong — fire-roasted, salt added, no soy sauce. Speaking of food, Fubao also famous酥饼 (crisp cakes). Mr. Gong says: "Big gentry Pi family hired a chef from out of town who made excellent crisp cakes — first deep-fried, then fire-roasted. Pi family banquets, best dish was crisp cakes. Later pastry shops all learned; on market days, sold everywhere, even to Chongqing. Dried tofu also sold everywhere; villagers carrying背篼 (back baskets) to market mostly buy a small pack. Now no one makes crisp cakes; young people like cake etc. Dried tofu not as fragrant as before." Old gentleman sighs deeply. Doing fieldwork, often hear elders' such "present not as good as past" sighs; I'm always half-believing, it contains too much nostalgic sentiment. Everything encountered in youth, in elders' memory, like their own youth, so beautiful. However, indeed many good things, because low profit, because labor-intensive, because requiring special patience to make, now lost. So I also feel a bit melancholy with Mr. Gong. Good things we've lost and will lose are truly too many.

The dried-tofu old man not eager for business, moves a bench to sit by threshold, looks up at raindrops resting. Old age, making dried tofu by old craft to sell, not for food and clothing, but a habit, a nostalgia for decades of life. Old people on this street probably all feel this way; so despite old houses very dilapidated, still refuse to move with children to new district. Where in new district is such eaves water? Crisp and rhythmic, accompanying old friends' voices, listened to for most of a lifetime. Street steps, up and down dozens, familiar since sitting in mother's back basket as a child! On market days, street so crowded that stepping on shoes can't bend to retrieve; looking out from mother's neck, sea of heads — how spectacular, how prosperous! After resting a while, old man picks up small basket, walks into rain again, without looking back, drops a word; landlady replies a sentence, I don't understand either. Bamboo hat rain patter gradually fades; Mr. Gong says: "Old friend," pauses, adds, "fewer and fewer." Such mood permeates old street's air. I myself am seventy-three, very sensitive to this air. We sit silent a while, eyes vacant.

The grocery landlady diagonally opposite picks up her rice bowl and sits under the eave; I ask old Mr. Gong one last Gelaohui question: do Gelaohui branches everywhere have unified organizational relations? Superior-subordinate leadership? He answers: no, all independent, only support each other in major matters. However, some places' Gelaohui and branch Duobazi have high prestige, great号召力, somewhat like leader figures. Early Republican era, Sichuan Vice Governor Xia Zhishi was from Hejiang, county's number one Daye. His wife Dong Zhujun founded Jinjiang Hotel in Shanghai; a few years ago her biographical TV drama "Century Life" filmed exterior scenes on Fubao street. Also a Hejiang county militia chief named Pei Yugao, also a Paoge Daye. Republican 36th year (1947), National Government held National Assembly elections; Hejiang's Paoge Daye He Suyong, with support of 69 Gelaohui members wielding knives and guns, became a delegate. Seems Paoge not only colluded with bandits, also with government. Landlady suddenly says loudly: "And that Fan Shaozeng!" "Who?" "Fan Shaozeng, you don't know? Ha'er (Fool) Commander!" Old gentleman interjects: "He's called Fan Ha'er, from Chongqing, Li-hao Dage. A lucky man, everything turns from danger to safety. Also on good terms with Chiang Kai-shek." Landlady continues: "Was division commander, then commander; Emei TV station made a drama, all true." Suddenly a woman behind me excitedly says: "'Fool Commander' — filmed right on this street!" I turn, see a spirited young woman, a child's head sticking out from her shoulder — that's her son standing in a back basket. Carrying children in back baskets is Sichuan custom; baskets woven of bamboo, hard yet elastic, child well protected. Basket middle has a fold; child can stand or sit comfortably on the fold, free to turn and look all around. Standing on ground, child's height below adult's knee; once in basket carried, eyes level with mother's, vision suddenly broadened — must be fun. This woman probably entered during our silence; she continues: "Below that high step in front of Fire Temple, opposite Tianlu Pavilion, temporarily set up a tofu pudding shop; Ha'er Commander carried off a big girl right there." We all get excited; old gentleman laughs heartily.

I care much about Gelaohui's fate during land reform. Old gentleman says: nothing, no longer active means fine. Several gentry, who were Paoge, classified as landlords, land distributed then became common people. Only those who served in old government, subject to mass supervision, "on-site reform," actually also ordinary. Several bandit Paoge were suppressed; one surnamed Pi, called Pi Dacai, had several dozen dan of rent, served as militia chief, then district chief, was Ren-hao Duobazi. Pi Dacai had several large houses, just west of north end of the central "bazi." Behind the house a watchtower, originally five stories; top floor rotted a few years ago, demolished leaving four.

The child-carrying woman hurriedly asks old gentleman if he saw the child's grandfather. Old gentleman probably answers "no"; woman about to leave, when from the street comes a tall, red-faced man with heavy steps; woman turns and slips out, taking him away. Bright top reflects a few跳动 red patches on wet bluestone road. Landlady watches their backs, softly praises: "What a fine woman!"

Lunchtime. Landlady stretches, hands on table, slowly stands. I help old Mr. Gong out; he lives next door, turn left and home. Rain still falling steadily; roof eaves wide, eaves water dripping below steps; old gentleman's doorway has a dry patch. His enthusiasm not spent, pulls a small bamboo chair for me, wants to tell me some bandit "切口" (argot). I just sit, he suddenly calls me "Lao Yan." I'm baffled; he laughs, chokes on air; after recovering, says Guizhou and Sichuan people, to friends, have affectionate special names — replacing friend's surname with a somewhat related word. "Lao Yan" is "Chen." Luo called Lao Xiang (echo), Bo called Lao Fei (fly), Tang called Lao Mi (honey), Zhong called Lao Zhuang (collision). Yang called Lao Mi (cat), probably Yang homophone of sheep (yang) → cat (mi). Du called Lao Cheng (撑/propping), from Du联想到 belly (du), full belly propped. Liu called Lao Shun (顺/obedient), first Liu homophone of willow (liu), then willow branches → obedient. Gu called Lao Beng (绷/taut), from Gu联想到 drum (gu), then drum taut. Some names impossible to infer: He called Lao Hui (ash), Wei called Lao Quan (circle), Zeng called Lao Ban (boss), Wang called Lao Huan (return). Mr. Gong一口气 says twenty or thirty surname names. I ask, is this bandit argot? "No," he answers. His elder daughter, visiting from Hejiang city, washing vegetables, hearing this, mutters: "If not bandit argot, it's Paoge slang." Old gentleman waves hands: "No, no!"

But he wants to tell me bandit argot; I wait. He composes himself, finally speaks: bandits robbing a market, called "赶混子" (chasing chaos) or "打混子" (beating chaos). Robbing gentry's home called "打窑子" (hitting the kiln). Rice called "粉子" (powder), eating called "吊粉子" (hanging powder), bowl called "莲花" (lotus), spoon called "耍子" (plaything), chopsticks called "划签" (drawing slips), cloth called "闭子" (closer), clothes called "大衫" (big robe), straw sandals called "划勾" (drawing hook). Sichuan has a kind of thick bamboo tobacco pipe, two people can smoke simultaneously, called "抬溜子" (carrying the slide). Because his elder daughter showed contemptuous annoyance at "argot" and "slang," old gentleman's enthusiasm dampened, said some then stopped. I feel regret; visibly, not having said it all, he also feels regret, almost a grievance of unfulfilled ambition. He has to change topic, then speaks well of Paoge again. Eyes brighten: Xianfeng 11th year (1861), Fubao Catholics ran rampant, oppressing people; Paoge Li Wending told his son Cheng Sheng to lead street young men, destroyed the church, quelled the religious disaster. This story I also saw in Republican "Hejiang County Annals" and 1986 "Hejiang County Social Customs Annals," very interested to learn more, but glancing inside, daughter has lifted the pot lid, so I take leave.

Walking and pondering, this Fubao Town — under big eaves, how many mysterious-colored stories hidden!

Open umbrella, rustle rustle, soft drizzle seems to cast a dreamy mood over my thoughts. So interesting, I think. Then I recall Li Jieren's "Ripple on Stagnant Water" — Tianhui Town's Paoge manager Luo Wai Zui, flesh-trade Liu Sanjin, gambling house scalding pig hair and skinning live dogs, opium dens where everyone can lie down puffing clouds — originally all existed exactly the same here. No wonder Sha Ting, returning to Sichuan market towns, can write good works; here the ground is full of novel material! But I didn't come to write novels.

sections.name: 走好，福宝场
sections.content_zh:
走好，福宝场

回龙街八十二号龚在书先生家的后院里，有一座古坟，荒圮已久，还看得出来是圆形的，直径有四米左右。环周本来砌一圈石条，现在只剩下正面左边大约两米长的一段了。正面朝西偏南，还很整齐，可惜石条下部被土埋没，有几个字也埋在里面了。式样大致是，上、下各有比较长的水平石条，夹住四根竖立的石条，石条之间填石板，形成一个三开间的构图。正中一间上面出楼，楼顶压一块石檐口。楼正面刻四个字"寝陵伟观"。最靠边的两根石条上刻一副对联，上联"山山水水常呈□□"，下联"子子孙孙永□□□"。上面的石条有精致的浮雕，已经风化剥蚀得很厉害了。中央的石板上，左上角雕日，右上角雕月。正中竖刻"皇清待赠诰曾祖……"，下款为"乾隆三十年……"。这座老坟，当年在镇上算得上体制宏大了。

坟的前面紧挨明月山西坡，很陡。半坡上斜着一幢房屋，看屋顶尺度很大，这是王氏宗祠。我们查《王氏族谱》，有十四世王瑗，"葬福宝王氏祠后，有碑，寅山申向"。从位置和朝向看，这座大坟大体可确定为王瑗的墓。王姓福宝祠始祖王宣为第九世，崇祯十四年（1641）以后迁来，照世代排比，也大致相合。不过现在福宝的王姓人氏都不知道这墓主的名字，只知道是他们的祖先，清明节还来供一炷香。我们打算把墓前的淤土挖一挖，看看这位曾祖的名字，但找不到可以负责的人，终于不敢挖。

我们从刘家巷绕到王氏宗祠正面，一看这房子现状还不错，又是个"长五间"，通面阔十四点五米，金柱直径三十厘米。住着五户人家，王本国先生就住在左梢间。他说，原本前面有院墙，正中立一个有瓦檐的木构院门。现在墙和门都没有了，不过前面是白色溪谷地，谷地对岸便是双河街新区，景色开阔，倒也很好。我正在张望，忽然发现脚下有一块残碑，还剩四个字，右边上下两个是"讳瑗"，左边上下两个是"蒲氏"，那么，这很可能是王瑗夫妇的墓碑。于是又引起了一个问题，它和祠后的那座墓有什么关系呢？王本国先生解释说，祠里原有六块大碑，许多小碑，供销社拿宗祠办过糖厂，那时把大小石碑都砸碎了。这块"讳瑗"残石，是小碑上的，小碑不一定是墓碑。这是个悬案，关系不大，不去管它。

值得注意的是，王姓人氏现在传说，这坟里埋的人是在山里被老虎吃了的，后人只抢回来一只脚，所以这坟叫独脚坟。

福宝场附近自古多虎豹出没。流传的山歌和民间故事里关于老虎吃人、吃牛、吃猪的情节很多。贾大戎先生说，20世纪50年代，当地驻军还专门组织过打虎除害的运动。

虎多是因为森林多。合江，尤其是它的南乡和西乡，曾经密布着原始森林。民国《合江县志·食货》说："邑南凡五区，幅员寥阔，纵长三百里，叠嶂重山，毗接黔徼……尤富竹木……蔽日干霄，掩映岩谷。""西二区毗连缁水县（即今习水），亦竹木之薮也，森林畅茂，亘数十里或十余里，采木者不能尽。问家之富，指林木以对。"林木曾是乡民的基本财富。

我到了福宝场，住在林场的招待所里，到回龙街上访问，除了粮站和供销社的职工宿舍外，几乎所有的庙宇都成了林场的职工宿舍。可是，我没有见到一片林木。四面山上都是些杂草灌木，被干黄的梯田弄得七零八落。经堂山上，有些垦地坡度早就超过了规定的极限二十五度。只有蒲江河岸的慈竹郁郁葱葱，还有东面林场园艺场里的橘子树挂着金色的果实。橘子本来是合江的特产，白沙场在清代曾建立过全四川最早的专征橘子税的关卡。现在，橘子树也并不成林，只在园艺场的天坛山上多一些。村里人说采橘子卖不了几个钱，没有兴致去采摘。不过在去园艺场路边几幢农舍的墙上刷着白灰字："私摘一只橘子罚款五元。"

几十年来，林业局的任务是砍林，而不是造林，是自己断自己的生路而不是把日子过得越来越红火。一年有伐几百万方木材的"指标"，却没有种几棵树的指标。

贾大戎先生和街上所有的朋友们都说，原来四周山上全是常绿阔叶林，因为当地无霜期长，冬季也没有黄叶，满目青翠。我所住的林场招待所二楼有一间大厅是林场办的退休老职工活动站，天天有几桌麻将。管理这个活动站的老人王其炳先生是林场的前任党委书记。于是我邀王老先生花一个晚上给我们讲一讲林场的过去和现状。

虽然自古这地区居民就主要以伐竹木为生，但当初人口稀少，运输困难，每年的砍伐量和蓄积量大体平衡，真正是"青山常在，永续利用"。1952年，为造成渝铁路，需要枕木，从此开始大量砍伐山林。铁路通车后，交通方便了，又从这里采伐大量开矿用的坑木外运。1958年大炼钢铁，伐木烧高炉，好好的木材烧成灰烬，钢铁也没有炼成。同时吃公共食堂，也用上好木材当柴烧，因为好木材容易劈也容易烧，火大。

20世纪60、70、80年代，福宝林场每年的生产指标都在四五百万方。1982年至1983年，联合国世界银行贷款改造林相，但林场把一大笔钱用来造了一条商业街。林相没有改良，贷款到期，于是大肆砍伐原始天然林去还债。但一直到那时候，砍伐的规模还不算最大，因为森林的归属不定，是贵州的还是四川的，争论不休。县界也不定，国有林和公社林也分不清。到了90年代，边界划定，便放手大伐，例如天堂坝，九十万亩森林砍光，只剩下几百亩山地可种一点农作物，困难得很。幸好汲取长江1998年大洪水的教训，中央决定保护天然林，1999年起福宝林场的生产指标降低到每年两万多立方米木材和三十万枝楠竹，林业工人的任务开始转向植树育林。

这样一来，福宝林场侥幸保存下来六十万亩天然常绿阔叶林。

听到这里，我大大舒了一口气。但是，生产规模小了，紧接着便发生了林业工人生活问题。林场是个"自收、自资、自给"的副科级事业单位，虽然政府给了几十万元"天保工程"补贴费，但维持不了。每年伐楠竹八万到十万枝，收入四十万元左右，只够还世界银行贷款的利息。

原有三百多职工，曾是福宝场的主要消费力量，对刺激福宝场的繁荣起过很大的作用。现在工资只能领到百分之七十，职工养猪和家禽，再种点儿蔬菜和粮食，勉强够吃。间伐一些小树，够烧。卖掉一点木柴，有零花钱，不多。

于是，职工和他们的成年子女只得外出打工。有百分之六十的职工办了"买断工龄"或者"停薪留职"手续，男男女女，年轻的都走。一个劳动力，在外地打工，正常状态一个月能得几百元，上了千元的就难保不大正经了。王老先生停顿了一下，心情显得很沉重。

我们到福宝镇水口附近的下蒲村去看旧地主何栋的大宅，那里原来住着二十二户林场工人，现在只剩下一户退休的了。大宅空荡荡的。我们看到一位老太太背着锄头回来，一问，九十多岁了，刚刚去锄了菜地。其余的二十一户工人，都自谋生路，走了。

供销社和粮站的职工以及他们的子女，也都走这一条路，并且也带动了四乡农民。

福宝镇现在继续起着一个地区内工农业产品交换市场的作用。我们在赶场的日子观察过，从称为"九条龙"的山路上来的男男女女，背篓里装的是玉米粒、红苕、春笋之类，很沉重，一清早就汗流浃背。回去的时候很轻松，背篓里装的是一点点农药、化肥和小农具，也有割一块猪肉的。还有人买了小鸭苗，在背篓里叽叽啾啾，叫得很欢。市上卖农业生产资料的店子也不多，一家化肥店，一家兼卖农药和种子的小农具店，镰、锄、耙、柴刀之类都是手工打的，福华街上就有红炉，铁匠已经很老了，没有带徒弟。

不过福宝镇新区，双河街和新河西街，却很繁华。仔细一调查，这繁华是靠打工仔和打工妹维持的。镇上和四乡农村一共三万多人，倒有八千人出去打工，我随意访问了十六户人家，家家有人打工，少的一个，多的竟出去了四个女儿。头几年打工纯粹卖力气，近几年有搞经营的了。王书记说，有一个在重庆干建筑业，大概已经有了一千万以上的资产。打工的寄了钱回家，第一件事便造房子。新区的房子，除了卫生院、学校和镇政府之类，都是打工人家造的。20世纪80年代初造的大多是二三层的砖混结构楼房，90年代末，造到五六层，现在甚至有两幢七层的了。在开发区，还有人独资造了几十米长的一排楼房。山坡上零散的新房子也都是打工仔的。他们家里人的消费水平在这个浅山农业地区就算很高的了，于是镇上就出现了一批与农业地区经济水平不符合的"高档"消费店铺。开店铺的人有打了几年工回来的，也有从老街和农村直接来的。还有从公家单位退出来的职工和他们的子女。一家店铺每月可得六百元上下的利润，老板们便也进入了"高消费"群体。打工的人大多会间歇性地回乡住些日子，他们出手比家人更"阔绰"一点，那就更加增大了街上的消费量，街上的消费性商业和服务业便不寻常地发达起来。酒家、饭铺至少有二十五家，其中有几家说得上"豪华"。最新款式的大量时装店多得无法统计，因为连成一大片摊架市场。老板娘们到泸州进货，每礼拜一趟，背回一大包来，把长途车天天塞得满满的。美容美发店竟有十一家之多，而中小学生们必需的文具店却只有半家。说它半家，是因为只在百货店里放了个柜台。

王书记说到美容美发店，就面带不屑之色，那里面，大约接近一半，都有不正经的勾当。王书记说，本地话叫"一、三、五"消费，便是"小姐"坐台费每次一百元，付老板娘三十元，茶资倒不贵，一杯只要五角。有几家美容美发店的老板娘是外面打工回来的，很懂得这种经营的门道，把店内店外装修得十分暧昧，门缝里透出紫色的灯光。几家客店、宾馆里也有干这种"服务"业的。每逢周末，新街上便会停着一长溜的轿车，都是从邻近县城赶来销魂的。

打工经济带来了很时髦的生活方式。年轻女子穿着一点也不比城市落伍，头发染成红色、黄色，"松糕鞋"足有几寸厚。在双河街有五家出售兼出租VCD（影音光碟）的店铺，居然还开着两家网吧。离我们住的林场招待所不远，竟有一家娱乐城、一家歌舞厅和一家滑冰场。我溜进滑冰场去看了一圈，水磨石的旱冰场正在维修，旁边有好几个关着门的厅室，也在重新装修，不知是干什么用的。大门上很长很宽的滑冰场横匾一头耷拉下来了，我期待它修好后拍一张照片，不料那横匾被拆下来拿去重新制作了，一直到我们离开也没有做好。街上的这些娱乐消费场所，大约是和美容店配套的，远道而来的顾客寻欢作乐还要"系列化"。

依靠外出打工造成的经济文化繁荣，是畸形的，不免脆弱。现在，攒钱比较多的打工仔、打工妹，已经不再在福宝安家，而到合江城里去买房子定居了。福宝的"开发区"看上去也没有多少生气，许多楼房是空的。想想，当年徽商和晋商的故乡，大概也是以类似的方式发展起来，又衰败下去的。

最引起我注意的倒是打工使浅山区小小一个福宝镇跟全国建立了密切的联系，非常开放。全镇连四乡农村只有三万八千三百多人口，2001年，程控电话有了两千门。有一天，到老西河街去，在新街上看见一家"中国移动联通公司代办处"，进去向坐在柜台后面看电视的营业员打听了一下，他说代办处在2000年11月开业，到2002年4月，每月平均有二三十户入网。这个数字不低，但他懒于给我们查一查确数，我们当然没有办法，只好退出来继续赶路。

新区街上有几个长途汽车站。到广东东莞、中山、深圳、广州，浙江温州、义乌、宁波，云南昆明，贵州贵阳，广西桂林都有来回车，是双层的卧铺车厢。旺季，如春节前后，大批民工回家、离家，天天有几班车。淡季，则要等候，凑足了一车的人数才会发车。到重庆、成都和泸州，每天都有好几趟定时班车。这些车的老板和司机，都是回乡的打工仔，大城市的打工生活教会了他们许多经营之道，把比较现代化的生意带到过去的穷乡僻壤里来了。福宝不再闭塞，现代化的信息技术和交通设施很快把福宝融进统一的大市场里去了。相应，福宝的新区已经看不出什么地方特色，除了沿街多豆花店之外。我所喜欢的很有特色的竹器，街上没有店铺卖，只有赶场日，有附近村民挑着来卖。但新款时装倒可以随时买到。2002年4月，有四川美术学院的一班学生来回龙街写生，来的时候正逢几十年未有的暖春，只穿了夏季的短衫裤，第二天忽然来了一场几十年未有的倒春寒，女孩子们冻得浑身起鸡皮疙瘩。她们跑到新区街上，立马就穿上了很时兴的绒衣，胸前印着几个英文字，左看右看都满意，高兴得几个人拥在一起嘻嘻哈哈。

我第二次到福宝，等过完了春节再出去打工的人还没有走尽。常常可以见到一群一群的年轻人，大多是女青年，带着提包，互相照应着上长途卧车。有一次，见一群女孩子正在上到东莞去的车，我问一个短发的："要乘多少钟头才到？""三十多个钟头。""辛苦吧！""哪里能安逸！像猪！想安逸就饿饭！"女孩子才十六岁，初中毕业，挺秀气的，却不得不背井离乡，远走海疆。但是，丢弃"五龙抱珠"的幻想，脱离土地，正是大部分农民走向现代化必须迈出的一步。

农村也只有在摆脱了过剩人口的压力之后，才能加快现代化。

四川人远出谋生，是早有传统的。记得少年时父亲亲自给我讲授的李白《长干行》，就写四川女子思念到湖楚一带"打工"的丈夫："……十六君远行，瞿塘滟滪堆。五月不可触，猿声天上哀。门前迟行迹，一一生绿苔。苔深不能扫，落叶秋风早。八月蝴蝶黄，双飞西园草。感此伤妾心，坐愁红颜老。早晚下三巴，预将书报家。相迎不道远，直至长风沙。"

现在，出去打工的以女子为多了。她们不再伤春悲秋，而是满怀对新生活的追求了。

愿福宝人走向未来的道路越来越健康，越宽阔。同时，愿福宝老场镇，那条古色古香的回龙街，能长久保存下去，给他们亲切的历史记忆，丰富他们的精神世界。

2002年秋
sections.content_en:
Farewell, Fubao Market Town

In the backyard of Mr. Gong Zaishu's home at No. 82 Huilong Street, there is an ancient tomb, long abandoned; still visible as circular, about four meters in diameter. Originally surrounded by a ring of stone strips, now only a section about two meters long on the left front remains. The front faces west-south, still neat; unfortunately the lower part of the stone strips is buried in soil, several characters also buried. The design is roughly: upper and lower each have relatively long horizontal stone strips, clamping four vertical stone strips, with stone slabs filling between them, forming a three-bay composition. The central bay has a tower above, topped by a stone eave. The tower front bears four characters "Qinling Weiguan" (Magnificent Mausoleum View). On the two outermost stone strips is carved a couplet: upper line "mountains and waters always present □□", lower line "descendants forever □□□". The upper stone strips have exquisite relief carvings, badly weathered and eroded. On the central slab, upper left carved sun, upper right carved moon. Center vertically carved "Imperial Qing awaiting bestowal, great-great-grandfather...", lower signature "Qianlong 30th year...". This old tomb, in its day, was grand in scale for the town.

Directly before the tomb, against the west slope of Mingyue Mountain, very steep. Halfway up the slope leans a building; judging by roof scale, large — this is the Wang Ancestral Hall. We checked "Wang Clan Genealogy": 14th generation Wang Yuan, "buried behind Fubao Wang Ancestral Hall, has stele, yin mountain shen orientation." From position and orientation, this large tomb can generally be identified as Wang Yuan's. The Wang clan's Fubao ancestral hall founder Wang Xuan was 9th generation, moved here after Chongzhen 14th year (1641); by generation count, roughly matches. However, now Wang people in Fubao don't know the tomb owner's name, only know he is their ancestor, still offer incense at Qingming. We planned to dig away the silt before the tomb to see this great-great-grandfather's name, but couldn't find a responsible person, finally didn't dare dig.

We went around from Liujia Lane to the front of Wang Ancestral Hall; the building's condition is not bad, a "long five-bay" structure, total facade width 14.5 meters, gold columns 30 cm diameter. Five households live there; Mr. Wang Benguo lives in the left end bay. He says originally there was a courtyard wall in front, with a wooden gate with tile eaves in the center. Now wall and gate gone, but in front is Baise Stream valley, across the valley is Shuanghe Street new district, view open, actually quite good. I was looking around when suddenly I发现 a broken stele at my feet, four characters remaining: right upper and lower "Hui Yuan" ( taboo name Yuan), left upper and lower "Pu Shi" (Lady Pu). So this is likely Wang Yuan and wife's tomb stele. This raises another question: what is its relation to the tomb behind the ancestral hall? Mr. Wang Benguo explains: the hall originally had six large steles, many small ones; the supply cooperative used the hall for a sugar factory, then smashed all large and small steles. This "Hui Yuan" fragment is from a small stele, small steles not necessarily tombstones. This is an unsolved case, not important, let it be.

Noteworthy: Wang clan people now legend says the person buried in this tomb was eaten by a tiger in the mountains; descendants only recovered one foot, so this tomb is called One-Foot Tomb.

Fubao area since ancient times has had many tigers and leopards. Circulating folk songs and stories have many episodes of tigers eating people, cattle, pigs. Mr. Jia Darong says in the 1950s, local garrison even organized tiger-hunting campaigns.

Many tigers because many forests. Hejiang, especially its south and west townships, was once densely covered with primeval forest. Republican "Hejiang County Annals · Food and Goods" says: "The county south has five districts, vast territory, 300 li long, layered mountains, bordering Guizhou... especially rich in bamboo and wood... blocking sun and sky, shading valleys." "West Second District borders Zishui (now Xishui), also a forest region, lush, extending tens of li or more, loggers cannot exhaust. Asking family wealth, they point to forests." Forests were once villagers' basic wealth.

I arrived at Fubao, stayed at the forest farm guesthouse, visited Huilong Street; except for grain station and supply cooperative staff housing, almost all temples have become forest farm staff housing. Yet I saw not a single forest. All four mountains are weeds and shrubs, scattered by dry yellow terraced fields. On Jingtang Mountain, some reclaimed slopes早已 exceed the prescribed limit of 25 degrees. Only Pujiang River banks have lush bamboo, and the east forest farm orchard's orange trees bear golden fruit. Oranges were originally Hejiang's specialty; Baisha Market in Qing dynasty established Sichuan's earliest special orange tax checkpoint. Now orange trees don't form forests either, only more on Tiantan Mountain in the orchard. Villagers say picking oranges sells little money, no enthusiasm to harvest. But on walls of several farmhouses along the road to the orchard, whitewashed characters: "Privately picking one orange fines five yuan."

For decades, the Forestry Bureau's task was cutting forest, not planting — cutting off one's own livelihood rather than making life more prosperous. A year has "quotas" of cutting millions of cubic meters of timber, but no quota for planting trees.

Mr. Jia Darong and all friends on the street say originally all four mountains were evergreen broadleaf forest; because local frost-free period long, winter also no yellow leaves, everywhere green. The second floor of the forest farm guesthouse where I stayed has a large hall as retired staff activity station, every day several mahjong tables. The old man managing this station, Mr. Wang Qibing, is the forest farm's former party secretary. So I invited old Mr. Wang to spend an evening telling us the forest farm's past and present.

Though since ancient times residents mainly lived by cutting bamboo and wood, initially population sparse, transport difficult, annual cutting and growth roughly balanced — truly "green mountains always there, sustainable use." In 1952, to build Chengdu-Chongqing railway, needed sleepers; from then began large-scale forest cutting. After railway opened, transport convenient, then harvested large quantities of mining pit props for export. 1958 Great Leap Forward steelmaking, cutting wood for blast furnaces; good timber burned to ash, steel not made. At the same time public canteens, also used good timber for firewood, because good timber easy to split and burn, big fire.

1960s, 70s, 80s, Fubao forest farm annual production quota 4-5 million cubic meters. 1982-1983, UN World Bank loan for forest improvement, but the forest farm used a large sum to build a commercial street. Forest not improved; loan due, so大肆 cut primeval natural forest to repay. But until then, cutting scale not yet largest, because forest ownership uncertain — Guizhou or Sichuan, endless dispute. County boundary also uncertain, state forest and commune forest indistinguishable. By 1990s, boundaries fixed, then unrestrained cutting; e.g., Tiantangba, 900,000 mu forest cut bare, only a few hundred mu left for some crops, very difficult. Fortunately learning from 1998 Yangtze flood, central government decided to protect natural forests; from 1999 Fubao forest farm production quota reduced to over 20,000 cubic meters timber and 300,000 bamboo poles annually, forestry workers' task began shifting to tree planting and forest cultivation.

Thus, Fubao forest farm luckily preserved 600,000 mu of natural evergreen broadleaf forest.

Hearing this, I breathed a big sigh of relief. But with production scale reduced, immediately came forestry workers' livelihood problems. The forest farm is a "self-collecting, self-funding, self-sufficient" deputy-section-level public institution; though government gave several hundred thousand yuan "Natural Forest Protection Project" subsidy, cannot sustain. Annual cutting 80,000-100,000 bamboo poles, income about 400,000 yuan, only enough to pay World Bank loan interest.

Originally over 300 staff, once Fubao's main consumer force, greatly stimulated Fubao's prosperity. Now wages only 70%; staff raise pigs and poultry, grow some vegetables and grain, barely enough to eat. Thinning some small trees, enough for firewood. Selling some firewood, pocket money, not much.

So staff and their adult children have to go out to work. 60% of staff completed "buying out工龄" or "unpaid leave" procedures; men and women, young all left. One laborer, working away, normally earns several hundred yuan a month; over 1,000 yuan then hard to guarantee decency. Old Mr. Wang paused, mood heavy.

We went to Xiapu Village near Fubao's water mouth to see old landlord He Dong's mansion; originally 22 forest farm worker households lived there, now only one retired household left. Mansion empty. We saw an old lady returning with a hoe on her back; asked, over 90 years old, just hoed her vegetable plot. The other 21 worker households, all found their own way, left.

Supply cooperative and grain station staff and their children, also took this path, and also带动 surrounding farmers.

Fubao Town now continues to function as a regional industrial-agricultural product exchange market. We observed on market days: men and women coming up the mountain paths called "Nine Dragons", back baskets loaded with corn kernels, sweet potatoes, spring bamboo shoots, heavy, sweating early morning. Returning light, back baskets with a little pesticide, fertilizer, small farm tools; some also cut a piece of pork. Some bought ducklings, chirping in back baskets, lively. Shops selling agricultural production materials not many: one fertilizer shop, one small farm tool shop also selling pesticide and seeds; sickles, hoes, rakes, firewood knives all hand-forged; on Fuhua Street there's a forge, blacksmith very old, no apprentices.

However, Fubao's new district — Shuanghe Street and Xinhe West Street — is very prosperous. Careful investigation: this prosperity is maintained by migrant workers and migrant women. Town and surrounding countryside total over 30,000 people, yet 8,000 go out to work; I randomly visited 16 households, every household has someone working away, minimum one, maximum four daughters all out. First few years working purely selling labor; recent years some go into business. Secretary Wang says one in Chongqing construction, probably has over 10 million yuan assets. Migrant workers send money home, first thing is build houses. New district houses, except health center, school, town government etc., all built by migrant worker families. Early 1980s mostly 2-3 story brick-concrete buildings; late 1990s, built to 5-6 stories; now even two 7-story buildings. In development zone, someone even sole-funded a row of buildings tens of meters long. Scattered new houses on hillsides also migrant workers'. Their families' consumption level is quite high for this shallow-mountain agricultural area; so the town has a batch of "high-end" consumer shops inconsistent with agricultural area economic level. Shop owners: some returned after working several years, some came directly from old street and countryside. Also staff retired from public units and their children. A shop earns about 600 yuan monthly profit, bosses also enter "high consumption" group. Migrant workers mostly intermittently return to stay, spending more "generously" than family, further increasing street consumption; consumer commerce and services unusually developed. Restaurants and eateries at least 25, several can be called "luxurious." Latest fashion clothing shops too many to count, because连成 a large stall market. Shop proprietresses go to Luzhou to buy goods, once a week, carrying back big packages, long-distance buses packed full every day. Beauty and hair salons as many as 11, while stationery shops essential for primary and secondary students only half a shop. Half because only a counter in a department store.

Secretary Wang, speaking of beauty salons, shows disdain; inside, about half, have improper activities. Secretary Wang says local dialect calls it "one, three, five" consumption — "miss" sitting fee 100 yuan each time, pay proprietress 30 yuan; tea not expensive, one cup only 50 cents. Several beauty salon proprietresses returned from working outside, know this business well, decorate inside and out very ambiguous, purple light seeping through door cracks. Several inns and hotels also engage in this "service" industry. Every weekend, new street has a long line of sedans, all from neighboring county towns coming for pleasure.

Migrant economy brought fashionable lifestyle. Young women dress no less than city, hair dyed red, yellow, "platform shoes" several inches thick. On Shuanghe Street five shops selling and renting VCDs, even two internet cafes. Not far from our forest farm guesthouse, an entertainment city, a song-and-dance hall, and a skating rink. I slipped into the skating rink: terrazzo roller rink under repair; beside several closed halls also being renovated, unknown purpose. The long wide skating rink sign on the gate sagged at one end; I expected to photograph after repair, but the sign was taken down for remaking, not done until we left. These entertainment venues on the street, probably配套 with beauty salons; distant customers seeking pleasure want "serialization."

Economic and cultural prosperity built on out-migration is deformed, inevitably fragile. Now, migrant workers and women who have saved more, no longer settle in Fubao, but buy houses in Hejiang city. Fubao's "development zone" also looks lifeless, many buildings empty. Think: the hometowns of Huizhou merchants and Shanxi merchants in old days, probably developed and declined in similar ways.

What most caught my attention: migration made this small shallow-mountain Fubao Town establish close ties with the whole nation, very open. Whole town plus countryside only 38,300+ population; in 2001, program-controlled telephones reached 2,000 lines. One day, going to Old Xihe Street, saw on new street a "China Mobile Unicom Agency"; went in, asked the clerk sitting behind counter watching TV; he said agency opened November 2000, by April 2002, monthly average 20-30 households subscribing. This number not low, but he was too lazy to check exact figure for us; of course we had no way, so left and continued.

New district has several long-distance bus stations. To Guangdong Dongguan, Zhongshan, Shenzhen, Guangzhou; Zhejiang Wenzhou, Yiwu, Ningbo; Yunnan Kunming; Guizhou Guiyang; Guangxi Guilin — all have round-trip buses, double-decker sleeper coaches. Peak season, like around Spring Festival, large numbers of migrant workers returning and leaving, several buses daily. Off-season, must wait, fill a bus then depart. To Chongqing, Chengdu, Luzhou, several scheduled buses daily. These bus owners and drivers are all returned migrant workers; big-city working life taught them many business ways, bringing relatively modern business to former remote poor areas. Fubao no longer isolated; modern information technology and transport facilities quickly integrated Fubao into the unified big market. Correspondingly, Fubao's new district shows no local特色, except many tofu pudding shops along the street. The distinctive bamboo ware I like, no shops sell on street; only on market days, nearby villagers carry them to sell. But latest fashion can be bought anytime. April 2002, a class of Sichuan Fine Arts Institute students came to Huilong Street to sketch; arrived during an unprecedented warm spring, only wore summer clothes; next day suddenly an unprecedented cold snap, girls shivering with goosebumps. They ran to new district street, immediately put on fashionable fleece tops with English letters printed on chest, looking left and right satisfied, happily huddled together laughing.

My second time to Fubao, those waiting until after Spring Festival to go out to work hadn't all left. Often see groups of young people, mostly young women, with bags, looking after each other boarding long-distance sleepers. Once, saw a group of girls boarding a bus to Dongguan; I asked a short-haired one: "How many hours to get there?" "Over thirty hours." "Hard work!" "How can it be comfortable! Like pigs! Want comfort then go hungry!" The girl only sixteen, junior high graduate, quite pretty, yet has to leave home, go far away. But abandoning the "five dragons embracing pearl" fantasy, leaving the land, is exactly the step most farmers must take toward modernization.

Rural areas can only accelerate modernization after摆脱 surplus population pressure.

Sichuan people going far to make a living has long tradition. Remember as a youth my father personally taught me Li Bai's "Ballad of Changgan", which writes a Sichuan woman missing her husband who went to "work" around Hubei-Hunan: "...at sixteen you went far away, to Qutang's Yanyu Reef. In fifth month cannot touch it, ape cries sad from sky. Before the door, your lingering footprints, one by one grown green with moss. Moss too deep to sweep, fallen leaves early autumn wind. Eighth month butterflies yellow, paired flying west garden grass. Moved by this my heart aches, sitting sorrowful my beauty ages. Sooner or later coming down Sanba, send word home in advance. To meet you I won't say far, even to Changfengsha."

Now, those going out to work are mostly women. They no longer grieve over spring and autumn, but full of pursuit of new life.

May Fubao people's road to the future become ever healthier, ever broader. At the same time, may Fubao old market town, that antique Huilong Street, be preserved long, giving them intimate historical memory, enriching their spiritual world.

Autumn 2002

sections.name: 碛口恋
sections.content_zh:
碛口恋

古镇碛口的调研工作，做得可有年头了。

1997年11月下旬，我们刚刚完成介休张壁村的田野调查，吕梁地区旅游总公司的侯克捷先生就用他那辆好像随时都可能解体的吉普车把我们接到了碛口。这时候，我们已经做了不少乡土建筑的调查研究，从鱼米之乡到戈壁高原都见识过了，一到碛口，看到黄河边上的镇子和附近几个山村，我们还是被大大地震动了。震动了我们的，第一是黄土高原特有的深沟大壑、秃峁断梁，那么荒寒枯瘠又庄严雄浑得惊心动魄；第二是碛口镇三百年兴衰的历史，那么独特又丰富多彩，紧紧联系着黄河河套和秦晋大峡谷中黄河河运的开发和明清两代对蒙古的政策，那是一曲商人和苦力的奋斗史；第三呢，在深沟里，在陡坡上，在悬崖顶，在黄河边，一座座窑洞村落，那么自然地惊险，自然地变化，自然地和天地山川生为一体。它们是自然的产物。稍一细看，墀头上装饰着精致的砖雕，门窗上的细棂也疏密有致，连碾子上的石磙和牲口的料槽还刻着花呐！只要有一丝可能，建筑都会洋溢出人们对生活的热爱，记录下人们在极其困苦的条件下的追求、斗争和创造。它们是碛口开发史的实物见证。

侯克捷先生和临县王成军副县长的满腔热情也很使我们感动，他们深深地懂得这些文化遗产的价值，迫切地希望把它们保护起来。他们接我们去，为的就是要我们和他们一起努力做好这件极有意义的工作。我们毫无保留地立即跟他们绾了同心结，决定把碛口和它周边的几个村落作为我们调研的对象。

第三天早晨六点钟，我们在离石坐长途客车回北京，过了石家庄，下起大雪来，车轱辘小心翼翼地滚，到北京已经晚上九点多了，幸好老侯塞给我们一包黄河边上特产的滩枣，又软又甜，这才没有饿瘪。

碛口的研究价值很高，工作的规模必须稍大一点才能体现出它的价值，我们不愿也不敢草草成书。而且，干起来也有些外在的困难。临县是个国家级贫困县，而我们这个研究小组也只有在别的课题上攒下点余钱来才买得起车票，于是，工作就做做停停，三天打鱼，两天晒网。不过，我们始终挂念着碛口，不断向电视台、报刊、学者、摄影家等等中外朋友们介绍碛口。我们还曾经正式推荐碛口和它周边的村落作为国家级文物保护单位，可惜太过匆忙，资料不足，手续不全，没有成功。一天天拖下去，我们肚子里的疙瘩越长越大。

1999年，我们把香港中文大学的何培斌教授拉到了碛口，他一看大为激动，过不了几天，带着录像师又来了两次。在他的支持下，我们在2000年写成了一本初步的研究报告。这以后，我们又在台湾龙文化基金会的支持下继续做碛口的工作，带着学生，陆陆续续测绘了几个村落的建筑，并且做了更深入一点的调查。就这样，算下来，到2003年，已经先后去了七八次之多。有一次是盛夏去的，天热得邪乎，风都烫人，李秋香和杜非在索达干往北七八里的黄河岸边抄两块碑，第二天浑身上下凡没有遮挡的部分都脱了一层皮。那天晚上在西云寺斜对面的高圪台上吃饸饹，停电了，点上蜡烛，我仿佛听到东市街上管账先生们的算盘声噼里啪啦地响了起来。老侯大概没有在幻觉中闻到饭店小伙计给管账先生们送去的夜宵的香气，而是闻到了我们四个人身上几天积攒下来的汗臭，临时决定，不再在乡政府的文件柜上过夜了，立即赶回县城去。好罢，我口袋里已经有了一整本关于陈敬梓的访问材料，有点儿不适当的满意，就钻进了那辆浑身吱吱嘎嘎乱叫叫人不大放心的吉普车。今年年初，我拿出那个笔记本来看，三年前的汗馊气依然扑鼻。

就这么的，到了2003年11月，忽然临县县委孙善文副书记来了电话，说是有了一笔经费，可以用来保护和开发碛口，要我们去帮着做点儿什么。这当然是个好消息，触发了压在我心底多年的愿望，我说，行，这就去。恰好那时候台湾汉声杂志社的黄永松先生在北京，我对他又劝又激再加上诱惑，他动了心，改了飞机票，决定跟我作伴。上午从北京出发，天黑之后到了太原。第二天，孙副书记的车载上我们，过离石拉上侯克捷先生，直奔碛口而去。先到招贤镇，刚刚扎进瓷窑沟，还来不及细看，见多识广、平日里一向不动声色最沉得住气的黄永松立马掏出了手机，放大嗓门，东打一个电话，西打一个电话，打了几个之后，对我说："都跳起来了，那几位都跳起来了。"还没有走出瓷窑沟，秋天里邀些境外专家在碛口开个小型讨论会的计划就大体形成了。我说，可不要开那种说几句话就走人的会，来了就得干点儿什么。黄永松说：那当然！

看过了碛口、李家山和西湾，跟孙副书记交换了些关于保护和开发的设想，确定了我们在第一阶段的工作，这里面就包括完成我们全面介绍碛口和它周边村落的书。这本书，一来可以深化对碛口的认识，把保护和开发的工作做得更准确、更完善，二来可以提高碛口的知名度，引起更多的人的关怀，促进保护和开发。黄永松则负责落实那个开会的计划。

不料，台湾的几位朋友看了黄永松带回去的照片之后，竟等不到秋天开会，立刻要求到碛口过正月十五。于是，我们一齐又去了一趟。刚到离石，王成军副县长候了个正着，给我们吃了顿山西省著名的莜面和荞面，看了看街上热火朝天的龙灯，当天下午就开始进村参观。

《汉声》杂志的出版人吴美云女士和台湾大学的夏铸九教授，走到哪里就喊到哪里，哇！哇！哇！最沉稳的是三联书店的前老总董秀玉女士，不喊，张着嘴笑，老也闭不拢。

吴美云以她的职业习惯，不断问我一些关于写书的问题。我回答：这座房子我们测绘过了，或者，这件事我们调查过了。说着说着，我发觉我们的准备工作确实已经做了不少，是到了动手完成这本书的时候了。夏教授则热心地对孙副书记表示，他们可以为保护和开发碛口做些实实在在的工作，他们在古迹保护方面和区域规划方面有丰富的经验。

台湾朋友走了之后，我独自留下来又和临县前工会主席王洪廷先生到樊家沟、南沟、索达干、高家塌几处去看了一趟，访问了一位行船的老艄。王洪廷先生近五年来一直从事《碛口志》的准备工作，积累了不少资料。他是碛口人，1997年我们第一次到碛口就访问过他。还有一位碛口人，县党校老师薛容茂先生也一直和我们联系着，对我们2000年调研初稿的写作很有帮助。

3月、4月、5月，我们又有人分头到碛口去，工作是调查碛口周边的几个村子，摄影，带同学去补充一些测绘。

王洪廷先生不断地给我们寄些访问记录来，还有他拍摄的照片，薛容茂先生也寄来几份资料。孙副书记则组织了县里的几位"秀才"分头调查了些我们希望得到的资料。可惜我们写的书不能篇幅太大，没能容纳这许多好材料。

七年来，我们这个乡土建筑研究组的全体成员都先后参加了这个课题。我照应总体的工作，负责调查和写作；李秋香负责调查访问和摄影，还主持历年的测绘并参与写作；罗德胤负责三个周边村子的调查、测绘和写作。楼庆西拍了不少照片。我们的"编外"朋友杜非博士参加了一些工作。

参加了田野工作的学生几年来前后几批一共三十六个。其中有一部分用这个题材写了毕业论文。因为人数众多，我们不一一列出他们的名字了。

这次碛口的工作，有一部分学生是利用国庆假期来做的，他们觉得这是一件很有价值的工作，所以宁愿放弃休息，来一厘米一厘米地测量、绘图，做这一份极细致又极枯燥熬人的事。

碛口的工作也有很大的困难。由于题材的特殊性，我们认为需要多做一些社会调查，例如货栈和过载店的经营，大商人的发迹史，等等，但是，我们几乎什么都没有得到。事情过去不过几十年，并不算久远，知道详情的人却已经找不到了。有一些事情和人物，在镇子上倒是留下一些传闻，但各人所传的又大不一样，而且无从取证，真假难分，善恶难辨，我们只好不写了。连一些十分简单的事，例如油筏子的结构和驾驶都弄不确切。王洪廷先生说，这恐怕要到包头去调查才成，我们做不到，写了个大概就过去了。本来还想写一点民俗，但民俗的变化很快，伞头秧歌唱的都是眼前的话，连龙灯也很现代化了，而我们要写的主要是碛口辉煌的当年。于是，也是提一句就算了。

拍照片也一样，眼前是一幅衰落破败的景色，中间夹一些现代化的零碎，很难教人回想起当年的繁华。

这些困难给我们的研究报告留下许多遗憾，但是，比遗憾更重要的是使我们更痛切地感到危机，再过几年，连我们当前写下的这些事情也不会有人知道了。我们国家好像还没有提倡、支持和组织过一批人系统地调查记录几百年来普通而平常的老百姓的生活史。倒是花了大力气去考证夏、商、周的断代问题。那么，我们民族的历史，将永远是"帝王家谱和断烂朝报"，我们的子孙后代，将永远无法知道或者只零七八碎地知道千千万万普通而平常的老百姓是怎样生活着并且创造过多么光辉的文化成就的了。

闲话少说，我们接着干罢，像精卫填海那样。

甲申年上元节，我（七十六岁）、王洪廷（六十五岁）和董秀玉（六十二岁）在黑龙庙戏台上挽着臂膀唱了几首五十几年前年轻人的歌。朋友给我们拍了照，我在照片下面写了几句：

如果你已经把青春忘记，

请和我们一起回忆；

乱石碛上也会开放花朵，

我们的生命化成了新泥。

2004年4月
sections.content_en:
Love for Qikou

Research work on the ancient town of Qikou has gone on for quite some years.

In late November 1997, we had just completed fieldwork at Zhangbi Village in Jiexiu, when Mr. Hou Kejie of Lüliang Regional Tourism Corporation picked us up in his jeep — which seemed ready to fall apart at any moment — and took us to Qikou. By then, we had done quite a bit of vernacular architecture research, having seen everything from land of fish and rice to Gobi plateau; but arriving at Qikou, seeing the town by the Yellow River and nearby mountain villages, we were still greatly shaken. What shook us: first, the Loess Plateau's characteristic deep gullies and great ravines, bald hilltops and broken ridges — so desolate, barren, yet solemnly and powerfully breathtaking; second, Qikou Town's three-hundred-year rise and fall history, so unique and rich, closely tied to the development of Yellow River shipping in the Yellow River Great Bend and Qin-Jin Grand Canyon, and to Ming-Qing policies toward Mongolia — a saga of merchants and laborers' struggle; third, in deep gullies, on steep slopes, on cliff tops, by the Yellow River, cave-dwelling villages — so naturally perilous, naturally varied, naturally one with heaven, earth, mountains and rivers. They are products of nature. Looking closer, gable ends (chitou) decorated with exquisite brick carvings, window and door latticework finely spaced, even the stone rollers on mills and livestock feed troughs bear carvings! Whenever there was the slightest possibility, architecture overflowed with people's love of life, recording their pursuits, struggles, and creations under extremely harsh conditions. They are physical witnesses to Qikou's development history.

Mr. Hou Kejie and Lin County Deputy Magistrate Wang Chengjun's warm enthusiasm also moved us deeply; they deeply understand the value of these cultural heritage sites, urgently hope to protect them. They took us there precisely to have us work with them on this highly meaningful task. We unreservedly immediately tied the knot with them, deciding to make Qikou and its surrounding villages our research object.

At six a.m. on the third day, we took a long-distance bus from Lishi back to Beijing; past Shijiazhuang, heavy snow began, wheels rolling cautiously; arriving in Beijing past nine p.m. Fortunately old Hou stuffed us a pack of beach jujubes, a Yellow River specialty — soft and sweet — so we didn't starve.

Qikou's research value is very high; the work scale must be somewhat large to reflect its value; we were unwilling and dared not rush a book. Moreover, there were external difficulties. Lin County is a national-level poverty county, and our research group could only afford tickets by saving surplus from other projects; so work went in stops and starts, three days fishing, two days drying nets. However, we always thought of Qikou, continuously introducing it to TV stations, newspapers, scholars, photographers, and other Chinese and foreign friends. We once formally recommended Qikou and surrounding villages as a national-level cultural relic protection unit; unfortunately too rushed, insufficient materials, incomplete procedures, didn't succeed. Day by day dragging on, the knot in our stomachs grew larger.

In 1999, we brought Professor He Peibin of Chinese University of Hong Kong to Qikou; he was greatly excited upon seeing it, within days came twice more with a videographer. With his support, we wrote a preliminary research report in 2000. After that, with support from Taiwan Dragon Culture Foundation, we continued Qikou work, bringing students, gradually surveying buildings in several villages, and doing somewhat deeper investigation. Thus, counting up, by 2003 we had gone seven or eight times. Once in midsummer, heat extreme, wind even burning; Li Qiuxiang and Du Fei copied two steles by the Yellow River bank seven-eight li north of Suodagan; next day all unprotected parts of their bodies peeled a layer of skin. That evening at the high terrace diagonally opposite Xiyun Temple, eating heluo (noodles), power went out, lit candles; I seemed to hear accountants' abacuses clattering on East Market Street. Old Hou probably didn't smell in his hallucination the aroma of late-night snacks the restaurant boy delivered to accountants, but smelled the sweat accumulated on our four bodies over several days; temporarily decided not to sleep on the township government's file cabinets anymore, immediately returned to county town. Well, I already had a whole notebook of interview material about Chen Jingzi in my pocket, somewhat inappropriate satisfaction, then climbed into that jeep creaking all over, not very reassuring. Early this year, I took out that notebook; the sweat stench from three years ago still pungent.

And so, in November 2003, suddenly Deputy Secretary Sun Shanwen of Lin County Party Committee called, saying a sum of funding had become available for Qikou protection and development, asking us to help do something. This of course was good news, triggering a wish pressed in my heart for years; I said, fine, going now. Coincidentally, Mr. Huang Yongsong of Taiwan Han Sheng Magazine was in Beijing; I persuaded, challenged, and tempted him; he was moved, changed his flight, decided to accompany me. Departing Beijing in the morning, arrived Taiyuan after dark. Next day, Deputy Secretary Sun's car picked us up, passed Lishi to pick up Mr. Hou Kejie, headed straight for Qikou. First to Zhaoxian Town, just entering porcelain kiln gully, before looking closely, the well-traveled, usually imperturbable Huang Yongsong immediately pulled out his mobile phone, raised voice, called here and there; after several calls, said to me: "They all jumped up, those few all jumped up." Before leaving the kiln gully, a plan to invite some overseas experts to a small symposium at Qikou in autumn had roughly formed. I said, don't hold the kind of meeting where people say a few words and leave; coming means getting something done. Huang Yongsong said: Of course!

After seeing Qikou, Lijiashan, and Xiwan, exchanging ideas on protection and development with Deputy Secretary Sun, we确定 our first-phase work, including completing our comprehensive book introducing Qikou and surrounding villages. This book, on one hand can deepen understanding of Qikou, making protection and development more accurate and complete; on the other hand can raise Qikou's profile, attract more concern, promote protection and development. Huang Yongsong was responsible for implementing the meeting plan.

Unexpectedly, after several Taiwan friends saw photos Huang Yongsong brought back, they couldn't wait for the autumn meeting, immediately demanded to go to Qikou for Lantern Festival (15th of first lunar month). So we all went again. Just arrived at Lishi, Deputy Magistrate Wang Chengjun was waiting, treated us to famous Shanxi youmian (oat noodles) and qiaomian (buckwheat noodles), watched the bustling dragon lanterns on the street, that afternoon began village visits.

Han Sheng Magazine publisher Ms. Wu Meiyun and National Taiwan University Professor Xia Zhujiu, wherever they went shouted: Wow! Wow! Wow! Most composed was Ms. Dong Xiuyu, former head of SDX Joint Publishing; didn't shout, mouth open smiling, never closing.

Wu Meiyun, by professional habit, constantly asked me questions about writing the book. I answered: we surveyed this building, or we investigated this matter. Talking and talking, I realized our preparatory work was indeed quite substantial; it was time to start completing this book. Professor Xia enthusiastically told Deputy Secretary Sun that they could do practical work for Qikou protection and development, with rich experience in heritage protection and regional planning.

After Taiwan friends left, I stayed behind and went with former Lin County Trade Union Chairman Mr. Wang Hongting to Fanjiagou, Nangou, Suodagan, Gaojiaota to look around, interviewed an old boatman. Mr. Wang Hongting has been preparing "Qikou Annals" for nearly five years, accumulated much material. He is a Qikou native; we interviewed him on our first Qikou visit in 1997. Another Qikou native, county party school teacher Mr. Xue Rongmao, has also kept in touch, very helpful to our 2000 research draft writing.

March, April, May, we again sent people separately to Qikou; work was investigating several surrounding villages, photography, bringing students to supplement some surveys.

Mr. Wang Hongting continuously sent us interview records and his photos; Mr. Xue Rongmao also sent several materials. Deputy Secretary Sun organized several county "scholars" to separately investigate materials we hoped for. Unfortunately our book cannot be too long, couldn't contain all this good material.

Over seven years, all members of our vernacular architecture research group participated in this project. I oversaw overall work, responsible for investigation and writing; Li Qiuxiang responsible for interviews and photography, also led annual surveys and participated in writing; Luo Deyin responsible for investigation, survey, and writing of three surrounding villages. Lou Qingxi took many photos. Our "external" friend Dr. Du Fei participated in some work.

Students participating in fieldwork over several years, several batches, total thirty-six. Some used this topic for graduation theses. Due to large number, we don't list their names one by one.

Part of this Qikou work, some students used National Day holiday; they felt this was valuable work, so宁愿 gave up rest, measuring and drawing centimeter by centimeter, doing this extremely meticulous and tedious work.

Qikou work also had great difficulties. Due to the topic's特殊性, we felt need for more social investigation, e.g., operation of warehouses and transit shops, great merchants' rise to wealth, etc.; but we got almost nothing. Events only decades past, not that remote, yet people knowing details already gone. Some events and figures left rumors in town, but accounts differ greatly, unverifiable, true-false indistinguishable, good-evil hard to tell; we had to not write. Even simple things, like oil raft structure and operation, couldn't be确定. Mr. Wang Hongting says this恐怕 requires investigation in Baotou; we couldn't, wrote a rough outline and moved on. Originally wanted to write some folk customs, but customs change fast; umbrella-head yangko sings of current matters, even dragon lanterns very modernized; while what we mainly write is Qikou's glorious past. So, just a mention.

Photography same:眼前 is a scene of decline and ruin, interspersed with modern fragments, hard to evoke past prosperity.

These difficulties left many regrets in our research report; but more important than regret is making us more acutely feel the crisis — in a few years, even what we currently write will be unknown to anyone. Our country seems not to have advocated, supported, or organized people to systematically investigate and record the life history of ordinary, common people over hundreds of years. Instead spent great effort verifying Xia, Shang, Zhou dynasty chronology. Then our nation's history will forever be "emperors' family trees and fragmentary court records"; our descendants will never know, or only know fragmentarily, how millions of ordinary, common people lived and what brilliant cultural achievements they created.

Enough idle talk, let's continue working, like Jingwei filling the sea.

On the Lantern Festival of Jiashen year (2004), I (age 76), Wang Hongting (65), and Dong Xiuyu (62) sang arm-in-arm on the Heilong Temple stage several songs of young people from over fifty years ago. Friends photographed us; I wrote a few lines below the photo:

If you have already forgotten youth,

Please recall with us;

Flowers also bloom on rocky rapids,

Our lives turn into new mud.

April 2004

sections.name: 《古村郭峪碑文集》序
sections.name_en: Preface to 'Stele Collections of Ancient Guoyu Village'
sections.content_zh:
《古村郭峪碑文集》序

中国有两千多年不曾间断的官修正史，世上独一无二。但是，正史所写的大都是统治阶级上层的事，所以大学者梁启超说，一部二十四史，无非是帝王家谱和断烂朝报，即使熟读了史官们的著作，仍然不知道我们民族的生存状态和它艰难的发展历程。所以，我们在许多重要问题上不得不借重各种私家著述，甚至笔记说部之类。但这些书所能提供的史料仍然偏于社会的上层，而且很零杂片断，真实性也难免有可疑之处。

整个二十四史或者二十五史所覆盖的历史时期，中国都是个农业社会。因此，要了解我们这个民族两千多年的生存状态和发展历程，必须了解农村，了解农民。要了解农村和农民，工作不得不从头做起。首先要有计划地大量做全面、深入、细致的个案调查。个案调查的一部分重要工作是搜集乡土文献资料，而乡土文献资料中，最基本的是宗谱和碑文，还有可供参考的地方志。宗谱和地方志早就引起了一些学术机构和史家的注意。但是，地方志写的是一个县的建制里的事，而且仍然是官家的史书，着重于本县的疆域、建置、山川、职官、科名、乡贤，再加上长长的贞女节妇名单。那些田亩、钱粮、户口，未必能反映真实的情况，而且常常见到历次所修的志，多有不明原因的难以解释的出入，所以，对研究农村个案来说，地方志的史料价值并不很大。

江南各省的农村，以一个姓氏为主的血缘村落比较多，宗族历来重视修谱，谱的篇幅大，内容丰富。除了必有的谱系之外，大多还有诸如族规、重要人物的传记、宗族的各项管理制度、大事记和艺文等等，它们大多能提供不少很有价值的史料，即使贞女节妇的小传，也能透视出生活的一角。但宗谱提供的史料也有很大缺点：一来是宗谱传人不传事，史料大多夹杂在人物传记里，比较零散，而且大多年代不详，难以整理成系统；二来是宗族内部难免有社会分化，人物传记之类，几乎全是记乡绅，尤其记修谱时候出钱多的人或者管事的人，内容也会扬善隐恶，有失实之处；三来是主持修谱的人大多是在乡知识分子，所谓士绅，他们深受儒家思想影响，于史实取舍或叙述之中片面性很大。例如，许多村落的繁荣，都因为从明代晚期起一批村人以从商致富，带动农村的建设，但宗谱里最喜欢说的是村人的科名成就，虽然只不过出了几个贡生之类；却不提商业和手工业的成就，虽然宗庙的巍峨、寺观的壮丽、宅居的富赡、书院的精雅、桥梁道路的便捷，其实大多仰赖商人捐资。被贬为"四民之末"的商人们的这些贡献，只在"义行"栏目里有点儿零星记载。

宗谱里最不可轻信的有两点，一是往往附会显赫的古人为自己的先祖，即使本姓里没有显赫的人物，也会编造故事说祖上某人因为某种事故而改易了姓氏，而原姓氏血缘本是某大人物之后。二是往往编造先祖迁徙来历，如四川人多来自湖北孝感，皖南人多来自徽州篁墩，福建客家人多从江西翻越武夷山经石壁迁来，而北方各省人多是从山西洪洞县来的。事实常常是，一个某姓的先祖初来的时候比较穷，人口又少，不会早早立谱，过了四五代甚至更久，境况好了，族人多了，才立意修谱，这时明白上代情况的族人已经很少，所以就聘请"谱师"来编。谱师是祖传的很专业又很封闭的职业，他们有很多"传子不传女"的秘密口诀，就包括给人续祖先和编造迁移路线。

北方各省，以一个大姓为主的血缘村落比较少，宗族势力比南方各省弱得多，或者根本没有宗谱，或者只有一份谱系图而已。因此，北方不少杂姓村落重要的管理方式是建立公选的"社"和"会"，它们的工作大多由"公议"决定，所以村里都有很多石碑，记载下大大小小的事件，从建村、造墙、修庙、铺路、禁赌、育林、纠纷、协议、天灾人祸、树木归属、风水保护、演戏舞龙直到打扫街巷的责任制度、过桥规矩、买卖章程等等，反映着杂姓村落的特点。这些碑文中有许多像地方法规、公告或者契约，措辞严谨，不能夸张虚饰；一事一碑，巨细不遗，公道诚实；甚至公布账目，直到几分几厘几丝几忽，所以它们的可信度比较高，史料价值很大，搜集起来，能够相当系统地刻划出乡村社会生活的整体面貌，具体而生动地勾划出村民的生存状态和对发展的追求。这种珍贵的史料，可惜还没像宗谱那样受到重视。

但是，这些石碑，半个世纪以来遭受的摧残很严重。不仅仅是因为"破四旧"，更是因为石料很有用处。统一的人民公社政权建立之后，传统的农村半自治的"社"和"会"的"公议"式的管理完全废除，这些石碑失去了现实的作用，便被用来铺地、填坑、搭桥、垒墙、墁猪圈、造厕所、当磨刀石，甚至砸碎了烧石灰。幸运一点的，被有点儿雅趣的人家搬去在院落里架起来摆花盆。如果再不赶紧抢救，连残存的一些也快要破坏完了，那么，中国农村的历史将有很大一部分会永远失去，我们将永远不能完整地、具体地、生动地了解我们民族的历史了。

郭峪村是山西省阳城县的一个大村，过去因产煤铁而很富裕，曾经有过二百九十多块明清时代的石碑。20世纪下半叶，像其他地方一样，石碑被"废物利用"，损毁殆尽。从2000年秋天起，郭峪村党总支和村委会认识到了这些石碑的重大文物价值，下决心加以收集，得到村民们的积极支持，经过多半年的努力，终于得到了七十多块。虽然只及原有石碑的四分之一，而且多有残缺和磨损，它们还是勾划出了郭峪村的一部分重要历史。这些历史，不但是郭峪村的，而且有更广泛的意义，例如关于明代末年李自成农民战争、郭峪村内部社会矛盾、煤矿纠纷、商人的经营和他们对乡里建设的贡献等等，甚至公共工程捐款的芳名录里也透露出工商业和金融业发展的信息。郭峪村党总支和村委会把这些碑文请人点校，编书出版，对我国的史学是一个很有意义的事件。更进一步的是，希望以这本书引起对农村的，也包括城市里的石碑和其他乡土史料的普遍关注，赶紧加以有规模、有计划地收集整理。这些石碑都是文物，应该得到文物的待遇，千万不要再失去它们。

为了充分认识郭峪村碑文的价值，应该先认识郭峪这个村子。

郭峪所在的晋东南阳城县，土地硗薄，不利稼穑，但富有煤、铁、硫磺等矿产。早在明代初年，铁产量就居全国前列，从而促进铁器手工业的发达。靠农业难以糊口的居民，纷纷以冶铁和贩运铁货为业。从明末到清末活跃在全国的晋商，其中有一支叫阳城帮，便是以铁货贸易起家的。郭峪村并不产铁，但产优质煤，冶铁离不开煤。郭峪村民因挖煤而积累了资金，就投入到商业中去。清代末年，以金融业为支柱的晋中大商户衰败之后，以矿业为支柱的阳城帮依然很活跃。民国年间，郭峪全村二百户，户户有人长期在外经商。村子比较富，文化也就跟了上来。郭峪村在明清两代出过六名进士，明代末年，有张好古一门三进士，有张鹏云一家祖孙兄弟科甲。张鹏云是万历进士，崇祯时任蓟北巡抚，他孙子张尔素是顺治进士，任刑部左侍郎。距郭峪不过一公里，有个黄城村，当年属郭峪管辖，那里出过一位著名人物陈廷敬，顺治进士，康熙时任文渊阁大学士，为《康熙字典》总裁官之一。黄城村本是郭峪陈氏的别业，陈廷敬上代是从郭峪村迁去的，他的母亲还一直住在郭峪村。

阳城是山西通往中原的隘口之一，古来兵家必争之地。战国时期的鬼谷子王诩便在境内云蒙山（古称"云梦山"）隐修。韩信、王莽、李渊都曾过阳城去夺天下。明末李自成的老十三营王自用部，多次攻击阳城，郭峪、黄城、上庄、砥泊都是反复血战之地，纷纷建造了坚固的防御工事。郭峪村于崇祯八年（1635）始建的寨墙最高处竟达十九米，遗憾的是东城门和北城门在"文化大革命"时拆掉了，村中心还有一座作瞭望和最后困守用的敌楼，叫豫楼，高三十余米。

郭峪村的居住建筑，包括陈廷敬故居和张鹏云故居，并不豪华。但郭峪村有一座宏大的汤帝庙。晋东南和晋南一带，是中华文明发源地之一，尧、舜、禹、汤的遗迹到处都有，奉祀他们的庙宇也分布很广，郭峪的汤帝庙是其中十分壮观的一座。大殿九开间，戏台和钟鼓楼飞檐相接，斗拱交错，是规格很高的木构建筑。村里有过一座文庙和一座先贤祠，规制也很宏丽，可惜都在"文化大革命"时期被拆除。

过郭峪村东门外樊河对岸山上有侍郎寨，也属郭峪村，但有独立的防御工程，不过因为造公路和长年失修，城墙已很残破。侍郎寨往北，山上有文昌阁、石山寺和晴雨塔，都是重要的景观建筑，也在"文化大革命"中被毁。

郭峪村经历过多种多样的历史场面，含蕴着丰富的历史信息。这些信息的很大一部分，用文字记载在那将近三百方的石碑里，这些石碑因而非常珍贵。现在，石碑虽然只剩下不到四分之一，仍然还可以见到一个晋商村落大致完整的历史面貌。因此，这本碑文集是很有价值的，希望引起史学界的重视。

2003年
sections.content_en:
Preface to "Collected Stele Inscriptions of the Ancient Village of Guoyu"

China has over two thousand years of uninterrupted official dynastic histories, unique in the world. However, official histories mostly record the upper ruling class; so the great scholar Liang Qichao said that the Twenty-Four Histories are nothing but emperors' family trees and fragmentary court records; even thoroughly reading historians' works, one still cannot know our nation's living conditions and its difficult development. Therefore, on many important issues we have to rely on various private writings, even notebooks and fiction. But the historical materials these books provide still lean toward the upper social strata, and are very fragmented, their authenticity inevitably questionable.

Throughout the historical period covered by the Twenty-Four or Twenty-Five Histories, China was an agricultural society. Therefore, to understand our nation's two-thousand-year living conditions and development, we must understand the countryside, understand farmers. To understand countryside and farmers, work has to start from scratch. First, systematically conduct comprehensive, in-depth, detailed case studies. An important part of case study work is collecting local documentary materials; among these, the most basic are clan genealogies (zongpu) and stele inscriptions (beiwen), plus local gazetteers for reference. Clan genealogies and local gazetteers have long attracted attention from academic institutions and historians. However, local gazetteers record matters within a county's administrative structure, and are still official histories, focusing on the county's territory, establishments, mountains and rivers, officials, examination successes, local worthies, plus long lists of chaste women and virtuous widows. Those farmland, grain tax, household figures may not reflect real conditions, and often successive editions have unexplained discrepancies; so for rural case studies, local gazetteers' historical value is not very great.

In Jiangnan (southern Yangtze) provinces' countryside, blood-line villages dominated by one surname are relatively common; clans have always valued compiling genealogies, which are lengthy and rich in content. Besides the necessary lineage charts, most also include clan rules, biographies of important figures, various clan management systems, chronicles, and literary works; they can provide much valuable historical material; even short biographies of chaste women can reveal a corner of life. But clan genealogies also have major shortcomings: first, they record people not events; historical material is mostly mixed in人物 biographies, relatively scattered, and mostly with unclear dates, hard to systematize; second, within clans social differentiation is inevitable, biographies almost entirely record local gentry, especially those who paid most or managed affairs during compilation, content may praise good and hide evil, with inaccuracies; third, those presiding over compilation are mostly rural intellectuals, so-called gentry, deeply influenced by Confucianism, highly one-sided in selecting or narrating facts. For example, many villages' prosperity came from late Ming villagers getting rich through commerce, driving rural construction; but genealogies most like to record villagers' examination successes, though only a few shengyuan (licentiate) level; not mentioning commercial and handicraft achievements, though ancestral halls' grandeur, temples' magnificence, residences' wealth, academies' elegance, bridges and roads' convenience, actually mostly relied on merchant donations. These contributions of merchants, demoted as "lowest of the four occupations," only have零星 records in the "righteous deeds" section.

Two points in clan genealogies are least trustworthy: first, often attributing illustrious ancient figures as ancestors; even if the surname has no illustrious figure, they fabricate stories that an ancestor changed surname due to some incident, and the original surname's bloodline descends from some great figure. Second, often fabricating ancestors' migration origins — e.g., Sichuan people mostly from Xiaogan, Hubei; southern Anhui people mostly from Huangdun, Huizhou; Fujian Hakka mostly crossed Wuyi Mountain from Jiangxi via Shibi; northern province people mostly from Hongdong, Shanxi. The fact often is: when a surname's ancestor first arrived, relatively poor, few people, wouldn't compile genealogy early; after four-five generations or more, circumstances improved, clan members increased, then decide to compile; by then few clan members know earlier情况, so hire a "genealogy master" (pushi) to compile. Genealogy masters are hereditary, highly professional and closed occupations; they have many secret formulas "passed to sons not daughters," including continuing ancestors and fabricating migration routes.

In northern provinces, blood-line villages dominated by one large surname are fewer; clan power much weaker than southern provinces, or no genealogy at all, or only a lineage chart.
